article_title: Affordance-Based Approach to Language Assessment
citation: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000
title: Six analytic foci operationalize affordance dimensions as observable assessment lenses
description: The paper consolidates six vantage points as operational foci of affordance-based assessment: emergence, reciprocity, resonance, negotiation, disruption and reclamation, and latent trajectories. Each focus is a practical lens where multiple affordance dimensions intersect and become observable in classroom interaction, functioning as methodological bridges that render the five constitutive dimensions accessible for assessment. Each focus is defined, illustrated with a classroom vignette, and connected to ecological theory, with rubric levels and documentation mechanisms proposed for each.
requirements: Rubrics with qualitative descriptors, observation logs, digital artifacts, and learner reflections for documentation
constraints: Vignettes are demonstrative rather than systematic empirical data, given the paper's conceptual nature
target_learning_goals: documenting emergent, reciprocal, resonant, negotiated, resilient, and delayed engagement with learning opportunities
key_sources: Quang Nhat Nguyen & Dung Thi Hue Doan. (2025). Affordance-based Approach to Language Assessment. Language Education & Assessment, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.29140/lea.v8n1.103000

article_title: SIPPS (Systematic Instruction in Phonological Awareness, Phonics, and Sight Words)
citation: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/
title: Three-level developmental progression of word-recognition instruction with an older-student variant
description: The curriculum organizes word-recognition instruction into "three developmental levels of progression in word recognition: simple alphabetic (SIPPS Beginning Level), spelling-pattern (SIPPS Extension Level), and polysyllabic/morphemic (SIPPS Challenge Level)." A separate variant, SIPPS Plus, covers the simple alphabetic and spelling-pattern phases but is designed specifically for older students in grades 4–12, allowing the same progression to serve adolescent struggling readers.
requirements: Placement testing to locate students at their points of need within a level and lesson
target_learners: K-12 students needing foundational word-recognition instruction
target_learning_goals: Progression from simple alphabetic to spelling-pattern to polysyllabic/morphemic word recognition
examples: SIPPS Plus addresses the simple alphabetic and spelling-pattern phases for students in grades 4-12
key_sources: SIPPS program description and outcomes review. (2022). https://www.evidenceforessa.org/

article_title: Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field
citation: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org
title: Six-element pattern for engaging training and technical assistance design
description: A reusable design pattern for training and technical assistance (TA) consisting of six elements the brief identifies as necessary for engagement: grounding in "clear expectations and common understanding," being "designed around the needs of the recipients," being "developed using ongoing recipient input," being "accessible for recipients," being "delivered by providers equipped to meet recipients' needs," and being "framed as a partnership between the provider and recipient." The pattern organizes TA design decisions around recipient engagement.
requirements: Providers equipped to meet recipients' needs
Ongoing recipient input during development
target_learners: Training and technical assistance recipients in human services and employment programs
target_learning_goals: Effective engagement with training and technical assistance
examples: The brief presents the six elements as the organizing framework for making training and TA engaging, drawn from interviews with 12 designers, providers, and recipients of TA.
key_sources: Kara Conroy, Annalisa Mastri, James Wholley. (2021). Engaging Training and Technical Assistance Recipients: Lessons from the Field. Mathematica. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/engaging-training-and-technical-assistance-recipients-lessons-from-the-field

article_title: 2014 Facts and Findings
citation: Mathematica Policy Research. (2014). Mathematica's Facts & Findings: A snapshot of significant research results. https://www.mathematica-mpr.com
title: Three-practice school improvement package promoted by SIG
description: The School Improvement Grants program promotes a package of school improvement practices for low-performing schools comprising three components: "using data to inform and differentiate instruction," "expanding technology access for teachers or using computer-assisted instruction," and "providing ongoing professional development in which teachers work collaboratively or that school leaders facilitate." An evaluation brief found over 96 percent of surveyed low-performing schools adopted all three practices, making this a widely implemented improvement pattern in SIG-funded settings.
requirements: Schools must be low-performing schools operating under the SIG program context in which the practices are promoted
constraints: The article reports adoption rates only and does not print evidence linking the package to improved student achievement
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional growth through collaborative ongoing professional development
examples: An evaluation brief on the adoption of school improvement practices promoted by SIG surveyed low-performing schools and found over 96 percent adopted the three practices
key_sources: Mathematica Policy Research. (2014). Mathematica's Facts & Findings: A snapshot of significant research results. https://www.mathematica.org/publications/2014-facts-and-findings-print

article_title: Teacher Evaluation in Chicago Public Schools
citation: Sartain, L., Zou, A., Gutiérrez, V., Shyjka, A., Hinton, E., Brown, E.R., & Easton, J.Q. (2020). Teacher Evaluation in CPS: Perceptions of REACH Implementation, Five Years In. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu
title: Make evaluator feedback specific, actionable, task-focused, relevant, balanced, and collaborative for it to improve practice
description: Teachers consistently reported that the value of observation feedback depends on its qualities. As the researchers summarize, "Teachers said that for feedback to be meaningful and useful, it must be specific, actionable, task-focused, relevant, balanced, and collaborative." Evaluators and school leaders should therefore design feedback conversations around these six characteristics rather than delivering generic ratings.
requirements: Evaluators must deliver feedback that is specific, actionable, task-focused, relevant, balanced, and collaborative
constraints: The article reports teachers' stated preferences about feedback qualities; it does not experimentally test which qualities cause practice change
target_learners: practicing K-12 teachers in evaluated schools
target_learning_goals: improving classroom instructional practice through evaluation feedback
examples: Teachers reported the REACH observation process accurately represented their teaching practice, provided opportunities to reflect, and resulted in practice changes
key_sources: Sartain, L., Zou, A., Gutiérrez, V., Shyjka, A., Hinton, E., Brown, E.R., & Easton, J.Q. (2020). Teacher Evaluation in CPS: Perceptions of REACH Implementation, Five Years In. Chicago, IL: University of Chicago Consortium on School Research. https://consortium.uchicago.edu

article_title: Principios de Aprendizaje de la Transición de Diseño para los Expedientes de Aprendizaje y Empleo: Co-diseño para la Equidad
citation: Page, K., Merritt Johnson, A., Franklin, K., Carter, B., Galindo, M., Solorzano, T., Lee, S., y Shah, Z. (2023, Julio). Principios de Aprendizaje de la Transición de Diseño para los Expedientes de Aprendizaje y Empleo: Co-diseño para la Equidad. Digital Promise https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/186
title: Siete principios de diseño de transición de aprendizaje co-diseñados para tecnologías LER
description: Treinta y un estudiantes y trabajadores de comunidades HSE co-diseñaron siete principios de diseño de transición de aprendizaje para guiar el desarrollo futuro de tecnologías LER: conectar a personas con apoyos; conectar a personas con oportunidades; incluir indicadores de destrezas y aprendizaje añadidos; ser inclusivo de la identidad, el movimiento y el lenguaje; capacitar con prácticas basadas en destrezas; adoptar un enfoque integral de la credencialización digital; e integración con diversas herramientas. Estos principios se centran en el valor y la utilidad de los LER para personas que experimentan transiciones en múltiples contextos.
requirements: Desarrollo con (y no para) los estudiantes y trabajadores de comunidades HSE, incorporando la experiencia contextual de quienes han vivido los retos que los LER aspiran a mitigar
constraints: Los principios se derivan de las percepciones y experiencias de un grupo específico de participantes HSE en Estados Unidos y México
target_learners: estudiantes y trabajadores de comunidades histórica y sistemáticamente excluidas, incluidos los que viven en la pobreza y estudiantes multilingües
target_learning_goals: apoyar transiciones múltiples y fluidas entre la educación y la fuerza de trabajo
examples: Los participantes compartieron cinco cosas que creen que las tecnologías LER deberían tener/hacer durante el segundo taller de co-diseño

article_title: Operation Outbreak: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Experiential Simulations in Education for Scalability
citation: Kelly McNeil, Sharin Jacob, Quinn Burke, and Stefani Pautz Stephenson. (2026). Operation Outbreak: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Experiential Simulations in Education for Scalability. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Implementation grains for simulations: single lesson, multi-week unit, and schoolwide event, with larger doses producing deeper learning when well-supported
description: The review organizes simulation integration into three time-based "grains": single-lesson simulations that are "the easiest to slot into a traditional schedule" but yield modest depth; multi-week units allowing students to "return to the simulation, test new ideas, and build on previous discoveries"; and schoolwide events like Operation Outbreak that are highly engaging but low-feasibility without strong support. The review concludes that "even small doses of simulation gameplay can be beneficial, but larger doses (time-span and scale) tend to produce deeper learning provided they are well-supported." Educators are advised to weigh feasibility against desired impact.
requirements: Single-lesson grains need clear, narrow learning goals and a brief debrief; multi-week units need curricular integration and ongoing assessment; schoolwide events need administrative approval, cross-subject coordination, and follow-up classroom activities.
constraints: Schoolwide events are typically rare without strong support and may be one-time annual events; the review notes students may remember the excitement more than the academic lessons without integrated reflection.
examples: The review cites River City implemented over about two weeks and EcoMUVE over multiple class sessions as multi-week grains, and Operation Outbreak as a schoolwide day-long or multi-day event grain.
key_sources: Kelly McNeil, Sharin Jacob, Quinn Burke, and Stefani Pautz Stephenson. (2026). Operation Outbreak: Exploring the Affordances and Challenges of Experiential Simulations in Education for Scalability. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/5b9d16cb-7253-49d0-9d95-e510b6951d4b

article_title: Designing for Technology Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory
citation: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Six design principles from adult learning theory for adult-learning technology
description: The report's summary distills its five theory sections into six considerations: base curriculum on "real world, authentic situations that learners are familiar with, and/or will encounter in the job market"; help learners do something with new information; create regular self, group, and peer reflection; design pace control; facilitate self-direction via self-assessments and planning tools; and incorporate alternative points of view.
requirements: Products should let students "control the pace of their learning, such as the ability to pause, repeat or control the order of material, or access learning material anytime, anywhere."
constraints: Application must stay adult-level: "no kid-oriented scenarios, no abstract made-up problems, no disconnected random problem sets."
target_learning_goals: adult basic education and ESL outcomes
examples: The summary's remaining bullets call for helping learners do something with new information, in a simulation or a real world problem, and for interaction with "alternative points of view" via projects or collaborations with diverse others.
key_sources: Designing Technology for Adult Learners: Applying Adult Learning Theory. (2016). https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/bb3f892f-a74d-4da1-8086-0334fd227316

article_title: Tech Talk: Co-Designing Youth Digital Well-Being Solutions
citation: Karim, S., Liberman, B., & Trettin, S. (2025). Tech Talk: Co-Designing Youth Digital Well-Being Solutions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/264
title: Six-step youth co-design process for digital well-being solutions
description: This pattern is a repeatable project-level process for engaging youth as partners in designing solutions: convene youth advisors, conduct focus groups to surface shared challenges, prioritize and refine promising ideas, define prototype focus and design session, facilitate an interactive prototyping session, and develop a solution for testing. The report states its "approach was grounded in research-based co-design and youth participatory methods that have been shown to result in more usable, appropriate, and effective solutions for young people than traditional research approaches." Youth advisors co-planned and co-facilitated focus groups, voted on prototyping ideas, and brainstormed the product in rapid-brainstorming rounds.
requirements: Recruit youth advisors with personal experience navigating the challenge, leadership and communication skills, and comfort facilitating conversations with peers; provide clear time commitments, permission forms, and compensation
constraints: The process was conducted virtually using platforms such as Zoom, Padlet, FigJam, and Google Suite, and sessions were not recorded due to privacy considerations
target_learning_goals: critical consciousness, confidence, and interpersonal skills through meaningful leadership roles in co-design
examples: Youth advisors provided input on focus group questions, led facilitation of the focus groups, and participated in a 1.5-hour virtual prototyping session with four rounds of rapid brainstorming
key_sources: Karim, S., Liberman, B., & Trettin, S. (2025). Tech Talk: Co-Designing Youth Digital Well-Being Solutions. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/264

article_title: EdTech Quality Indicators Guide: Leveraging the Five EdTech Quality Indicators to save time and money, reduce risk, and improve student outcomes
citation: Digital Promise. (2026). EdTech Quality Indicators Guide: Leveraging the Five EdTech Quality Indicators to save time and money, reduce risk, and improve student outcomes. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six-step edtech procurement process from needs analysis to sustain-and-scale
description: The guide structures district edtech procurement as six steps: Analyze & Inventory, Discover & Decide, Design & Plan, Mobilize & Implement, Evaluate & Reflect, and Sustain & Scale. Each step frames key questions and points to practical resources and templates. The guide says the steps "represent a comprehensive process that districts and schools can engage with to discover, pilot, and procure edtech tools to meet a given need," grounding the articulated need in data before exploring solutions and returning to Discover & Decide if a pilot shows a tool is not the right fit.
requirements: Cross-departmental teams analyze student and operational data first; a cross-functional team defines vision and purpose before piloting
constraints: Steps assume district capacity to run pilots and maintain meeting cadences with providers
target_learners: District and school education leaders involved in edtech procurement
target_learning_goals: Formalizing intentional, data- and evidence-driven procurement processes
examples: Step 5 directs teams to leverage interim and summative pilot data to decide whether a tool is the right fit or whether to return to Discover & Decide
key_sources: Digital Promise. (2026). EdTech Quality Indicators Guide: Leveraging the Five EdTech Quality Indicators to save time and money, reduce risk, and improve student outcomes. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/f1e0fd08-9047-42e7-9a2d-190ccb4d10dd

article_title: Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools
citation: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/publications/practiceguides
title: Signal the need for dramatic change with strong leadership
description: In a failing school, the leader should make a clear commitment to dramatic changes from the status quo and signal the magnitude and urgency of those changes. The guide states that "Leadership is key, but it alone is not adequate" and that the leader must show dramatic changes are necessary. Leaders signal change by communicating a clear purpose, creating high expectations, sharing leadership, and eliminating distractions so classroom time focuses on instruction.
requirements: A change in leadership practices is essential: either install a new principal or have the existing leader radically alter leadership practices
constraints: Strong turnaround leadership sometimes met resistance, including calls from parents for leaders to resign
target_learners: students in chronically low-performing K-12 schools
target_learning_goals: raising student achievement in mathematics and reading within one to three years
examples: New principals entered schools with a clear purpose, set expectations from the first day, and spent long hours studying the school before making immediate changes; one principal led an aggressive community campaign to change the school's perception
key_sources: Herman, R., Dawson, P., Dee, T., Greene, J., Maynard, R., Redding, S., and Darwin, M. (2008). Turning Around Chronically Low-Performing Schools: A practice guide (NCEE #2008-4020). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/7

article_title: REL Northwest's Guide to Community Engagement Data Collection and Analysis
citation: Collecting and Making Sense of Community Engagement Data. (2025). Regional Educational Laboratory Northwest. https://ies.ed.gov/rel-central/2025/01/dissemination-plan-template
title: Six-element quality checklist for community engagement session questions
description: A handout adapted from a program evaluation toolkit assesses each drafted session question against six key elements: the question should be 'Pertinent', 'Answerable', 'Reasonable', 'Specific', 'Evaluative', and 'Complete', each with yes/no ratings and notes. For example, 'Reasonable' asks whether the question 'link[s] to what the agency can practically and realistically achieve or influence', and 'Evaluative' asks whether it will 'produce actionable answers and inform next steps.'
requirements: Assess the quality of each question after drafting initial session questions
target_learners: Education agency staff drafting community engagement session questions
target_learning_goals: Write and prioritize high-quality engagement questions
examples: A companion handout rates each question's importance and urgency from 1 to 5 to set high, medium, or low priority

article_title: Preventing Dropout in Secondary Schools
citation: Rumberger, R., Addis, H., Allensworth, E., Balfanz, R., Bruch, J., Dillon, E., Duardo, D., Dynarski, M., Furgeson, J., Jayanthi, M., Newman-Gonchar, R., Place, K., & Tuttle, C. (2017). Preventing dropout in secondary schools (NCEE 2017-4028). Washington, DC: National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance (NCEE), Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Assign a single primary advocate to each student who needs intensive, individualized support
description: For students who have fallen off track and face significant challenges, the guide recommends assigning one person as the student's primary advocate who provides intensive monitoring and personalized intervention. The principle states: "For each student identified as needing individualized support, assign a single person to be the student's primary advocate." Advocates draw on a menu of support options and receive ongoing professional learning and tracking tools. This recommendation carries a Moderate Evidence rating from the panel.
requirements: Advocates need a menu of support options to use with students
Advocates need ongoing professional learning opportunities and tools for tracking their work
constraints: Some recommended practices, such as hiring individuals to serve as advocates, may require expenditures
target_learners: Secondary students (grades 6-12) who have fallen off track and face significant challenges to success
target_learning_goals: Staying in school, progressing in school, and graduating from high school
examples: The guide suggests responsibilities for advocates and case managers, key advocate qualifications, a sample support menu addressing student and family needs, and a sample monitoring sheet for student tracking.

article_title: Using Technology to Support Postsecondary Student Learning
citation: Dabbagh, N., Bass, R., Bishop, M., Costelloe, S., Cummings, K., Freeman, B., Frye, M., Picciano, A. G., Porowski, A., Sparrow, J., & Wilson, S. J. (2019). Using technology to support postsecondary student learning: A practice guide for college and university administrators, advisors, and faculty. Washington, DC: Institute of Education Sciences, What Works Clearinghouse. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Use simulation technologies that help students engage in complex problem-solving
description: The guide recommends using simulation technologies that help students engage in complex problem-solving, including online simulation tools and immersive technologies, with tips for group problem-based learning assignments. Simulations allow postsecondary students to work through complex, realistic problems that are difficult to enact in traditional instruction.
requirements: Simulations should engage students in complex problem-solving rather than simple drill
constraints: The panel assigned a minimal level of evidence, based on a single study providing evidence for this recommendation
target_learners: postsecondary students at 2- and 4-year colleges and universities
examples: The California Budget Challenge as a sample online simulation tool

article_title: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM)
citation: Strategic Instruction Model (SIM). (2024). University of Kansas Center for Research on Learning. https://sim.ku.edu
title: SIM implementation requires distributed teacher capacity, leadership support, coaching time, and a Literacy Leadership Team over a three-to-five-year adoption
description: The review specifies that successful SIM implementation depends on staffing and organizational conditions: content and support teachers willing and able to implement the routines and strategies, leadership willing to support teachers, provide time for coaching, and create school schedules that accommodate such instruction, plus a Literacy Leadership Team of core content and support teachers and school leadership to guide implementation. Initial adoption takes place over a three-to-five-year period as staff work through planning, implementing, and sustaining phases.
requirements: Leadership must provide time for coaching and create school schedules that accommodate the instruction
A Literacy Leadership Team must be created to guide implementation
constraints: Initial adoption takes place over a three-to five-year period
examples: The review lists staffing requirements including a Literacy Leadership Team created by core content and support teachers and school leadership

article_title: Fostering Powerful Use of Technology Through Instructional Coaching
citation: Bakhshaei, M., Hardy, A., Francisco, A., Noakes, S., & Fusco, J. (2018). Fostering Powerful Use of Technology Through Instructional Coaching: Results from the Pilot Year of the Dynamic Learning Project. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.org
title: Six core attributes of an effective instructional coaching program
description: From pilot-year data across 50 schools, the authors identified six core attributes of an effective coaching program: "partnerships, personalization, voluntary nature, situated in school/classroom, non-evaluative, and sustained." Coaching works as a partnership in which the teacher drives decisions; it is personalized to each teacher's context; participation is voluntary rather than compliance-based; the coach is situated on site; the relationship is non-evaluative so teachers feel safe experimenting; and support is sustained across cycles.
requirements: Coaches must be protected from evaluative roles and other assignments; teachers must be able to choose to participate; coaching must provide sustained one-on-one time (on average at least 19 hours of coaching support over the school year).
constraints: The attributes were identified in one pilot year across underserved middle schools; the report notes the appropriate balance of coaching depth versus breadth may change depending on school characteristics and teacher aptitude.
target_learning_goals: Teacher professional growth in technology integration
examples: 77 percent of participating DLP teachers received at least 30 minutes of one-on-one coaching per week, with 43 percent receiving more than an hour each week.
key_sources: Bakhshaei, M., Hardy, A., Francisco, A., Noakes, S., & Fusco, J. (2018). Fostering Powerful Use of Technology Through Instructional Coaching: Results from the Pilot Year of the Dynamic Learning Project. Digital Promise. https://digitalpromise.dspacedirect.org/items/540c3325-fd5f-408e-a347-2409f57848dd

article_title: The Science Student Electronic Exit Ticket (SEET) System: Visualizations to Help Teachers Notice and Reflect on Classroom Inequalities
citation: Ali Raza, Tamara Sumner and William R. Penuel. (2024). The Science Student Electronic Exit Ticket (SEET) System: Visualizations to Help Teachers Notice and Reflect on Classroom Inequalities. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(1), 87-100. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8199
title: Design equity visualizations that embody simplicity and familiarity while providing access to disaggregated data
description: Because teachers underused the equity visualizations in favor of easier whole class displays, the article argues that designers need "further investigation into new visualization types that embody simplicity and familiarity while still providing access to finer-grained data on student participation by race/ethnicity and gender." The principle holds that ease-of-use, familiarity, and simplicity are prerequisites for adoption of learning analytics visualizations in practice, and that equity visualizations must reconcile this with their necessarily more complex data types. Trust is flagged as an important attribute for visualizations displaying sensitive data.
requirements: Visualization types familiar to teachers, such as bar and line charts, or supports that build visualization literacy
constraints: Equity visualizations necessarily embody more complex data types, suggesting new visualization literacies may be needed
target_learning_goals: sustained teacher use of equity analytics to reflect on instructional practice
examples: The disaggregated bar chart was ranked the most preferred of the equity visualizations, consistent with teachers' familiarity with bar charts
key_sources: Ali Raza, Tamara Sumner and William R. Penuel. (2024). The Science Student Electronic Exit Ticket (SEET) System: Visualizations to Help Teachers Notice and Reflect on Classroom Inequalities. Journal of Learning Analytics, 11(1), 87-100. https://doi.org/10.18608/jla.2024.8199

article_title: AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators
citation: Prado, Y.; Ruiz, P.; Fusco, J.; DuVall, D.; Hinkel, D.; Perkoff, M.; Rocha, O. (2026). AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/291
title: Responsible AI policy in schools should rest on six principles including human oversight, transparency, access, privacy, instructional purpose, and evidence-based procurement
description: The guidance brief holds that "Strong AI policies and guidance are built on several key principles": AI supports decisions rather than making them, students and families understand when and how AI is used, tools do not widen opportunity gaps, student data is protected, use aligns to learning goals, and tools are approved under evidence-based district guidelines. The central question guidance should answer is how AI can support teaching and learning without replacing human judgment.
requirements: Schools need clear, shared expectations; policy should be shared in practical, values-driven, flexible ways
examples: The brief points to district examples such as the Indian Prairie School District Generative AI Strategy and Policy and the Iowa City Community School District GenAI Guidelines Website
key_sources: Prado, Y.; Ruiz, P.; Fusco, J.; DuVall, D.; Hinkel, D.; Perkoff, M.; Rocha, O. (2026). AI in Education: A Set of Four Essential Resource Briefs for Educators. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/291

article_title: Strengthening Policies and Practices for the Initial Classification of English Learners: Insights from a National Working Session
citation: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org
title: Districts within a state and states within an ELP consortium should use a single ELP assessment for initial EL classification unless comparability evidence exists
description: Because commercially available ELP assessments measure and weight language domains differently, multiple classification instruments can produce multiple understandings of English language proficiency and complicate interpreting transferring students' proficiency levels. The report states that "Practically all participants agreed that having a common initial classification assessment was preferred", and that states allowing multiple instruments should first provide compelling empirical evidence that the instruments' scores are comparable, such as a table of comparative scores.
requirements: If multiple instruments are allowed, compelling empirical evidence of score comparability must be provided first
constraints: States using multiple instruments face challenges understanding transferring ELs' proficiency levels from districts using different instruments
target_learners: Potential English learners moving within and across states and consortia
target_learning_goals: Comparable initial EL classification decisions across districts, states, and consortia
examples: Seven states permit LEAs to choose among multiple commercial screeners, and half of WIDA Consortium member states allow a choice between two consortium screeners
key_sources: H. Gary Cook & Robert Linquanti. (2015). Issues and options associated with initially classifying English learners (ELs). Council of Chief State School Officers. https://www.ccsso.org

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Six foundational leadership knowledge areas for NGSS implementation
description: Domain 1 of the framework identifies six distinct but related knowledge bases leaders need: NGSS and the Innovations in NGSS; Equity and Access for All Learners; Instructional Materials, Curriculum, and Assessment; Professional Learning; Systems Change; and Continuous Improvement. The article states "leaders need in-depth knowledge within six distinct, but related knowledge bases (Figure 1.1)." These areas were identified through a summit with national experts and interviews with leaders in two states, and they inform all critical actions in Domain 2.
requirements: Leaders at all levels need to develop knowledge in each of the six areas and understand intersections among them; depth needed may vary by role and system level.
constraints: No prior guidance existed on what knowledge leaders need for NGSS implementation; the areas were derived from the project's own literature review, summit, and interviews.
target_learners: State, district, regional, and school science education leaders
target_learning_goals: Understanding NGSS innovations, equity, curriculum and assessment quality, professional learning, systems change, and continuous improvement
examples: Regional and district leaders designing professional learning need deeper understanding of the NGSS and how to design and facilitate professional learning.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation
citation: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies
title: Six system drivers influencing NGSS use in classroom practice
description: Domain 3, Impacting NGSS Teaching and Learning, places standards-based teaching and learning at the center, with interactions among teachers, the NGSS, and students, surrounded by six system drivers: Standards; Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment; Policies; Key Stakeholders; Funding; and Professional Learning. The article states "Surrounding this center are six system drivers that most influence the use of the NGSS in classroom practice." Leaders' critical actions are both informed by and focused on these drivers, with equity and access encompassing the classroom.
requirements: Leaders gather data to gauge the extent to which their actions are influencing and leveraging each system driver.
constraints: The focus of NGSS implementation should always be on standards-based teaching and learning in the classroom for all students.
target_learners: Leaders charged with supporting and implementing the NGSS at all system levels
target_learning_goals: Focusing implementation efforts on the levers that most influence classroom NGSS teaching and learning
examples: The framework graphic shows arrows connecting leaders' critical actions to the Impacting NGSS Teaching and Learning domain.
key_sources: Stiles, K., Mundry, S., & DiRanna, K. (2017). Framework for Leading Next Generation Science Standards Implementation. San Francisco: WestEd. https://www.nextgenscience.org/appendix-d-case-studies

article_title: Balancing Act: State and District Roles in School Improvement under ESSA
citation: Dunn, L., & Ambroso, E. (2019). Balancing act: State and district roles in school improvement under ESSA. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. http://centeronschoolturnaround.org
title: Six key strategies characterize how SEAs implement SEA and LEA roles in school improvement under ESSA
description: From interviews with school improvement leads in 10 SEAs, the authors identified six strategies present in every SEA's approach: taking on multiple roles with LEAs, balancing support and accountability, differentiating support by district characteristics, building district capacity for sustainable change, prioritizing local contexts and needs, and leveraging ESSA requirements to specify roles. The authors state, "From these interviews, we identified six key strategies that were present in each of the 10 SEAs' approaches to implementing SEA and LEA roles in improvement." They present the set as building "a comprehensive, cohesive, and coherent system of support for school improvement."
requirements: SEAs must work with and through LEAs, which ESSA positions as key levers for school improvement
constraints: Strategies were identified from interviews with 10 purposively selected SEAs chosen for well-established and varied approaches, so breadth beyond these states is not established
target_learners: State education agency and local education agency staff supporting school improvement
target_learning_goals: Improving outcomes in comprehensive support and improvement (CSI) and targeted support and improvement (TSI) schools
examples: Louisiana leverages ESSA to require identified schools to choose high-quality English and math curricula and a professional development vendor, and competitively allocates its 7% school-improvement set-aside
key_sources: Dunn, L., & Ambroso, E. (2019). Balancing act: State and district roles in school improvement under ESSA. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED602966

article_title: Serving the Whole Person: An Alignment and Coherence Guide for Local Education Agencies
citation: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies
title: Six-chapter alignment and coherence process from student understanding through strategic communication
description: The guide's core reusable design is a six-chapter team process: "Chapter 1. Identify the Strengths, Needs, and Aspirations of Your Students; Chapter 2. Describe How These Strengths, Needs, and Aspirations Inform Your Vision for Serving the Whole Person in Your District; Chapter 3. Identify a Focus Area for Coherence; Chapter 4. Tailor the Implementation of Your Whole-Person Initiatives for Alignment With Your Focus Area; Chapter 5. Create an Action Plan; Chapter 6. Plan for Strategic Communication That Reinforces the Work." Each chapter follows a consistent structure of purpose, collaborative activities, hypothetical district responses, and reflection questions.
requirements: A cross-departmental team with defined facilitation must carry out the chapters collaboratively; the guide also directs teams to assess readiness before starting
constraints: The guide recommends choosing no more than one or two focus areas to start, and notes teams may work more quickly or more slowly than the guide indicates
target_learning_goals: aligned and coherent whole-person initiatives that advance equitable outcomes
examples: Chapter 3 directs teams to articulate a focus area using a 'so that' coordinating conjunction connecting the focus area to the district's broader whole-person vision
key_sources: Walrond, N. (2021). Serving the whole person: An alignment and coherence guide for local education agencies. WestEd. https://www.wested.org/resources/whole-person-alignment-and-coherence-guide-for-local-education-agencies

article_title: Balancing District Impacts and Community Interests: Considerations for District Charter Authorizers
citation: Chait, R. (2022). Balancing district impacts and community interests: Considerations for district charter authorizers. WestEd. http://www.WestEd.org
title: Charter authorizers should balance district impact assessments with six community- and district-oriented factors: demonstrated need, community demand, unique offerings, track record, fiscal impact, and long-term value to the district
description: The brief proposes that authorizers weigh six factors when deciding whether to authorize a new charter school: demonstrated need, community demand, unique offerings, track record, fiscal impact, and long-term value to the district. It argues this enables "informed and inclusive charter school authorizing decisions rooted in evidence of local communities’ wants and needs as well as analysis and projections about the impact on traditional public schools." Demonstrated need is assessed via achievement, performance, and attainment data; community demand via surveys and focus groups.
requirements: Conducting a community needs assessment reviewing existing student achievement, performance, and attainment data for all student populations
Assessing community demand through community surveys, focus groups, and other community engagement activities
Creating processes, collecting data, and conducting analyses for fiscal impact and long-term value considerations
constraints: The brief acknowledges that assessing negative long-term fiscal impact "is an admittedly complicated assessment"
Past performance as a track record indicator is described as not a perfect future predictor
target_learners: Students and families in communities served by district charter authorizers, including students with disabilities, English Learners, and students from low-income families
target_learning_goals: Ensuring new charter schools meet unmet student needs and community demand for schooling options and programs
examples: The brief illustrates the balancing problem with a hypothetical high-quality STEM charter application supported by families, located within 5 miles of an existing but poorly implemented and underenrolled STEM program, in an area with sufficient student population to support an additional school
The brief suggests authorizers may conduct needs and demand analyses on their own or in partnership with community-based organizations that have existing relationships with families
key_sources: Chait, R. (2022). Balancing district impacts and community interests: Considerations for district charter authorizers. WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED620722

article_title: Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools Can Develop Systems That Support Student Mental Health
citation: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group.
title: Six design components of welcoming and affirming school environments for student mental health
description: The report identifies six strategies as important components of comprehensive approaches to creating welcoming and affirming environments: culturally responsive practices, predictable routines, positive expectations, explicit SEL instruction, supportive relationships, and self-care strategies such as mindfulness, exercise, meditation, yoga, and calming routines. It states these have been "identified as important components of comprehensive approaches to creating welcoming and affirming environments to improve student mental health in schools."
requirements: Strategies must correspond with school and community values and be implemented through programmatic support and commitments that shape school climate and culture
target_learners: K-12 students in charter schools, with attention to historically marginalized students and students of color
examples: Valor Collegiate Academy implements welcoming-environment practices through its Compass Model, restorative-justice discipline policies, and weekly Compass Circles of 15 to 20 students
key_sources: National Charter School Resource Center, Browning, A., & Larbi-Cherif, A. (2022). Creating Communities of Care: How Charter Schools can Develop Systems that Support Student Mental Health. Manhattan Strategy Group. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED625528

article_title: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science
citation: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Provide English language development and comprehensible content instruction simultaneously rather than delaying content until English proficiency
description: The report argues that equal educational opportunity for English learners requires ELD or ESL instruction combined with engaging content instruction made comprehensible through specific techniques, and that "Both of these instructional opportunities should be provided simultaneously." Delaying content instruction until sufficient English proficiency relegates students to a role where they lack the content knowledge expected at their grade level. Scaffolding—limiting contextual complexity and gradually removing limits—amplifies the language of content.
requirements: Teachers use scaffolds such as concept maps, graphic organizers, realia, pre-taught vocabulary, collaborative projects, and sentence frames
constraints: Without proper instruction, the language demands of content disciplines can compromise English learners' content understanding
target_learners: English learners, including newcomers and U.S.-educated students
target_learning_goals: Content knowledge and academic language acquired together
examples: The report's Montebello K-4 program blended science and language so student thinking came first and authentic language developed as students described their thinking
key_sources: Equal Access to Content Instruction for English Learners: An Example from Science. (2012). WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED580362

article_title: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity
citation: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity. (2021). Spencer Foundation & Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/summer-learning-creating-equity
title: Six Design Principles for Summer Learning and Beyond framework
description: The report's organizing framework is a set of six interrelated design principles, or stances toward learners and learning: center relationships; create a culture of affirmation and belonging; build from students' interests and take a whole child approach; engage students' and families' knowledge in disciplinary learning; provide creative, inquiry-based forms of learning; and address educator needs and learning. The report states these are "essential for creating intellectually rigorous and equitable learning settings" and provide "a holistic framework for designing goals, practices, and activities for summer learning and beyond." The principles are grounded in a view of learning as cognitive, physical, emotional, social, and cultural at once, and are meant to be used together.
requirements: The principles are an interrelated set meant to be used together, not in isolation
constraints: The framework was developed for post-pandemic summer learning design and beyond, in response to pandemic and racialized trauma contexts
target_learners: K-12 students returning to school after pandemic virtual learning, their families, educators, and communities
target_learning_goals: Intellectually rigorous and equitable learning; social-emotional development; academic engagement
examples: The Cajon Valley Union School District applies the principles through advisory spaces, the Launchpad career and interest center, TEDxKids@ElCajon, co-design sessions with families, and Camp Cajon summer programming
key_sources: Summer Learning and Beyond: Opportunities for Creating Equity. (2021). Spencer Foundation & Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/summer-learning-creating-equity

article_title: UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community
citation: Karen Hunter Quartz. (2023). UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org
title: Six key practices of a community school serving immigrant, multilingual communities
description: The report distills UCLA Community School's approach into six key practices: knowing and building on a community's history, assets, and culture; developing and articulating desired core competencies; nurturing shared leadership and collective agency; creating space for collaborative inquiry, professional autonomy, and teacher development; using data and stories to elevate the school's vision and track progress; and affirming everyone's role. The report says these practices "contribute to its success" and offers them as takeaways for practitioners.
requirements: A cross-sector partnership structure with a primary university partner and community school coordination to sustain the practices
constraints: Practices are documented at one TK-12 school in central Los Angeles serving a large immigrant population; the report presents them as an example, not a tested recipe
target_learners: TK-12 students in immigrant, low-income, multilingual communities
examples: UCLA-CS built a multilingual program in Spanish, Korean, and English and increased the percentage of graduates earning the State Seal of Biliteracy
key_sources: Karen Hunter Quartz. (2023). UCLA Community School: Celebrating Language, Culture, and Community. Learning Policy Institute. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED642538

article_title: State Approaches to Developing Educational Leaders
citation: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572
title: Six-function taxonomy of state leadership development initiatives
description: The report organizes state initiatives by the specific leadership development "functions" they perform beyond generally enhancing leaders' skills: "providing role-specific professional learning," supporting induction of early-career leaders, facilitating career advancement for aspiring leaders, supporting leadership teams, providing differentiated assistance for school improvement, and facilitating training for supervisors. The authors present these categories as "a useful heuristic for understanding important points of variation across states' leadership development initiatives," with Table 2 mapping functions to states (role-specific learning in 21 states; induction 9; career advancement 7; teams 10; differentiated assistance 5; supervisor training 5).
requirements: Initiatives must be ongoing statewide programs so their functions can be identified and mapped across states
constraints: The authors state the categories are a heuristic; some programs serve a single function while others serve multiple, often overlapping, functions
target_learning_goals: Understanding the range of leadership development functions states support
Informing design of statewide leadership initiatives
key_sources: Fitz, J., Wechsler, M. E., & Levin, S. (2024). State approaches to developing educational leaders. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/795.572

article_title: Design Principles for Instructionally Relevant Assessment Systems
citation: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528
title: Six design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems
description: The report proposes a framework of six principles that state assessment systems should incorporate to have a net positive impact on instruction: Authentic, Curriculum-Anchored, Educative, Developmental and Asset-Oriented, Reflective of and Responsive to Learners, and Useful for Informing Decisions That Impact Instruction. The principles are designed to "Build upon current conceptions of alignment to standards" and to "focus on the most discerning features of assessment system design," triangulating among instructional shifts, key users, and evidence-based behaviors to influence. Each principle is elaborated with rationale and critical features.
requirements: State assessment systems defined as all instruments, supports, and communications from the state education agency about assessment
constraints: The principles are intentionally focused on features of state summative assessments rather than optional local activities
target_learners: K-12 students assessed by state large-scale assessment systems
target_learning_goals: Disciplinary knowledge and practice aligned to state standards
Positive instructional impact of assessment systems
examples: The report details each principle with rationale and critical features, using science assessment examples from states pursuing innovative systems
key_sources: Badrinarayan, A. (2024). Design principles for instructionally relevant assessment systems. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/111.528

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: North Carolina
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: NORTH CAROLINA. https://edtrust.org
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce into six strategies: making educator diversity data "visible and actionable to stakeholders"; setting clear state and district goals; investing in educator preparation programs to increase enrollment and improve preparation of teachers of color; targeting resources to districts and schools to recruit and hire a diverse workforce; investing in retention efforts that improve working conditions and provide growth opportunities; and using federal COVID-related relief funds for these strategies. Each strategy is operationalized with criteria and a three-level rating scale applied to North Carolina.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and analyze educator workforce data to lead targeted, data-informed efforts
constraints: Framework is addressed to state-level policymakers, advocates, and educators; ratings reflect one state's status in 2022
target_learning_goals: increasing the racial and cultural diversity of the educator workforce
improving student access to diverse educators
examples: North Carolina is rated green on sharing program-level candidate demographics, hosting the DRIVE Summit, GYO investment, teacher academies, and induction/mentoring; yellow on data visibility, goals, licensure interrogation, and district partnerships; red on scholarships, program approval standards, MSI investment, hiring-manager training, residencies, and leadership development
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: NORTH CAROLINA. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622852

article_title: Investing in a High-Quality Teacher Workforce: Lessons from Texas Teacher Preparation Programs
citation: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327
title: Site coordinator role combining field supervision, coaching, seminar teaching, mentor training, and governance facilitation
description: The site coordinator, a role common to US PREP residency transformation sites, fulfills the responsibilities of traditional university field supervisors—"supervising, coaching, and conducting observations for residents during their clinical experience"—while also teaching practicum seminars and methods courses, training and collaborating with mentor teachers, supporting residents emotionally, and facilitating quarterly governance meetings with partner districts. Because site coordinators' work touches many dimensions of candidates' experiences, candidate support structures are well scaffolded and aligned.
requirements: Sufficient staffing to maintain a low ratio of teacher candidates to site coordinators, enabling frequent, meaningful feedback to each candidate
Personnel with both coaching and instructional expertise
constraints: The report recommends recruiting site coordinators from educators nearing retirement, senior teachers, and instructional leaders, implying supply considerations
target_learners: Teacher residents in yearlong clinical placements
target_learning_goals: Clinical skill development through frequent observation, coaching, and feedback
examples: At UH, site coordinators guide residents through scaffolded, graduated teaching responsibilities alongside mentor teachers
key_sources: Bland, J. A., Ralph, K., Wei, W., Wang, V., Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wechsler, M. E. (2025). Investing in a high-quality teacher workforce: Lessons from Texas teacher preparation programs. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/871.327

article_title: Cultivating Math Mindsets: Teaching Practices That Enable Equitable Classroom Learning
citation: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406
title: Composite daily math lesson structure with six engagement-oriented components
description: The observed middle school math lessons shared a common structure of six components: a warm-up, direct instruction, group activity, share-out, note-taking, and demonstration of understanding. Each teacher integrated at least five of these six components, whether the class period was 45 or 90 minutes. The structure deliberately builds in social interaction, with "Random assignment to groups; not ability-based grouping" at standing whiteboard stations, and low-stakes warm-ups and checks "with no grade."
requirements: Class time structured so students can move around and socially interact with a variety of classmates
constraints: Documented in 45- to 90-minute middle school periods across five California middle schools
examples: Table 2 describes each component's goal, structure, and teacher and student roles, e.g., the share-out goal to "Celebrate multiple ways to represent and solve math problems."
key_sources: Price, H., & Fitz, J. (2026). Cultivating math mindsets: Teaching practices that enable equitable classroom learning. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/810.406

article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: Six design principles for embedding incidental learning into developer-agent interactions
description: The article proposes six early design principles that "any approach embedding incidental learning into human-agent interactions should satisfy": Contextual (tied to the specific code or decision just engaged with), Grounded (based on the agent's reasoning, not artifacts alone), Ambient (out-of-band, flow-respecting), Selective (intervening only on genuine learning moments), Adaptive (calibrated to developer expertise), and Closed-Loop (verifying internalization via comprehension checks). They "do not specify a system" but "define what any such system must do".
requirements: Learning opportunities must be grounded in the agent's reasoning trace, which carries information such as alternatives considered and uncertainty that cannot be reconstructed from code artifacts alone.
constraints: The authors present the principles as early proposals and "invite the community to refine and extend them".
target_learners: Software developers at varying expertise levels using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Incidental acquisition of concepts such as API choices, design decisions, alternatives, and trade-offs during agent-assisted coding
examples: SHIELD is presented as an early instantiation that operationalizes these principles.
key_sources: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Illinois
citation: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://edtrust.org
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing educator workforce diversity
description: The brief organizes state-level action into six strategies: making educator diversity data "visible and actionable to stakeholders"; setting clear state and district goals; investing in educator preparation programs; targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting and hiring a diverse workforce; investing in retention through working conditions and growth opportunities; and using federal COVID relief funds for diversity strategies. Each strategy is operationalized as criteria rated on a three-level scale (meets all or most, some, one or no requirements), and Illinois is rated against each. The framework treats workforce diversity as a policy-design problem spanning data, goals, preparation, recruitment, and retention.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share useful and timely educator workforce data so stakeholders can set goals and chart a path forward
constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions; it rates what states do, not district or classroom practice
target_learners: K-12 public school students in Illinois, particularly students of color
target_learning_goals: Equitable student access to a racially diverse, high-quality educator workforce
examples: Illinois earned greens for scholarship programs, GYO funding, residency pathways, and numeric diversity goals, but reds or no-evidence ratings for investing in minority-serving institutions and for leader cultural-competence training
key_sources: EdTrust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: ILLINOIS. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED622786

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions into six strategies: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, investing in educator preparation programs, targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting a diverse workforce, investing in retention of teachers of color, and using federal COVID-related relief funds. Each strategy is rated on a three-level scale from "Meets all or most of the requirements within the goal" down to "Meets one or no requirements within the goal", with printed rating methodologies for each criterion. The framework is applied to score Michigan's actions.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share timely, publicly available educator workforce data so stakeholders can make targeted workforce decisions
constraints: Ratings reflect policy conditions as documented for Michigan in 2022; the brief states efforts to recruit teachers of color are compromised when districts struggle to retain them
target_learning_goals: increasing student access to diverse educators
recruiting, preparing, and retaining teachers of color
examples: Michigan earned green ratings for posting school-level workforce demographics, its stakeholder-input Top 10 Strategic Education Plan, Grow Your Own funding, and a three-year induction and mentoring program; it earned red for lacking scholarships and loan forgiveness targeting students of color
key_sources: The Education Trust. (2022). Educator Diversity State Profile: Michigan. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/

article_title: Educator Diversity State Profile: Texas
citation: The Education Trust. (2022). Texas Educator Diversity State Profile. https://edtrust.org/educator-diversity/
title: Six-strategy state policy framework for increasing the racial diversity of the educator workforce
description: The brief organizes state policy conditions for a diverse educator workforce into six strategies: making educator diversity data visible and actionable, setting clear state and district goals, investing in educator preparation programs, targeting resources to districts and schools for recruiting and hiring, investing in retention of teachers of color, and using federal COVID-related relief funds. States are rated on each strategy using a three-level scale from "Meets all or most of the requirements within the goal" down to "Meets one or no requirements within the goal," with printed criteria and rating methodologies for each sub-component. The framework is applied to rate Texas green, yellow, or red on each criterion.
requirements: State education agencies must collect and share useful and timely educator workforce data so stakeholders "can make targeted, strategic workforce decisions at the school, district, and state level."

constraints: The framework addresses state-level policy conditions; it rates states against printed criteria rather than measuring the effects of the strategies on workforce diversity.

target_learning_goals: Equitable student access to a racially and culturally diverse, high-quality educator workforce

article_title: Authentic Student Work in College Admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business
citation: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774
title: Six-step implementation process for an admissions portfolio review system
description: The report documents the process the Ross Undergraduate Admissions team used to build and run portfolio review: align the portfolio to central admission processes, establish technological capacity, develop rubrics, build reader capacity, conduct outreach, and iterate. Rubrics align with "skills and mindsets students need to flourish in the Ross program and community—including critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and curiosity." The pattern balances a standard review's efficiency with qualitative portfolio depth inside existing university timelines.
requirements: Rubrics with clear criteria and detailed performance indicators for reliable qualitative review
A technology platform (SlideRoom) to accept and transfer media submissions
A hired team of 20 to 25 short-term contractual professional readers
constraints: Implemented within the University of Michigan's existing application deadlines, review timeline, and decision release, avoiding university-wide change
target_learning_goals: Reliable evaluation of applicants' critical thinking, problem-solving, collaboration, and curiosity
examples: In year one (2016), every submission was reviewed by the Ross Admissions Review Committee to determine whether submissions met the goals and identify needed guidance adjustments
key_sources: Willis, L., & Martinez, M. R. (2022). Authentic student work in college admissions: Lessons from the Ross School of Business. Learning Policy Institute. https://doi.org/10.54300/756.774

article_title: Investing in Texas Teacher Preparation: Key Features of Successful Residency Programs
citation: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief
title: Six common features of high-quality teacher residencies: yearlong clinical experience, practice-based coursework, EPP–district partnerships, trained mentors, site coordinators, and stipends
description: Texas has used state guidance, grant provisions, and regulatory changes to incentivize residency programs to adopt a set of common features, "six of which stand out in contributing to quality preparation": a yearlong clinical experience, integrated practice-based coursework, partnerships between preparation programs and school districts, trained and experienced mentor teachers, clinical faculty site coordinators, and resident stipends. The features are based on the state's definition of a high-quality residency in which "the teacher candidate is paired with an experienced, highly effective mentor teacher for a full year of clinical training and co-teaching in a K–12 classroom."
requirements: State guidance, grant provisions, and administrative code changes that incentivize programs to adopt the features
constraints: The features are most difficult to establish and sustain in communities with higher needs, including smaller, under-resourced, and more rural districts
examples: TCLAS-funded EPP–district partnerships launched with residency programs already meeting the state's vetted residency definition
key_sources: Wojcikiewicz, S. K., & Wei, W. (2024). Investing in Texas teacher preparation: Key features of successful residency programs [Brief]. Learning Policy Institute. https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/texas-teacher-preparation-brief

article_title: AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems
citation: Tripathi, P., & Kapralos, B. (2026). AI-Enabled Serious Games: Integrating Intelligence and Adaptivity in Training Systems. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21962
title: Six-phase historical arc of adaptive training systems (1969–present)
description: The chapter synthesizes a chronological progression of adaptive training systems through six phases: Phase I (1969–1980s) parameter-control CAI with behaviorist foundations; Phase II (1980s–1990s) model-based intelligent tutoring systems with explicit learner models; Phase III (1990s–2000s) dynamic difficulty adjustment from commercial games; Phase IV (2000s–2010s) structured authoring and modular platforms; Phase V (2010s–2020s) mastery learning and learning analytics; Phase VI (2020–present) AI-enabled runtime adaptivity. The arc reveals that "each phase solved one problem and introduced a new one" and that AI "inherits all unsolved problems simultaneously."
requirements: Understanding the arc requires documenting learner modeling depth, diagnostic specificity, adaptation timescale, and policy sophistication for each phase
constraints: The historical arc reveals "an upper limit on achievable intelligence: an architectural constraint not correctable by better implementation alone" in pre-AI systems
target_learners: Designers and researchers of serious games and adaptive training systems
target_learning_goals: Understanding how computational learning systems have attempted to integrate instructional intelligence and runtime adaptation

citation: F. Rogosch, A. Schrader. (2026). AI-Generated Interactive Fiction for Educational Use: A Pilot Study of Perceived Comprehensibility, Coherence, and Engagement. Proceedings of EDULEARN26 Conference. https://doi.org/10.21125/edulearn.2026.1075

description: SINE is the stimulus-generation system used in this study: "a previously described domain-agnostic pipeline that generates choice-based IF scenarios from structured educational content using an open -weight LLM, with deterministic validation and a repair stage". In this study the pipeline was kept unchanged, with the inference backend moved to Qwen3 14B via the OpenRouter cloud API. It produced a controlled pool of 48 scenarios from 20 media-technology seeds after automated playability and validation filtering.

citation: Yuchen Liu, Roberto Martinez-Maldonado, Riordan Alfredo, Paola Mejia-Domenzain, Dwi Rahayu, and Sadia Nawaz. (2026). AI-Driven Analytics of Team-Teaching Talk: Acoustic Patterns across Experience, Cohorts and the Learning Design. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.09831
title: Six-behaviour spatial pedagogy coding scheme for team teaching
description: An observation coding scheme adapted from prior work that integrates spatial pedagogy space types with team-teaching research. "The final coding scheme distinguished six spatial pedagogy behaviours organised into three broader categories": Instruction (Lecturing), Interaction (Ts-S interaction, T-S interaction, T-Ss interaction), and Collaboration (Assisting, T-T interaction). Supervisory and Personal space behaviours were not retained because they typically involve little or no sustained speech. Inter-rater reliability on a pilot session reached a Cohen's Kappa of 0.75.

constraints: Behaviours associated with Supervisory and Personal space types were excluded from the analytical scheme because they typically involve little or no sustained speech

article_title: Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students
citation: Buket Bilgiç and Demet Sever (2026). Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights from faculty members and students. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00601-0
title: Six-theme multidimensional ethical structure of AI use in higher education
description: Thematic analysis of semi-structured interviews with faculty members and students organized perspectives on ethical AI use into six themes: "Ethical Risks, User Approaches to Ethical Risks, Ethical Risk Management, Resources and Support, and Long-Term Effects", alongside participants' AI tool use and perceived benefits. Together these themes reveal what the article calls "a multidimensional ethical structure in the use of AI in education", spanning risks, user orientations, management practices, support structures, and anticipated long-term consequences. Faculty and student perspectives are presented separately within each theme.
requirements: Semi-structured interviews with both stakeholder groups, analyzed through Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis combining inductive and deductive coding.
constraints: The study is situated within a specific context, and the results reflect participants' reported views and experiences regarding the ethical use of AI in education.
target_learning_goals: understanding ethical dimensions of AI use in learning and teaching
examples: Themes were derived from interviews with 23 students and 14 faculty members selected through maximum variation sampling.

citation: Gheisari, S., & Salarian, H. (2024). Analysis and Prediction of At-Risk Students using Machine Learning Algorithms. https://scholar.google.com/scholar?q=Analysis+and+Prediction+of+At-Risk+Students+using+Machine+Learning+Algorithms
title: SISTC integrated student dataset of 1,027 cleaned records with 14 features for dropout prediction
description: A de-identified institutional dataset built by joining three SISTC sources: course/credit enrollment, subject-wise performance, and demographic/enrollment history. "The integration of these datasets resulted in 2,405 student records. However, after data cleaning and preprocessing, only 1,027 records were retained." It carries 14 features (origin, study duration, age, subjects attempted/completed/failed/exempted, gender, visa type, nationality, course name, course attempts, GPA, enrollment status) and a binary Status target (Graduated/Completed = 1, Withdrawn/Canceled = 0).
requirements: Categorical variables encoded numerically and numerical variables normalized and standardized before model training
constraints: Only records classified as Graduated/Completed or Withdrawn/Cancelled were retained after cleaning
target_learners: higher education students at SISTC, largely international
target_learning_goals: early identification of students at risk of withdrawal or enrollment cancellation
examples: The cleaned dataset contained 716 Withdrawn/Cancel and 311 Graduated/Completed records (Table 3)
