article_title: The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning
citation: Mario Brcic, Stjepan Frljic. (2026). The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26181
title: The six moves: Prime, Probe, Point, Attach, Strengthen, Test as a model of learning one new idea
description: The article models what a student knows as a knowledge map of dots and links, and learning one new idea as growing a new dot and tying it into the map through six ordered moves. As printed, "We call them the six moves: Prime, Probe, Point, Attach, Strengthen, Test, shown on Figure 1." Probe and Test are the protected moments where the student's own work must remain visible; Point, Attach, and Strengthen are guarded-support moments. Each move is mapped to a teacher role, a permitted AI role, and supporting evidence in Table 1.
requirements: A motivated, engaged student; the article states the sequence assumes what it cannot itself supply
constraints: Scope is one idea, on first encounter, in a single pass; long-term retention via review and spacing is a separate layer above the model
target_learners: K-12 and higher-education students learning a new idea
target_learning_goals: Building durable, transferable understanding of a new concept
examples: The article runs survivorship bias through all six moves as a worked lesson plan (Table 4, Figure 2), with AI in at Prime, Attach, and Strengthen and out at Probe and Test
key_sources: Mario Brcic, Stjepan Frljic. (2026). The Effortless Trap: Productive Struggle, AI, and the Illusion of Learning. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.26181

article_title: Conversational AI agents in education: an umbrella review of current utilization, challenges, and future directions
citation: Amrita Ganguly, Nafisa Mehjabin, Aqdas Malik, Aditya Johri. (2025). Conversational AI agents in education: an umbrella review of current utilization, challenges, and future directions for ethical and responsible use. AI and Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-025-00916-0
title: Six-theme framework of directions for ethical and responsible CAI use in education
description: This review organizes directions for ethical and responsible use of CAI in education into six themes derived from thematic analysis of the included reviews: "Ethical governance and policy frameworks; Privacy and data protection measures; Fostering academic integrity and fair use; AI literacy, training and awareness; Design and technical solutions; and Equity, inclusion and human oversight". Each theme aggregates codes such as institutional guidelines, GDPR/HIPAA compliance, AI detection and assessment adaptation, educator and student training, bias mitigation and watermarking, and human oversight. The framework serves as the review's answer to RQ3's second part and underpins its proposed roadmap.
requirements: Institutional adoption of governance, privacy, integrity, literacy, design, and equity measures together, as the review presents them as complementary directions
constraints: Directions are synthesized from review articles published 2020-2025 and reflect the field's stated needs rather than tested interventions
target_learning_goals: responsible and ethical use of conversational AI in learning contexts
examples: The review cites suggested measures such as compliance with data protection regulations like GDPR and HIPAA, adapting assessment methodologies to reduce AI-assisted cheating, and digital watermarking and metadata tagging for content attribution

article_title: Designing faculty standards for technology integration in higher education institutions: a design-based research study
citation: Helen Crompton, Diane Burke and Christine Nickel. (2026). Designing faculty standards for technology integration in higher education institutions: a design-based research study. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00584-y
title: Six-standard framework for faculty technology integration in higher education: Instructor, Coordinator, Leader, Researcher, Learner, and Contributor
description: The study's final theory of ontological innovation is a framework of six standards covering the three faculty workload areas of teaching, research, and service. The article states the standards are "specifically designed for higher education faculty to support their diverse roles in teaching, research, and service by intentionally integrating technology across all areas". Each standard is accompanied by indicators that illustrate what effective technology integration looks like in practice, such as designing inclusive digital learning experiences under Instructor and using digital tools for data analysis under Researcher. The framework was developed and revised through two design-based research macro cycles with surveys and interviews.
requirements: Standards must be paired with actionable tools such as self-assessments, rubrics, and measurable outcomes to be effective in practice
constraints: The article notes cultural variations in governance, academic hierarchies, and pedagogical traditions can shape how faculty interpret and enact the standards, so adopters should consider local contexts
target_learners: Higher education faculty including full-time, part-time, adjunct, and clinical instructors
target_learning_goals: Effective, ethical, and contextually relevant technology use across teaching, research, and service
examples: The final standards table lists indicators such as designing learning opportunities that integrate digital tools and resources, and mentoring students using technology-enhanced guidance and support

title: Six NGSS-aligned middle school student drawing assessment dataset
description: A dataset of student-generated scientific drawings from middle school modeling assessments in the northeastern United States, covering six items (red dye diffusion, Jane's inflated ball, melting butter, hot shower effect, heated cup of water, Jennifer's teapot) with totals from 453 to 816 responses per item. Following the annotation protocol, "each drawing is assigned to one of three ordered proficiency levels:Beginning, Developing, orProficient", scored independently by domain experts. Example drawings are released in the GitHub repository.

constraints: Collected from middle school classrooms in one region of the United States, so representational practices may reflect local curricular contexts

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts
citation: Miguel Rodriguez and Peter Wulff. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22578
title: Six fundamental components of prompt engineering, ordered from task and context down to tone
description: The article presents a six-component account of prompt engineering, stating there are six fundamental components to prompt engineering, from most important to least important: 1) task, 2) context, 3) exemplar, 4) persona, 5) format, and 6) tone. Task is the instruction the AI is expected to carry out and is the most critical component; context provides background details; exemplars illustrate desired style; persona, format, and tone shape delivery but are less essential. These principles are reflected in the article's example prompts.
requirements: Task and context must be included for the prompt to guide the model's behavior effectively
target_learning_goals: effective use of generative AI for learning
examples: The article's exploration context prompt opens by setting task and context and repeats the instruction to maintain the guide role

article_title: Collaborative Making of a Boundary Object for Classifying Generative AI Learning Activities
citation: Dohn, N. B., Markauskaite, L., Huber, E., Wardak, D., Yang, H., Zeivots, S., Casey, A., van Diggele, C., Dohn, N. B., Mannix, K., Mantai, L., Pressick-Kilborn, K., Spence, N., Vallis, C., & Wilson, S. (2026). Collaborative Making of a Boundary Object for Classifying Generative AI Learning Activities. Postdigital Science and Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s42438-026-00671-3
title: Six-category taxonomy for characterising GenAI learning activities
description: The article proposes a taxonomy comprising six categories for characterising GenAI learning activities: Learning Objective (intentionality), Content/GenAI Objects and Processes (what students engage with), Representation Format (media selection), Epistemic Engagement (methodology), Human-GenAI Labour Distribution (role distribution), and Artefacts (material resources). The framework fuses Heimann's German-Scandinavian didactic theory with the ACAD approach to address the postdigital entanglement of humans and technology. As the authors state, "these frameworks complement each other and provide six categories that are important in characterising learning activities across design, presentation and analysis."
requirements: Each category must be specified with a GenAI focus and a set of terms denoting different forms of traits
The taxonomy must accommodate both learning about GenAI and learning within another academic domain using GenAI
constraints: No taxonomy can capture the specificity and entanglement among various elements of learning activities
Histories and traditions influence how general categories are interpreted in a particular context
The field is rapidly changing and any proposed taxonomy risks becoming quickly obsolete
examples: Applied to a financial report writing task in business where students use institutional chatbots
Applied to a law client consultancy role-play with a GenAI-simulated client
Used to construct a ball game fundamentals activity where groups ask GenAI to invent games

article_title: Epistemic Dependence in AI-Mediated Learning
citation: Du Y, Yuan Y (2026) Epistemic dependence in AI-mediated learning. AI & SOCIETY. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00146-026-03294-1
title: Six diagnostic criteria for distinguishing productive epistemic reliance from harmful epistemic dependence
description: The review operationalises the boundary between productive reliance and harmful dependence through a six-criterion diagnostic table: "contestability, recoverability, transfer, traceability, distributed responsibility and epistemic plurality". Each criterion is stated as a contrast — e.g. transfer means capability persists when the system is absent, whereas dependence means performance collapses when AI support is withdrawn. The criteria are offered as diagnostic questions for research, design and pedagogy, not as a psychometric scale.
requirements: Empirical validation: the review states the criteria are not a psychometric scale and need empirical validation
constraints: No single criterion is decisive in every context; the pattern matters, as does the importance of the delegated judgement
target_learners: Learners in AI-mediated educational settings across disciplines
target_learning_goals: Developing epistemic judgement and responsible use of AI for knowledge-related tasks
examples: Table 2 contrasts productive reliance (learner can reconstruct main reasoning with reduced support) with harmful dependence (learner can reproduce a product but cannot explain how the conclusion was reached)

article_title: Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education
citation: Henrique Mohallem Paiva. (2026). Curriculum as Code: An AI-Assisted Architecture for Instructional Design in STEM Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.07364
title: Six-phase AI-assisted instructional design pipeline under the Curriculum as Code paradigm
description: The article formalizes instructional material creation as an engineering process analogous to CI/CD pipelines, composed of six sequential phases: Context Injection, Pedagogical Calibration, Technical Calibration, Planning, Iterative Implementation, and Review. It "replaces unstructured human-AI interactions with a systematic, stage-gated pipeline" that embeds the instructor's tacit knowledge via few-shot calibration, enforces cognitive load theory constraints, and generates LaTeX/Beamer slides plus Python figures through text-based interfaces. Validation occurred in a PBL higher-education institution across eight modules and 28 project contexts.
requirements: Instructor-supplied foundational scoping documents (syllabus, Project Charter), previously validated teaching materials for few-shot calibration, and an institutional custom Beamer class defining visual identity rules
constraints: Validated with a single authoring instructor in a single institution; generative models exhibit behavioral drift after provider updates, occasionally requiring prompt recalibration
target_learners: Undergraduate computing and business administration students in project-based learning programs
target_learning_goals: STEM content mastery (mathematics, computing, engineering topics) delivered through contextualized, active-learning instructional materials
examples: First-year common core modules IN01-IN04 adapted to 24 distinct PBL project contexts, plus specialized modules SE05, AD06, CS11, SE12

citation: Dahal N, Hasan MK and Islam MT (2026). GenAI and AI tools for STEAM educators: evidence-informed strategies and resources for the future of teaching. Front. Educ. 11:1948064. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1948064
title: Six-type taxonomy of generative AI systems for STEAM educators
description: The review distinguishes six types of GenAI systems relevant to STEAM classrooms: text-generation, image-generation, audio-generation, video-generation, code-generation, and multimodal systems that integrate two or more functions. It states that "For STEAM educators, it is useful to distinguish six types of GenAI systems", naming examples such as ChatGPT, DALL·E, Runway ML, and GitHub Copilot. Multimodal systems are described as especially relevant to STEAM projects requiring learners to move between words, images, numbers, models, and computational artifacts.
requirements: Educators need both distinctions and connections among rule-based, adaptive, and generative systems to make informed classroom choices
constraints: GenAI should not be equated with all AI in education; predictive analytics, dashboards, automated scoring, and intelligent tutoring are not necessarily generative

target_learning_goals: informed selection of generative tools for interdisciplinary tasks

article_title: A Framework for Institutional Change in the Age of AI
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A framework for institutional change in the age of AI. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00649-4
title: Six-dimension framework for adapting institutional change models to the AI era
description: The framework identifies six diagnostic dimensions along which prior interactive-engagement (IE) change models must be reconsidered for generative AI: three concerning tools (evidence base, rate of change, scope) and three concerning people (faculty agency, change agent role, student role). It is grounded in sociocultural activity-system models in which tools transform activity. The authors state: "Our framework identifies six dimensions along which existing IE change models must be reconsidered in light of generative AI’s arrival." It is intended as a diagnostic lens, not a new change model.

constraints: The authors do not claim the six dimensions are exhaustive; they offer a starting point

article_title: A Taxonomy of Metacognitive Learning Scenarios in Professional Contexts: Integrating Systems Theory with Empirical Constraints
citation: Gibson, D. C., Azukas, M. E., & Yilmaz Soylu, M. (2025). A Taxonomy of Metacognitive Learning Scenarios in Professional Contexts: Integrating Systems Theory with Empirical Constraints.
title: Six-node open systems model of metacognition
description: The article proposes a six-node open systems architecture synthesizing Flavell, Nelson and Narens, Koriat, and COPES: "Environment (external context and task demands), Input (information entering the learner's system), Processes (active cognitive/metacognitive operations), Structures (stable knowledge representations, beliefs, standards), Output (generated products and behaviors), and Feedback (information about output quality and environmental response)." Monitoring is modeled as upward Processes→Structures flow and control as downward Structures→Processes flow, with a mandatory external backbone Output→Feedback→Environment→Input. It serves as the common language for enumerating learning scenarios.
requirements: Cross-cluster connections must preserve psychological realism: Input always flows into the internal system and Output always flows from it
constraints: The six-node model necessarily simplifies complex processes; Structures aggregates diverse metacognitive knowledge into a single node
examples: The model was implemented in the DOT Framework and used to generate 216 combinatorial learning scenarios for an AI-enabled Coach

article_title: Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance
citation: Gabelmann, J., Jahn, F., Baum, K., van Rossum, S., Wuenscher, E., Gros, T. P., Wolf, V. (2026). Modularizing Educational LLM-Agency for Fostering Responsible Learning Assistance. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.30187
title: Six design desiderata for responsible LLM-based educational systems
description: The article derives six design desiderata for responsible LLM-based educational systems: differentiated pedagogical control, preservation of epistemic agency, process-level transparency, effective human oversight, explicit handling of value conflicts, and anticipatory robustness and revisability. These are stated as 'a selection of necessary design conditions for responsible AI in this context, rather than as a complete or sufficient specification'. Each desideratum constrains how a system must be built, not merely how it should behave.
requirements: Desiderata must be specific to the educational deployment context and have direct architectural implications
constraints: They are necessary conditions, not a complete or sufficient specification of responsible educational systems
target_learning_goals: responsible AI-supported exercise solving and skill development

article_title: Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities
citation: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154v1
title: Simulated-respondent framework: fine-tuning an LLM to reproduce option-choice patterns across discretized ability levels so item parameters can be read off the resulting curves
description: The framework bins student ability into L labeled intervals (Table 2, from Foundational to Elite mastery), prompts the LLM to answer as a student of a given ability level with the correct answer supplied, and trains it with an MSE loss on next-token option probabilities against interval-averaged MCM/3PL probabilities. As the abstract states, "By learning to reproduce the systematic error patterns of students across a discrete range of abilities, the LLM implicitly captures the underlying response probabilities encoded in the 3PL and MCM curves", allowing difficulty to be approximated from predicted option probabilities.
requirements: A calibrated dataset of responses with independently derived student ability levels, and IRT-fitted 3PL/MCM target curves per item
constraints: Each mapping arrow in the pipeline introduces approximation error, so reported correlations are best read as lower bounds
LoRA was applied only to Gated Attention components, adapting roughly a quarter of the layers a conventional transformer would expose
target_learners: students at discretized ability levels answering multiple-choice mathematics items
target_learning_goals: item difficulty estimation for assessment design and test form assembly
examples: The framework was applied to 4,848 mathematics items generated from 970 item models, with stimuli and options allowed to carry image components combined into a single image
key_sources: Christopher Ormerod and YoungKoung Kim. (2026). Multimodal Item Parameter Estimation using Simulated Response Probabilities. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.10154

article_title: Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education
citation: Tabares-Cruz YB, Cevallos-Sánchez HA, Arteaga-Pita IG, Rodriguez-Alava LA, Carreño-Mendoza AL, Cedeño-Barreto MdlÁ, Castro-Castillo GJ, Cobacango-Villavicencio JG and Moreira-Choez JS (2026) Predictors of the ethical use of generative artificial intelligence in higher education. The endogenous construct "captures whether these principles are translated into responsible academic practice across multiple domains." article_title: AI literacy and scenario-based ethical judgment about generative AI among undergraduate students
citation: Reed, J. M., Ferdig, R. E., Dodson, T. M., Gunstad, J., & Hughes, J. W. (2026). AI Literacy and Scenario-based Ethical Judgment About Generative AI Among Undergraduate Students. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09757-w
title: Six adapted GenAI ethical scenarios for assessing scenario-based ethical judgment
description: A six-scenario measure adapted with permission from Dodson et al. (2025), presenting dilemmas mirroring common academic situations where AI might be used, with response options of ethical, unethical, or unsure. Three scenarios depict learning-support uses and three depict substitutionary uses. The article notes "Internal consistency for the six-item measure was modest (KR-20 = 0.61)", which the authors attribute to the ceiling effect and limited variability.
requirements: Scenarios are scored dichotomously as correct or incorrect, with unsure coded as incorrect
constraints: Modest internal consistency (KR-20 = 0.61)
Pronounced ceiling effect limited ability to differentiate judgment in ambiguous situations
Fixed presentation order means order or priming effects cannot be excluded
target_learning_goals: ethical judgment about generative AI use in academic contexts
examples: Q1 presents a student using AI to summarize textbook notes and verifying with her professor; Q5 presents a student minimally editing an AI-generated assignment before submitting it
key_sources: Reed, J. M., Ferdig, R. E., Dodson, T. M., Gunstad, J., & Hughes, J. W. (2026). AI Literacy and Scenario-based Ethical Judgment About Generative AI Among Undergraduate Students. Journal of Academic Ethics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10805-026-09757-w

article_title: Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments
citation: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842
title: Six specialized role-assigned prompts sharing a four-part structure for assignment generation and guardrails
description: Taklif.AI's prompt engineering pipeline assigns distinct LLM roles and tasks across six prompts (personalize-assignment, simplify-assignment, assignment-guardrails, interest-guardrails, output-guardrails, pdf-ocr). The article states: "We employ six specialized prompts, each assigned a distinct LLM role and task (Table 3). All prompts follow a consistent four-part structure": role definition, task specification, context and constraints, and output formatting. Zero-shot prompting is adopted to maximize generalizability, with prompts iteratively refined using LangSmith evaluation tools.
requirements: Structured output enforcement (JSON/Markdown with LaTeX rules) for downstream integration, and iterative refinement using LangSmith's evaluation tools measuring coherence, personalization depth, and safety compliance
constraints: Zero-shot prompting (no in-context examples) is used rather than few-shot exemplars
target_learning_goals: personalized and simplified assignment generation with safety and relevance validation
examples: The personalize-assignment prompt assigns a Learning Experience Designer role with customization, creativity, cultural sensitivity, and fairness skills, and outputs JSON with a title and Markdown content
key_sources: Zaki Kurdya, Mohammed Zuqlam, Salem Amassi, Shady Telbany, Motaz Saad. (2026). Taklif.AI: LLM-Powered Platform for Interest-Based Personalized College Assignments. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05842

article_title: Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning
citation: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613
title: Simulation-based framework for evaluating learner task-selection strategies and system constraints in mastery-based ITS
description: A simulation framework that models mastery learning as a repeated problem-level decision cycle in which simulated learners select skills via predefined strategies, the system selects problems, performance is generated via AFM, and mastery is updated via BKT with a 95% mastery threshold. It is grounded in real student interaction data from two math ITS datasets and enables "controlled comparison of learner strategies and system constraints under standardized conditions" prior to classroom deployment. The framework supports close-the-loop experimentation by identifying which learner behaviors warrant targeted system constraints.
requirements: Real student interaction data to fit AFM and BKT parameters and derive typical solution paths
A mastery threshold (95% posterior mastery probability) and predefined task-selection decision rules
constraints: Models a limited set of strategies and constraints and does not capture motivational, metacognitive, or affective factors
Focuses on a task-selection-first setup and does not model direct problem-selection, multi-task-selection, or fully system-driven sequencing
Learner strategies are modeled as static rather than adapting over time
target_learners: middle school and high school mathematics students in ITS environments
target_learning_goals: efficient skill mastery in multi-step mathematical problem solving
examples: Simulations of 1,000 learners per condition using PSLC DataShop datasets for equation solving (58 problems, 10 skills) and graph interpretation (31 problems, 13 skills), with open-source simulation and analysis code
key_sources: Haley Noh, Aarna Chowdhary, Jeroen Ooge, Vincent Aleven, Conrad Borchers. (2026). Simulating Learners' Task-Selection Strategies and System Constraints in Mastery Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21613

article_title: Findings of the First Teaching Monster Challenge: A Benchmark of Pedagogical Content Knowledge in AI Agents
citation: Lin, Yi-Cheng; Guo, Yu-Kai; Chen, Szu-Chi; Feng, Bo-Han; Hsu, Yun-Man; Hsieh, Hsiang; Lin, Yu-Jung; Wu, Yue-Ling; Dong, Jia-Kai; Cheng, An-Yu; Huang, Yu-Han; Ieong, Lok-Lam; Chen, Kuan-Yu; Tchouang, Ming-Douo; Sun, Shao-Hua; Lin, Che; Ding, Jian-Jiun; Lee, Hung-yi. (2026). Findings of the First Teaching Monster Challenge: A Benchmark of Pedagogical Content Knowledge in AI Agents. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08852
title: Six-stage cascade architecture for end-to-end instructional video generation
description: Nearly all submissions instantiate a six-stage cascade: "persona parsing and routing, lesson planning, slide and script composition, visual rendering, narration synthesis, and assembly." Recurring design choices include structuring the persona as JSON conditioning for every stage, difficulty-based model routing, web-search grounding of lesson plans, Bloom's-taxonomy constraints enforced by closed-loop LLM review, HTML/CSS slide templates with reviewer–fixer loops, split handling of conceptual versus mathematical figures, two-step planning for Manim animation, and word-level forced alignment of narration to animation.
requirements: Each stage consumes artifacts from earlier stages; persona parsing into structured JSON conditions every following stage.
constraints: Web-search grounding lowers but does not eliminate factual errors in lesson plans; one-shot LLM generation of Manim code fails frequently without a storyboard split.
target_learners: learners described by persona across grade levels and attention spans
examples: Eight of the top 10 Layer 2 teams parsed the free-text persona into a structured JSON profile; one team routed lesson planning to Claude Opus 4 for normal attention spans and Claude Sonnet 4 for short ones.

article_title: ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting
citation: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9
title: Six-dimensional prompt quality vector as a diagnostic, comparable, and policy-relevant representation
description: ARPG+ models prompt quality as a six-dimensional vector covering "structural completeness, semantic clarity, contextual grounding, task specificity, constraint explicitness, and output conventions." The representation is described as diagnostic (each dimension maps to concrete coaching actions), comparable across time (enabling progress tracking), and policy-relevant (feeding safety and benefit terms). The authors state the dimension choice is "an informed design commitment rather than the output of an empirical dimensionality search," anchored in prior prompt-engineering and AI-literacy work.
requirements: Each dimension maps to concrete coaching actions (e.g., low structural completeness suggests adding a skeleton; low semantic clarity triggers a disambiguating question).
constraints: The authors state the six dimensions are an informed design commitment, not the output of an empirical dimensionality search; empirical refinement including confirmatory factor analysis on real-learner corpora is identified as a priority.
target_learners: Novice LLM users learning to prompt
examples: Each dimension maps to a micro-action: low structural completeness yields a skeleton hint; weak contextual grounding suggests a citation or data reference; missing output conventions offers a format example.
key_sources: Ye, P.-G., Mo, K., Long, Y., Liu, M., Sang, H., & Zheng, J. (2026). ARPG+: a simulation-based study of real-time coaching for educational LLM prompting. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-026-00606-9

article_title: Designing for Authentic Assessment: A Scoping Review
citation: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Zilu Du. (2025). Designing for authentic assessment: a scoping review. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-025-01588-9
title: Six-dimensional framework of authentic assessment characteristics in and beyond workplaces
description: The review proposes a six-dimensional framework for authentic assessment (AA) characteristics consisting of authenticity in assessment, cognitive challenges, assessment criteria, feedback, student agency and social collaboration. It extends prior frameworks (Gulikers et al. 2004; Ashford-Rowe et al. 2014; Villarroel et al. 2018) by distinguishing multiple meanings of authenticity — assessment, professional, digital, self and social authenticity — and by adding student agency and social collaboration as design elements. The review states it 'underscores the design of student agency, which enables students to integrate their knowledge, actions and identity across various practices'. The framework was used to code the 37 included studies.
requirements: Assessment designs must be coded against all six dimensions to determine whether and how design elements are incorporated
constraints: The framework's novelty rests on few studies addressing the broader (student and societal) perspectives of authenticity
target_learners: undergraduate and postgraduate students in higher education
target_learning_goals: authentic assessment design that supports meaningful engagement, employability and societal contribution
examples: The authors used the framework to systematically code how 37 empirical studies designed authentic assessment, calculating the number of studies mentioning each design element.
key_sources: Ying Zhan, David Boud, Zilu Du. (2025). Designing for authentic assessment: a scoping review. Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10734-025-01588-9

article_title: Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher
citation: Mireia Vendrell, Samantha-Kaye Johnston. (2026). Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100572
title: Six essential intellectual processes underpinning critical thinking in AI-mediated learning
description: Drawing on Bloom's revised taxonomy, Halpern's model of critical thinking and the APA Delphi Report, the article articulates 'six essential and interrelated processes: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity'. Each is defined and mapped in Table 1 to the risks of unstructured LLM use and to ethical foundations such as human agency and epistemic responsibility. The processes are both cognitive and dispositional.
requirements: Processes must be 'intentionally scaffolded through pedagogy' rather than assumed to emerge spontaneously
examples: Table 1 maps each process to a risk (e.g., cognitive offloading threatens conceptual interpretation) and to theoretical foundations
key_sources: Mireia Vendrell, Samantha-Kaye Johnston. (2026). Scaffolding critical thinking with generative AI: Design principles for integrating large language models in higher education. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100572

article_title: The Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (SFAILQ): Assessing AI Literacy in Adolescents, Young Adults, and Midlife Adults
citation: Liu Qingqi, Miao Wenjiao, Li Jingjing, Lei Yuju. (2026). The Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (SFAILQ): Assessing AI Literacy in Adolescents, Young Adults, and Midlife Adults. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1110. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071110
title: Six-facet model of AI literacy: affective experiences, usage skills, cognitive evaluation, ethical norms, responsible use, and self-development
description: The article proposes a six-facet model of AI literacy building on the ABCE and KSAVE models by adding two new factors. The authors define AI literacy as "the responsible use of AI within ethical standards, characterized by the experience of positive emotions, proficiency in employing AI tools, clear and rational cognitive frameworks, and a commitment to continually enhancing one's theoretical understanding and practical proficiency in AI for the purpose of fostering self-development." Responsible use combines prudent engagement and self-accountability; self-development captures dynamic future potential alongside static competencies.
requirements: Scale items must be designed from the outset to suit adolescents, young adults, and midlife adults to achieve cross-age equivalence
constraints: The authors note the model's dimensions map onto DigCompEdu only partially, since DigCompEdu focuses on educators and broader digital technologies
target_learning_goals: AI literacy: affective, skill, cognitive, ethical, responsible-use, and self-development competencies
examples: The SFAILQ was developed from this model with 32 items across the six dimensions
key_sources: Liu Qingqi, Miao Wenjiao, Li Jingjing, Lei Yuju. (2026). The Six-Facet Artificial Intelligence Literacy Questionnaire (SFAILQ): Assessing AI Literacy in Adolescents, Young Adults, and Midlife Adults. Behavioral Sciences, 16(7), 1110. https://doi.org/10.3390/bs16071110

article_title: A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities
citation: Wang, N., Zou, D., Xie, H., & Qin, S. J. (2026). A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities, and insights from the frontier agent paradigm, exemplified by OpenClaw. Computers and Education: Artificial Intelligence, 11. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2026.100653
title: Six-dimensional agentic capability framework rated on a 1–5 ordinal scale, grounded in activity theory and scaffolding theory
description: The review develops a coding rubric rating six agentic capability dimensions — autonomy and proactivity; planning and reasoning depth; memory and context management; tool and environment interaction; multi-agent collaboration; and robustness, explainability and governance — each on "A 1–5 ordinal scale" capturing thresholds from non-agentic to fully agentic behaviour. Activity theory anchors the dimensions educationally (e.g., autonomy maps to the subject, governance to rules), and scaffolding theory supplements interpretation of planning, memory, and governance dimensions.
requirements: Dimensions must be ratable from reported agent architecture, interaction design, and evaluation setup without fine-grained interaction logs or proprietary benchmarks.
constraints: The article states the framework "is not a psychometric measurement tool" and that formal external expert validation was not conducted, so capability scores should be interpreted with this in mind.
target_learners: Researchers and coders of educational agentic AI literature
target_learning_goals: Mapping and evaluating the agentic capabilities of educational AI systems
examples: The rubric was pilot-tested on 20 randomly selected studies with two independent coders, and level descriptors were refined with LLM assistance before full corpus coding.

A scoping review of generative AI-powered agentic AI in education: Research landscape, agentic capabilities, and insights from the frontier agent paradigm, exemplified by OpenClaw. article_title: A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education
citation: Simon Baradziej. (2026). A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education. Social Sciences & Humanities Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2026.103418
title: Six-role taxonomy of agentic AI in higher education
description: The review organises the agentic-AI-in-higher-education literature into a role-based taxonomy derived from thematic synthesis of 48 included studies. As the review states, "six discrete thematic roles for agentic AI in higher education were identified: personalised learning and adaptive tutoring; automated assessment and feedback; teaching assistance and augmentation; administrative and student support; curriculum design and workforce alignment; and research support and academic operations." Roles are not mutually exclusive; Table 5 reports their frequencies (18, 12, 11, 8, 5, and 4 studies respectively).
requirements: Systems must meet at least three of four agentic criteria (autonomy, planning, tool use, persistent memory) to fall within the taxonomy's scope
constraints: Roles are not mutually exclusive in practice; several studies reported systems serving more than one function
target_learning_goals: understanding the roles agentic AI assumes across university functions including teaching, assessment, administration, curriculum, and research
key_sources: Simon Baradziej. (2026). A systematic review of the roles of agentic AI in higher education. Social Sciences & Humanities Open. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssaho.2026.103418

article_title: Self-Monitoring Interventions for Students with ASD: a Meta-analysis of School-Based Research
citation: Davis, J.L., Mason, B.A., Davis, H.S., Mason, R.A., & Crutchfield, S.A. (2016). Self-Monitoring Interventions for Students with ASD: a Meta-analysis of School-Based Research. Review Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, 3, 196–208. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40489-016-0076-y
title: Corpus of 16 single-subject self-monitoring studies with 28 unique participants with ASD
description: The meta-analysis synthesized a corpus of "Sixteen single subject studies ... with 28 unique participants", drawn from school-based research on self-monitoring for students with ASD. Included studies (marked with asterisks in the reference list) span preschool through high school settings and targets including on-task behavior, social initiations, stereotypy, and academic engagement.
requirements: Studies met single-subject design inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis
target_learners: students with autism spectrum disorders in school settings
target_learning_goals: behavioral and academic outcomes addressed by self-monitoring

article_title: The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021
citation: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5
title: Six categories of AI applications in STEM education with sub-categories
description: The review's central taxonomy classifies AI applications in STEM education into six categories: learning prediction, intelligent tutoring system, student behavior detection, automation, educational robots, and others. Each category is further divided into sub-categories, e.g., learning prediction splits into learning performance prediction (N = 14) and at-risk student prediction (N = 4); intelligent tutoring systems split into instructional content delivery, recommendation of personalized learning path, and resource recommendation. The taxonomy emerged from content analysis of 63 empirical studies published 2011–2021 and serves as the review's answer to its first research question.
requirements: Classification was based on a GST-derived coding scheme applied by two raters with consensus on conflicting codes
constraints: Only AI-supported robots were included, since robots contain various techniques and the review considered the research topic
target_learners: STEM learners from kindergarten through higher education
target_learning_goals: Selecting and applying AI techniques to support STEM instruction and learning
examples: Learning prediction was the largest category (N = 18, 29%), followed by intelligent tutoring systems (N = 16, 25%) and student behavior detection (N = 13, 21%)
key_sources: Weiqi Xu and Fan Ouyang. (2022). The application of AI technologies in STEM education: a systematic review from 2011 to 2021. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-022-00377-5

article_title: Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory
citation: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1
title: Span-task battery distinguishing STM (simple span) from WM (complex span) in children
description: A set of memory tasks administered to 7- to 13-year-olds: digit, letter, and word span as traditional simple span STM measures, and reading span, listening span, and least number span as complex span WM measures requiring concurrent processing. As the article states, "WM was assessed with three tasks in which children remem-bered information while concurrently performing other cognitivetasks." Each span was defined as the largest set recalled perfectly from both sets. The battery also included PIAT-R Reading Recognition for decoding and Woodcock-Johnson Visual Matching and Cross-Out for processing speed.
requirements: Administration in a single session in a constant task order, with order not counterbalanced so individual differences would not be confounded with task order
constraints: Letter span was administered only in Study 1; digit span and least number span only in Study 2
target_learning_goals: measuring distinct memory constructs and their links to word decoding and processing speed
examples: Reading span required children to read sentences aloud, judge truth, and recall final words; least number span required reading three numbers, naming the smallest, then recalling the smallest numbers in order
key_sources: Robert Kail and Lynda K. Hall. (2001). Distinguishing short-term memory from working memory. Memory & Cognition, 29(1), 1-9. https://link.springer.com/journal/13421/29/1

article_title: Effects of a 6-week, co-taught literacy unit on preservice special educators' literacy-education knowledge
citation: Pufpaff, L. A., & Yssel, N. (2010). Effects of a 6-Week, Co-Taught Literacy Unit on Preservice Special Educators' Literacy-Education Knowledge. Psychology in the Schools, 47(5). https://doi.org/10.1002/pits.20485
title: Six-week co-taught literacy unit embedded in special education methods courses
description: An intensive 6-week literacy unit embedded within two existing special education methods courses (mild interventions and intense interventions licensure programs) at a midsize Midwest university. "The 6-week curriculum was developed based on the NRP's (2000) Þve key areas essential for learning to read (i.e., phonemic awareness, phonics, ßuency, vocabulary, and comprehension)" plus emergent literacy and writing/spelling. The unit aimed to give candidates knowledge and skills to implement research-based practices suited to individualized student needs, not a curriculum to teach from directly.
requirements: Candidates must be enrolled in both special education methods courses, which are restricted to students accepted into the Teaching Curriculum for either licensure program.
constraints: The unit is taught during the second half of the semester, which "leaves little time for participants to plan and implement literacy assessment and intervention activities at the conclusion of the unit."
target_learners: Preservice special education teacher candidates in mild and intense interventions licensure programs
target_learning_goals: Knowledge of literacy assessment and instruction across the five critical components of reading, emergent literacy, and writing/spelling for diverse learners with disabilities
examples: Each week addressed one critical component of reading, with the sixth week focused on handwriting, composition, and spelling; an emergent literacy presentation was added in the first week.

article_title: “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children's metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities
citation: Ebru Aydın, Çağlayan Dinçer. (2022). “I did it wrong, but i know it”: Young children’s metacognitive knowledge expressions during peer interactions in math activities. Thinking Skills and Creativity 45 (2022) 101104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tsc.2022.101104
title: Sixteen mathematical measurement activities across length, area, weight, and volume dimensions designed to elicit peer interaction
description: The study designed and implemented sixteen activities based on the dimensions of mathematical measurement skills of length, area, weight, and volume, with four activities per dimension. Activities were prepared from outcomes and indicators in the Turkish Preschool Education Program, organized and finalized as 13 outcomes and 60 indicators after expert consultation with a preschool education specialist and a mathematics education specialist. The activities "allow peer interactions and they are ordered from easy to difficult." Examples include Animal Shelters (selecting objects of appropriate length), How to Cover It? (covering a surface), Bags (comparing weights), and Cylinders (comparing volumes). All activities were video-recorded with three cameras from different angles.
requirements: Outcomes and indicators based on children's measurement skills selected from the Preschool Education Program
Expert consultation with specialists in preschool education, mathematics education, and early childhood education
constraints: Implemented two days a week, one activity per day, over approximately 10 weeks excluding holidays
Designed for a kindergarten class of 18 children aged 60–68 months, with two children as focal participants
target_learning_goals: Mathematical measurement skills (length, area, weight, volume) and metacognitive knowledge expression
examples: Measuring Rods activity: children create measuring rods with cardboard sticks and place unit lines with objects such as paper clips, sticks, straws, or buttons

article_title: Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom
citation: Beebe, D. W., Rose, D., & Amin, R. (2010). Attention, Learning, and Arousal of Experimentally Sleep-Restricted Adolescents in a Simulated Classroom. The Journal of Adolescent Health. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jadohealth.2010.03.005
title: Simulated classroom assessment with educational films, quizzes, and video/EEG monitoring
description: A laboratory analogue of a classroom used to measure learning, attention, and arousal objectively. Participants were "seated behind a table" viewing "30-minute educational films presented on a 19-inch television ~6 feet away", then completed 12-item multiple-choice quizzes; a subset was video-recorded and EEG-monitored. Inattentive behavior was coded by a condition-blind rater in 30-second epochs as look-aways of ≥3 consecutive seconds.
requirements: Educational films of developmentally-appropriate content (The Western Tradition series)
Condition-blind behavioral raters and, for arousal, EEG equipment
constraints: The authors state the technique "has not been previously validated and warrants psychometric attention"
examples: Used to compare quiz scores, inattentive behaviors, and theta power after sleep-restricted versus healthy-sleep weeks in a counterbalanced design

article_title: The genetic and environmental etiologies of the relations between cognitive skills and components of reading ability.
citation: Christopher, M. E., Keenan, J. M., Hulslander, J., DeFries, J. C., Miyake, A., Wadsworth, S. J., Willcutt, E., Pennington, B., & Olson, R. K. (2016). The Genetic and Environmental Etiologies of the Relations between Cognitive Skills and Components of Reading Ability. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 145(4), 451-466. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0000146
title: Simple view of reading as a genetic etiological model
description: The study tests the simple view of reading (Hoover & Gough, 1990), which posits that "successful reading comprehension is the product of word reading and listening comprehension skills". The nested and hierarchical reading models provide etiological support: all phenotypic variance in reading comprehension was captured by the common reading latent variable, with word reading and listening comprehension showing independent genetic variance.
requirements: Multiple measures of word reading, listening comprehension, and reading comprehension to model as latent variables
constraints: Findings are specific to the Colorado Front Range sample with English as a first language

article_title: Experiences of racism and subjective cognitive function in African American women
citation: Coogan P, Schon K, Li S, Cozier Y, Bethea T, Rosenberg L. (2020). Experiences of racism and subjective cognitive function in African American women. Alzheimer's & Dementia: Diagnosis, Assessment & Disease Monitoring. https://doi.org/10.1002/dad2.12067
title: Six-question subjective cognitive function scale from the STIDA telephone dementia screener
description: The article ascertained subjective cognitive function in 2015 using "six yes/no questions" developed for the short Structured Telephone Interview for Dementia Assessment (STIDA), a telephone screener for dementia. Each positive response was assigned 1 point for a total score ranging from 0 to 6, categorized as good (0), moderate (1-2), or poor (3-6). The article reports that "Scores based on the questions have correlated well with results from more extensive cognitive assessments", and cites evidence that self-awareness of poor memory predicts dementia and AD onset.
requirements: Administered as six yes/no questions; scoring assigns 1 point per positive response for a 0-6 total
constraints: Measures subjective rather than objectively assessed cognition; the article notes it would be optimal to have objective measures
target_learning_goals: Subjective assessment of memory and cognitive function in epidemiological research
examples: In the BWHS analytic cohort, 60.0% of participants fell in the good SCF category, 28.1% in moderate, and 12.0% in poor

article_title: Dose-Related Effects of Alcohol on Cognitive Functioning
citation: Dry MJ, Burns NR, Nettelbeck T, Farquharson AL, White JM (2012) Dose-Related Effects of Alcohol on Cognitive Functioning. PLoS ONE 7(11): e50977. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0050977
title: Six-test repeated-measures cognitive battery (UFOV, SOPT, IT, TSP, SART, TMT)
description: A battery of six widely used psychometric tests administered in a fixed order (UFOV, SOPT, IT, TSP, SART, TMT) at four time-points, chosen because each measures a process previously shown to be alcohol-sensitive, each is well-known and easily accessible, and each is "suitable for repeated measures designs". The battery could be completed in 40-50 minutes, minimizing variability from rising and falling BACs. TMT forms were symmetrically transformed to remove learning effects across presentations.
requirements: Tasks must be free of strategies producing abrupt outcome changes, or alterable to achieve this, for repeated administration
constraints: The battery requires approximately 40-50 minutes per test-run, which the authors note constrains testing within a stable BAC window
target_learning_goals: measuring dose-related changes across processing speed, working memory, strategic optimization, vigilance, response inhibition, cognitive flexibility and psychomotor function
examples: Participants completed the battery three times on day 1 for practice and once at baseline plus three dosed time-points on day 2
key_sources: Dry MJ, Burns NR, Nettelbeck T, Farquharson AL, White JM (2012) Dose-Related Effects of Alcohol on Cognitive Functioning. PLoS ONE 7(11): e50977. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0050977

article_title: Efficacy of Learning Strategies Instruction in Adult Education
citation: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291
title: Four SIM learning strategies taught in the trial: Bridging, Building Fluency, Prediction, and Summarization
description: The study taught four SIM learning strategies using the existing SIM strategy template: "The Bridging Strategy, The Building Fluency Strategy, The Prediction Strategy, and The Summarization Strategy." Bridging is a word-level decoding strategy using the mnemonic PART with a FIND subroutine for syllabication; Fluency uses two cycles of repeated reading, first word-level then passage-level, re-reading lists 3 to 7 times to mastery; Prediction uses the CLUE mnemonic (check for clues, link to prior knowledge, unveil predictions, examine the reading); Summarization uses the READ mnemonic (review, evaluate, answer with paraphrase, determine a summary). Each strategy presents short sequenced steps with a mnemonic to cue cognitive and metacognitive actions.
requirements: Delivery through the explicit four-phase instructional method
Reading materials appropriate for adults
constraints: Validated with adolescents with SLD in secondary settings with up to 36 weeks available for instruction; in this trial planned instruction was shortened to 19 to 34 hours
target_learners: Adult basic education learners at NRS educational functional levels 2 through 6
target_learning_goals: Prediction and prior-knowledge activation before reading
examples: Bridging teaches readers to underline familiar letter groups in an unfamiliar word, blend the sounds, and check whether the word makes sense in the sentence before moving to later steps
key_sources: Hock Michael F., Mellard Daryl F. (2011). Efficacy of learning strategies instruction in adult basic education. Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness, 4(2), 134-153. https://doi.org/10.1080/19345747.2011.555291

article_title: Sight word acquisition in first grade students at risk for reading disabilities: an item-level exploration of the number of exposures required for mastery
citation: Steacy LM, Fuchs D, Gilbert JK, Kearns DM, Elleman AM, Edwards AA. (2020). Sight Word Acquisition in First Grade Students At-Risk for Reading Disabilities: An Item-Level Exploration of the Number of Exposures Required for Mastery. Annals of Dyslexia. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11881-020-00198-7
title: Sight Word Challenge: a one- to three-minute daily timed sight word reading activity with mastery-based word removal
description: The Sight Word Challenge was a timed word recognition activity embedded in a yearlong multicomponent decoding intervention for at-risk first graders. Students read from lists of the 500 most frequent words (Educator's Word Frequency Guide) for one minute, with the tutor correcting errors by pronunciation only; "When a student read a word correctly on three consecutive days, the word was removed from the student's list." Tutors reviewed up to three unmastered words and awarded certificates at benchmarks of 10, 50, or 200 words mastered.
requirements: One-on-one tutoring in a quiet space outside the classroom, with tutors tracking student progress across sessions
constraints: No semantic feedback was provided during the activity; the measure was developed based on word frequency and not to explore specific grapheme-phoneme correspondences
target_learners: First grade students at risk for reading disabilities
target_learning_goals: Automatic recognition of high-frequency sight words
examples: 93 students in the study mastered the same 145 words, which formed the item set for the exposure analyses
key_sources: Steacy LM, Fuchs D, Gilbert JK, Kearns DM, Elleman AM, Edwards AA. (2020). Sight Word Acquisition in First Grade Students At-Risk for Reading Disabilities: An Item-Level Exploration of the Number of Exposures Required for Mastery. article_title: Teacher–Student Dialogue During Classroom Teaching: Does It Really Impact on Student Outcomes?
citation: Howe, C., Hennessy, S., Mercer, N., Vrikki, M., & Wheatley, L. (2018). Teacher-Student Dialogue during Classroom Teaching: Does it Really Impact upon Student Outcomes? To appear in The Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://gtr.ukri.org/projects?ref=ES/M007103/1
title: Six-component student outcome assessment battery (three SATs, science test, reasoning test, PASS)
description: The study assessed six outcomes: Mathematics, SPAG and Reading SATs supplied by teachers, a specially prepared Year 6 science test on inheritance and evolution and fair testing, a specially designed general reasoning test, and the PASS attitude survey. For the science test, "Pilot data indicated that the items had excellent scale properties (Cronbach's alpha across all items=.95; mean square out-fit scores all below 2.00 on Rasch analysis)"; the reasoning test alpha was .98 and PASS alpha .93.
requirements: Teacher-supplied anonymized SAT scores
Trained markers with a scoring manual for science short-text items
Start-of-year NFER baselines matched to each outcome
constraints: Mathematics SAT analyses were based on 61 classes because classes where a colleague taught mathematics were discounted
The science test was omitted in classrooms that had not covered inheritance and evolution
target_learners: Year 6 students in English primary schools (N up to 1784)
target_learning_goals: Curriculum mastery in mathematics, literacy and science
Attitudes to school, self as learner and relationship with teacher
examples: Science items covered fossilization, heritability including of acquired characteristics, and inter-generational adaptation

article_title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic computer-supported collaborative learning environments in schools
citation: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7
title: Simulation versus hybrid approaches distinguished by whose goals and purposes the activities serve
description: The article reframes the prevailing participant/setting classification of authentic designs: the crux of the distinction is conceptualized as the extent of students' direct interaction with practitioners and the setting, but the review concludes the decisive criterion is "whose goals and purposes" the activities serve. Simulations aim for classroom culture to "more closely resemble, align with, or approximate the authentic culture" via boundary objects; hybrids place learners in direct interaction with practitioners on activities serving practitioners' purposes, and are therefore preferable termed hybrids rather than full participation.
requirements: Classifying a design requires information about the purpose of activities, not only who participates and where
constraints: Participant and setting information alone does not determine the approach: both approaches can include teachers, non-authentic practitioners, or authentic practitioners
target_learners: designers and researchers of authentic CSCL environments
target_learning_goals: conceptualizing and organizing design variations for authenticity
examples: Radinsky et al.'s (2001) mutual benefit partnership was treated as a simulation-variation C case because the telecommunications company was not an authentic culture and student benefit was a service rather than learning industry practice
key_sources: Yotam Hod, Ornit Sagy. (2019). Conceptualizing the Designs of Authentic Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning Environments in Schools. http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007%2Fs11412-019-09300-7 https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-019-09300-7

article_title: The role of first-language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self-efficacy in CSCL
citation: Natalia Reich-Stiebert, Jan-Bennet Voltmer, Jennifer Raimann, Stefan Stürmer. (2023). The role of first-language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self-efficacy in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 18:513–530. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09411-2
title: SIDE-based account: linguistic cues in computer-mediated collaboration trigger social categorization and stereotype processes
description: The article uses the social identification model of deindividuation effects (SIDE) to explain how first-language heterogeneity harms CSCL interactions. It argues that computer-mediated communication's "relative lack of individualizing cues" increases reliance on "easily available surface-level social categorical information", and that "Linguistic features are generally strong markers of ethnic and cultural category membership", potentially triggering stereotyping, stereotype threat, intergroup bias, and paternalistic communication patterns. The study did not attempt to separate these stereotype-based processes from task-related communication barriers; both are treated as candidate mechanisms behind the heterogeneity effect.
requirements: expressly framed as applying to computer-mediated, written-language CSCL contexts
constraints: the article states it "did not intend to differentiate between task-related and stereotype-based processes as contributors"
target_learners: distance-education university students in CSCL groups
target_learning_goals: online interaction self-efficacy for academic collaboration
key_sources: Natalia Reich-Stiebert, Jan-Bennet Voltmer, Jennifer Raimann, Stefan Stürmer. (2023). The role of first-language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self-efficacy in CSCL. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn 18:513–530. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-023-09411-2

article_title: Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment
citation: Aaron J. Peltoniemi, Joni Lämsä, Sami Lehesvuori, Raija Hämäläinen. (2025). Understanding the role of I-positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09447-6
title: Six discourse functions mapped onto inquiry-based knowledge construction categories
description: The article inductively derived a coding taxonomy: "This resulted in the following six DF: reviewing directions and strategies, sharing and confirming information, brainstorming, empirical evaluation, clarification and elaboration, and submission and reflection." These map onto inquiry-based learning phases — orientation (reviewing directions, sharing information), conceptualization (brainstorming), investigation (empirical evaluation), discussion (clarification and elaboration) and conclusion (submission and reflection) — as a means of segmenting CSCL dialogue by its function for knowledge construction.
requirements: Dialogue chunks whose relevance to a discourse function could not be agreed by all authors are excluded
Coding decisions reviewed by the other three authors through intersubjectivity
constraints: Derived inductively from one thermodynamics task with ten students in one course
examples: Orientation mapped to reviewing directions and strategies plus sharing and confirming information, following Pedaste et al.'s inquiry phases

article_title: Fun beyond gamification: Universal elements to enhance children’s learning
citation: Kokarida, P., Markopoulos, P., & Tisza, G. (2026). Fun beyond gamification: Universal elements to enhance children's learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:30. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09780-9
title: Six non-gamification elements of fun in formal learning for primary students
description: A thematic framework identifying six elements primary school students aged 9–12 perceive as making learning fun beyond gamification: "a sense of agency, challenge, diversity in learning, pleasure, a low-stress climate, and peer interaction." Derived via reflexive thematic analysis combining deductive coding against the FunQ model and inductive coding of focus group and observation data, then contextualized by an expert interview. It extends the FunQ model for formal primary settings.
requirements: Qualitative elicitation of student perspectives, since the elements are defined by students' own reported experiences of fun
constraints: Derived from one public primary school in Heraklion, Greece, in music and art sessions with students aged 9 to 12
target_learning_goals: motivation and engagement in formal learning activities
examples: Themes were corroborated by classroom observations of 48 students and reviewed by an expert in creative and fun learning
key_sources: Kokarida, P., Markopoulos, P., & Tisza, G. (2026). Fun beyond gamification: Universal elements to enhance children's learning. Instructional Science (2026) 54:30. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09780-9

article_title: Facilitating small-group learning: A comparison of student and staff tutors' behavior
citation: Moust, J. C. & Schmidt, H. G. (1995). Facilitating small-group learning: a comparison of student and staff tutors' behavior. Instructional Science 22: 287-301. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251
title: Six-component framework of tutor behavior: subject-matter input versus process facilitation
description: The article organizes tutor behavior into two main components, each with three elements: the subject-matter-input component comprises use of expertise, cognitive congruence and assessment orientation, while the process-facilitation component comprises authority, role congruence and focus on cooperation. The framework was operationalized as a 39-item rating scale whose subscales were validated by generalizability study and confirmatory factor analysis. The authors state that "two main components of the tutor role were distinguished: the way a tutor handles the knowledge students must acquire, and the way a tutor establishes a personal relationship with the members of the group". It underpins the study's hypotheses about how student and staff tutors differ.
requirements: Ratings require judgements from about 11 students per tutorial group for satisfactory generalizability coefficients
constraints: Confirmatory factor analysis indicated the six-subscale model did not entirely fit the data; the six components were retained for theoretical reasons despite mixed empirical support
target_learners: first-year university law students in problem-based tutorial groups
target_learning_goals: self-directed learning of subject-matter through small-group problem discussion
examples: The six subscales were used to compare student and staff tutors in two first-year law courses, with items such as 'The tutor was able to understand problems we had with the materials' for cognitive congruence.
key_sources: Moust, J. C. & Schmidt, H. G. (1995). Facilitating small-group learning: a comparison of student and staff tutors' behavior. Instructional Science 22: 287-301. https://link.springer.com/journal/11251

article_title: Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation
citation: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5
title: Engineer the simulation environment as a safe container before the debriefing to support shared experience and epistemic outcomes
description: The article shows that debriefing outcomes depend on upstream engineering of the learning environment: briefing establishes trust, expectations, and role delegation before the scenario. "The explicit aim of this preparation is to establish the entire simulation, including the debriefing, as a "safe container" where threats to professional identity can be managed in ways conducive to learning". Observational templates also distribute the cognitive labor of observing against the learning goals.
requirements: Pre-simulation briefing covering learning targets, environment familiarisation, and role delegation; artifacts such as NEWS scorecards and ISBAR templates to distribute cognitive labor
constraints: Simulations can be highly stressful for learners, so building trust and managing expectations is crucial
examples: In the analysed case, two students conducted systematic observations using template documents, and the facilitator called closed-loop dialogue the most important tool at their disposal
key_sources: Mads Solberg, Charlott Sellberg. (2025). Debriefing as epistemic engineering: conversational remembering and socially distributed metacognition in healthcare simulation. Instructional Science (2026) 54:7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09760-5

article_title: Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process
citation: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0
title: Eight characteristics of the design of training simulator specifications
description: The article characterises the design of training simulator specifications as a task with 'eight main characteristics', including complex domains requiring extensive task analysis, multiple and contradicting constraints, long time-consuming processes, incomplete and insecure information, and timing problems. The authors state these characteristics 'reﬂect the ill-structured nature of design problems and the iterative nature of the instructional design process'.
requirements: Designers of simulator specifications need extensive knowledge of the task domain, the technical systems to be used, learning, and instructional design.
constraints: The characteristics are attributed to earlier analyses of simulator specification projects (Verstegen, 2003; Verstegen & van der Hulst, 2000) rather than tested in this study.
target_learners: domain experts and instructors tasked with simulator specification
target_learning_goals: understanding the ill-structured, iterative nature of simulator specification design
examples: The study case: designing functional specifications for a simulator to train analysts of thermal images collected with Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAV).
key_sources: Verstegen, D.M.L., Barnard, Y.F. & Pilot, A. (2006). Which events can cause iteration in instructional design? An empirical study of the design process. Instructional Science 34, 481–517. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-005-3346-0

article_title: Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others
citation: Floris M. van Blankenstein, Diana H. J. M. Dolmans, Cees P. M. van der Vleuten, Henk G. Schmidt. (2011). Which cognitive processes support learning during small-group discussion? The role of providing explanations and listening to others. Instructional Science 39, 189–204. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-009-9124-7
title: Simulated video group discussion method for isolating cognitive activities in collaborative learning
description: A laboratory research method in which participants watch a video-recorded group discussion performed by actors, so that all participants share the same prior knowledge and are exposed to the same group process. "The effects of explanation on learning could be studied by stopping the video at various points in time and instructing the participants to respond to the discussion during these 'gaps'." An edited version with the main explainer's contributions removed was used for the explanation condition and the integral version for the listening condition, allowing explaining to be compared with listening while controlling for random group dynamics.
requirements: Actors and scripts recorded in advance; participants instructed to use knowledge from a pre-experiment instruction text
constraints: The authors note it is debatable whether processes induced by watching a simulated discussion are equivalent to those in a real group discussion, which may be more dynamic and include off-topic talk
target_learning_goals: studying the cognitive processes (explaining, listening) that support learning during group discussion
examples: The radar problem discussion was performed by four drama-club students and shown to participants in isolated computer rooms
