article_title: SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation
citation: O'Hare, S., Kajamaa, A., Conn, R., & Gormley, G. (2025). SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09734-7
title: SimLab: a condensed four-session Change Laboratory pattern combining in-situ simulation with facilitated expansive learning discussions
description: SimLab adapts the Change Laboratory formative intervention — typically up to ten-plus sessions — into four sessions designed "for the demands of the general practice workplace". Each session pairs an in-situ simulation or CHAT-guided group interview with facilitation of double stimulation: video footage of the simulation and observations serve as mirror data, while the activity system model, laminated guidelines and prior-session summaries serve as second stimuli. Reflection walls and diaries capture disturbances and aha moments between sessions. The pattern is described as potentially transferable to other clinical settings.
requirements: Requires mirror data (ISS video footage, guidelines, prior-session summaries), a researcher interventionist facilitator, and flexible reflection tools between sessions
constraints: Designed and evaluated in a time-poor general practice setting; sessions ran at lunchtime when the practice was closed
examples: Session 1: anaphylaxis ISS with video playback and CHAT-guided interview; session 3: meningitis ISS testing the newly designed emergency trolley and grab bags
key_sources: O'Hare, S., Kajamaa, A., Conn, R., & Gormley, G. (2025). SimLab: an intervention to promote expansive learning and organisational change in team-based emergency care simulation. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-025-09734-7

article_title: Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review
citation: Jina Kang, Chungsoo Na, Morgan Diederich, Hillary Swanson, Lili Yan. (2026). Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09803-5
title: Situate data practices in broader personal, social, and historical contexts rather than procedural tool engagement alone
description: The review argues, citing Wilkerson and Polman (2020) and Wise (2020), that science instruction should go beyond technical fluency with data tools. It reports that "instructional approaches often emphasize procedural engagement with data tools while neglecting opportunities for students to engage in deeper sense-making", and recommends situating data practices within environmental, social, political, and historical contexts and connecting them to students' personal lives to enhance engagement and agency.
requirements: Learning activities must move beyond procedural engagement with data tools to include critical interpretation of data and its broader implications
constraints: Grounded in the review's synthesis of prior scholarship rather than a tested intervention in this article
examples: The review cites work connecting data practices to students' personal lives as enhancing engagement and agency in data practices
key_sources: Jina Kang, Chungsoo Na, Morgan Diederich, Hillary Swanson, Lili Yan. (2026). Cultivating science data literacy in K-16 science education through data practices: A systematic review. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-026-09803-5

article_title: The keyword effect: A conceptual replication, effects on bias, and an optimization
citation: Waldeyer, J., & Roelle, J. (2021). The keyword effect: A conceptual replication, effects on bias, and an optimization. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 37–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09235-7
title: Situation model account of the keyword effect
description: According to the situation model approach to metacomprehension, "the underlying mechanism via which generating keywords after a delay fosters judgment accuracy is that it requires learners to access their situation model-level representation of the respective texts". Accessing this representation yields diagnostic cues (e.g., generation fluency, keyword quality) that learners incorporate into their judgments of learning. Immediate keyword generation does not serve this function because learners can then rely on surface- and textbase-level representations, which decay faster and are not tapped by comprehension tests; with increasing delay, access to the situation model becomes more likely.
requirements: Keyword generation must occur after a delay so that surface- and textbase-level representations have decayed and learners access their situation model-level representation
constraints: The article notes learners without external standards scarcely exploit keyword quality as a cue, and that which cues learners use to form their JOLs remains widely unclear
target_learners: university students learning from expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate metacomprehension judgments of text comprehension
examples: In the experiment, keyword and keyword+external standard conditions generated five keywords per text after reading all four texts, before judging their comprehension
key_sources: Waldeyer, J., & Roelle, J. (2021). The keyword effect: A conceptual replication, effects on bias, and an optimization. Metacognition and Learning, 16, 37–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-020-09235-7

article_title: To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights
citation: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6
title: Situation-model approach to metacomprehension within the cue-utilization framework
description: The cue-utilization framework holds that learners lack direct access to their cognitive states and must infer comprehension from cues, with accuracy depending on how strongly cues tie to the mental text representation determining test performance. The situation-model approach specifies that judgments are accurate when cues tap the situation-model level of representation, since "The situation model represents a learner's deep understanding and what is typically referred to as text comprehension." Interventions are designed to help learners "generate, attend to, or select situation-model cues."
requirements: Comprehension tests must assess the situation model, requiring inferences or application rather than recall of specific textual information
constraints: Learners tend to default to heuristic or memory-based cues rather than situation-model cues, per self-report studies cited
target_learners: university students learning from expository texts
key_sources: Anja Prinz & Stefanie Golke & Jörg Wittwer. (2020). To What Extent Do Situation-Model-Approach Interventions Improve Relative Metacomprehension Accuracy? Meta-Analytic Insights. Educational Psychology Review (2020) 32:917–949. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09558-6

article_title: Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging
citation: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3
title: Situative synthesis: motivation as primarily a social phenomenon with individual accounts as special cases
description: The article contrasts aggregative reconciliation (exemplified by Bandura's collective efficacy as aggregated individual judgments) with Greeno's situative synthesis. Under the situative synthesis, "motivation is primarily a social phenomenon; individual experiences, theories, and measures are presumed to be secondary 'special cases' of activity that resides in social, cultural, and material contexts beyond individual participants." Organized activity, not individual beliefs, is the primary unit of analysis. The authors adopt this as an interventionist design argument rather than a naturalistic claim about the nature of motivation.
requirements: Study of individuals must include analysis of the meaning systems in which those individuals exist
constraints: The authors frame this as an interventionist argument about educational practice, not a naturalistic claim about the nature of motivation
target_learners: All learners studied through situative accounts of motivation
target_learning_goals: Understanding how goals and values emerge in learning environments and sociocultural contexts
examples: Greeno's 1997 response to Anderson, Reder, and Simon arguing the situative perspective can provide a broader framework that includes individual cognitive functioning but goes beyond it
key_sources: Daniel T. Hickey, Charmian Lam. (2026). Further Redefining Motivation with Situated Cognition, Power, and Belonging. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10219-3

article_title: Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework
citation: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9
title: Situated expectancy-value theory with three value beliefs and three costs
description: The review describes situated expectancy-value theory (Eccles & Wigfield) as a modern framework in which expectancy of success and subjective task values are proximal explanatory factors shaped by goals, self-schemas, and sociocultural background. The article states that "The value component of the situated model is divided into three types of value beliefs and three types of costs that contribute to approaching or avoiding certain tasks." Value beliefs are attainment, intrinsic, and utility value; costs are opportunity, effort, and emotional costs. In the action model, expectation of success links self to outcome, and the values and costs attach to different stages.
requirements: Expectancy and value beliefs are assumed to jointly predict achievement-related choices and performance
constraints: The article notes the earlier Atkinson assumption of an inverse relation between expectancy and value was not tenable
target_learning_goals: explaining and predicting achievement-related choices and behavior
examples: The article locates opportunity costs at the goal, effort costs at the action, and emotional costs at the anticipated consequences within the action model
key_sources: Detlef Urhahne · Lisette Wijnia. (2023). Theories of Motivation in Education: an Integrative Framework. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09767-9

article_title: Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses and Self- and Socially- Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations
citation: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses, Self- and Socially-Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations. Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0
title: Mapping medical simulation phases onto SRL phases: beginning, escalation, and peak
description: The article proposes mapping the three segmented phases of a medical simulation onto the phases of an SRL model. The "beginning" maps onto task definition and goal setting and planning, where trainees establish a goal and collect information on the patient's condition; the "escalation" maps onto enacting study tactics and strategies, where trainees execute a developed course of treatment; and the "peak" maps onto adaptation, where trainees analyze how to adjust their plan to meet new demands and ensure patient survival. The article states these phases "could be interpreted as having a gradual increase in requirements," potentially coinciding with increases in arousal.
requirements: Segmentation of simulation videos into beginning, escalation, and peak phases, guided by simulation scripts and patient deterioration events
constraints: Medical simulations may not have a resolution and can end abruptly after the script is completed
target_learners: medical residents in team-based simulation training
target_learning_goals: team regulation under escalating task demands
key_sources: Moreno, M., Grewal, K., Cutumisu, M., & Harley, J.M. (2025). Employing Machine Learning to Predict Medical Trainees’ Psychophysiological Responses, Self- and Socially-Shared Regulated Learning Strategies While Completing Medical Simulations. Education Psychology Review, 37 (70), 1-29. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10044-0

article_title: What Works for Teaching Word Reading to Adolescents? A Meta-Analytic Investigation
citation: Julia J. Yi, A. Angelique Aitken, Emily Sharp, Adiba Nusrat, Micheal Sandbank. (2026). What Works for Teaching Word Reading to Adolescents? A Meta-Analytic Investigation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10124-9
title: Simple View of Reading: word reading and language comprehension as the two critical elements of reading comprehension
description: The article adopts the Simple View of Reading (SVR) as its organizing framework for defining and selecting word-reading interventions. The SVR is described as "a well-validated reading framework that identified word reading as one of two critical elements of reading comprehension, with the other being language comprehension" (Gough & Tunmer, 1986; Hoover & Gough, 1990). The meta-analysis uses this model to justify narrowing its analytic lens to interventions with a primary focus on word-reading instruction, defining multi-component interventions as those combining word reading with language comprehension components.
requirements: Interventions are classified by whether their word-level reading component comprises at least 50% of instructional time, following the SVR distinction between word reading and language comprehension.
constraints: The article applies the framework to English, characterized as a morphophonemic language with deep orthography; findings are not assumed generalizable to other orthographic systems.
target_learners: Adolescents in middle school and high school (grades 6-12, ages 11-21)
target_learning_goals: Word reading, decoding, and related foundational literacy skills
examples: The inclusion criteria required the word-level reading intervention to comprise at least 50% of instructional time, and non-language-based interventions (e.g., color overlays, medical treatments) were excluded.
key_sources: Julia J. Yi, A. Angelique Aitken, Emily Sharp, Adiba Nusrat, Micheal Sandbank. (2026). What Works for Teaching Word Reading to Adolescents? A Meta-Analytic Investigation. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10124-9

article_title: How Does Initial Teacher Education Research Frame the Challenge of Preparing Future Teachers for Student Diversity in Schools? A Systematic Review of Literature
citation: Rowan, L., Bourke, T., L'Estrange, L., Lunn, J., Ryan, M., Walker, S., & Churchward, P. (2021). How does Initial Teacher Education Research frame the challenge of preparing future teachers for student diversity in schools?: A systematic review of literature. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 112-158. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979171
title: Six-code thematic framework for knowledge claims in ITE-diversity research: content, teaching-to-diversity, program approaches, ITE-student challenges, teacher-educator challenges, and transformative commitment
description: The review developed an inductive, iterative coding framework to classify knowledge claims about preparing teachers for diverse learners. It began with two broad issues — "Issues of ITE diversity content" and "Issues of ITE delivery relevant to diversity" — and expanded these into six codes, including arguments about knowledge needed, specific program approaches such as specialist courses and partnerships, challenges relating to ITE students' beliefs, challenges relating to teacher educators' context, beliefs and skills, and a final code for "Papers marked by an overt commitment to social justice and social transformation through education". The framework was tested for inter-coder agreement and applied to all 209 papers.
requirements: Coding required iterative reading and negotiation of subcodes among three chief investigators, with conceptual saturation reached after coding 20 + 20 papers
constraints: The authors acknowledge the analysis is shaped by their own ideological positions as researchers committed to educational and social justice, and that some concepts and positions are more difficult to illustrate than others
target_learning_goals: understanding how teacher education research frames preparation for student diversity
examples: Three lead authors coded all 209 abstracts in Phase 1; in Phase 2, 19 of 20 test papers were coded identically by all three lead authors, and a random-sample check of Codes 1, 2 and 6 revealed 100% agreement
key_sources: Rowan, L., Bourke, T., L'Estrange, L., Lunn, J., Ryan, M., Walker, S., & Churchward, P. (2021). How does Initial Teacher Education Research frame the challenge of preparing future teachers for student diversity in schools?: A systematic review of literature. Review of Educational Research, 91(1), 112-158. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320979171

article_title: Inclusive Strategies for Children With Developmental Disabilities in Mainstream Classrooms in African Countries: A Systematic Review of Stakeholder Experiences, Attitudes, and Perspectives
citation: Genovesi Elisa, Gaches Akhina, McKenzie Judith, Hanlon Charlotte, Hoekstra Rosa A. (2024). Inclusive Strategies for Children With Developmental Disabilities in Mainstream Classrooms in African Countries: A Systematic Review of Stakeholder Experiences, Attitudes, and Perspectives. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241288247
title: Six interrelated themes organize stakeholder perspectives on inclusive strategies for children with DD in African mainstream classrooms
description: The review's reflexive thematic analysis of extracts from 28 qualitative African studies developed a thematic map of six interdependent themes with subthemes: meeting learners' needs, targeted support and feedback, whole-class approach, inclusive environment, engaging teaching, and fit with the evidence base. The authors state that "Our interpretation of the data lead to the development of six interdependent themes, each with subthemes, as shown in the thematic map in Figure 1." Subthemes were closely interrelated across themes.
requirements: Studies must be qualitative reports of stakeholder experiences of inclusive education for children with DD in mainstream African classrooms
constraints: Synthesis focused on approaches, drivers, and aims of strategies rather than technical details such as specific tasks, needs assessment or timings
Not all studies are equally represented in the synthesis; five contributed only one or two short relevant extracts
target_learners: children with developmental disabilities in mainstream primary and secondary schools in non-Arab African countries
target_learning_goals: inclusive education for learners with developmental disabilities
examples: The thematic map in Figure 1 exemplifies subthemes with extracts and participant quotes from 13 synthesized papers

Inclusive Strategies for Children With Developmental Disabilities in Mainstream Classrooms in African Countries: A Systematic Review of Stakeholder Experiences, Attitudes, and Perspectives. article_title: A Systematic Review of International Higher Education Scholarships for Students From the Global South
citation: Anne C. Campbell and Emelye Neff. (2020). A Systematic Review of International Higher Education Scholarships for Students From the Global South. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320947783
title: Six-rationale taxonomy of international higher education scholarship programs for Global South students
description: The review proposes a taxonomy of six primary and distinguishable rationales connecting scholarship programs to intended outcomes: skills and knowledge acquisition for human capital development; diplomatic aims, relations with former colonies, or solidarity; social change or social justice; international or sustainable development; internationalization of universities; and providing access to higher education. The authors state that "The thematic analysis of international scholarship literature discerned six primary and distinguishable rationales for international scholarships for students from the Global South." Rationales featured prominently in five or more sources were treated as major, and the review also applies a micro (individual), meso (institutional), macro (societal) level framework to the rationales.
requirements: A rationale is defined as the concept that logically connects a program to its intended outcome; sources lacking an explicit goal had the rationale inferred from intended outcomes or program description
constraints: Only English-language peer-reviewed sources published 2010-2019 were included; the ordering of rationales reflects the number of articles stating them as primary, not the actual number of programs
target_learners: students from Global South (World Bank low- and middle-income) countries pursuing higher education abroad
target_learning_goals: clarifying program goals and designs of international scholarship programs
examples: The review coded each of 105 sources with one of six rationale categories in an inductive thematic analysis, then summarized each rationale subgroup separately
key_sources: Anne C. Campbell and Emelye Neff. (2020). A Systematic Review of International Higher Education Scholarships for Students From the Global South. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/0034654320947783

article_title: A Best-Evidence Synthesis and Meta-analysis on Effective Reading Programs in Spanish
citation: José L. Arco-Tirado, Francisco D. Fernández-Martín, Mirian Hervás-Torres, Gracia Jiménez-Fernández, Nuria Calet, Sylvia Defior, Amanda J. Neitzel, Robert E. Slavin. (2024). A Best-Evidence Synthesis and Meta-analysis on Effective Reading Programs in Spanish. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241297668
title: Six-component conceptual framework for Spanish reading instruction: the NRP five pillars plus concepts about print
description: The review adopts a conceptual framework with "six targeted components": the five pillars of the NRP (2000) framework — phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and reading comprehension — plus a sixth component, concepts about print, meaning that children understand that print carries meaning and books "work" in a particular way. This framework structures the review's inclusion criteria, outcome coding, and decision to conflate all six components into an overarching reading-outcomes construct for the meta-analysis.
requirements: Included studies must target one or more of the six components as quantitative reading outcomes in Spanish for grades K–6.
constraints: The article notes its search found no studies of Spanish reading including Active View of Reading factors (motivation, background knowledge, self-regulation) as predictors.
target_learners: K–6 students in Spanish-speaking countries learning to read in Spanish as their first language

article_title: Research Avenues Supporting Embodied Cognition in Learning and Instruction
citation: Juan C. Castro-Alonso, Paul Ayres, Shirong Zhang, Björn B. de Koning, Fred Paas. (2024). Research Avenues Supporting Embodied Cognition in Learning and Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09847-4
title: Six research avenues framework for embodied cognition effects on learning and instruction
description: The review organizes embodied learning research into six interconnected avenues: physical activity, generative learning, and offloaded cognition explain benefits of making human movements; specialized processor and signaling explain benefits of observing movements; and social cognition applies to both. As the review states, "The first three research avenues (physical activity, generative learning, and offloaded cognition) apply when students make human movements." Each avenue is paired with influencing features (e.g., movement relevance, working memory load, redundancy, meaningfulness) that modulate the size of embodied learning effects.
requirements: Movements must be made or observed in instructional settings, primarily hand gestures and object manipulation
constraints: The avenues are complementary and not mutually exclusive; the review's primary focus is on hand movements rather than whole-body movements
target_learners: students across domains including math, science, statistics, and astronomy
target_learning_goals: learning enhanced by making or observing gestures and object manipulations
examples: Table 1 lists each avenue with its explanation, example, influencing feature, and a review article, e.g., offloaded cognition illustrated by using manipulative objects for complex calculations
key_sources: Juan C. Castro-Alonso, Paul Ayres, Shirong Zhang, Björn B. de Koning, Fred Paas. (2024). Research Avenues Supporting Embodied Cognition in Learning and Instruction. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09847-4

article_title: Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective
citation: Televantou, I., Marsh, H. W., Xu, K. M., Guo, J., & Dicke, T. (2023). Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09816-3
title: SIMS80 cross-national longitudinal database
description: The Second International Mathematics Study (SIMS80), administered by the IEA in the 1980s, is a cross-national database of 13-year-old students from the USA, Canada (Ontario), and New Zealand (13,656 students, 340 schools). Uniquely among IEA and PISA collections, "SIMS80 is based on a pre- and post-measurement design, allowing for controls for the effects of prior achievement on subsequent achievement." The study used forty common mathematics test items across four rotated forms, four-item mathematics self-concept measures, and rich student- and class-level background variables.
requirements: Pre- and post-measurement design enabling prior-achievement controls
constraints: Data are dated (1980s), which the authors state limits their use for informing current educational policy
target_learning_goals: mathematics achievement and mathematics self-concept outcomes
examples: Re-analysis replicating Zimmer and Toma (2000) with a subset of SIMS80 data; data publicly available in SPSS format without restrictions

Peer Spillover and Big-Fish-Little-Pond Effects with SIMS80: Revisiting a Historical Database Through the Lens of a Modern Methodological Perspective. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09816-3

article_title: Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories?
citation: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5
title: Six options for integrating propositions across theories (Table 2 heuristic model)
description: The article presents a heuristic model of six ways to integrate causal or predictive propositions: identical effects, reciprocal effects, chains of effects, joint causes, joint outcomes, and new effects. Options such as joint causes and joint outcomes reduce the number of propositions by merging constructs, while the new-effects option increases propositions but "allows new insights and creates a broader theory that contains the original theories as subtheories." Options 4 and 5 require functional homogeneity of the merged constructs.
requirements: Constructs subsumed under a merged umbrella construct must show functional homogeneity — the same effects on the outcome — or explanatory power is lost
constraints: Options 4 and 5 lose explanatory power if the functional homogeneity principle is violated; option 6 increases rather than decreases the number of propositions
examples: Reciprocal-effects models integrated self-enhancement and skill-development models of self-concept and achievement; joint-cause merging of emotions into positive and negative affect works for hedonic well-being but not task performance
key_sources: Reinhard Pekrun. (2024). Overcoming Fragmentation in Motivation Science: Why, When, and How Should We Integrate Theories? Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09846-5

article_title: The Development, Testing, and Refinement of Eccles, Wigfield, and Colleagues’ Situated Expectancy-Value Model of Achievement Performance and Choice
citation: Jacquelynne S. Eccles · Allan Wigfield. (2024). The Development, Testing, and Refinement of Eccles, Wigfield, and Colleagues' Situated Expectancy-Value Model of Achievement Performance and Choice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09888-9
title: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT) of achievement performance and choice
description: SEVT holds that achievement-related performance and choice are most directly influenced by individuals' "expectations for success at and the subjective task value (STV) of the action chosen compared to" available alternatives. Subjective task value comprises four components: intrinsic value, utility value, attainment value, and perceived cost. Expectancies and values are themselves shaped by task-specific beliefs, goals, self-schemata, and affective memories, which develop through socializers' beliefs and behaviors, prior achievement experiences, and the cultural milieu. The 2020 renaming to situated expectancy-value theory emphasizes that beliefs, values, and decisions are situated and specific rather than global, and that cultural influences are infused throughout the model rather than only exogenous.
requirements: Validated measures of the central constructs; the authors note attaining consensus on measurement is a key future need
constraints: The article states trying to test all proposed links in one study would not be possible; support is built gradually, part by part
The figure depiction does not fully capture the situative and culturally infused character the authors intend; a new depiction is in preparation
target_learning_goals: achievement-related choices such as course enrollment and career choice
examples: The 1976 precursor model had four boxes including cultural norms and expectations, current situational factors, socialization in home and schools, and personal attitudes and values
The model was developed to explain why girls were less likely to participate in STEM courses and careers
key_sources: Jacquelynne S. Eccles · Allan Wigfield. (2024). The Development, Testing, and Refinement of Eccles, Wigfield, and Colleagues' Situated Expectancy-Value Model of Achievement Performance and Choice. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09888-9

article_title: Integrating Human Movement in Learning: Advancements in Language Instruction, Multimedia, and Theory
citation: de Koning, B., Zhang, S., & Sepp, S. (2025). Integrating Human Movement in Learning: Advancements in Language Instruction, Multimedia, and Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10027-1
title: Six interrelated research avenues explaining why embodied cognition can enhance learning and instruction
description: The review describes Castro-Alonso et al.'s (2024) framework of "six interrelated research avenues that explain why embodied cognition can enhance learning and instruction." Three avenues concern mechanisms underlying making movements: physical activity, generative learning, and offloaded cognition. Two avenues pertain to observing movements: the specialized processor and signaling. A final avenue, social cognition, applies to both making and observing movements. For each avenue the authors discuss supporting evidence, key influencing factors, and instructional implications.
requirements: For each avenue, supporting evidence, key influencing factors, and instructional implications are discussed.
constraints: The review notes the authors emphasize the need for future research to consider instructional, cognitive, and cultural aspects to deepen understanding of embodiment in learning.
target_learners: learners in physical and digital learning environments
target_learning_goals: learning supported by making or observing movements
examples: Generative activities such as sketching, drawing, gesturing, and acting out concepts and processes are discussed as benefiting learners.
key_sources: de Koning, B., Zhang, S., & Sepp, S. (2025). Integrating Human Movement in Learning: Advancements in Language Instruction, Multimedia, and Theory. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10027-1

article_title: Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology
citation: Matthew T. McCrudden · Macy Bowman · Gala Sofia Campos Oaxaca. (2025). Reporting of Methodological Rigor in Empirical Mixed Methods Research in Educational Psychology. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10090-8
title: Six-element coding scheme for evaluating reporting of methodological rigor in mixed methods articles (adapted from Harrison et al., 2020)
description: A scoring rubric the authors adapted from Harrison et al. (2020) to evaluate reporting quality across six elements: aims and purposes, mixed methods study design, data collection, data analysis, integration, and elements of writing, each scored high/medium/low (Table 1). Two reviewers independently coded all 57 articles; pre-reconciliation agreement was 94.7% (324/342 ratings) with Cohen's kappa of 0.925 overall, and the first author adjudicated 18 adjacent score differences.
requirements: Two independent trained raters coding all articles, with reconciliation of differences by adjudication
constraints: Eligibility was limited to articles with primary quantitative AND primary qualitative data collection and analysis; data-transformation studies were excluded
target_learning_goals: evaluating and improving reporting of methodological rigor in mixed methods research
examples: The rubric's design element distinguished clearly labeled designs from identifiable-but-unlabeled and difficult-to-identify designs

article_title: A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables
citation: Julian F. Lohmann, Nils Machts, Jens Möller, Steffen Zitzmann. (2025). A More Comprehensive, More Reliable Multilevel Approach for Assessing and Modeling Teacher Judgment Accuracy Using Latent Variables. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10029-z
title: Simulated classroom environment for assessing pre-service chemistry teachers' judgment accuracy
description: The article's first empirical application used a simulated classroom environment in which pre-service chemistry teachers interacted with 12 virtual eighth-graders by selecting and posing questions, with three false answers and one correct answer per question covering four chemistry competence domains. Participants were 'required to assess the correctness of the given responses themselves' and after a 30-minute virtual lesson rated each student's ability on a 0–100 scale. Student ability levels were randomly sampled per student and teacher, so the true benchmarks varied across participants. The sample consisted of N = 53 pre-service chemistry teachers.
requirements: Benchmark ability levels defined by the simulation's student-specific probabilities of correct answers
Participants rating students on a 0–100 scale after the virtual lesson
constraints: The article text available here ends before the application's results are reported, so no outcome findings from this study are recorded
target_learners: pre-service chemistry teachers (teacher students) preparing to teach at upper track secondary schools
target_learning_goals: judgment accuracy (rank, level, differentiation) regarding student ability in chemistry
examples: Moderators tested in this application were education status (Bachelor = 0, Master = 1) and the number of questions asked during the virtual class

article_title: Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
citation: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9
title: Six-moderator framework for reading intervention efficacy in Chinese children
description: The article organizes its meta-analysis around six potentially important moderators of reading intervention efficacy for Chinese children: "intervention outcome, intervention method, intervention timing, participant type, intervention form, and intervention implementer". Interventions were classified into five types based on core linguistic components for reading acquisition (phonological, morphological, orthographic, fluency, and working memory), grounded in the Interactive Dynamic Literacy Model. Meta-regression analyses tested each moderator's influence on effect sizes.
requirements: Studies must use a pretest–posttest control-group randomized controlled design and report at least one word-level literacy indicator
constraints: Limited to school-aged native Chinese speakers from preschool to sixth grade; only RCTs were included
target_learners: typically developing Chinese children in preschool through grade 6
examples: The meta-analysis coded 49 effect sizes from 28 studies on these six moderators with interrater Cohen's kappas ranging from 0.68 to 1
key_sources: Yijun Ruan, Urs Maurer, Catherine McBride. (2024). Effectiveness of Reading Interventions on Literacy Skills for Chinese Children with and Without Dyslexia: a Meta-analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09915-9

article_title: Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach
citation: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5
title: Simple view of reading: reading comprehension as the product of decoding and language comprehension, implying four reader quadrants
description: The article describes the simple view of reading (SVR; Hoover & Gough, 1990) as a prominent theory in which "reading comprehension can be modeled as the product of language comprehension (LC) and decoding (D) abilities". Decoding is the ability to recognize printed words accurately and quickly; language comprehension is the ability to extract and construct literal and inferred meaning from spoken discourse. "The multiplicative nature of the model implies a difficulty in compensating for deficits in one of the two abilities with improved performance in the other", yielding four quadrants: good readers, poor readers, poor decoders, and poor comprehenders.
requirements: Measures of both decoding and language comprehension (here syntactic comprehension and vocabulary as two indicators) are needed to classify readers into the four quadrants
constraints: The article acknowledges the SVR does not fully describe all possible aspects of reading performance, citing Castles et al. (2018)
examples: The study used the SVR to label the four latent profiles and to predict that poor comprehenders benefit from comprehension-targeted instruction
key_sources: Tetzlaff, L., Edelsbrunner, P., Schmitterer, A., Hartmann, U., & Brod, G. (2023). Modeling Interactions Between Multivariate Learner Characteristics and Interventions: a Person-Centered Approach. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09830-5

article_title: The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review
citation: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8
title: Distinction between simultaneous and sequential visuospatial working memory
description: The review adopts a working-memory framework in which the visuospatial sketchpad is subdivided into simultaneous and sequential VSWM components, citing evidence of a double dissociation. Simultaneous VSWM tasks present all information at once and require recall of stimulus positions, as in the visual patterns task, while sequential tasks present stimuli in a sequence, as in the Corsi block task. The review treats this distinction as an organizing axis for assessing the predictive power of VSWM for mathematics.
requirements: Tasks must separately tap each component, since the review states there is evidence for the dissociation of these tasks supporting their independent investigation
constraints: The review notes no included studies investigated the influence of sequential VSWM on Mathematical Reasoning, highlighting a gap in the research
target_learners: school-aged children aged 0–16 in mainstream schools
target_learning_goals: mathematics performance (numerical operations and mathematical reasoning)
examples: Included studies used simultaneous tasks such as the visual patterns task and dot matrix, and sequential tasks such as the Corsi block task
key_sources: Katie Allen & Steve Higgins & John Adams. (2019). The Relationship between Visuospatial Working Memory and Mathematical Performance in School-Aged Children: a Systematic Review. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-019-09470-8

article_title: Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention
citation: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005
title: Present complementary problem-solving strategies simultaneously in speech and gesture rather than sequentially
description: When teaching a concept paired with a complementary procedure, deliver the conceptual strategy in speech while simultaneously performing the procedural strategy in gesture, rather than presenting the two messages one after the other. The article concludes that "for an instructor's gesture to facilitate deep learning, generalization, and retention over time, it must be presented simultaneously with speech." In the supporting experiment, only simultaneous presentation produced delayed retention and generalization advantages; sequential cross-modal presentation was no better than speech alone.
requirements: The gesture must convey a strategy complementary to, not redundant with, the spoken strategy
Both strategies must be presented within a single presentation of the problem, without a break
constraints: Sequential speech-then-gesture presentation may cause children to discount the gestured information as meaningless movement
The article did not test gesture-first sequencing, which prior work it cites suggests might sometimes help learners with high prior knowledge
target_learners: learners naive to the taught material
target_learning_goals: retention of taught procedures over days and weeks
integration of conceptual and procedural strategies
examples: In the experiment, children in the simultaneous condition heard the Equalizer explanation while watching Add-Subtract hand movements on the same equation, and showed the highest delayed performance (e.g., .64 mean proportion correct on generalization problems at four weeks)
key_sources: Congdon Eliza L., Novack Miriam A., Brooks Neon, Hemani-Lopez Naureen, O'Keefe Lucy, Goldin-Meadow Susan. (2017). Better together: Simultaneous presentation of speech and gesture in math instruction supports generalization and retention. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2017.03.005

article_title: Improving (meta)comprehension: Feedback and self-assessment
citation: Hepner, S. L., Oudman, S., Carlson, T. E., van de Pol, J., & van Gog, T. (2024). Improving (meta)comprehension: Feedback and self-assessment. Learning and Instruction, 92, 101922. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2024.101922
title: Situation-Model Approach to Metacomprehension (cue-utilization account)
description: The article frames monitoring accuracy via the Situation-Model Approach to Metacomprehension, built on Koriat's cue-utilization framework: learners lack direct insight into comprehension and rely on cues, some diagnostic (e.g., summarizing gist) and some not (e.g., ease of reading, interest, font size). Generative activities like delayed diagramming give access to diagnostic cues about the situation model, because the diagram is completed from the mental model in long-term memory rather than degraded surface features. The study tests whether model-answer feedback adds further diagnostic cues.
requirements: Learners must engage in a generative activity (e.g., diagramming) that exposes the quality of their situation model, ideally at a delay so judgments rest on the mental model rather than surface features
constraints: Effects of diagramming on monitoring accuracy are described as only moderate (g = 0.72 in prior meta-analytic work cited by the article), leaving room for further improvement
target_learners: secondary school students reading expository texts
target_learning_goals: accurate comprehension monitoring and self-regulated learning from text
examples: Participants read four texts and completed delayed causal diagrams of the texts' underlying causal structure before making judgments of learning

article_title: Category change in the absence of cognitive conflict.
citation: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22
title: Test cognitive-conflict necessity in simple, successful learning scenarios with manipulation checks and independent tracking of unlearning and re-learning
description: The article argues that weak effects of cognitive conflict interventions in complex classroom scenarios are uninterpretable because learning has multiple determinants. It recommends that "One response to this problem is to study simple situations in which there are fewer factors that determine the outcome, and those factors can be identified, measured, or controlled." It further recommends studying scenarios where learning is already successful, implementing an accurate manipulation check that learners experienced conflict, and using assessments that track reliance on the prior and new conceptions independently of each other.
requirements: Learning scenarios simple enough that determinants of outcome can be identified, measured, or controlled
A manipulation check verifying learners actually experienced the intended conflict
Assessment forms that track unlearning of the prior conception and learning of the new conception independently
constraints: In complex, realistic subject matters where outcomes have many determinants, a negative outcome of a conflict intervention is not interpretable; the recommendation is limited to simple scenarios with successful baseline learning
target_learners: Researchers designing studies of conceptual change; instructors of science topics
target_learning_goals: Evaluating whether cognitive conflict is a necessary prerequisite for non-monotonic conceptual change
examples: The authors applied this approach themselves: the re-categorization paradigm offers experimental control over prior knowledge, simple subject matter, controlled feedback content, and posttests probing reliance on initial versus target categories
key_sources: Ramsburg, J. T., & Ohlsson, S. (2015). Category Change in the Absence of Cognitive Conflict. https://www.google.com/search?q=%22Category+Change+in+the+Absence+of+Cognitive+Conflict%22

Challenge and Threat Appraisal of Tests in High School: Integrating Educational Psychology and Biopsychology Improves Understanding of How Students Take Tests. title: Automated Matlab signal pipeline synchronizing EDA, EEG, and survey data
description: The signal pipeline is an autonomous Matlab program into which raw signals from the Empatica E4, the CytonRK headsets, and Qualtrics survey data are fed, producing a synchronized and processed dataset without subjective human intervention. Each recording has an independent layered database so raw data or any processing step can be revisited, and a graphical interface allows visual inspection of each stage, including automated peak-alpha frequency identification.
requirements: Individual per-participant data files were needed because some steps, such as Fourier transforms into time slices, took nearly 10 hours to process
constraints: Ledalab's conservative curve-matching approach may produce false negatives, so the research measured event amplitude rather than frequency
target_learning_goals: processing multimodal physiological and survey data for observational classroom research
examples: Raw EDA data were batch-processed outsourced to Ledalab for deconvolution and flowed back into the pipeline

article_title: A developmental extension to the multidimensional structure of interests.
citation: Akkerman, D. M., Vulperhorst, J. P., & Akkerman, S. F. (2020). A developmental extension to the multidimensional structure of interests. Journal of Educational Psychology, 112(1), 183-203. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000361
title: Six-dimensional framework underlying the development of interests
description: The article organizes interest development around six dimensions identified in prior literature: "time, value, agency, frequency, intensity, and mastery". These dimensions serve as the measurement structure for characterizing students' multiple interests and how their profiles of scores change across contexts and over time. The framework is used empirically to test developmental models of interest rather than proposed as a new taxonomy.
requirements: Empirical measurement of interests on all six dimensions, here via experience sampling, to support developmental models of interest
constraints: The dimensions are identified in prior literature, not derived anew in this article
target_learning_goals: Understanding the structure and development of individual interests as a basis for learning
examples: The six dimensions structured latent profile analyses of 7,226 interest reports from 204 students at two time points

article_title: The cost of multiple representations: Learning number symbols with abstract and concrete representations.
citation: Amy Bennett, Matthew Inglis and Camilla Gilmore. (2018). The Cost of Multiple Representations: Learning Number Symbols with Abstract and Concrete Representations.
title: Design number books and early number materials with simple, consistent representations of quantity
description: Because learning from multiple concrete representations was less effective than learning from a single consistent representation, the authors recommend that materials introducing number words and symbols use simple representations. The implications statement concludes that "number books designed to introduce children to the magnitude meanings of number words and symbols should consider using simple representations", whether a single concrete item set or abstract dot arrays. This challenges the dominant number-book convention of varying counted items page by page.
requirements: Materials should pair each number word or symbol with a consistent set of representations so learners can map magnitude without extraneous variation
constraints: Evidence comes from artificial symbol learning with children aged roughly 6-10 in short training sessions; the authors note their setting differs from how children typically first encounter Arabic numerals
target_learners: preschool and early primary school children learning number words and symbols
target_learning_goals: attaching magnitude meanings to number words and symbols
examples: Across three experiments, children trained with dot arrays or one repeated picture set outperformed children trained with twenty different familiar pictures varying from trial to trial
key_sources: Amy Bennett, Matthew Inglis and Camilla Gilmore. (2018). The Cost of Multiple Representations: Learning Number Symbols with Abstract and Concrete Representations. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000318

citation: SIGNALING IN MULTIMEDIA LEARNING: THE INFLUENCE OF PRIOR KNOWLEDGE. (2007). https://eric.ed.gov/

description: The article's supplemental material describes a larger data set collected in a multidisciplinary project, stating that "the data is part of a larger data set with overall up to 400 participants from 15 classes". The table lists every variable collected, spanning standardized reading comprehension, domain-specific self-concept and interest, prior knowledge, post-learning knowledge, subjective ratings, usability, log file data and a delayed test. Only a subset of variables are analyzed in the attached manuscript.

article_title: Sex differences in mathematics anxiety and attitudes: Concurrent and longitudinal relations to mathematical competence.
citation: Geary, D. C., Hoard, M. K., Nugent, L., Chu, F., Scofield, J. E., & Hibbard, D. F. (2019). Sex Differences in Mathematics Anxiety and Attitudes: Concurrent and Longitudinal Relations to Mathematical Competence. Journal of Educational Psychology, 111(8), 1447-1461. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000355
title: Mathematics efficacy and utility beliefs form a single mathematics-attitudes construct in this sample
description: Unlike studies separating utility (value) beliefs from self-efficacy, the article's principal components, parallel, and MAP analyses indicated utility and efficacy items defined a single factor for mathematics, so an overall mathematics attitudes score (7 items, α = .84) was used. The authors suggest the collapse may reflect uniformly high utility ratings across students, reducing variation and discriminating power.
requirements: Attitude items assessing both self-evaluated efficacy and long-term utility beliefs, e.g., "How much do you like doing math?" on a 1-to-7 scale, with factor-structure checks before compositing.
constraints: The single-factor result may be sample- or era-specific; the article notes it might reflect a secular increase in students' beliefs about the importance of mathematics.
examples: The Michigan Study of Adolescent and Adult Transitions attitudes measure was analyzed with PCA, parallel, and MAP procedures before compositing.

article_title: Within-year stability and changes in adolescents’ cross-domain motivational profiles: Predictions on academic achievement and educational choices.
citation: Polso, K.-M., Tuominen, H., Ihantola, P., & Niemivirta, M. (2025). Within-year stability and changes in adolescents' cross-domain motivational profiles: Predictions on academic achievement and educational choices. Journal of Educational Psychology, 117(6), 960-979. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000955
title: Situated expectancy-value theory: socialization and interpretation of prior experiences shape goals, self-concepts, expectancies, and subjective task values that drive achievement and choices
description: Situated expectancy-value theory (SEVT), the renamed framework of Eccles' expectancy-value theory, explains educational outcomes such as achievement and program choice through domain-specific motivational beliefs. The article states that "These beliefs are tightly intertwined with identity formation and impact success expectancies as well as the subjective task value in a given activity or, for example, school subject." Task value comprises intrinsic, attainment, and utility facets plus perceived cost, and the study uses these constructs to profile ninth-graders' math and language arts motivation. The framework underpins the study's four research questions on profiles, stability, predictors, and outcomes.
requirements: Motivational beliefs are measured as domain-specific (subject-specific) expectancies, values, and costs rather than global traits
constraints: The framework emphasizes the context-specific and dynamic nature of motivational processes, so findings are situated in the specific educational transition context studied
target_learners: adolescents in the final year of lower secondary education
target_learning_goals: educational pathway choices and academic achievement
examples: The study operationalized SEVT constructs as self-concept, intrinsic value, attainment value, utility value, and opportunity cost for math and language arts, measured twice across the ninth-grade year.
key_sources: Polso, K.-M., Tuominen, H., Ihantola, P., & Niemivirta, M. (2025). Within-year stability and changes in adolescents' cross-domain motivational profiles: Predictions on academic achievement and educational choices. article_title: The reading comprehension and vocabulary knowledge of children with poor reading comprehension despite adequate decoding: Evidence from a regression-based matching approach.
citation: Spencer, M., Wagner, R. K., & Petscher, Y. (2019). The Reading Comprehension and Vocabulary Knowledge of Children with Poor Reading Comprehension despite Adequate Decoding: Evidence from a Regression-Based Matching Approach. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000274
title: Simple View of Reading classification system and its additive versus multiplicative variants
description: The Simple View of Reading holds that reading comprehension is the product of decoding and linguistic comprehension, and it underwrites a four-group classification: adequate reader, dyslexia, SCD, and mixed deficit/garden-variety poor reader. The article tests whether the SCD cell's predicted oral-language weakness is sufficient to explain its comprehension difficulty, contrasting additive (main-effects) and multiplicative (interactive) variants. It concludes the results "do not support an additive version the Simple View of Reading" and that vocabulary and decoding are "necessary but not sufficient components of reading comprehension."
requirements: Decoding and linguistic comprehension must each be measured to classify readers into the four groups
constraints: The article states an interactive version still lacks "a theoretical explanation with empirical support of any interactive effect that is observed"
examples: The study classified second graders as SCD or typical readers using SAT-10 reading comprehension and DIBELS-6 NWF decoding percentile cutoffs and tested the additive versus multiplicative models via the magnitude of vocabulary versus comprehension weaknesses.

description: This element is the article's first empirical application of the SINM to "the PISA 2015 data of 2 countries, that is, the Netherlands and Colombia". It served to illuminate the structure of interactions among interest indicators in networks of different groups of adolescents and to identify structurally important variables, with the article noting a first empirical test of the model.

constraints: Findings concern these two countries; the article also reports sourcecode and supplemental materials are available

article_title: Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching
citation: Gabriel, F., Kennedy, J.P., Marrone, R. & Leonard, S. (2025). Pragmatic AI in education and its role in mathematics learning and teaching. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00315-4
title: Six objects of transformation mapping AI implementation to learning-design goals
description: Working from their conceptual model, the authors "propose six general areas where AI may be able to provide mechanisms or approaches that support the learning process". Table 1 maps each object of transformation to an AI implementation, design goals, and positive and negative worked examples: task-demand and cognitive-quality matching, agency and cooperation, improved value induction, feedback strategies that preserve sense of control, retraining attributions for failure and success, and fostering self-regulation of emotions.
requirements: Semi-supervised arrangements allowing classroom teachers to provide input and fine-tune algorithms in a straightforward way where resource producers build the systems
constraints: Each area's worked examples include failure modes, such as AI platforms mis-assessing learning patterns and delivering inappropriately matched tasks
target_learning_goals: Reduced maths anxiety and positive emotional responses
examples: Table 1 pairs each object of transformation with AI implementations, design goals, and plus and minus example scenarios such as an emotion-aware system failing to detect a student's frustration

article_title: EEG analysis of brain dynamics in a simulated multi-task and multi-stage learning environment
citation: Hui Xie, Chunli Jia, Yanxia Luo, Jiangshan He, Zexiao Dong, Dan Liang, Ziqi Ren, Mingzhe Jiang, Xinbo Gao & Xueli Chen. (2025). EEG analysis of brain dynamics in a simulated multi-task and multi-stage learning environment. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00376-5
title: Semester-long simulated-MOOC EEG dataset from an 11-lesson biology course
description: This dataset comprises weekly 14-channel EEG recordings (Emotiv EPOC+ headsets, 128 Hz sampling) from undergraduates completing an 11-week elective biology course simulating a MOOC, with lecture, virtual lab, and quiz tasks each session and three course stages. As the authors state, "the data were analyzed for stage classification using machine learning models" on 7,544 samples of 84 relative-PSD features. The dataset supports stage-wise EEG analyses and the article's machine-learning experiments.
requirements: Data must pass the article's quality screening; participants with more than two stages containing over 40% poor-quality segments were excluded
Preprocessing with EEGLAB filtering, ICA artifact removal, and segment rejection rules
constraints: Only six participants' high-quality data were ultimately retained for analysis
Some segments were excluded due to poor electrode contact and external noise interference
target_learners: undergraduate students in an engineering elective course
target_learning_goals: capturing neural activity during information acquisition, virtual experimentation, and knowledge application tasks
examples: Stage sample sizes printed in the article are 2717 (Stage 1), 2453 (Stage 2), and 2374 (Stage 3), totaling 7,544 samples

article_title: Unveiling the neural mechanisms of supernatural fiction comprehension using fNIRS
citation: Xiaodong Xu, Cheng Jia, Kang Chen & Lijuan Chen. (2025). Unveiling the neural mechanisms of supernatural fiction comprehension using fNIRS. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00327-0
title: The simulation account of fiction comprehension
description: The simulation account holds that readers comprehend actions and events that cannot occur in reality by mentally simulating them with perceptual, motor and mentalizing resources. As the article puts it, "The simulation theory positsthat individuals engage their sensorimotor system and associated brain networks (e.g., IFG) to mentally simulate events that they cannot physically enact". The study tests this account against a cognitive-difficulty alternative and interprets its sensorimotor activation, connectivity and mediation findings as direct evidence for simulation during supernatural reading.
requirements: Readers must engage their sensorimotor system and associated networks such as the IFG to mentally simulate events they cannot physically enact.
constraints: The article notes it did not explicitly measure the extent to which participants mentally simulated characters' actions, and cannot entirely rule out a world-knowledge-inconsistency explanation.
target_learning_goals: Comprehension and interpretation of fictional and supernatural narratives
examples: The study contrasted supernatural Harry Potter excerpts (SF), the same scenarios with realistic names (SR), and realistic versions (RR), using a within-item design drawn from the HP Collection.
key_sources: Xiaodong Xu, Cheng Jia, Kang Chen & Lijuan Chen. (2025). Unveiling the neural mechanisms of supernatural fiction comprehension using fNIRS. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-025-00327-0

article_title: Simulated Learners in Educational Technology: A Systematic Literature Review and a Turing-like Test
citation: Käser, T., & Alexandron, G. (2023). Simulated Learners in Educational Technology: A Systematic Literature Review and a Turing-like Test. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00337-2
title: Taxonomy of purposes for simulated learners in educational technology
description: The review organizes the applications of simulated learners into several purposes: teacher training, hypothesis generation and evaluation about human learning, adaptive learning algorithm development, collaborative virtual worlds, and testing learning environments. As the abstract states, simulated learners can be used "for teacher training, for generating and evaluating hypotheses on human learning, for developing adaptive learning algorithms". This taxonomy frames the trends the review traces over 2010-19.
requirements: Computational models that simulate learner interactions and data must be built for the chosen purpose
constraints: Simulated learner models tend to represent only narrow aspects of student learning
target_learners: teacher trainees working with simulated students
examples: The review lists teacher training, hypothesis evaluation, adaptive algorithm development, virtual worlds with simulated pals, and testing learning environments as uses

article_title: Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems
citation: Aleven, V., Roll, I., McLaren, B. M., & Koedinger, K. R. (2016). Help Helps, But Only So Much: Research on Help Seeking with Intelligent Tutoring Systems. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0089-1
title: Evaluation framework distinguishing 16 possible effects of SRL interventions
description: The article proposes a framework for evaluating interventions supporting self-regulated learning, built on four distinctions: targeted SRL processes versus domain-level learning; current versus future learning; same versus a new learning environment; same versus a different domain. "These four items define a space of 16 possible effects on learning that interventions to support SRL may have." It relates the Help Tutor studies to this space and argues future research should test additional cells, such as effects on future domain-level learning. The authors see measuring SRL both during and after an intervention as key to moving the field forward.
requirements: Researchers must operationalize and measure SRL outcomes both during and after the intervention to evaluate lasting effects
constraints: Only a sampling of the 16 possibilities was addressed in the Help Tutor studies; transfer to other environments cannot be taken for granted
target_learners: Students using advanced learning technologies with SRL support
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning skills and domain-level learning
examples: The Help Tutor studies measured current domain learning, and current and future help-seeking behavior via logs, hypothetical scenarios, and post-test items with embedded help

article_title: AIED—Coming of Age?
citation: Wayne Holmes. (2024). AIED—Coming of Age?. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-023-00352-3
title: Six challenges for the AIED community's coming of age
description: The author enumerates six challenges the AIED community should engage: generative AI, researcher responsibility for misuse, AI literacy, openness to other fields, ethics and human rights, and anthropomorphic language. He frames them as provocation, not criticism: 'raising these challenges is not a criticism of the work to date of the AIED community. Instead, it is a recognition of the successes of the AIED community alongside the fact that the world has changed.'
requirements: The community must debate and engage with each challenge rather than continue its traditional focus unchanged
constraints: The author raises the challenges 'although (because of space) not explore in enough detail'
target_learners: AIED researchers and the AIED research community
target_learning_goals: Responsible and ethical research practice in AI in education
examples: The Special Issue's fifteen opinion pieces from inside and outside the AIED community respond to the Durham panel provocation

article_title: Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs
citation: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 25:118–156. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0030-z
title: Sierra's impasse-and-repair theory of the origin of learners' procedural errors
description: Sierra, as presented in the article, is "a theory to explain the origin of learners' procedural errors (VanLehn 1990)" proposing "plausible cognitive processes that could lead learners to execute incorrect steps." Errors arise when learners face impasses — situations in which their current knowledge is insufficient — and apply one of three repair strategies: no-op, back-up and barge-on. The article reports the theory was validated by a computational model of learning applied to subtraction that successfully modeled the acquisition of multiple errors observed in learners' behavior, and Astus takes inspiration from it to diagnose errors.
requirements: Modeling errors via impasse and repair requires a hierarchical goal structure that meets Sierra's criterion for a hierarchical goal structure
constraints: Little effort has been made to incorporate elements of the Sierra theory into ITSs, according to the article
target_learning_goals: understanding and diagnosing learners' procedural errors
examples: The article describes how a no-op repair ignores an unachievable goal, a back-up repair returns to a previously unfinished goal, and a barge-on repair modifies procedural knowledge to resolve the impasse.
key_sources: Luc Paquette, Jean-François Lebeau, Gabriel Beaulieu & André Mayers. (2015). Designing a Knowledge Representation Approach for the Generation of Pedagogical Interventions by MTTs. article_title: A Simulated Student Can Improve Collaborative Learning
citation: Aurora Vizcaíno. (2005). A Simulated Student Can Improve Collaborative Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197303
title: Simulated Student agent added to a collaborative synchronous system for learning programming
description: The Simulated Student is an agent embodying the features of the proposed architecture, added to a collaborative, synchronous system used for learning programming. Its role is to detect and avoid off-topic conversations, passive behaviour, and problems related to students' learning. The article describes it as a "Simulated Student, which has the features described in the model", deployed to check the model's efficiency in a real case.
requirements: Must be integrated into a collaborative, synchronous learning system where the three negative situations can arise
examples: A Simulated Student with the architecture's features was added to a collaborative, synchronous system for learning programming and tested in an experiment

article_title: A Simulated Student Can Improve Collaborative Learning
citation: Aurora Vizcaíno. (2005). A Simulated Student Can Improve Collaborative Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00197303
title: Simulated Student architecture for detecting and avoiding negative situations in collaborative learning
description: The Simulated Student architecture is a model of a simulated peer agent that monitors collaborative learning interactions to detect and avoid situations that decrease the benefits of learning in collaboration. It targets three named situations: off-topic conversations, students with passive behaviour, and problems related to students' learning. The article presents it as a model whose features are instantiated in an agent added to a real collaborative system, and evaluates whether the model is adequate in the avoidance of negative situations.
requirements: A collaborative learning environment whose interactions the simulated student can monitor
Detection mechanisms for the three targeted negative situations
examples: The architecture's features were implemented in a Simulated Student added to a synchronous collaborative programming system

article_title: Towards Trustworthy AutoGrading of Short, Multi-lingual, Multi-type Answers
citation: Johannes Schneider, Robin Richner, Micha Riser. (2023). Towards Trustworthy AutoGrading of Short, Multi-lingual, Multi-type Answers. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00289-z
title: Similarity-threshold autograding architecture with teacher-controlled error constraints and a human-deferred uncertainty zone
description: The article proposes an autograding framework in which fine-tuned multilingual transformer models embed question-answer pairs and score similarity to the correct answer. "Using two thresholds on the score, we can place a question-answer pair into one of three categories" — likely correct, uncertain, or likely incorrect — with uncertain pairs deferred to a human. Teachers specify minimum accuracy levels (maximum false-negative and false-positive rates), from which thresholds are computed to maximize the fraction of samples autograded while honoring the constraints. A validation procedure then compares accuracy on manually and automatically graded answers per exam.
requirements: A dataset of question-answer pairs with teacher-provided correct/incorrect marks as ground truth
Teachers must specify minimum accuracy thresholds for answers classified as correct and incorrect
Difficult samples within the threshold range must be graded manually by a human
constraints: Restricted to questions whose answers can be marked as correct or incorrect
Accuracy of about 90% on autograded samples is deemed insufficient for fully automatic grading of high-stake exams
Relying only on semantic similarity may not suffice because an autograder cannot reason logically
target_learners: students studying at home for exam preparation
target_learning_goals: accurate assessment of short free-text and numeric answers across subjects and languages
examples: The system was trained and evaluated on about 10 million answers and 990000 questions from Classtime, covering languages including Ukrainian, English, Russian and German
