article_title: Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring
citation: Matsuda, N., Cohen, W. W., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0020-1
title: SimStudent: a machine-learning agent that learns an expert model through tutored problem solving
description: SimStudent is a domain-general machine-learning agent that learns an expert model of a target task through tutored problem solving, using the same tutor interface crafted for the target cognitive tutor. It learns production rules representing individual cognitive skills, with an if-part (information retrieval path and preconditions) and a then-part (operator function sequence). Three machine-learning techniques are combined: version spaces for the information retrieval path, FOIL inductive logic programming for preconditions, and iterative-deepening depth-first search for the operator function sequence. The domain dependency is implemented as background knowledge comprising a WME structure, feature predicates, and operator functions.
requirements: Background knowledge including a WME structure, feature predicates, and operator functions must be provided prior to learning.
constraints: SimStudent does not learn strategic knowledge to select among equally available productions, so accuracy reflects both correct and incorrect production applications.
target_learning_goals: Authoring expert models for cognitive tutors
key_sources: Matsuda, N., Cohen, W. W., & Koedinger, K. R. (2015). Teaching the Teacher: Tutoring SimStudent Leads to More Effective Cognitive Tutor Authoring. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-014-0020-1

article_title: Studying the Effect of a Competitive Game Show in a Learning by Teaching Environment
citation: Matsuda, N., Yarzebinski, E., Keiser, V., Raizada, R., Stylianides, G. J., & Koedinger, K. R. (2013). Studying the Effect of a Competitive Game Show in a Learning by Teaching Environment. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0009-1
title: SimStudent as a machine-learning teachable agent with high cognitive fidelity, including incorrect learning
description: SimStudent is "a machine-learning architecture that learns procedural skills inductively from examples", integrated into APLUS where students tutor it with yes/no feedback, hints, quizzes, and self-explanation prompts. Its unique characteristic is the ability "to model both correct and incorrect learning": given prior knowledge based on surface features, it makes induction errors from correct examples, producing overly specific or general productions mirroring common algebra errors. The authors hypothesize such "high cognitive fidelity" teachable agents offer better learning-by-teaching opportunities.
requirements: Students provide feedback, demonstrations, and explanations during tutored problem-solving
constraints: SimStudent does not understand students' free-text responses; question answering is designed to promote reflective thinking
target_learning_goals: procedural skill in solving linear equations
examples: Students tutor SimStudent via the APLUS Tutoring Interface, posing equations and giving flagged feedback

title: Six-stage UX design process for website products (definition, research, user analysis, information architecture, prototyping, testing)
description: The article adopts a six-stage UX design process diagram (Fig. 1) for website products: product definition, information search including competitor review, user analysis via personas and journey maps, information architecture, prototype design as sketches/wireframes/mockups, and testing with possible iteration. It structures which stages GenAI tools support in the studied courses.
requirements: Course projects organized around campaign briefings; teams of students per stage
constraints: The article notes barriers applying generative tools to Web development tasks
target_learners: undergraduate design and creative technology students
examples: PCI courses followed this staged process from campaign briefing ideation through Web prototype development

article_title: Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary
citation: Goodman, B., Linton, F., & Gaimari, R. (2016). Encouraging Student Reflection and Articulation Using a Learning Companion: A Commentary. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 474–488. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0041-4
title: Simulated peer in an ITS ensures collaborator availability while retaining individualized tutoring
description: The article describes a design pattern in which "[a] simulated learning companion, acting as a peer in an intelligent tutoring environment ensures the availability of a collaborator and encourages the student to learn collaboratively, while drawing upon the instructional advantages that ITSs provide." This blends ITS individualized coaching with CSCL peer learning, avoiding the need for a second human participant. The companion's role and knowledge extent are defined by the instructional designer and controlled at runtime, adapting behavior to individual student needs — an advantage over human collaborators.
requirements: A differentiated peer role, since students have higher expectations for communication from a tutor than from a peer
constraints: Menu-based dialogues made the interaction unnatural and not always the most appropriate
examples: LuCy in the PROPA ITS prompted students to explain reasoning behind actions and justify decisions via menu-driven dialogue

article_title: Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom
citation: Jennifer K. Olsen & Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven. (2021). Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 31:24–56. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00228-w
title: Six design desires for shared control of co-orchestrated social transitions between teacher and system
description: The article formulates six design desires (Table 2) for balancing teacher and system responsibilities when orchestrating fluid social transitions. They specify that 'Teachers are the instigators of the lesson-designing process', that the system carries out real-time orchestration decisions within the confines of the teacher's lesson design, that teachers can make real-time changes and override system decisions, that the system provides monitoring with visible decisions and explanations, that teachers handle behavior, help-giving and reviewing system decisions, and that the system communicates transition information to students. Desires 4 and 5 were updated after Study 2.
requirements: Co-orchestration must be designed according to the teacher's values and classroom culture for the technology to be adopted in the long term
constraints: The desires were derived from primary-school teachers' perspectives; involving students is left for future work
target_learning_goals: fluid social transitions between individual, small-group and whole-class learning in technology-enhanced classrooms
examples: The desires were implemented in a mid-fidelity prototype of an orchestration system for specific social transition scenarios used in Study 2

Designing for the co-Orchestration of Social Transitions between Individual, Small-Group and Whole-Class Learning in the Classroom. citation: Hossain, Z., Bumbacher, E., Brauneis, A., Diaz, M., Saltarelli, A., Blikstein, P., & Riedel-Kruse, I. H. (2018). Design Guidelines and Empirical Case Study for Scaling Authentic Inquiry-based Science Learning via Open Online Courses and Interactive Biology Cloud Labs. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-017-0150-3
title: Present real experiments and modeling side by side so students can compare and recognize divergences
description: The article recommends that "real experiments and modeling should be presented to the student side by side, where the correspondence between both should be easily understandable." This bifocal modeling approach helps students understand key properties of the real system through the model while recognizing its subtleties by seeing how real and model behavior diverge. Even simple models capturing only overall tendencies can provide powerful lenses for understanding complex biological systems.
requirements: Equivalent symbolism between model and real experiment representations
Mechanistic models that capture overall behavioral tendencies
constraints: Even simple models may not capture all real-system behaviors such as light-intensity-dependent variability
examples: Students compared a parameter-fitting simulation of Euglena to real experiment videos and reported differences in light-intensity sensitivity, spinning behavior, and reaction lag

article_title: The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment
citation: Conejo, R., Guzmán, E., & Trella, M. (2016). The SIETTE Automatic Assessment Environment. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education, 26, 270–292. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0078-4
title: Siette: a domain-independent web-based automatic assessment environment
description: Siette is a web-based automatic assessment system developed over 16 years at the University of Málaga. It supports classical test theory, item response theory, and computer adaptive testing, and integrates them with multidimensional student models used by intelligent educational systems. The system is designed as "a web-based assessment component that can be semantically integrated with intelligent systems or with large LMSs, such as Moodle." Teachers use an authoring tool to create large item pools of multiple-choice, open answer, generative, and complex task items.
requirements: A user-friendly authoring tool so that teachers can create and maintain item pools
Interoperability with other systems via web services and APIs
constraints: Not an open-source project; free academic use granted upon request
Designed mainly for higher education
target_learning_goals: formative and summative assessment across multiple skills
examples: Integrated with Moodle at the University of Málaga virtual campus serving 2500 staff and 35000 students per year
Used for botany assessment in a laboratory using QR codes attached to dried plant sheets

article_title: Supporting Coordination and Peer Editing in Students’ Online Collaborative Writing Processes
citation: Maya Usher, Ido Roll, Orly Fuhrman, Ofra Amir. (2025). Supporting Coordination and Peer Editing in Students’ Online Collaborative Writing Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 35. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-024-00450-w
title: SITU: a minimalist group awareness tool embedded in Google Docs
description: SITU is a Google Docs add-on group awareness (GA) tool designed to "support productive coordination and encourage peer editing in the context of OCW tasks". It has two functionalities: a traffic-light color rating (red/yellow/green, with three 'S' logo shapes) letting students anonymously mark paragraph readiness, and a to-do list of up to 200 words of written feedback about required editing. Anonymity is intended to reduce the guilt and anxiety of editing a co-author's work, and the document itself serves as the organizing mechanism for interactions rather than an external dashboard.
requirements: Deployed as a Google Docs add-on within a shared OCW document; relies on students rating paragraph readiness and providing written feedback to co-authors
constraints: The article states the to-do list did not provide specific suggestions or instructions on how or what to revise, leaving decisions to students
target_learning_goals: task coordination in asynchronous group work
examples: In the main study, experimental-group documents contained six pre-rated paragraphs (two red, two yellow, two green) and students could re-rate paragraphs or rate new ones

article_title: Evaluation Methods for Intelligent Tutoring Systems Revisited
citation: Jim Greer & Mary Mark. (2015). Evaluation Methods for Intelligent Tutoring Systems Revisited. Int J Artif Intell Educ 26:387–392. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0043-2
title: Six emerging evaluation approaches for intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning environments
description: The article organizes its survey around six approaches that "hold great promise for evaluating educational environments": using the open web and crowd sourcing, comparing decisions of adaptive environments with human experts, using simulated learners, washing out selection bias, examining learning curves, and performing evaluations derived from mega quantities of micro measurements. Each is presented as an expansion of the 1993 survey, enabled by increases in computer speed, storage, and connectivity. The framework spans formative and summative evaluation of smart, intelligent, or adaptive educational environments.
requirements: Increases in computer speed, storage and connectivity that made techniques such as crowdsourcing and educational data mining feasible
constraints: The broad 1993 concept of an ITS has narrowed to stand-alone one-on-one computer tutors, so the methods apply to a wider range of adaptive environments
target_learners: AIEd researchers and developers evaluating adaptive learning environments
target_learning_goals: rigorous evaluation of intelligent tutoring and adaptive learning systems
examples: The article briefly comments on each of the six approaches, indicating ways the 1993 survey might be expanded.

article_title: Problem Order Implications for Learning
citation: Nan Li, William W. Cohen, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2013). Problem Order Implications for Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0005-5
title: SimStudent as a computational model of skill learning with where, when, and how learners
description: SimStudent is a machine-learning agent that inductively learns skills to solve problems from demonstrated solutions and problem-solving experience, using a variation of the version space algorithm, inductive logic programming, and iterative-deepening depth-first search. It learns production rules with three parts — perceptual information (where), precondition (when), and operator function sequence (how) — each acquired by a corresponding learning mechanism. The article uses SimStudent as a precise, unambiguous computational model of the problem-order question, tutoring it with automatic tutors on problems previously used with human students. The authors report it has been shown to find high-quality models of student learning across domains and to discover student models that predict human student behavior better than human-generated models.
requirements: Requires a perceptual hierarchy, a set of feature predicates, and a set of operator functions provided as prior knowledge before learning
constraints: Does not assume a memory limitation, which differs from human students
Presents a bias towards more generalized skills over specific ones without considering computational cost
Does not model aspects of human learning such as motivation
target_learners: Simulated students modeling human learners in math and science domains
target_learning_goals: Acquisition of problem-solving skills (production rules) in domains such as fraction addition, equation solving, and stoichiometry
examples: In the equation solving domain, SimStudent was tutored on problems such as −3x + 2 = 8 and learned production rules like the divide rule with perceptual information, precondition, and operator sequence parts
key_sources: Nan Li, William W. Cohen, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2013). Problem Order Implications for Learning. Int J Artif Intell Educ. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0005-5

article_title: Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers’ self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence
citation: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1
title: Six-dimension model of teachers' AI competence
description: Based on a systematic literature review and qualitative interviews with 35 stakeholders, the article identifies six dimensions of AI competence for teachers: Theoretical Knowledge about AI, Legal Framework and Ethics, Implications of AI, Attitude toward AI, Teaching and Learning with AI, and Ongoing Professionalization. The article states that "AI competence in the context of education is a set of skills that enable teachers to ethically responsible develop, apply, and evaluate AI for learning and teaching processes." The model is holistic and multidimensional, distinguishing itself from frameworks that focus on a single construct.
requirements: Ongoing teacher professionalization and training to maintain the competence set
constraints: The PF and AT dimensions did not fit the final single-factor measurement model in their current form
target_learning_goals: Developing AI competence for ethical and responsible use of AI in teaching
key_sources: Delcker, J., Heil, J., & Ifenthaler, D. (2025). Evidence-based development of an instrument for the assessment of teachers' self-perceptions of their artificial intelligence competence. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-024-10418-1

article_title: Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving
citation: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y
title: Six-session weaving workshop with graduated math goals from shape recognition to sequence exploration
description: A reusable instructional design at the unit level: six one-hour sessions during the school day in which youth use laser-cut frame looms and grid paper to plan and create woven artifacts. Sessions progress from introducing weaving designs and warping looms, through planning on grid paper and completing initial projects, to a second project exploring relationships between materials, number, shape, and sequence, ending with reflection on connections to math. Youth were encouraged to make at least two projects and to try new techniques and styles in their second design.
requirements: Frame looms laser-cut from an open-source pattern
Grid paper for planning designs
Yarn in multiple colors and thicknesses, string for warping, scissors, pencils, tapestry needles
constraints: Youth sometimes created small projects, abandoned projects, or wanted to continue working beyond the scope of the workshop
target_learners: middle-school youth (grades 6-8) in a mixed-age classroom
target_learning_goals: recognize how shapes, patterns, motifs emerge on grid structure
reason about how sequence and shape intersect
explore relationships between materials, number, shape, sequence
examples: Youth used an over one, under one sequence in first projects and progressed to over two, under two or over three, under two sequences in second projects
key_sources: Thompson, N. (2024). Weaving in: shifts in youth mathematical engagement through weaving. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10316-y

article_title: Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience
citation: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3
title: Situational cognitive training game framework
description: The article proposes a three-component framework for designing cognitive training games that balances training effectiveness, motivation, and context. As printed, "this study proposes a situational cognitive training game framework that integrates cognitive training foundation, motivational design framework, and human–computer interaction framework". The cognitive foundation adopts classic inhibition trainings (Simon and Stroop tasks); the motivational design framework draws on Keller's ARCS model and Yee's gameplay motivation framework, using game elements to enhance challenge, confidence, and satisfaction; the human–computer interaction framework incorporates authentic contexts to promote immersion and engagement.
requirements: Classic inhibition trainings as the cognitive design basis to ensure training effectiveness
Game elements aligned with ARCS factors and Yee's achievement and immersion components
Authentic real-life contexts grounded in the human–computer interaction framework
constraints: Developed and evaluated for inhibition ability, one EF sub-skill, with university students
examples: Four games were built on the framework: two button-selection games based on the Simon task and two voice-recognition games based on the Stroop task, set in soccer, baseball, sushi-eating, and pet-training situations
key_sources: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3

article_title: Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience
citation: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3
title: Situational training game design pattern: authentic scenarios plus progressive challenge and real-time feedback
description: A reusable lesson/game-level design pattern for cognitive training games: embed classic cognitive tasks in authentic real-life situations and layer motivational game elements. The article states that "the game integrated key design elements, including authentic scenarios, sound effects, animations, progressive difficulty stages, time limits, and scoring mechanisms". Progressive stages, timers and scoring serve achievement-oriented motives, while authentic contexts such as restaurants and apartments with animated transitions and sound effects foster presence, relatedness and autonomy.
requirements: Tasks must target a specific EF sub-skill based on classic cognitive assessments
Staged progression with selectable difficulty levels
Immediate feedback via sound effects and animations
constraints: Evaluated in 15-minute single-session training; long-term effects unknown
examples: The sushi-eating game is based on the Stroop task, requiring participants to inhibit the interference of color words; the baseball game adds a third-stage rule change requiring response inhibition of previous habitual actions
key_sources: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3

article_title: Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience
citation: Sora Chi-Fang Huang, Zhi-Hong Chen, Yu-Tzu Lin. (2026). Enhancing inhibition ability through situational training games: effectiveness, motivation and experience. Education Tech Research Dev 74. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10593-3
title: Four situational inhibition training games (button-selection and voice-recognition)
description: A series of four digital inhibition training games developed with Construct 3 per the situational cognitive training game framework. As printed, "the game system comprises two types of games: button-selection and voice-recognition games". Button-selection games are based on the Simon task and require suppressing automatic responses across three difficulty stages; voice-recognition games are based on the Stroop task and require verbally responding while inhibiting conflicting visual and textual information. Situations include soccer, baseball, sushi-eating, and pet training, and the system provides immediate feedback and accurate response-time recording.
requirements: Built with Construct 3 for digitalized delivery with precise response-time recording
Tasks derived from classic inhibition trainings (Simon and Stroop tasks)
constraints: Voice recognition accuracy was noted by participants as needing improvement
examples: In the baseball button-selection game, the third stage introduces a new rule so that when the pitcher faces right and lowers his leg, the correct response is the left button, opposite from the prior rule

article_title: Understanding and managing the complexities in situated learning in immersive virtual environments
citation: Wang, M., Dede, C., Grotzer, T. A., & Chen, J. (2025). Understanding and managing the complexities in situated learning in immersive virtual environments. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10519-5
title: Framework of three complexity types surrounding situated learning
description: The article presents a conceptual framework delineating "the complexities of real-world problems, the complexities in exploring real-world problems, and the complexities in reflecting on problem exploration experience." It argues that real-world problems are ill-structured, involving "incomplete information and the lack of well-determined algorithms," and that exploration and reflection each pose distinct difficulties. The framework is intended as "a guide for designing situated learning curricula, evaluating situated learning practices, and addressing situated learning challenges."
requirements: A holistic understanding of complexities is needed so that scaffolding does not undermine the open-ended nature of situated learning
constraints: The authors state a limitation: "a lack of a systematic review of relevant studies before proposing the framework"
target_learners: secondary school students learning in immersive virtual environments

article_title: Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs
citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). Simulation research and design: a dual-level framework for multi-project research programs. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09876-0
title: Simulations can be classified by modality (live, role-play, digital) and purpose (assessment, facilitation, research)
description: The article defines simulations as "authentic models of professional situations that can be manipulated by participants", distinguished from simulators as the technical devices used to conduct them. It classifies simulations by modality into live simulations with trained standardized persons, role-play simulations with briefly prepared participants, and digital simulations run on computers, and by purpose into assessment, facilitation, or research. The framework offers specific recommendations for these two critical features.
requirements: Design processes should consider modality and purpose as critical features; simulations and simulators are distinct artifacts that have to be designed separately
constraints: The framework targets simulations that assess and train knowledge and competences, excluding simulations emphasizing skills such as motor skills
target_learners: learners in medical education and teacher education
target_learning_goals: knowledge and competence acquisition and assessment in simulated professional situations
examples: COSIMA 4 simulated a medical interview using live simulations with professional actors, digital simulations, and role-play simulations

citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). title: Simulation components: learning and testing environments, simulation scenarios, case vignettes, briefings, and debriefings
description: The article classifies the simulation components typically developed in simulation research programs (Table 2). Learning environments "pursue the goal of facilitating knowledge and competence acquisition and include instructional support", while testing environments assess without instructional support. Simulation scenarios are professional situations in which an agent can demonstrate competences; case vignettes depict persons with specific characteristics and a task; briefings include a familiarization and fiction contract; debriefings let learners compare their solution to the designated solution.
requirements: Components must be designed separately and embedded in the learning and testing environment according to the experimental procedure
target_learners: higher education learners in simulated professional situations
target_learning_goals: facilitation and assessment of knowledge and competences in simulations
examples: COSIMA 4 created case vignettes from a blueprint specifying critical features, with an expert workshop evaluating their accuracy and difficulty

citation: Fink, M. C., Radkowitsch, A., Bauer, E., Sailer, M., Kiesewetter, J., Schmidmaier, R., Siebeck, M., Fischer, F., & Fischer, M. R. (2020). title: Research materials for simulation studies: assessment instruments, educational intervention, and experimental procedure
description: Table 1 of the article classifies the materials developed for research purposes in simulation-based studies. Instruments that assess knowledge treat it as a prerequisite of performance, while competence instruments "operationalize this construct as observable results and processes in simulations", including computer-based tests, coding schemes, and rating scales. The educational intervention is the treatment condition examined, such as instructional support like prompts, and the experimental procedure consists of the measurement procedure and an experimenter's guide.

target_learning_goals: assessment and facilitation of knowledge and competences
examples: The COSIMA research committee created a common test battery including motivational and cognitive scales and a common measurement procedure for all projects

article_title: Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats
citation: Webb, M. E., Fluck, A., Magenheim, J., Malyn-Smith, J., Waters, J., Deschênes, M., & Zagami, J. (2021). Machine learning for human learners: opportunities, issues, tensions and threats. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09858-2
title: Six explanation types for machine learning systems in industry guidance
description: Initial industry guidance on AI explainability, cited in the article, identifies six main types of explanation. As printed, "This guidance identifies six main types of explanation (Itransition 2019; ICO and Turing 2019, p. 19) as follows." They are: rationale explanation (the reasons behind a decision in accessible terms), responsibility explanation (who is involved and who to contact for human review), data explanation (what data was used and how), fairness explanation (steps ensuring unbiased, equitable decisions), safety and performance explanation (accuracy, reliability, security, robustness steps), and impact explanation (effects on individuals and wider society).
requirements: Explanations must be delivered in a form accessible and non-technical to the recipient
constraints: There are no agreed metrics for the quality of explanation methods, so comparisons across contexts are difficult
target_learners: recipients of machine learning decisions including students and teachers
target_learning_goals: understanding and evaluating machine learning systems

article_title: Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education
citation: Rob J. Nadolski, Hans G. K. Hummel, Ellen Rusman, Kevin Ackermans. (2021). Rubric formats for the formative assessment of oral presentation skills acquisition in secondary education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-021-10030-7
title: Six-step formative assessment method for oral presentation skills with analytic rubrics
description: The article's formative assessment method structures classroom rubric use into a recurring cycle applied around each oral presentation. As printed, "The formative assessment method consisted of six steps: (1) study the rubric; (2) practice and conduct an oral presentation; (3) conduct a self-assessment; (4) consult feedback from teacher and peers; (5) Reflect on feedback; and (6) select personal learning goal(s) for the next oral presentation". The method is embedded in project-based education and repeated across two projects, with advice on the second presentation targeting subskills performed insufficiently in the first. It was applied with twelve- to thirteen-year-old students in Dutch secondary schools.
requirements: Analytic rubrics validated for the domain and target group must be available in a digital tool supporting self-, peer-, and teacher-assessment
Teachers and students require condition-specific workshops on rubric usage and feedback provision
constraints: Teachers regarded the classroom scenarios as relatively time-consuming; only two oral presentations could receive feedback within the study
target_learning_goals: Oral presentation skills acquisition through formative assessment and reflection
examples: Students practiced two consecutive projects with presentations; after Project 2 experimental students compared dashboard progress across both presentations during the second reflection assignment

article_title: The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students’ privacy awareness
citation: Luca Botturi, Tiffany Fioroni, Chiara Beretta, Davide Andreoletti, Alessandro Ferrari, Felipe Cardoso, Anna Picco-Schwendener, Suzanna Marazza, Silvia Giordano. (2024). The iBuddy experience: A digital simulation-based approach to enhance secondary school students' privacy awareness. Education Tech Research Dev 72. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-023-10309-x
title: Two-phase session design: playful narrative simulation followed by modular debriefing
description: The iBuddy session is designed in two phases: (a) a highly engaging narrative-based playful simulation playable with all age groups, and (b) a flexible modular debriefing adjustable to the age group and to questions emerging in each session. The debriefing has two steps: behind-the-scenes modules (what happened, emotions, technical features, data deletion) and real-life modules (how the internet works, personalization, advertising, data value, profiles, terms of use, alternatives), combined usually 3 or 4 at a time.
requirements: Half of the session time is devoted to debriefing
Cliffhangers or pointers to the debriefing are integrated during the simulation design
A presenter leads and an operator prepares safe custom questions
constraints: The debriefing path depends on participants' questions, age group and available time
The debriefing is less interactive and engaging than the simulation
target_learners: students aged 11–20 in secondary, high school and university classes
target_learning_goals: understanding of data collection and processing
examples: Debriefing part 1 always includes modules 1.1, 1.3 and 1.4 with optional 1.2; part 2 offers modules M2.0–M2.6 from which the presenter combines 3 or 4

citation: Patience E. Idoga, Dokun Iwalewa Oluwajana, Ibrahim Adeshola. (2022). Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-022-10150-8
title: Six-construct instructor e-learning acceptance questionnaire (299 respondents, Nigerian universities)
description: A structured questionnaire measuring six constructs — self-efficacy, educational quality, technological complexity, perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use, and behavioral intention — using a five-point Likert scale with three indicators per construct adapted from prior studies (e.g., Mohammadi 2015; Davis 1986). It was administered to instructors of three private schools across three geopolitical zones in Nigeria; "299 respondents (90.60%) were included in this study". Factor loadings ranged from 0.74 to 0.92, AVE from 0.589 to 0.802, and Cronbach's alpha from 0.651 to 0.876.

constraints: Purposive sampling of three private schools may introduce researcher bias, as the authors state
target_learning_goals: Measuring determinants of instructors' technology acceptance
examples: Sample indicators include 'I feel confident using the e-learning platform' (SE2, loading 0.85) and 'I intend to use the e-learning platform in the future' (BI1, loading 0.80).

article_title: Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty’s and students’ perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education
citation: Hoda Harati, Gretchen McAllister, Yingying Liu. (2026). Cultivating inclusive mindsets exploring faculty's and students' perspectives on using online simulations for inclusive pedagogy in teacher education. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10662-7
title: Situated learning plus simulation-based learning as a framework for simulation-supported inclusive pedagogy preparation
description: The study grounds its simulation design in two complementary frameworks. Situated learning holds that "professional knowledge develops through participation in socially and contextually meaningful activity rather than through abstract instruction alone" (Lave & Wenger, 1991), while simulation-based learning provides "structured opportunities for rehearsal, reflection, and decision-making in low-risk environments that approximate the complexity of real practice" (Levin & Frei-Landau, 2023). Together they position the simulation as a pedagogical space where candidates test responses, reflect on consequences, and develop readiness for inclusive practice in contested contexts.
requirements: Realistic dilemmas, stakeholder perspectives, and reflective opportunities within the simulation to support professional reflection and decision-making
constraints: The article frames the frameworks as interpretive lenses for perception data, not as tested mechanisms; findings reflect self-reported perceptions rather than observed practice
examples: The discussion interprets candidates' movement from abstract to practical strategies through legitimate peripheral participation and features of a community of practice.

article_title: Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective
citation: Katai, Z. (2020). Promoting computational thinking of both sciences- and humanities-oriented students: an instructional and motivational design perspective. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-020-09766-5
title: Six-stage hearing–seeing–doing e-learning session with interleaved motivation questionnaires
description: A lesson-level sequence that alternates motivational phases with measurement points: a hearing introduction, a dance-performance phase to arouse curiosity, an animation phase supporting abstracting, three doing phases (reconstruction, white-box orchestration, black-box orchestration) implementing active involvement and progressive challenge, and a closing parallel simulation arousing aesthetic emotions. Nine questionnaires (Q1–9) are interleaved between stages to track emotions, challenge, and involvement. The article states that during the doing phases "students are invited to actively participate in the animations (Mayer and Chandler 2001) according to the principle of moderate-progressive challenge".
requirements: Help-buttons indicating the next operation, and repeatable tasks on randomly generated inputs until solved correctly without help, to reduce anxiety and promote a sense of achievement
constraints: The article notes that if e-learning materials are interesting only because they are novel, they may lose their appeal as learners become accustomed to them
examples: In the reported experiment both groups followed the session Q1–2, s1, Q3, s2, Q4, s3, Q5, s4, Q6, s5, Q7, s6, Q8–9 in computer labs with individual access to the online tool.

article_title: Army television research activities
citation: Joseph H. Kanner. (1951). Army Television Research Activities. https://eric.ed.gov
title: Signal Corps experimental mobile color television unit
description: An experimental production unit built for Army television research on color instruction. The article states: "The Signal Corps operates an experimental mobile color unit which consists of three color cameras and associated equipment mounted in an air-conditioned van." Transistor use makes the cameras lighter than predecessors though bulkier than standard image orthicons. It supported the color-versus-monochrome teaching study at Fort Monmouth and Huntsville.

constraints: The cameras remain bulkier than standard image orthicons despite being lighter due to extensive use of transistors
target_learners: Army trainees at the Signal School and the Ordnance Guided Missile School
target_learning_goals: Military teaching and training delivered over television
examples: Used at the Signal School, Fort Monmouth, and the Ordnance Guided Missile School, Huntsville, Alabama, across a wide variety of subject matter

article_title: A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies
citation: Tondeur, Jo; Aesaert, Koen; Prestridge, Sarah; Consuegra, Els. (2018). A multilevel analysis of what matters in the training of pre-service teacher's ICT competencies. Computers & Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.compedu.2018.03.002
title: Six strategies of the teacher training institution for preparing pre-service teachers' ICT competencies
description: The article enumerates six strategies pre-service teachers experience in their teacher training institution: "1) using teacher educators as role models, 2) reflecting on the role of technology in education, 3) learning how to use technology by design, 4) collaboration with peers, 5) scaffolding authentic technology experiences, and 6) continuous feedback." These strategies together form the institutional component of the tested model and were measured as perceived occurrences in the survey of 931 pre-service teachers.
requirements: Teacher training institutions must deliberately enact all six strategies so pre-service teachers perceive their occurrences
constraints: Studied in the context of Flemish final-year teacher education; effects are on perceived ICT competence
target_learners: pre-service teachers in teacher training institutions
target_learning_goals: competence to use ICT for learning processes and to strengthen instructional practice

article_title: What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence
citation: de Hoop, T., Klochikin, E., & Stone, R. (2016). What Works to Improve Reading Outcomes in Latin-America? A Systematic Review of the Evidence. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Abstract Template, American Institutes for Research. https://www.air.org
title: Simple View of Reading as the theoretical framework for appraising non-intervention reading research
description: The review adopts the Simple View of Reading (attributed to Gough & Tunmer, 1986) as its theoretical lens for appraising studies that focus on reading outcomes but are not tied to a specific intervention. In this framework, "reading success is contingent upon two main abilities: language ability and decoding abilities, and the sub-skills of each of these". The reviewers will determine the extent to which non-intervention studies take this approach into consideration, then narratively synthesize that evidence.
requirements: Applied to critically appraising non-intervention studies of reading outcomes, which are then narratively synthesized
target_learners: Children from birth through grade 3 in the Latin-American and Caribbean region
target_learning_goals: Early grade reading outcomes, including language ability and decoding sub-skills
examples: The review plans to judge how far non-intervention quantitative and qualitative studies consider the two-abilities framework before narrative synthesis

article_title: Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis of the Impact of EEF Trials on the Educational Attainment of Pupils on Free School Meals: 2011-2019
citation: Bilal Ashraf, Akansha Singh, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, Tahani Coolen-Maturi, Jochen Einbeck, Steve Higgins and Adetayo Kasim. (2021). Individual participant data meta-analysis of the impact of EEF trials on the educational attainment of pupils on Free School Meals: 2011 - 2019. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Simplified IPD meta-analysis model (sIPD) for educational trials with heterogeneous outcome scales
description: The sIPD model is a three-level Bayesian individual participant data meta-analysis model adapted for educational trials, where pupils are nested within schools and schools within trials. Because outcome scales differ across trials, the authors "first eliminate heterogeneity between trials by scaling the post-test and pre-test outcome data to a unit variance of 1 per trial", then fit a model with fixed intercept and pre-test gradient, trial-specific treatment effects, and school and pupil random effects, pooling via inverse-variance weights. Attainment gaps are estimated by adding a treatment-by-FSM interaction term.
requirements: Outcome and pre-test data must be standardised within each trial to unit variance before pooling
Bayesian fitting with vague priors and MCMC convergence checking (three chains, 200,000 iterations, Rhat and trace plots)
constraints: The scaling approach is described as statistically not the most desirable, offering a trade-off between model challenges and meaningful results
It may distort outcome distributions if outcomes do not come from a common underlying construct
Shrinkage of trial-specific effects may disadvantage less heterogeneous trials
target_learners: pupils eligible for Free School Meals in English primary and secondary schools
examples: Applied to 88 EEF trials from 2011-2019 with over half a million pupils, estimating pooled effects on FSM pupils and FSM-non-FSM attainment gaps in literacy and mathematics.
key_sources: Bilal Ashraf, Akansha Singh, Germaine Uwimpuhwe, Tahani Coolen-Maturi, Jochen Einbeck, Steve Higgins and Adetayo Kasim. (2021). article_title: Student perceptions of technology-enhanced simulation resources in laparoscopic training: a scoping review and implications for surgical instrumentation.
citation: Vega Ochoa AD, Pinto Bautista HL, Weber Ipuana WJ, González Cuello MÁ, Díaz Pérez A. (2026). Student perceptions of technology-enhanced simulation resources in laparoscopic training: a scoping review and implications for surgical instrumentation. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10009-z
title: Integrate simulation technology into structured pedagogy — objectives, faculty facilitation, feedback and assessment — rather than treating it as effective by default
description: This principle holds that the educational value of technology-enhanced simulation resources depends on their pedagogical integration: "Simulation and immersive tools are more likely to support learning when they are embedded in structured curricula, facilitated by trained faculty, supported by deliberate practice and assessed through competency-based criteria." The review explicitly rejects a technology-centered interpretation, arguing VR, AR, box trainers and portable simulators "are not educationally effective by default."
requirements: Learning outcomes must be defined; faculty must be trained; assessment should use checklists or objective metrics and evaluate both perception and performance
constraints: The review presents these as implementation hypotheses derived from indirect evidence and one direct study, not a finalized curriculum guideline
target_learners: Health sciences students in surgical training, including Surgical Instrumentation students
target_learning_goals: Psychomotor skill acquisition, procedural familiarity, learner confidence, safe transition to clinical practice
examples: The review recommends that programs define learning outcomes, ensure faculty training, combine low-cost and technology-enhanced resources when appropriate, use checklists or objective metrics, and evaluate both perception and performance.

article_title: Competence and confidence of health care professionals in using clozapine: a qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis.
citation: Secchi Agostina, Whiskey Eromona, Nair Sajitha, Shergill Sukhi, Thomas Trudy. (2025). Competence and confidence of health care professionals in using clozapine: a qualitative systematic review and thematic synthesis. Acta Neuropsychiatrica. https://doi.org/10.1017/neu.2025.10024
title: Six-theme framework of factors influencing professionals' competence and confidence in clozapine management
description: The review's thematic synthesis of 34 studies organises the factors influencing health care professionals' competence and confidence in clozapine management into six analytical themes. As the review reports, "Six themes were identified: attitude toward and knowledge about clozapine, misconceptions (regarding side effects, monitoring and co-morbidities), guidelines, education, training and experience." The framework links these factors to clozapine underuse and variation in prescribing practice.
requirements: Studies of health care professionals caring for adults with treatment-resistant schizophrenia on clozapine, published in English after 1989
constraints: Based on 34 included studies, most using self-report surveys; only a few studies involved non-medical professionals
target_learners: medical professionals such as psychiatrists and trainee doctors
non-medical professionals such as nurses, pharmacists and allied health workers
target_learning_goals: competence in clozapine prescribing and management
confidence in adhering to guidelines and managing side effects
examples: Thematic analysis following Thomas and Harden (2008) was applied to data extracted independently by two reviewers from 34 studies

article_title: Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review.
citation: González-Sanz A, López-García JC, Sutil-Rodríguez E, Juárez-Vela R, Santos-Sánchez JÁ, Navas-Echazarreta N, Martínez-Sabater A, Sancho-Sanchez C. (2026). Simulation-Based Training for Nursing Students to Improve Patient Safety: Systematic Review. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/87898
title: Taxonomy of simulation modalities and fidelity levels for patient safety education
description: The review organizes simulation-based education by modality and fidelity. Fidelity is "the degree to which the simulation reproduces the conditions of actual clinical practice," classified as low, medium, or high; modalities per the Healthcare Simulation Dictionary include role-playing, virtual or online simulations, task trainers, high-tech mannequins, and immersive simulations with standardized patients. Across the 20 included studies, high-fidelity simulators (n=9), standardized patients (n=8), virtual reality (n=4), role play (n=2), and board simulations (n=1) were used, with categories not mutually exclusive. The combination of modality and fidelity level allows simulation to be adapted to different educational contexts and clinical competencies.
requirements: Simulation design must not compromise the psychological and physical integrity of participants, per the review's framing of safe training processes
constraints: Modality categories are not mutually exclusive because several studies combined HFS with SP or VR
target_learning_goals: patient safety competencies including communication, teamwork, and medication safety
examples: High-fidelity simulation predominated, with 16 studies using this modality; low-fidelity role-playing was used for interprofessional communication, medication administration, and incident reporting

Each theme carries subthemes with study distributions detailed in supplemental tables, and figure 4 summarises the key strengths and challenges of each learning format. The taxonomy organises how CBL, PBL and TBL are used and experienced in public health programmes.

article_title: Psychometric properties of instruments assessing the ethics of teaching: a COSMIN-based systematic review.
citation: Chaimo Kesinee, Thanasilp Sureeporn. (2026). Psychometric properties of instruments assessing the ethics of teaching: a COSMIN-based systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://doi.org/10.3352/jeehp.2026.23.12
title: Six ethics-of-teaching instruments: ESSQ, ELS, EEQ, TEPI, TCPERSS, and MCI

The review reports that "The number of items ranged from 10 to 56, and the number of domains ranged from 1 to 7," and that most are "self-report Likert-type questionnaires, except for the TCPERSS scale, which incorporates peer assessment." Target populations were primarily teachers and faculty members in Iran, Türkiye, and the United States, totaling more than 3,000 participants.

constraints: None were specifically designed for health professions education

article_title: The effectiveness and perceived value of feedback used in cardiac arrest simulation education: a mixed-method systematic review.
citation: Vella Rachael, Baker Elise, Akerjordet Kristin, Thyer Liz. (2025). The effectiveness and perceived value of feedback used in cardiac arrest simulation education: a mixed-method systematic review. Scandinavian Journal of Trauma, Resuscitation and Emergency Medicine. https://doi.org/10.1186/s13049-025-01456-6
title: Six-category taxonomy of feedback comparisons in cardiac arrest simulation education
description: The review developed six deductive categories for classifying feedback comparisons based on methodological design: "1) human feedback versus a control or as an intervention only, 2) device feedback versus a control or as an intervention only, 3) human versus human feedback, 4) device versus device feedback, 5) human versus device feedback and 6) multiple comparators." This taxonomy organises the diverse feedback literature into comparable groups, enabling thematic synthesis across studies with consistent comparators. The multiple comparator group was excluded from coding due to wide variation in outcomes, which reduced the clarity and usefulness of insights.

constraints: The multiple comparator group was not coded due to wide variation in outcomes, which reduced the clarity and usefulness of insights compared to studies with consistent comparators

article_title: Artificial intelligence in orthopaedic education, training and research: a systematic review.
citation: Banskota Bibek, Bhusal Rajan, Yadav Prkash Kumar, Banskota Ashok Kumar. (2025). Artificial intelligence in orthopaedic education, training and research: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08162-y
title: Six-theme framework for AI integration in orthopaedic education and training
description: The review organises its findings into six key themes: "(a) AI-driven simulation and Virtual Reality in Orthopaedic Training, (b) Adaptive Learning Platforms and Personalized Education Pathways, (c) Computer Vision and Objective Skill Assessment, (d) AI Applications in Orthopaedic Research, (e) Predictive Analytics for Surgical Education and Outcome Prediction, and (f) Challenges and Ethical Considerations in AI Integration." This framework maps the landscape of AI applications across orthopaedic education and research, distinguishing between mature technologies (VR/AR simulators) and nascent ones (generative AI), and highlighting cross-cutting concerns of bias, cost, validation gaps and ethical considerations.

constraints: Evidence is constrained by heterogeneity in study designs and outcome measures, precluding meta-analysis
examples: The review's thematic synthesis identified six themes through open coding and reflexive discussion among the research team.

article_title: Competencies of nurses to participate in safe medication management practices for biologics: A scoping review.
citation: Li Wansheng, Li Li, Li Linbo, Xiaodong Cardenas, Chen Mudiao, Liu Hongye, Li Peirao. (2025). Competencies of nurses to participate in safe medication management practices for biologics: A scoping review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317750
title: Six-domain competency framework for nurses in safe medication management of biologics
description: The review proposes a framework organizing nurse competencies for safe biologics management into six domains: clinical specialized knowledge, critical thinking and problem-solving skills, safe medication skills, health education skills, communication and coordination skills, and technological literacy. The framework is mapped against the American Nurses Association's Nursing Scope and Standards of Practice (NSSP) four domains of knowledge, skills, ability, and judgment. It is intended to clarify nursing roles and inform education and training for clinical nurses.
requirements: Applicable to nurses involved in safe medication management of biologics across hospital, family practice, and home-visit contexts
constraints: Only English-language articles were included, which might have introduced publication bias
Content regarding nurses' prescribing rights may be lacking

article_title: Simulation tools in neuro-oncological surgery: a scoping review of perioperative and training applications.
citation: Menna Grazia, Riva Dora, Marino Salvatore, Garber Jocelyn, Gerritsen Jasper Kees Wim, Mattogno Pier Paolo, Young Jacob Stewart, Olivi Alessandro, Doglietto Francesco, Berger Mitchel Stuart, Della Pepa Giuseppe Maria. (2025). Simulation tools in neuro-oncological surgery: a scoping review of perioperative and training applications. Journal of Neuro-Oncology. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11060-025-04972-8
title: Six-category taxonomy of simulation technologies in neuro-oncological surgery
description: The review organizes neuro-oncological simulation research into six categories: 3D models, AR, MR, and VR in presurgical planning and intraoperative navigation, plus AR and VR in surgical training. The review reports that "Augmented Reality (AR) in Presurgical Planning and Intraoperative Navigation: 25 articles" formed the largest group, while 3D models (5 articles) and VR for planning/navigation (4 articles) were least studied. The taxonomy maps distinct roles: 3D-printed models for presurgical planning, AR for intraoperative navigation overlay, and VR/MR for deeper real-time integration.

constraints: Limited to studies published in English; heterogeneity of study designs prevented meta-analysis

article_title: Effectiveness of non-technical skills training in intensive care units: a systematic review.
citation: Fernandes Pimenta Isac Davidson Santiago et al. (2025). Effectiveness of non-technical skills training in intensive care units: a systematic review. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07037-6
title: Use simulation-based training as the primary strategy for teaching non-technical skills in ICUs
description: The review identifies simulation training as the predominant teaching strategy across included studies, often combined with lectures, game play, online modules, interactive activities, and clinical case discussion. The authors cite the argument that "simulation-based training is the most effective for teaching NTS, promoting authentic use of communication, leadership, and teamwork techniques." Positive learning results in one study were attributed to simulation in the curriculum versus a classroom-based approach.
requirements: Facilitators with sufficient experience in learning, particularly for practical simulation contexts
constraints: Many programs combined simulation with traditional strategies; the relative contribution of each component was not isolated
target_learning_goals: Non-technical skills: teamwork, situational awareness, leadership, communication
examples: Included studies used simulation sessions with briefing and debriefing, often alongside lectures, game play, online modules and case discussions

article_title: The impact of simulation on the development of critical thinking and reflection among nursing and medical students: a systematic review.
citation: Loubbairi S, Lahlou L, Amechghal A, Nassik H. (2025). The impact of simulation on the development of critical thinking and reflection among nursing and medical students: a systematic review. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.334
title: Simulation-Based Learning Evaluation Scale (SBLES)
description: The SBLES is a 37-item instrument across five subscales used to assess reflection in simulation-based learning. The review reports that it "demonstrated good reliability and validity" in the one included study that measured reflection among nursing students using standardized patient role-play.
requirements: Used to assess reflection attitudes in simulation-based learning contexts.

article_title: Teaching methods for critical thinking in health education of children up to high school: A scoping review.
citation: Prokop-Dorner Anna, Piłat-Kobla Aleksandra, Ślusarczyk Magdalena, Świątkiewicz-Mośny Maria, Ożegalska-Łukasik Natalia, Potysz-Rzyman Aleksandra, Zarychta Marianna, Juszczyk Albert, Kondyjowska Dominika, Magiera Agnieszka, Maraj Małgorzata, Storman Dawid, Warzecha Sylwia, Węglarz Paulina, Wojtaszek-Główka Magdalena, Żabicka Wioletta, Bała Małgorzata M. (2024). Teaching methods for critical thinking in health education of children up to high school: A scoping review. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0307094
title: Six dimensions differentiate teaching methods for critical thinking in school health education
description: The review's qualitative synthesis, coded in MAXQDA from the included articles, categorizes health-education teaching methods along six analytical themes. As the article states, "Six dimensions that differentiated the teaching methods were identified: central teaching component, central educator, pupils' activity level, teaching context, educational materials, and significance of critical thinking." These dimensions organize the review's descriptive synthesis of how interventions teach critical thinking.
requirements: Studies must report enough detail on teaching methods and their implementation for coders to classify them on each dimension
constraints: Dimensions were derived from 115 included studies in school health education (ISCED 0–3) and depend on the reporting quality of the primary articles
target_learners: pupils in preschools, primary schools, and secondary schools (ISCED 0–3)
target_learning_goals: critical thinking within health education and health literacy
examples: The coding book was developed and tested on 5% of included articles, and coded data were summarized and compared using graphical tools to identify patterns

article_title: Core Competencies for Serious Illness Conversations: An Integrative Systematic Review.
citation: Susanna Pusa, Rebecca Baxter, Sofia Andersson, Erik K. Fromme, Joanna Paladino, Anna Sandgren. (2024). Core Competencies for Serious Illness Conversations: An Integrative Systematic Review. Journal of Palliative Care. https://doi.org/10.1177/08258597241245022
title: Three-theme taxonomy of core competencies for serious illness conversations
description: The review proposes a taxonomy of clinician core competencies for serious illness conversations (SICs), defined as "a mixture of attributes comprising applied knowledge, skills, and attitudes". Thematic synthesis of 53 included articles produced three themes — conversation resources, intrapersonal capabilities, and interpersonal capabilities — with subthemes describing how each is applied, and a conceptual model (Figure 2) depicting circular interactions between the themes.
requirements: Competencies were sought only in articles pertaining to the Serious Illness Care Program and/or Serious Illness Conversation Guide
constraints: The review states that because it only examined SICP/SICG-related articles, the competencies likely reflect some of the program's or guide's content
target_learning_goals: conducting effective serious illness conversations with seriously ill patients
examples: The review screened 313 records at title/abstract, assessed 96 full texts, and included 53 articles appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute checklists and synthesized thematically

article_title: Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review.
citation: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020
title: Learning outcomes in simulation depend more on scenario design, debriefing, and feedback than on simulator fidelity
description: Drawing on prior healthcare education research, the review argues that simulation effectiveness "relies less on fidelity and more on well‐designed clinical scenarios, appropriate debriefing, and effective feedback", which enhance learning outcomes regardless of the simulation's complexity. It treats low- and high-fidelity simulation as complementary, with fidelity matched to the learner's stage rather than treated as inherently superior.
requirements: well-designed clinical scenarios
appropriate debriefing
effective feedback
constraints: Prior research indicates mixed effectiveness between low- and high-fidelity simulations, with high-fidelity gains not always translating to clinical practice
examples: Included studies used low-fidelity models such as oranges, avocadoes, and a grapefruit ulcer model for initial practice, alongside high-fidelity mannequins and pulsatile flow simulators
key_sources: Anning Naomi, Tehan Peta. (2024). Simulation in podiatry teaching and learning: A scoping review. Journal of Foot and Ankle Research. https://doi.org/10.1002/jfa2.70020

article_title: Teaching heart valve surgery techniques using simulators: a systematic review.
citation: EL-Andari R, Bozso SJ, Kang JJH, Fialka NM, Adams C, Nagendran J. (2023). Teaching heart valve surgery techniques using simulators: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1503/cjs.017921
title: Fidelity taxonomy of surgical simulators: low-, middle- and high-fidelity devices for valve surgery training
description: The review organizes heart valve surgery simulators along a fidelity axis: "Surgical simulators can generally be divided into low-and high-fidelity devices." Low-fidelity simulators use readily available, cost-effective materials (e.g., tubing, boxes, plastic cups) but lack realistic look and feel; high-fidelity simulators replicate actual anatomy using animal or human tissue and realistic procedures, at high cost. Middle-fidelity models (e.g., silicone-over-clay aortic roots) and patient-specific 3D-printed models sit between these poles. The review uses this taxonomy to describe aortic and mitral valve simulators and to frame cost-versus-realism trade-offs.
requirements: High-fidelity simulators require cost and accessibility resources; the review notes many are prohibitively expensive for widespread adoption into surgical programs.
constraints: Low-fidelity simulators "often do not provide a realistic look or feel"; even high-fidelity simulators cannot replicate individual patient variation, unexpected complications, and team communication skills.
target_learning_goals: heart valve repair and replacement surgical technique
minimally invasive and robotic valve procedures
examples: Examples include a sub-US$20 aortic simulator from household materials, a cadaver-based beating-heart model with intra-aortic balloon pump, and 3D-printed patient-specific mitral models from echocardiography data.
key_sources: EL-Andari R, Bozso SJ, Kang JJH, Fialka NM, Adams C, Nagendran J. (2023). Teaching heart valve surgery techniques using simulators: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1503/cjs.017921

article_title: Simulation training in suicide risk assessment and intervention: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Richard Océane, Jollant Fabrice, Billon Grégoire, Attoe Chris, Vodovar Dominique, Piot Marie-Aude. (2023). Simulation training in suicide risk assessment and intervention: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2199469
title: Taxonomy of simulation techniques for mental health and suicide prevention training
description: The review organizes simulation-based education, defined as "techniques that creates a situation or environment to allow persons to experience a representation of a real event for the purpose of practice, learning, evaluation, testing", into named techniques with definitions and psychiatric applications: role play, simulated patient, standardized patient, virtual reality/virtual patient, voice simulation, manikins, and OSCE. Role play was the main type used in the reviewed studies (77 of 96 studies), and each technique is presented with its characteristic use, such as voice simulation letting students hear auditory hallucinations to build empathy and reduce stigma.
requirements: Techniques require appropriate implementation, e.g. simulated patients must be carefully coached, and virtual reality necessitates programming and equipment and software to implement
constraints: The review notes authenticity of psychiatric simulations has been questioned, and some studies reported induction of psychological symptoms for simulated patients without previous training
target_learning_goals: empathy and reduced stigma toward suicidal patients
examples: Role play was the main simulation format across the reviewed studies (77 of 96 studies); virtual reality was used in 7 studies including Coleman et al.'s avatar-based college-student training
key_sources: Richard Océane, Jollant Fabrice, Billon Grégoire, Attoe Chris, Vodovar Dominique, Piot Marie-Aude. (2023). Simulation training in suicide risk assessment and intervention: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2199469

article_title: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound.
citation: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485
title: Simulation as a waypoint to semiautonomous supervised clinical practice
description: The review frames high-fidelity ultrasound simulation not as a replacement for clinical training but as "a waypoint to allow the learner to transition to semiautonomous practice in a supervised, clinical setting." On this account, simulation is best used for acquisition of technical skills and image optimization, augments traditional learning, and, when integrated into curricula with self-directed learning, lets trainees contribute to clinical service while learning a complex skill. The framework draws an analogy to aviation, where simulators are integrated into training, assessment, and licensing.
requirements: Integration into training curricula rather than optional, unguided access
A strong focus on specific, objective, and measurable clinical outcomes with audit and curriculum revision based on learner feedback
constraints: Current simulators focus on technical skills proficiency while ignoring communication, distractions, and clinical management; none address the clinical context in which the trainee will eventually work
target_learners: novice ultrasound operators, including obstetrics and gynecology trainees, emergency medicine and radiology trainees, and allied health professionals
examples: The authors' own training curricula were challenged by simulation-based training and assessment, using simulation to augment traditional learning with objective outcomes and curriculum revision
key_sources: Dromey Brian P. MBChB, MRCOG; Peebles Donald M. MBBS, MD, MRCOG; Stoyanov Danail V. PhD. (2021). A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of the Use of High-Fidelity Simulation in Obstetric Ultrasound. Simulation in Healthcare. https://doi.org/10.1097/SIH.0000000000000485

article_title: Comparison of ultrasonography learning between distance teaching and traditional methodology. An educational systematic review.
citation: Duarte ML, dos Santos LR, Iared W, Peccin MS. (2022). Comparison of ultrasonography learning between distance teaching and traditional methodology. An educational systematic review. São Paulo Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.1590/1516-3180.2021.1047.R.19052022
title: Sixteen-study comparative evidence base on distance versus traditional ultrasonography teaching
description: The evidence base assembled by this systematic review: after screening 5,048 records and evaluating 61 in full, the reviewers included 16 studies of sufficient methodological quality comparing traditional and distance teaching of ultrasonography. Eleven studies evaluated doctors, residents or medical students, one evaluated nurses, and four evaluated physical therapy students in Spain. The review states that "from these, 16 presented sufficient methodological quality for their inclusion", and summarizes each study's design, learners, examination type, intervention and Kirkpatrick level in Table 2.
requirements: Studies had to compare teaching of ultrasonography for healthcare professionals between traditional methods and electronic means through distance-learning, e-learning, m-learning or web-based learning
constraints: One study (Socransky et al.) was excluded due to loss to follow-up of over 50% of initial participants; five studies involved no practical evaluation and relied only on questionnaires
target_learning_goals: improved ultrasound skills to achieve an accurate diagnosis
examples: Included studies taught FAST ultrasound, thoracic structures, pneumothorax, point-of-care ultrasound, musculoskeletal structures, and venous or arterial access procedures

article_title: Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured.
citation: Albarqouni Loai, Hoffmann Tammy, Glasziou Paul. (2018). Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1284-1
title: Six high-quality EBP assessment instruments (Fresno Test, Berlin Questionnaire, ACE tool, Taylor et al., Utrecht questionnaire, MacRae et al.)
description: The review identifies six instruments rated high quality because they achieved "≥3 types of established validity evidence". Four (Fresno Test, Berlin Questionnaire, Taylor et al., ACE tool) measure both EBP knowledge and skills; the Utrecht questionnaire measures knowledge and MacRae et al. measures skills. The Fresno Test, Berlin Questionnaire and ACE tool evaluate the ask, acquire, and appraise-and-interpret steps; none covers all five steps.
requirements: Instruments must be supported by established inter-rater reliability (if applicable), objective non-self-reported outcome measures, and multiple (≥3) types of established validity evidence, including discriminative validity
constraints: None of the six high-quality instruments was designed to evaluate all five EBP steps; the highest coverage is three steps
target_learners: Health professionals across undergraduate, postgraduate, and continuing education
target_learning_goals: Evidence-based practice knowledge, skills, and attitudes
examples: The Fresno Test consists of two clinical scenarios with 12 open-ended questions, needs about 40-60 min to complete and 10-15 min to mark using standardised grading rubrics
key_sources: Albarqouni Loai, Hoffmann Tammy, Glasziou Paul. (2018). Evidence-based practice educational intervention studies: a systematic review of what is taught and how it is measured. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-018-1284-1

article_title: What is a good doctor?
citation: Steiner-Hofbauer Verena, Schrank Beate, Holzinger Anita. (2017). What is a good doctor? Wiener Medizinische Wochenschrift. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10354-017-0597-8
title: Six-category taxonomy of good-doctor attributes
description: The review groups the attributes of good doctors extracted from 20 included studies and questionnaires into six superordinate categories: "(1) General interpersonal qualities, (2) Communication and patient involvement, (3) Medical competence, (4) Ethics, (5) Medical management, (6) Teaching, research, and continuous education." The authors state the categories' "boundaries remain fuzzy" and that several items were difficult to assign to a single category, but found the classification "conclusive and practical useful" as a framework for future research.
requirements: Future research on the concept of a good doctor should consider all six areas of interest, per the authors' recommendation
constraints: Category boundaries remain fuzzy and several items could fit more than one category; other clusters or labels would also be possible
target_learning_goals: understanding the attributes that define a good doctor across stakeholder perspectives
examples: Attributes from all included qualitative and quantitative studies and patient-satisfaction questionnaires were extracted into a pool of equivalent statements and grouped into the six categories by author consensus
