article_title: Simulation training in vitreoretinal surgery: a systematic review.
citation: Rasmussen Rasmus Christian, Grauslund Jakob, Vergmann Anna Stage. (2019). Simulation training in vitreoretinal surgery: a systematic review. BMC Ophthalmology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12886-019-1098-x
title: Gallagher et al.'s six validation benchmarks for surgical simulation instruments
description: The review adopts an article by Gallagher et al. defining six types of validation benchmarks for surgical training instruments: face, content, construct, concurrent, discriminate and predictive validity. Construct validity is defined as "an evaluation of whether an instrument measures what it was designed to," usually tested as the ability to differentiate novices from experts. The review uses this taxonomy to categorize the validity evidence of each included study and to argue that future work should move to higher levels of validity.
requirements: Proving validity is described as a vital part of assessing simulator training
constraints: Face validity is described as highly subjective and difficult to use for broader conclusions
None of the included studies provided discriminate or predictive validity
target_learners: surgical trainees and novices in vitreoretinal surgery
target_learning_goals: valid assessment of surgical skills acquired through simulation
examples: The review categorizes four included studies as providing construct validity, one as providing face validity, and argues Jonas et al. could be argued to provide concurrent validity via enucleated pig eyes

article_title: Acute surgical wound-dressing procedure: Description of the steps involved in the development and validation of an observational metric.
citation: Hegarty Josephine, Howson Victoria, Wills Teresa, Creedon Sile A., Mc Cluskey Pat, Lane Aoife, Connolly Aine, Walshe Nuala, Noonan Brendan, Guidera Fiona, Gallagher Anthony G, Murphy Siobhan. (2019). Acute surgical wound‐dressing procedure: Description of the steps involved in the development and validation of an observational metric. International Wound Journal. https://doi.org/10.1111/iwj.13072
title: Six-stage iterative metric development pattern: scoping review, video capture, task analysis, reliability stress testing, and Delphi consensus
description: The article describes a reusable development sequence underpinned by PBPT principles: a team of clinicians, academics, and researchers developed the metric "using an iterative six‐stage process, culminating in a Delphi panel meeting". A scoping review supplied background perspective; forehead-mounted GoPro video recordings of real and simulated procedures were repeatedly and iteratively deconstructed into steps, errors, and sentinel errors; the metric was stress tested for clarity, scorability, and inter-rater reliability; and a Delphi panel verified face and content validity. The authors state this methodology provides a framework for developing validated metrics and performance standards.
requirements: A metric development group combining academic and clinical expertise (the study used 8 academic and 4 clinical experts)
video recordings capturing procedures from start to waste disposal and hand hygiene
constraints: The task analysis and initial stress testing took the team 2.5 days (20 hours); technical difficulties with the GoPro camera were encountered
target_learners: health care professionals being trained in procedural skills
target_learning_goals: objective characterisation and assessment of procedural skill performance
examples: Videos were recorded with a GoPro mounted on nurses' foreheads during routine wound dressings, with nurses self-selecting and not interrupted or guided during the procedure.

article_title: A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology.
citation: Lee Roxanne, Raison Nicholas, Lau Wai Yan, Aydin Abdullatif, Dasgupta Prokar, Ahmed Kamran, Haldar Shreya. (2020). A systematic review of simulation-based training tools for technical and non-technical skills in ophthalmology. Eye. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0832-1
title: Use simulation to enable focussed, competency-based skills training before treating patients, and strengthen research before full curricular implementation
description: The review argues that the apprenticeship model, in which competence is assumed after a minimum number of procedures, is undermined by inconsistent clinical exposure and by quantity not equating to quality. "Simulation models offer a platform for trainees to improve their clinical and surgical skills, enabling focussed, competency-based training without putting patients at risk." Because most models lack robust evidence, the review recommends that "More robust research is needed to enable effective implementation of simulation tools into current training curriculums."
requirements: Objective assessment of proficiency prior to treating patients, using validated simulator metrics rather than procedure counts.
constraints: The review found poor quality of study design, predominance of descriptive reports, and few studies investigating effects on patient outcomes, so widespread curricular integration is not yet evidence-supported for most models.
examples: The review's evidence base spans 131 studies across virtual reality, wet-lab, dry-lab and e-learning modalities, with the Eyesi family the only comprehensively investigated models.

article_title: Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies.
citation: McManus IC, Dewberry Chris, Nicholson Sandra, Dowell Jonathan S, Woolf Katherine, Potts Henry WW. (2013). Construct-level predictive validity of educational attainment and intellectual aptitude tests in medical student selection: meta-regression of six UK longitudinal studies. BMC Medicine. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3827328/
title: Six UK longitudinal cohort studies of medical student selection and performance (1972–2009 entry)
description: A set of six prospective cohort studies providing the data for the meta-regression: the Westminster Study (entry 1972–1980, with full AH5), the 1980, 1985 and 1990 St. Mary's cohort studies (with applicant as well as entrant data; the 1990 cohort also has an abbreviated AH5), the UCLMS Cohorts (entry 2001–2004, detailed follow-up including MRCP(UK)), and the UKCAT-12 Study (entry 2007–2009, 12 medical schools, largest study, UKCAT and first-year outcomes). Four are proper selection studies with applicant data enabling range-restriction correction; outcomes span basic medical science, finals, MRCP(UK) and Specialist Register entry.

Longitudinal linkage of selection data to undergraduate and postgraduate outcomes via GMC numbers and examination records
constraints: The Westminster and UCLMS cohorts have entrant data only, so selection ratios for them were modeled rather than observed
UKCAT-12 outcomes analyzed here are limited to first-year performance

target_learning_goals: predicting undergraduate medical examination performance and postgraduate outcomes (MRCP(UK), Specialist Register) from secondary-school attainment and aptitude tests

article_title: The effect of virtual endoscopy simulator training on novices: a systematic review.
citation: Qiao Weiguang, Bai Yang, Lv Ruxi, Zhang Wendi, Chen Yuqing, Lei Shan, Zhi Fachao. (2014). The Effect of Virtual Endoscopy Simulator Training on Novices: A Systematic Review. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0089224
title: Use virtual endoscopy simulator training as an alternative to conventional teaching for novice gastroscopy learners
description: The review concludes that virtual endoscopy simulator training, in which novices follow a structured training schedule on a virtual endoscopy simulator, can substitute for bedside teaching for gastroscopy novices. It states that "virtual simulator training method could be considered as an alternative to conventional teaching for novices", based on pooled RCT evidence showing superior independent completion and less required assistance for gastroscopy. The recommendation is limited to gastroscopy; the review explicitly finds no supporting data for colonoscopy.
requirements: Novices receive a structured training schedule based on the virtual endoscopy simulator, as defined in the review's inclusion criteria
constraints: The review concludes no data is available to support simulator training effectiveness for colonoscopy
GRADE rated the gastroscopy completion evidence low due to imprecision and lack of instructor blinding
examples: The review pooled 15 RCTs (n=354), 9 for colonoscopy and 6 for gastroscopy training, comparing simulator training with bedside teaching or other interventions

article_title: Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review.
citation: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4028539/
title: Simulation-based crisis resource management (CRM) training programs for healthcare teams
description: Simulation-based CRM training programs teach non-technical skills — task management, teamwork, situation awareness, and decision-making — that can be safely practiced in a simulated crisis, with the ultimate goal of increasing patient safety and producing better patient outcomes. Eight of the nine included studies used "a combination of didactic and simulation training approaches in teaching CRM principles", and one study used only simulated mock codes. Interventions included high-fidelity simulation, in situ simulation delivered in the clinical setting, and mock code programs, compared against no intervention or didactic teaching alone.
requirements: The intervention must include simulation-based CRM teaching; interventions not explicitly mentioning CRM terms but teaching relevant non-technical skills during a medical crisis also qualified
constraints: The review excluded papers where teaching and/or assessment of technical skills could not be separated from non-technical skills in an acute care context, and excluded studies measuring only simulated outcomes
target_learners: Healthcare providers including physicians, nurses, respiratory therapists, physician assistants, perfusionists, and paramedics, from trainees to staff
target_learning_goals: Non-technical CRM skills — leadership, communication, task management, decision-making, situation awareness, and teamwork — applied to emergency and high-stakes clinical situations
examples: One study randomized trauma teams to simulation-enhanced CRM teaching or no extra teaching and compared outcomes during real trauma activations; another randomized subjects to scenario-based didactic sessions or scenario-based, simulator-enhanced teaching
key_sources: Boet Sylvain, Bould M. Dylan, Fung Lillia, Qosa Haytham, Perrier Laure, Tavares Walter, Reeves Scott, Tricco Andrea C. (2014). Transfer of learning and patient outcome in simulated crisis resource management: a systematic review. Canadian Journal of Anaesthesia. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4028539/

article_title: Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review.
citation: Kyriakoulis Konstantinos, Patelarou Athina, Laliotis Aggelos, Wan Andrew C, Matalliotakis Michail, Tsiou Chrysoula, Patelarou Evridiki. (2016). Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5066070/
title: Single versus multifaceted intervention categorization scheme for EBP teaching studies
description: The review categorizes the educational interventions in its 20 included studies into two types: single interventions (SI) covering a workshop, conference, lecture, journal club, or e-learning, and multifaceted interventions (MI) where a combination of strategies had been assessed. This categorization organizes the review's synthesis and underpins its conclusion that multifaceted approaches may be best suited for teaching EBM to health students.
requirements: Educational interventions that can be classified as either a single format or a combination of formats
constraints: The categorization was applied to studies of EBP teaching for undergraduate health students published 2005–2015
examples: The review lists 13 studies as single interventions and 6 as multifaceted interventions in its synthesis of results
key_sources: Kyriakoulis Konstantinos, Patelarou Athina, Laliotis Aggelos, Wan Andrew C, Matalliotakis Michail, Tsiou Chrysoula, Patelarou Evridiki. (2016). Educational strategies for teaching evidence-based practice to undergraduate health students: systematic review. Journal of Educational Evaluation for Health Professions. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5066070/

article_title: Effectiveness of simulation-based nursing education depending on fidelity: a meta-analysis.
citation: Kim Junghee, Park Jin-Hwa, Shin Sujin. (2016). Effectiveness of simulation-based nursing education depending on fidelity: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0672-7
title: Fidelity continuum of simulation modalities in nursing education
description: The article organizes simulation-based nursing education along a continuum of simulator fidelity, coding fidelity level by the physical equipment used: "LFSs were defined as static models or task trainers primarily made of rubber body parts"; medium-fidelity simulators were full-body manikins with embedded software controlled by an external handheld device; HFSs were life-sized computerized manikins with realistic anatomical structures and high response fidelity. Hybrid simulators combined two or more fidelity levels, and standardized patients were persons trained as an individual in a scripted scenario for instruction, practice, or evaluation. This taxonomy structures the meta-analysis's subgroup comparisons.
requirements: Fidelity level was coded according to the physical equipment used because selected studies did not indicate their debriefing methods
constraints: The categorization does not capture learning-related factors such as debriefing method, reflection, or feedback
target_learning_goals: cognitive, psychomotor, and affective learning outcomes
examples: The 40 included studies were coded as HFS, MFS, LFS, hybrid, or SP, with half of the studies comparing high-fidelity simulators to a control group and ten studies utilizing standardized patients
key_sources: Kim Junghee, Park Jin-Hwa, Shin Sujin. (2016). Effectiveness of simulation-based nursing education depending on fidelity: a meta-analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-016-0672-7

article_title: Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers
citation: Chojnacki, G., Eno, J., Liu, F., Meyers, C., Konstantopoulos, S., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2013). Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://www.sree.org
title: Sixteen-point instructional log instrument for measuring teacher practice
description: Teachers completed 16 online instructional checklists across the school year, roughly one every two weeks, with separate math and ELA versions. The math checklist had seven topic areas (number sense; computation; algebra and function; geometry; measurement; problem solving; and data analysis and probability); the ELA checklist had nine topic areas, modeled on Rowan and Correnti's (2009) checklist. For each of eight randomly sampled students per teacher, teachers indicated topics taught, instructional grouping method, and whether instruction was at the remedial, regular, or enriched level, yielding binary practice measures.
requirements: Teachers complete checklists online for the same eight randomly selected students throughout the year
constraints: The relatively small sample of teachers completing checklists harms the study's power, per the authors
target_learners: 5th grade students in treatment and control schools
target_learning_goals: Measuring instructional practices as intermediate outcomes of an interim assessment intervention
examples: Binary measures included whether a student received instruction on each topic that day, received any remedial or enriched instruction, and received small-group or individual format instruction
key_sources: Chojnacki, G., Eno, J., Liu, F., Meyers, C., Konstantopoulos, S., Miller, S., & van der Ploeg, A. (2013). Do Interim Assessments Influence Instructional Practice in Year One? Evidence from Indiana Elementary School Teachers. SREE Fall 2013 Conference Abstract. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563059

article_title: Testing the Efficacy of a Tier 2 Mathematics Intervention: A Conceptual Replication Study
citation: Doabler, C. T., Clarke, B., Kosty, D. B., Kurtz-Nelson, E., Fien, H., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2016). Testing the efficacy of a tier 2 mathematics intervention: A conceptual replication study. Exceptional Children, 83, 92–110. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916660084
title: Situate replication studies within larger a priori frameworks of systematic replication and report treatment-response rates across studies
description: The article recommends planning replications inside multi-year research programs rather than as one-off studies: "a logical next step for our research on ROOTS would be to conduct a series of increasingly distal replication studies." It reports grounding its IES-funded ROOTS efficacy project in a systematic replication framework aiming to accumulate converging evidence across four cohorts from two regions, and proposes adding rates of treatment response to the replication conversation. It cautions that statistical power and available resources must be taken into full consideration when planning such series.
requirements: Replication series must be planned a priori within large-scale efficacy projects, attending to statistical power and available resources
constraints: The article notes that factors such as statistical power and available resources must be taken into full consideration when planning replication studies in large-scale projects
target_learning_goals: establishing and generalizing evidence of intervention efficacy
examples: The ROOTS project planned four replications of the intervention's efficacy across cohorts; the Boston study held constant dosage, measures, analyses, and eligibility criteria while varying region, timing, and counterfactual
key_sources: Doabler, C. T., Clarke, B., Kosty, D. B., Kurtz-Nelson, E., Fien, H., Smolkowski, K., & Baker, S. K. (2016). Testing the efficacy of a tier 2 mathematics intervention: A conceptual replication study. Exceptional Children, 83, 92–110. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916660084

article_title: Strategic and Interactive Writing Instruction: An Efficacy Study in Grades 3-5
citation: Wolbers, K., Dostal, H., Graham, S., Branum-Martin, L., Kilpatrick, J., & Saulsburry, R. (2018). Strategic and Interactive Writing Instruction: An Efficacy Study in Grades 3-5. Journal of Educational and Developmental Psychology, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jedp.v8n1p99
title: SIWI framework for writing instruction with deaf and hard of hearing students
description: SIWI is a framework for writing instruction guided by three major principles: strategic instruction, interactive instruction, and linguistic competence and metalinguistic knowledge. The first two draw on evidence-based practices with hearing writers; the third addresses the specific language needs of d/hh children. Instruction uses guided, co-construction of authentic text with a language zone for repairing communication breakdowns and contrasting ASL and English.
requirements: Teachers need ongoing, longitudinal professional development with supported practice to implement SIWI faithfully
constraints: The article reports average instructional fidelity of 75% in this study, with interactive instruction principles enacted more than strategic or linguistic/metalinguistic ones
target_learners: 3rd-5th grade deaf and hard of hearing students
target_learning_goals: metalinguistic knowledge of ASL and English
examples: Units begin with establishing an audience and purpose for the writing and end with publication; students collaboratively engage in all aspects of the writing process using strategic and visual tools
key_sources: Wolbers, K., Dostal, H., Graham, S., Branum-Martin, L., Kilpatrick, J., & Saulsburry, R. (2018). Strategic and Interactive Writing Instruction: An Efficacy Study in Grades 3-5. Journal of Educational and Developmental Psychology, 8(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/jedp.v8n1p99

article_title: Impact of Consciousness-Raising Activities on Young English Language Learners' Grammar Performance
citation: Hamidreza Fatemipour & Shiva Hemmati. (2015). Impact of Consciousness-Raising Activities on Young English Language Learners’ Grammar Performance. English Language Teaching, 8(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n9p1
title: Six-step inductive grammar consciousness-raising activity sequence
description: The article structures its GCR treatment as a six-step inductive sequence drawn from Ellis (1991) and Willis and Willis (1996): setting the scene with an authentic text, comprehension questions, noticing via highlighting, hypothesizing, checking hypothesis, and confirmation of hypothesis. Learners "make their own assumption and formula about the grammar point" and the teacher confirms rather than lectures. The pattern operates on written and conversational texts in pairs or groups.
requirements: An authentic text with adequate examples of the target structure
Activities done in pairs or groups rather than individually
constraints: If the teacher explains via a ten-minute grammar explanation, the article states the purpose of consciousness-raising will be lost
target_learners: young EFL learners aged 11–16 at pre-intermediate level
target_learning_goals: explicit knowledge of target grammar structures
examples: The experimental group worked through texts with highlighted target structures, formed hypotheses in pairs, checked them against examples, and had correct assumptions confirmed and summarised by the teacher on the board
key_sources: Hamidreza Fatemipour & Shiva Hemmati. (2015). Impact of Consciousness-Raising Activities on Young English Language Learners’ Grammar Performance. English Language Teaching, 8(9). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/elt.v8n9p1

article_title: The Power of Fiction: Reading Stories in Abnormal Psychology
citation: Janit, Adrian; Hammock, Georgina; and Richardson, Deborah. (2011). The Power of Fiction: Reading Stories in Abnormal Psychology. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2011.050116
title: Situation-model account of narrative encoding: story propositions are encoded into episodic memory within a cohesive situation model, facilitating recall
description: The article proposes that expository and narrative texts are encoded into different memory loci: expository texts go into semantic memory, while narrative texts are compartmentalized into episodic memory. A proposition read in a story is "encoded as part of a cohesive situation model", the mental representation of the story, so the reader more easily recalls the fact together with its narrative context. Readers invoke vivid autobiographical memories and partake vicariously in characters' experiences, producing emotional and cognitive arousal at encoding. The authors used this account to design their story with realistic characters, surprise, suspense, curiosity, and rich description.
requirements: Story characters with whom readers identify
Literary elements such as surprise, suspense, and curiosity
Highly descriptive discourse to facilitate a rich situation model
constraints: Tested only with one story in one discipline (abnormal psychology)
target_learning_goals: recall and recognition of factual information about psychological disorders
examples: The authors wrote an eight-page story, Fugue, embedding 20 target propositions from the textbook about dissociative fugue, and tested it against the textbook excerpt in two classroom experiments.
key_sources: Janit, Adrian; Hammock, Georgina; and Richardson, Deborah. (2011). The Power of Fiction: Reading Stories in Abnormal Psychology. International Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning. https://doi.org/10.20429/ijsotl.2011.050116

article_title: Effects of Concept Cartoons on Mathematics Self-Efficacy of 7th Grade Students
citation: Sare Şengül. (2011). Effects of Concept Cartoons on Mathematics Self-Efficacy of 7th Grade Students. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(4), 2305-2313. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/estp
title: Sixteen researcher-developed concept cartoons for algebraic expressions and equations
description: The study's instructional artifact is a set of 16 concept cartoons on "Algebraic Expressions and Equations", created by the researcher and three mathematics education specialists and reviewed for content and suitability to students' level. Inter-evaluator agreement was computed with the Miles and Huberman formula, yielding "Concordance percentage was calculated 91". The cartoons were used as worksheets, projected on screen, and handed out as colour printouts during the four-week unit.
requirements: Content and student-level suitability review by the researcher and three mathematics education specialists
constraints: Developed for the 7th-grade Turkish algebra unit on algebraic expressions and equations
examples: Cartoons were projected with an overhead projector and distributed as colour printouts; a different group shared each activity sheet's dialogues with the class
key_sources: Sare Şengül. (2011). Effects of Concept Cartoons on Mathematics Self-Efficacy of 7th Grade Students. Educational Sciences: Theory & Practice, 11(4), 2305-2313. https://dergipark.org.tr/en/pub/estp

article_title: The Effect of Simulation-Based Learning on Prospective Teachers' Inference Skills in Teaching Probability
citation: Timur Koparan, Gül Kaleli Yılmaz. (2015). The Effect of Simulation-based Learning on Prospective Teachers’ Inference Skills in Teaching Probability. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031101
title: Use simulation-based environments to teach experimental probability because visualizing variability improves inference skills
description: The article recommends simulation-based probability teaching because it lets learners generate large numbers of random samples, visualize variability, and compare outcomes with predictions, which paper-and-pencil methods cannot achieve at scale. The authors state that "Simulation, when combined with the use of technology, is the most appropriate strategy to focus better on the concepts and reduce the technical calculations" and that the visuality needed for experimental probability problems cannot be achieved in traditional environments. Their findings showed improved prediction and inference skills.
requirements: A learning environment equipped with computers and dynamic statistical software
Learners must learn to build correct simulation models, since incorrect application can change the output
constraints: Simulation errors are a disadvantage; each model is unique and does not generate optimal solutions, and simulation results never match theoretical results exactly, so learners must return to probability theory
examples: 28 prospective teachers completed computer-assisted experimental probability activities over 4 weeks while 27 controls solved the same problems with paper and pen
key_sources: Timur Koparan, Gül Kaleli Yılmaz. (2015). The Effect of Simulation-based Learning on Prospective Teachers’ Inference Skills in Teaching Probability. Universal Journal of Educational Research 3(11). https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2015.031101

article_title: Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons
citation: Teke, H., Dogan, B., & Duran, A. (2015). Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(2), 111-118. https://www.ijres.net
title: Simulation-supported lesson structure: review questions, presentation with simulations, closing question round
description: In the experimental group each lesson opened with about five minutes of questions reviewing prior content and checking readiness, then the subject "was taught with the support of relevant presentations and simulations", and the final five minutes were devoted to questions and answers so unclear points could be identified and re-explained. Simulations were drawn from mebvitamin.com and youtube.com and projected with computer-aided projection in audio-visual quality.
requirements: Access to simulation resources and a computer-aided projector providing audio-visual quality
Four hours per week of course time across five weeks
constraints: The pattern was applied to one seventh-grade science-and-technology unit in a single school
target_learning_goals: Understanding of human body systems (digestive, urinary, nervous systems and sense organs)
examples: The experimental group studied the digestive system in week one, urinary system in week two, nervous system in week three, and sense organs in weeks four and five under this structure
key_sources: Teke, H., Dogan, B., & Duran, A. (2015). Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(2), 111-118. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105195

article_title: Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons
citation: Teke, H., Dogan, B., & Duran, A. (2015). Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(2), 111-118. https://www.ijres.net
title: Use simulations to make science topics concrete and observable when live demonstration is impossible
description: The article recommends simulations where phenomena are hard to observe directly: "Simulation provides the opportunity to demonstrate certain phenomena that are difficult or even impossible to observe and discern in other ways." Virtual laboratory implementations let students learn through trial and error and replay videos whenever they wish, and the conclusion adds that models and simulations can make science-and-technology subjects concrete and make instruction of scientific terms more influential.
requirements: Computer-aided education programs using GIFs and graphics to draw students' attention
Materials that fit individual student needs and learning styles
constraints: The article's own evidence covers one seventh-grade human-body unit; the conclusion states simulations were superior to traditional lecture in terms of students' learning for that context
target_learning_goals: Understanding scientific phenomena and terms that are difficult to observe directly
examples: The experimental group's human-body unit instruction used simulations from mebvitamin.com and youtube.com projected in audio-visual quality
key_sources: Teke, H., Dogan, B., & Duran, A. (2015). Influence of the Simulation Method on 7th Grade Students' Achievements in Science and Technology Lessons. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 1(2), 111-118. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105195

article_title: The Affordances of Fiction for Teaching Chemistry
citation: Randy K Yerrick, Tiffany Simons. (2017). The Affordances of Fiction for Teaching Chemistry. Science Education International, Volume 28, Issue 3. https://www.stemedu.org/science-education-international/
title: Six roles for fiction insertions in chemistry instruction
description: During a pilot year the teacher employed science fiction excerpts in six distinct instructional roles: "Introduction of topics vis-à-vis discrepant fictional events", "exemplars of embodied concepts following traditional instruction", "fictional artifacts for small group student debates", complements to lecture, "venues for follow-up applications after teaching concepts", and "artifacts for student prompts facilitating formative assessments". Each fiction insertion in the intervention year was accompanied by an experiment or activity, and students were asked to critically examine the media even where depictions were scientifically inaccurate.
requirements: Each fiction insertion was accompanied by an experiment or activity, and fictional resources were evaluated and strategically planned for the instructional unit well in advance.
constraints: The pattern was developed and observed in one teacher's college-preparatory chemistry classrooms in an urban Northeastern U.S. high school.
target_learners: high school chemistry students in college-preparatory classes
target_learning_goals: reaction classification (single replacement, double replacement, synthesis, decomposition)
examples: Fiction used in the intervention included Honey I Shrunk the Kids (conservation of mass), Breaking Bad (thermite reaction), Chain Reaction (hydrogen flammability), Big Hero 6 (decomposition reaction), and a The Martian book excerpt (synthesis/decomposition).
key_sources: Randy K Yerrick, Tiffany Simons. (2017). The Affordances of Fiction for Teaching Chemistry. Science Education International, Volume 28, Issue 3. https://www.stemedu.org/science-education-international/

article_title: Efficacy of the Social Skills Improvement System--Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS-CIP) in the Primary Grades
citation: DiPerna, J. C., Lei, P., Bellinger, J., & Cheng, W. (2014). Efficacy of the Social Skills Improvement System – Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS – CIP) in the Primary Grades. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Six-phase social skills lesson model: coaching, modeling, role play, practice, feedback, generalization
description: Each SSIS-CIP lesson follows a six-phase instructional sequence in which skills are first coached, then modeled, rehearsed by students through role play and practice, reinforced with teacher feedback, and finally generalized to other settings. The article states each lesson follows "a 6-phase instructional model (coaching, modeling, role playing, practice/rehearsal, feedback from teachers, and generalization of skills through practice in other settings such as the lunch room or at home)." This pattern structures each 20-25 minute lesson within the 10-week curriculum.
requirements: Teacher-delivered lessons of 20-25 minutes with opportunities for role play, rehearsal, feedback, and practice in other settings
target_learning_goals: Acquisition and generalization of specific prosocial classroom skills
examples: Lessons on skills such as listening to others and controlling anger during conflicts were delivered in three-lesson units following this six-phase sequence
key_sources: DiPerna, J. C., Lei, P., Bellinger, J., & Cheng, W. (2014). Efficacy of the Social Skills Improvement System – Classwide Intervention Program (SSIS – CIP) in the Primary Grades. SREE Spring 2014 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED562704

article_title: Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus
citation: Rina Oktaviyanthi, Yani Supriani. (2015). Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus. IndoMS-JME, Volume 6, No. 1, January 2015, pp. 53-76. https://journal.unnes.ac.id/nju/index.php/ujme
title: Six pedagogical purposes structure technology use during Calculus lectures
description: The study organized Microsoft Mathematics activities during lectures based on three main purposes of using a tool in teaching and learning (Wilson, 2008), presented in Table 1 as six uses: problem solving, calculation, visualization, graphing, exploratory, and confirmatory. For example, "Students utilized Microsoft Mathematics to facilitate the better visualization of a function, the concept that is taught or problem situation", with stated pedagogical benefits such as direct feedback linking parameters to graphical representation.
requirements: Activities must be planned around stated purposes of tool use (drill and practice, visualization, exploration, confirmation)
constraints: Described and applied in the context of first-year university Calculus instruction
examples: Students changing parameters of a Calculus function and observing changes in graphical characteristics; students validating answers in problem-solving tasks
key_sources: Rina Oktaviyanthi, Yani Supriani. (2015). Utilizing Microsoft Mathematics in Teaching and Learning Calculus. IndoMS-JME, Volume 6, No. 1, January 2015, pp. 53-76. https://journal.unnes.ac.id/nju/index.php/ujme

article_title: Students as Game Designers vs. "Just" Players: Comparison of Two Different Approaches to Location-Based Games Implementation into School Curricula
citation: Slussareff, M. and Boháčková, P. (2016). Students as Game Designers vs. 'Just' Players: Comparison of Two Different Approaches to Location-Based Games Implementation into School Curricula. Digital Education Review, 29, 284-297. http://greav.ub.edu/der
title: Situated learning as the theoretical basis for location-based learning
description: The article grounds location-based learning in situated learning theory, quoting Squire: "all learning takes place within a specific context and the quality of the learning is a result of interactions among the people, places, objects, processes, and culture within and relative to that given context". It lists the theory's central claims (action grounded in the concrete situation; knowledge does not transfer between tasks; training by abstraction is of little use; instruction in complex, social environments) and extends social learning and social development theory.
requirements: Rich interaction within a real-like situation, mediated by mobile devices providing portability, context sensitivity, connectivity and individuality
constraints: Anderson et al. (1996) point out that not all those characteristics support better knowledge acquisition and transfer as it is overstressed; some cognition is context-independent
target_learners: students in formal schooling using mobile devices in real environments
examples: The study's designers created location-based interviews and puzzles tied to real sites in their town, embodying situated learning
key_sources: Slussareff, M. and Boháčková, P. (2016). Students as Game Designers vs. 'Just' Players: Comparison of Two Different Approaches to Location-Based Games Implementation into School Curricula. Digital Education Review, 29, 284-297. http://greav.ub.edu/der

article_title: An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education
citation: Katharina Spintzyk, Friederike Strehlke, Stephanie Ohlberger, Bernd Gröben, and Claas Wegner. (2016). An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education. Science Educator, Vol. 25, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?q=An+Empirical+Study+Investigating+Interdisciplinary+Teaching+of+Biology+and+Physical+Education
title: Situated learning account of interdisciplinary teaching effectiveness
description: The article explains IdT's effectiveness through situated learning: knowledge is bound to the situation in which it is acquired and transferable only to a limited extent, so lessons must provide authentic situations, multiple perspectives, articulation and reflection phases, and social cooperative contexts. The authors write that "IdT lessons support the students' practical knowledge by making them aware of other relevant perspectives and situations of application in class and providing them with authentic lessons". This account is used to interpret the test group's superior knowledge growth.
requirements: Lessons must consider potential situations of application in advance and, if possible, make learning and application situations correspond
constraints: Following strictly constructivist theory, transferring knowledge to different contexts is possible to a limited extent only
target_learners: German grammar school students in fifth and sixth form
target_learning_goals: Cross-linked and applicable knowledge in biology and physical education
examples: The IdT unit linked biology explanations of muscle contraction, energy supply and training principles with practical endurance training in a fitness studio
key_sources: Katharina Spintzyk, Friederike Strehlke, Stephanie Ohlberger, Bernd Gröben, and Claas Wegner. (2016). An Empirical Study Investigating Interdisciplinary Teaching of Biology and Physical Education. Science Educator, Vol. 25, No. 1. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110252

article_title: Concept Mapping Strategy: An Effective Tool for Improving Students' Academic Achievement in Biology
citation: Sakiyo, J. & Waziri, K. (2015). Concept mapping strategy: An effective tool for improving students' academic achievement in biology. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(1), 56-62. www.jeseh.net
title: Six-procedure concept map construction sequence
description: The article prints Novak's (2004) six procedures for constructing a concept map: identify and list key concepts, rank them with the broadest most inclusive idea at the top, work down adding more specific concepts, connect concepts with labeled lines whose linking words form propositions, add specific examples below concept labels, and reconsider alternative map arrangements. The article stresses "there is no one way to draw a concept map", which it calls the source of the strategy's power and flexibility.
requirements: Linking words must define the relationship between two concepts so the connection reads as a true statement or proposition
constraints: Identifying the broadest, most inclusive concept can be difficult and requires awareness of the context of the concepts
target_learning_goals: organizing and representing knowledge in a subject area
examples: The article's plant cell example lists major concepts and arranges them hierarchically, connecting concepts with lines or arrows to indicate relationships
key_sources: Sakiyo, J. & Waziri, K. (2015). Concept mapping strategy: An effective tool for improving students' academic achievement in biology. Journal of Education in Science, Environment and Health (JESEH), 1(1), 56-62. www.jeseh.net. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1105286

article_title: The Effect of Discovery Learning Method Application on Increasing Students' Listening Outcome and Social Attitude
citation: Hanafi. (2016). The Effect of Discovery Learning Method Application on Increasing Students' Listening Outcome and Social Attitude. Dinamika Ilmu, Vol. 16 No. 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1411-3031
title: Six-step discovery learning cycle mapped onto the scientific approach and three-phase listening
description: A lesson-level pattern in which the discovery learning cycle of "stimulation, problem statement, data collection, data processing, verification, and generalization" is sequenced onto the scientific approach processes of observing, asking, collecting information, associating, and communicating, and onto pre-, while-, and post-listening phases. The article reports the "sixth section of the core activities ... proven to improve students' English listening scores" in its discussion of the intervention.
requirements: A planning phase defining objectives, materials and media, and an assessment phase, per the Kemdikbud implementation phases the article prints
constraints: Evidence comes from a single one-group pretest-posttest class with no control group
target_learning_goals: social attitudes such as politeness, honesty, discipline, confidence, and responsibility
examples: Section 4 combined data processing with while-listening; Section 5 combined verification with post-listening where students checked their work.
key_sources: Hanafi. (2016). The Effect of Discovery Learning Method Application on Increasing Students' Listening Outcome and Social Attitude. Dinamika Ilmu, Vol. 16 No. 2. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1411-3031

article_title: Two Modalities of the Contextualized Courseware in Three Modalities of Classroom Use
citation: Yavuz Akpinar, Özlem Şengül. (2018). Two Modalities of the Contextualized Courseware in Three Modalities of Classroom Use. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Two Adobe Flash courseware sets for the logic unit: a single space-journey context and a multiple-context set
description: Two specially designed sets of courseware taught the high-school logic unit. The single-context courseware used "circumstances and events of a journey to one of the pl anets", in which students manage a space vehicle, repair parts, and code sockets with logical propositions. The multiple-context courseware required students to interpret components of propositions under calendar, weather, social sciences, science, communication, and arithmetic contexts. Both were programmed in Adobe Flash and developed with mathematics teachers.
requirements: Developed in collaboration with mathematics teachers and aligned to the unit's propositional and compound proposition objectives
target_learning_goals: conceptual and procedural knowledge of propositional logic
examples: Group A studied the multiple context courseware with teacher support; group B the single context courseware without support; group C the single context courseware with support; group D received teacher-only conventional instruction
key_sources: Yavuz Akpinar, Özlem Şengül. (2018). Two Modalities of the Contextualized Courseware in Three Modalities of Classroom Use. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 17(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1165740

article_title: Investigating the Effect of Reduced Forms Instruction on EFL Learners' Listening and Speaking Abilities
citation: Mohammad Saber Khaghaninezhad & Ghasem Jafarzadeh. (2014). Investigating the Effect of Reduced Forms Instruction on EFL Learners' Listening and Speaking Abilities. English Language Teaching, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n1p159
title: Six-stage 35-minute lesson sequence for teaching reduced forms through video-based listening
description: The article's experimental treatment followed a recurring six-stage lesson structure totaling 35 minutes: a pre-listening stage explaining unknown words and providing background, a listening comprehension checking stage, a fill-in-the-blank stage on reduced forms, a stage "Raising students' awareness of "reduced forms"" by focusing on sound changes and rules, perception exercises in which learners wrote similar examples, and paired production exercises speaking on chosen topics using the taught forms. The course met twice a week for 10 weeks.
requirements: Sessions must include both perception exercises (writing similar reduced-form examples) and paired production exercises using previously taught reduced forms
constraints: The pattern was evaluated with intermediate Iranian EFL learners at a private language institution, so its effects are demonstrated in that setting
target_learning_goals: recognizing reduced forms in spoken English
examples: Each 35-minute session moved from pre-listening preparation through comprehension checking, dictation fill-in-the-blanks, explicit rule explanation, perception exercises, and paired speaking practice
key_sources: Mohammad Saber Khaghaninezhad & Ghasem Jafarzadeh. (2014). Investigating the Effect of Reduced Forms Instruction on EFL Learners' Listening and Speaking Abilities. English Language Teaching, 7(1). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n1p159

article_title: Statistical Analysis of Cooperative Strategy Compared with Individualistic Strategy: An Application Study
citation: Tawfik A. Saleh. (2011). Statistical Analysis of Cooperative Strategy Compared with Individualistic Strategy: An Application Study. The Journal of Effective Teaching, 11(1), 19-27. https://www.uncw.edu/jet/
title: Six principles for implementing cooperative learning groups
description: The article enumerates six principles drawn from the cooperative learning literature that it uses as the basis for implementing cooperative learning in the chemistry laboratory: "Individual accountability", "Positive interdependence", "Cooperation as a value", "Equal participation", "Simultaneous interaction", and "Promotive interaction" (face-to-face interaction in at least part of the task). The authors state these elements have "a solid foundation in educational research" and structured the experimental group's group functioning around them.
requirements: All students contribute to and master the material and share knowledge with teammates
Group members' success is linked through shared goals and materials
Goal structures must encourage fair, equal participation
More than one member actively engaged at a time, with face-to-face interaction in at least part of the task
target_learners: university students in general chemistry laboratory courses
examples: The experimental group was instructed and encouraged to function as units in conducting experiments, related laboratory concepts, calculations, and reporting of data.
key_sources: Tawfik A. Saleh. (2011). Statistical Analysis of Cooperative Strategy Compared with Individualistic Strategy: An Application Study. The Journal of Effective Teaching, 11(1), 19-27. https://www.uncw.edu/jet/

article_title: Effects of Early Writing Intervention Delivered within a Data-Based Instruction Framework
citation: Pyung-Gang Jung, Kristen L. McMaster, and Robert C. delMas. (2017). Effects of Early Writing Intervention Delivered Within a Data-Based Instruction Framework. Exceptional Children, 83(3), 281–297. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916667586
title: Simple view of writing: transcription, text generation, and executive functioning components
description: The article adopts the simple view of writing (Berninger & Amtmann, 2003) as its theoretical model, which "specifies three components of writing: transcription, text generation, and executive functioning," each constrained by attention and memory. As transcription becomes automatic, more cognitive resources are available for higher-level processes, which should improve overall writing proficiency. This model motivates the study's focus on handwriting and spelling intervention for beginning writers.
requirements: Intervention targeting lower-level transcription skills to free cognitive resources for higher-level writing
constraints: The article notes a focus on transcription alone may not have been sufficient for students at risk, per tutors' expressed need for more text generation activities
target_learners: Beginning writers in early elementary grades with or at risk for disabilities
target_learning_goals: Handwriting and spelling fluency supporting overall writing proficiency
examples: The CASL early writing intervention used in the study targeted transcription skills (handwriting and spelling activities) based on this model
key_sources: Pyung-Gang Jung, Kristen L. McMaster, and Robert C. delMas. (2017). Effects of Early Writing Intervention Delivered Within a Data-Based Instruction Framework. Exceptional Children, 83(3), 281–297. https://doi.org/10.1177/0014402916667586

article_title: The Effect of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on ESP University Students Critical Thinking and Writing Achievement
citation: Ali A. Qoura & Faten A. Zahran. (2018). The Effect of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on ESP University Students Critical Thinking and Writing Achievement. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p68
title: The 6+1 trait writing model as a rubric-based framework integrating assessment with writing instruction
description: The 6+1 trait writing model is a supplementary means for theorizing and evaluating adequate writing, built on rubrics assessing seven characteristics: ideas, organization, voice, word choice, sentence fluency, conventions, and presentation. It "integrates evaluation with the teaching process" and its "main focus is on using rubrics to provide students with feedback through self-assessment, peer assessment, and teacher feedback at different phases of the writing process". In this study it was operationalized as a method giving students the traits of adequate writing and the opportunity to develop critical thinking and writing achievement.
requirements: Requires rubrics that give students a clear explanation of why they received the score they did, so feedback can guide revision
constraints: The article states it is not a replacement of the writing curriculum but is used with the existing curriculum to offer a structure for feedback
target_learning_goals: critical thinking skills (explanation, inference, evaluation, self-regulation)
writing skills across the seven traits
examples: The study's training program taught six types of paragraph development and two essay types across ten sessions, with students evaluating their own writings and noting difficulties
key_sources: Ali A. Qoura & Faten A. Zahran. (2018). The Effect of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on ESP University Students Critical Thinking and Writing Achievement. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p68

article_title: The Effect of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on ESP University Students Critical Thinking and Writing Achievement
citation: Ali A. Qoura & Faten A. Zahran. (2018). The Effect of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on ESP University Students Critical Thinking and Writing Achievement. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p68
title: Ten-session 6+1 trait training program for ESP pharmacy students
description: A researcher-constructed training program based on the 6+1 traits model, aiming to develop ESP university students' critical thinking skills, writing skills, and study skills for lifelong learning such as communication and autonomy. "The program consisted of eight topics that were distributed over ten sessions (six sessions for paragraph writing and four sessions for essay writing." Each session was 105 minutes alongside one semester, applied over 11 weeks during the academic year 2017/2018. Students were evaluated on their contribution and participation in paragraph and essay writing and were allowed to evaluate their own writings.
requirements: Instruments validated through jury validation; reliability established with alpha Cronbach (0.709 for the critical thinking test, 0.738 for the writing skills test)
constraints: Delimited to first-year students at faculty of pharmacy from Horus University, aged seventeen to eighteen
target_learners: first-year ESP university students at faculty of pharmacy
examples: Students were taught six types of paragraph development (definition, comparison, contrast, classification and analysis, cause and effect, argument and recommendation) and two essay types (descriptive and cause and effect)
key_sources: Ali A. Qoura & Faten A. Zahran. (2018). The Effect of the 6+1 Trait Writing Model on ESP University Students Critical Thinking and Writing Achievement. English Language Teaching, 11(9). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v11n9p68

article_title: The Effectiveness of Multiple Intelligences Based Teaching Strategy in Enhancing the Multiple Intelligences and Science Process Skills of Junior High School Students
citation: Winarti, A., Yuanita, L., & Nur, M. (2019). The effectiveness of multiple intelligences based teaching strategy in enhancing the multiple intelligences and Science Process Skills of junior high school students. Journal of Technology and Science Education, 9(2), 122-135. https://doi.org/10.3926/jotse.404
title: Six-stage MI-based lesson pattern with dominant-intelligence grouping at the expression stage
description: A reusable lesson-level instructional pattern built on Gagne's instructional events, in which students first work in mixed groups and then express understanding in groups of similar dominant intelligence. The six stages are self-reflection, concept introduction, question formulation, SPS-based concept deepening, expression of understanding matched to dominant intelligence, and conclusion. The article states "The characteristic of this learning strategy lies in step (5), in which students were grouped based on the dominant type of intelligence."
requirements: A MI questionnaire administered before learning to identify each student's dominant intelligence type
Activities at stages 1–4 that involve all MI aspects, with stage 5 activities matched to students' dominant intelligences
constraints: The article reports the strategy was applied in junior high school science lessons over 12 weeks and does not claim effectiveness outside that setting
examples: Students with musical intelligence composed music, visual-spatial students painted, and logical-mathematical students planned further study to express their understanding of the subject matter
key_sources: Winarti, A., Yuanita, L., & Nur, M. (2019). The effectiveness of multiple intelligences based teaching strategy in enhancing the multiple intelligences and Science Process Skills of junior high school students. article_title: A Complete Review for Metacognitive, Cognitive, and Social/Affective Strategies as Essential Components of Learning Strategies and Their Relationships with EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Promotion
citation: Mahdiyeh Seyed Beheshti Nasab & Seyyed Fariborz Pishdadi Motlagh. (2015). A Complete Review for Metacognitive, Cognitive, and Social/Affective Strategies as Essential Components of Learning strategies and their relationships with EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Promotion. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.3p.166
title: Sixteen-session three-group learning-strategy training program with TOEFL reading passages
description: The study's instructional element is a quasi-experimental training program in which "The participants in all three experimental groups participated in sixteen sessions of strategy training". Ninety upper-intermediate learners, screened as homogeneous from 130 via a placement test, were divided into three classes of 30, each receiving one main strategy from Brown's (2000) taxonomy — metacognitive, cognitive, or social/affective — taught according to Oxford's (1990) training model. Three reading passages from Longman Complete Course for the TOEFL Test with 50 multiple-choice questions served as the outcome measure.
requirements: A proficiency/placement test to establish homogeneous groups before treatment
Reading passages appropriate to participants' proficiency level
constraints: Quasi-experimental design with three intact experimental classes rather than random assignment
examples: Each session familiarized students with subcategories of their group's strategy — e.g., monitoring, planning, evaluating for metacognitive; note taking, summarizing, translating, repeating for cognitive
key_sources: Mahdiyeh Seyed Beheshti Nasab & Seyyed Fariborz Pishdadi Motlagh. (2015). A Complete Review for Metacognitive, Cognitive, and Social/Affective Strategies as Essential Components of Learning strategies and their relationships with EFL Learners' Reading Comprehension Promotion. Advances in Language and Literary Studies. https://doi.org/10.7575/aiac.alls.v.6n.3p.166

article_title: Applying Sight Translation as a Means to Enhance Reading Ability of Iranian EFL Students
citation: Moslem Fatollahi. (2016). Applying Sight Translation as a Means to Enhance Reading Ability of Iranian EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p153
title: Sight translation as a mixed mode combining translation and interpreting
description: The article defines sight translation, citing Gonzalez, Vasquez and Mikkelson (2012), as "the act of the oral translation of a written text and is a combination of translation and interp reting" — the oral reproduction in the target language of a source-language document for listeners or readers. It is widely applied in translation pedagogy, and the article treats it as a language-teaching tool as well as an interpreter-training activity. Related accounts describe it as requiring quick analysis and creative, exact recreation of a text, and as cognitively demanding.
requirements: Requires a written source-language text that the learner renders orally into the target language for receivers present in the communicative situation
constraints: The article notes sight translation of texts longer than 100 words is regarded as quite challenging for interpreters
target_learning_goals: Reading comprehension ability in English as a foreign language
examples: In the experimental classes students read textbook English passages and simultaneously rendered them into speech in Persian, using about one fourth of the class hour
key_sources: Moslem Fatollahi. (2016). Applying Sight Translation as a Means to Enhance Reading Ability of Iranian EFL Students. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p153

article_title: Effects of Goal-Setting Skills on Students'academic Performance in English Language in Enugu Nigeria
citation: Abe, Iyabo Idowu; Ilogu, Guy Chibuzoh; Madueke, Ify Louisa. (2014). Effects of goal-setting skills on students' academic performance in english language in Enugu Nigeria. New Approaches in Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.2.93-99
title: Six-week weekly goal-setting training package for academic performance
description: The intervention pattern consisted of eighty minutes of training and discussion once per week for six consecutive weeks, delivered in students' own classrooms, while the control group received no training until two weeks after the programme. Sessions covered the concept of goal-setting, skills and special abilities involved, setting motivating and SMART goals, setting goals in writing, making an action plan and sticking to it, and accepting feedback and rewards, using goal-setting strategies and worksheets.
requirements: Participants selected via baseline assessment; those scoring below 40 on the average of GSPI and ATEL totals deemed poor performers
constraints: Delivered within intact classes in two public schools; to avoid contamination, students were treated in their various schools
target_learners: Senior Secondary II students with poor baseline performance in English
target_learning_goals: Improved English language performance through goal-setting skills
examples: Discussion, explanation, demonstration and drilling were used across the six sessions covering all parts of English Language
key_sources: Abe, Iyabo Idowu; Ilogu, Guy Chibuzoh; Madueke, Ify Louisa. (2014). Effects of goal-setting skills on students' academic performance in english language in Enugu Nigeria. New Approaches in Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.7821/naer.3.2.93-99

article_title: Vocabulary Teaching in Foreign Language via Audiovisual Method Technique of Listening and Following Writing Scripts
citation: Ebubekir Bozavlı. (2017). Vocabulary Teaching in Foreign Language via Audiovisual Method Technique of Listening and Following Writing Scripts. International Education Studies, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n5p129
title: Present new vocabulary with simultaneous voice and written script so learners hear pronunciation while following the text
description: The article recommends presenting vocabulary through simultaneous audio and written input: learners see concepts in a written text while hearing their pronunciation, following the script with their eyes rather than reading aloud. The study found learners taught this way attained "a success rate of around double of those subject to conventional methods" in learning speed and retention. The author attributes this to simultaneous use of multiple sense organs, citing the claim that a person remembers 50% of what he saw and heard versus 20% of what he heard alone.
requirements: Video or audio pronunciation of the target text, ideally by native speakers
A written transcript of the pronunciation for learners to follow
Repeated presentation of the material
constraints: Evidence comes from one small experimental study (two groups of 14) with percentage-based descriptive analysis and no inferential statistics
target_learners: advanced (C1) foreign language learners in university language-teaching departments
target_learning_goals: vocabulary learning efficiency and long-term retention in unnatural (non-immersion) environments
examples: Experimental-group participants listened to video pronunciations while following the decrypted written text, repeated four times, then discussed 15 chosen words and formed sentences with them
key_sources: Ebubekir Bozavlı. (2017). Vocabulary Teaching in Foreign Language via Audiovisual Method Technique of Listening and Following Writing Scripts. International Education Studies, 10(5). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v10n5p129

article_title: A Study of Geometry Content Knowledge of Elementary Preservice Teachers
citation: Fatma Aslan-Tutak and Thomasenia Lott Adams. (2015). A Study of Geometry Content Knowledge of Elementary Preservice Teachers. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(3), 301-318. https://www.iejee.com
title: Six principles of activity development for learning-for-teaching geometry activities
description: From the synthesis of qualitative findings, methods course resources, and teacher education literature, the researchers derived "six principles of activity development" guiding the intervention activities: addressing content alongside pedagogy, targeting weak 2-D geometry topics such as quadrilaterals, discussing content before pedagogical practices, sequencing from easier to more advanced topics, using visual aids, and combining small group and individual work. The activities also progressed through van Hiele levels from level 0-1 sorting to level 2 true-false tasks.
requirements: Activities must address content in addition to pedagogical practices in the methods course
Instruction must flow from easier topics to more advanced topics due to varied participant backgrounds
constraints: Developed for preservice elementary teachers with limited mathematics experience in a single methods course setting
target_learners: elementary school preservice teachers in a mathematics methods course
target_learning_goals: geometry content knowledge for teaching, especially quadrilaterals and shape classification
examples: Participants sorted 33 cut-out shapes in pairs, found non-belonging figures in 10 groups, and built a tree diagram classifying polygons, followed by whole-class discussions
key_sources: Fatma Aslan-Tutak and Thomasenia Lott Adams. (2015). A Study of Geometry Content Knowledge of Elementary Preservice Teachers. International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 7(3), 301-318. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1068059

article_title: Effect of Computer Simulations on Secondary School Students' Academic Achievement in Chemistry in Anambra State
citation: Okwuduba Emmanuel Nkemakolam; Offiah Francisca Chinelo; Madichie Chinyere Jane (2018). Effect of Computer Simulations on Secondary School Students’ Academic Achievement in Chemistry in Anambra State. Asian Journal of Education and Training, 4(4): 284-289. https://doi.org/10.20448/journal.522.2018.44.284.289
title: Use computer simulations to teach hazardous chemistry concepts that cannot be safely practiced hands-on
description: The article recommends that chemistry teachers incorporate computer simulation as one method for teaching hazardous concepts, since some contents cannot be taught with hands-on activities due to the hazardous nature of the experiments. Simulations provide a near-authentic environment and "providing a real life experiment for dangerous chemistry practicals".
requirements: Access to computer simulation software and display facilities (the study used teacher projection on a white board)
constraints: Findings come from public coeducational secondary schools only, which the authors say made generalisation difficult
target_learning_goals: Understanding hazardous or impractical chemistry concepts such as gas laws
examples: The study taught gas laws and states of matter with PhET simulations instead of hands-on laboratory experiments

Effect of Computer Simulations on Secondary School Students’ Academic Achievement in Chemistry in Anambra State.
