article_title: Physics Learning Achievement Study: Projectile, Using Mathematica Program of Faculty of Science and Technology Phetchabun Rajabhat University Students
citation: Artit Hutem, Supoj Kerdmee. (2013). Physics Learning Achievement Study: Projectile, using Mathematica program of Faculty of Science and Technology Phetchabun Rajabhat University Students. European J of Physics Education, Vol.4 Issue 3. https://www.europeanjournalofphysicseducation.com
title: Use simulation software such as Mathematica for physics experiments so students can experiment at home or university and learn at any time
description: The article recommends computer-based simulation as an aid to physics experimentation because it removes constraints of physical apparatus. The authors state the Mathematica program "can be experimented at home or at university" and "inspires students to study because it's strange and new for studying", linking this to the Thai education act's aims of autonomous, enjoyable learning. In the study this use produced higher achievement than the physical experiment set.
requirements: Students need access to the simulation program (Mathematica) on their own or institutional computers
constraints: Evidence comes from one small quasi-experiment on projectile motion at a single Thai university
target_learning_goals: physics conceptual understanding and achievement in projectile motion
examples: Fifty students studied projectile motion with Mathematica worksheets while fifty used a physical projectile motion experiment set, then both took the same 30-item post-test
key_sources: Artit Hutem, Supoj Kerdmee. (2013). Physics Learning Achievement Study: Projectile, using Mathematica program of Faculty of Science and Technology Phetchabun Rajabhat University Students. European J of Physics Education, Vol.4 Issue 3. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1052425

article_title: An Effective Teaching Method to Enhance History-Taking Skills for Chinese Medical Students
citation: Simin Huang, Peng Xu, Lie Feng, Chunting Lu & Jing Yang. (2018). An Effective Teaching Method to Enhance History-Taking Skills for Chinese Medical Students. International Journal of Higher Education, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v7n2p144
title: Six standardized clinical case scenarios for history-taking role-play training
description: The article selected and designed six typical and significant clinical cases — chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, acute myocardial infarction, upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, diabetes mellitus, rheumatoid arthritis and acute pyelonephritis — as scenarios aligned with the "Basic Clinical Skill" teaching syllabus. After standardization, they were used to train the observation group in role-play activities, with two cases trained in one course across four weekly one-hour sessions.
requirements: Cases standardized in accordance with the objectives and requirements of the teaching syllabus
target_learners: third-year medical students in a clinical medicine major
examples: Two cases were trained in one course during the 2nd to 5th week of the semester
key_sources: Simin Huang, Peng Xu, Lie Feng, Chunting Lu & Jing Yang. (2018). An Effective Teaching Method to Enhance History-Taking Skills for Chinese Medical Students. International Journal of Higher Education, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5430/ijhe.v7n2p144

article_title: Improving Resilience and Self-Esteem among University Students with Entrepreneurship Simulation Board Game
citation: Prihadi, K., Cheow, D. Z. Y., Yong, J. H. E., & Sundrasagran, M. (2018). Improving Resilience and Self-Esteem among University Students with Entrepreneurship Simulation Board Game. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 7(1), 48-56. http://iaescore.com/journals/index.php/IJERE
title: Use simulation games with lower risk than real ventures to prepare learners for entrepreneurial reality
description: Learning entrepreneurial skills through simulation games offers lower risks and a safer approach to preparing learners' readiness for reality, as long as gameplay simulates reality accurately. The article states learning "can be done through playing simulation games, because of its lower risks and safer approach to prepare the learners' readiness for reality." A board game was chosen over digital apps because it encourages face-to-face interaction without hidden identities, and the game's apparent safety allows difficult emotional content to be expressed legitimately.
requirements: Gameplay must simulate reality as accurately as possible
constraints: Bankruptcy or victimization in a board game is not life-threatening, so spiritual and social-support resilience factors are not engaged
examples: TBG was chosen as a board game rather than an online digital app to encourage interpersonal interaction
key_sources: Prihadi, K., Cheow, D. Z. Y., Yong, J. H. E., & Sundrasagran, M. (2018). Improving Resilience and Self-Esteem among University Students with Entrepreneurship Simulation Board Game. International Journal of Evaluation and Research in Education (IJERE), 7(1), 48-56. http://iaescore.com/journals/index.php/IJERE

article_title: The Effect of the Six Hats Based on Program in the Development of the Pivotal Thinking of Islamic Concepts Students in Hussein University
citation: DR.PH omar salem alkhateeb. (2015). The Effect of the Six Hats Based on Program in the Development of the Pivotal Thinking of Islamic Concepts Students in Hussein University. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.2. https://www.iiste.org
title: De Bono's Six Thinking Hats framework: six colored thinking modes for parallel thinking
description: The Six Thinking Hats, attributed to Edward de Bono, is a thinking-education framework that divides thinking into six patterns, each treated as a hat worn or removed according to the thinker's current mode: white (objective facts), red (emotions and intuition), black (negative aspects and failure points), yellow (optimism and positive change), green (creativity and new ideas), and blue (thinking about thinking and process control). The article describes it as "an effe ctive thinking encourages parallel thinking tool", simplifying thinking by dealing with one issue at a time and allowing thinkers to shift modes without personal threat. The study operationalized it as a training program for pivotal thinking skills.
requirements: Early training so that wearing the six hats becomes a habit, per de Bono as cited
constraints: The hats are symbolic ways of thinking, not real hats; the method is a tool for managing attention across six dimensions
target_learning_goals: pivotal thinking skills including comparison, classification, arrangement, prediction, and summarizing
examples: The researcher built a 20-session training program on the theoretical framework of the six hats and applied it in teaching Islamic concepts
key_sources: DR.PH omar salem alkhateeb. (2015). The Effect of the Six Hats Based on Program in the Development of the Pivotal Thinking of Islamic Concepts Students in Hussein University. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083817

article_title: The Effect of the Six Hats Based on Program in the Development of the Pivotal Thinking of Islamic Concepts Students in Hussein University
citation: DR.PH omar salem alkhateeb. (2015). The Effect of the Six Hats Based on Program in the Development of the Pivotal Thinking of Islamic Concepts Students in Hussein University. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.2. https://www.iiste.org
title: Twenty-session six-hats training program for pivotal thinking
description: The study's experimental intervention is a training program defined as "a set of a ctivities and strategies of training consisting of (20) formed a lecture", each lecture a 50-minute training session. It was validated by 10 arbitrators in educational and psychological sciences, with adjustments made from their recommendations. Training covered each hat in individual sessions, merged the six hats in comprehensive application sessions, and ended with a discussion session and post-test administration.
requirements: Validation by arbitrators before application; sessions sequenced from individual hats to merged application
constraints: Implemented during the first semester of the academic year 2014/2015 at Al-Hussein Bin Talal University
target_learning_goals: pivotal thinking skills and achievement in Islamic concepts
examples: Training on each hat through individual sessions of four sessions, then merging the six hats in comprehensive application and training positions for six sessions
key_sources: DR.PH omar salem alkhateeb. (2015). The Effect of the Six Hats Based on Program in the Development of the Pivotal Thinking of Islamic Concepts Students in Hussein University. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.2. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083817

article_title: Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme for Enhancing the English Language Efficiency among Primary School Students
citation: Tupe, N. (2015). Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme for Enhancing the English Language Efficiency among Primary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 8(2). https://www.e-iji.net
title: Situated, scenario-based learning with multimedia as anchoring context
description: The article grounds MSBLP in situated, problem-based scenario learning: problems are presented before the learner, who plays a role according to the context to solve them. Following McLellan, the context may be the actual work setting, a realistic surrogate, or an anchoring context such as a video or multimedia programme; here the multimedia programme itself serves as the anchoring context, so the learner is completely involved and interest increases. Authentic context and authentic activities let tasks integrate across subject areas and let learners detect relevant and irrelevant material, with constructivist and social-constructivist assumptions that knowledge is actively constructed.
requirements: Authentic context reflecting how knowledge will be used in real life
Problem-based scenarios providing coaching, scaffolding, collaboration, reflection and articulation
constraints: The article warns many interactive multimedia programs fail to account for real-world problem solving by interspersing steps, hints and clues that neatly add up to the correct solution
target_learners: Primary school children in remedial English programmes
target_learning_goals: Meaningful, situated English language learning rather than rote drilling
examples: In MSBLP the multimedia programme itself was developed as the anchoring context, with learners identifying their role to play in the scenario.
key_sources: Tupe, N. (2015). Multimedia Scenario Based Learning Programme for Enhancing the English Language Efficiency among Primary School Students. International Journal of Instruction, 8(2). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1085304

article_title: The Development and Implementation of Learning Material on Exposition Text to Improve Students' Achievement on Bahasa Indonesia
citation: Wenny Silaban, Biner Ambarita & Usman Hadi. (2018). The Development and Implementation of Learning Material on Exposition Text to Improve Students' Achievement on Bahasa Indonesia. International Education Studies, 11(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n11p53
title: Learning material structured from simple to complex with contextual examples, illustrations, and integrated writing projects
description: The material's design pattern arranges content in good order from introduction through main concepts, examples, illustrations and problem examples, moving from easy to difficult texts and finally abstract passages, with contextual examples from daily life serving as models and four projects integrated for guided practice. The article reports that "the projects steps available in the learning material are able to guide the students to learn Bahasa Indonesia" and that contextual examples are used as a model to guide essay writing.
requirements: Examples integrated from students' daily-life contexts; supporting figures, tables and illustrations relevant to the text
constraints: Validated for senior high school Bahasa Indonesia under the Indonesian national curriculum 2013
target_learning_goals: Constructing and writing exposition text with a process in academic reports
examples: Project 1 asks students to identify thesis, argument and recommendation in an academic article; Project 4 asks them to rearrange main and explanation ideas into exposition text
key_sources: Wenny Silaban, Biner Ambarita & Usman Hadi. (2018). The Development and Implementation of Learning Material on Exposition Text to Improve Students' Achievement on Bahasa Indonesia. International Education Studies, 11(11). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n11p53

article_title: Using Online Games to Teach Personal Finance Concepts
citation: Chin-Wen Huang, Chun-Pin Hsu. (2011). Using Online Games To Teach Personal Finance Concepts. American Journal of Business Education – December 2011 Volume 4, Number 12. https://www.cluteinstitute.com
title: Set of six free online games and simulations mapped to personal finance topics
description: The experimental group completed a curated set of free online games and one market simulation, selected for "relevancy, level of rigor, time to complete, and ease of use". Role-playing games from the Doorways to Dreams Fund (Farm Blitz, Refund Rush, Celebrity Calamity) reward desired financial behaviors such as confining spending to budgeted limits and saving regularly; Financial Football, Gen I Revolution, and the Wall Street Survivor trading simulation cover money management, consumer credit, financial services, and investing. Each role-playing game took around 30 minutes.
requirements: Games must cover a wide range of personal finance concepts without difficult finance-course calculations
Assignments submitted by finishing games online or handing in written learning reports
constraints: Games were not customized to the course, so not all scenarios could be referenced back to the course textbook
Only selective portions of Gen I Revolution's 15 missions were assigned due to semester time constraints
target_learners: undergraduate non-business majors in a personal finance course
examples: Farm Blitz, inspired by Bejeweled and Farmville, was ranked the favorite among the assigned games
key_sources: Chin-Wen Huang, Chun-Pin Hsu. (2011). Using Online Games To Teach Personal Finance Concepts. American Journal of Business Education – December 2011 Volume 4, Number 12. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1056617

article_title: E-Learning Strategy for Earning Learners
citation: G. Singaravelu. (2011). E-Learning Strategy for Earning Learners. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, Vol. 6 No. 4. https://www.i-manager.com
title: Researcher-made 50-mark English achievement test with test-retest reliability of 0.89
description: The study's instrument is the investigator's self-made achievement test, prepared on the basis of a blue print and used for both pre-tests and post-tests of both groups. Items are objective type, one mark each, totalling "50 marks", testing methods of teaching English; sample items ask, for example, which strategy teaches spelling to high-school students. Validity was established by jury opinion and reliability by the test-retest method, yielding a calculated value of 0.89, which the author calls quite significant and reliable.
requirements: Administered identically as pre-test and post-test to both control and experimental groups to evaluate English competency
constraints: Content validity rests on subject experts' and experienced teachers' opinions; reliability computed by test-retest only
target_learners: In-service B.Ed teachers in distance education mode
target_learning_goals: Competency in methods of teaching English
examples: The same question paper served both pre- and post-tests for control and experimental groups
key_sources: G. Singaravelu. (2011). E-Learning Strategy for Earning Learners. i-manager's Journal of School Educational Technology, Vol. 6 No. 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1102735

article_title: Alleviating Mathematics Anxiety of Elementary School Students: A Situated Perspective
citation: Sharma, Y. (2016). Alleviating mathematics anxiety of elementary school students: A situated perspective. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(2), 509-517. https://www.ijres.net
title: Situated learning lesson set distributing mathematics content across the model's eight components
description: A reusable unit-level design in which a mathematics topic sequence is distributed across the situated learning model's components rather than taught as formula presentation and board practice. The article reports: "The lessons were developed on these eight key components of situated leaning model - four each on reflection, and technology; three each on cognitive apprenticeship, articulation of learning skills and collaboration; and two each on stories and multiple practice." Reflection was supported with specific prompts, and multiple practice used linear programmed instruction material.
requirements: Lessons in English per the prescribed grade VII syllabus; component-specific supports such as prompts for reflection and programmed material for multiple practice
constraints: Treatment lasted 25 days at 35 minutes per day, which the author calls a relatively short treatment period
target_learners: grade VII students in English-medium schools
target_learning_goals: grade VII mathematics content learned with reduced mathematics anxiety
examples: The experimental group received these lessons for 25 days at 35 minutes per day while the control group covered the same topics via traditional lecture, blackboard problem solving, and home assignments
key_sources: Sharma, Y. (2016). Alleviating mathematics anxiety of elementary school students: A situated perspective. International Journal of Research in Education and Science (IJRES), 2(2), 509-517. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1110268

article_title: Problem Solving Instruction for Overcoming Students' Difficulties in Stoichiometric Problems
citation: Mandina Shadreck, Ochonogor Chukunoye Enunuwe. (2017). Problem Solving Instruction for Overcoming Students' Difficulties in Stoichiometric Problems. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 10, Number 4. https://adi.uab.ro
title: Chemistry content should be presented in a simple, logical and coherent manner to minimise student difficulties in stoichiometry
description: In its recommendations the article states that "Chemistry book writers and publishers should present content in a simple, logical and coherent manner so as to minimise the occurrence of student difficulties in stoichiometry." The principle addresses instructional materials as well as teaching: since the study traced stoichiometry difficulties to gaps in conceptual understanding of basic concepts, well-organised presentation of content is proposed as a way to reduce the occurrence of those difficulties.
requirements: Content materials (textbooks and other resources) designed with logical, coherent sequencing
constraints: Stated as a recommendation; the study did not manipulate textbook presentation as a variable
target_learning_goals: Understanding stoichiometric concepts and solving stoichiometric problems
examples: The study identified conceptual gaps (mole concept, balancing equations, limiting reagent) as the root of the difficulties the principle targets
key_sources: Mandina Shadreck, Ochonogor Chukunoye Enunuwe. (2017). Problem Solving Instruction for Overcoming Students' Difficulties in Stoichiometric Problems. Acta Didactica Napocensia, Volume 10, Number 4. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1164987

article_title: Reading Comprehension and Strategy Awareness of Grade 11 English Second Language Learners
citation: Cekiso, M. (2012). Effects of strategy instruction on the reading comprehension and strategy awareness of Grade 11 English Second Language learners in the Eastern Cape. Reading & Writing 3(1), Art. #23. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v3i1.23
title: Six-stage explicit reading strategy instruction session structure with before-, during- and after-reading strategy organisation
description: The article's instructional programme organised each session into six stages adapted from Wilhelm (2001): how to use the strategy; why, when and where to use it; teacher modelling via Think-Aloud; teacher scaffolding that is gradually decreased or removed; independent learner practice; and integrated use with other materials. Strategies were grouped as 'Before Reading', 'During Reading' and 'After Reading', and the benefit of each strategy was linked to learners' reading profiles so students could see the necessity of strategy use.
requirements: Sessions must include teacher modelling with Think-Aloud and scaffolding that is gradually decreased or removed as learners succeed
constraints: The programme as evaluated lasted three months with Grade 11 ESL learners taught by the same teacher
target_learners: Grade 11 English Second Language learners in secondary school
examples: Over three months the experimental group practised predicting, guessing word meaning from context, identifying main ideas and summarising, with an example prediction lesson using a Predictions and Support chart in Appendix A.
key_sources: Cekiso, M. (2012). Effects of strategy instruction on the reading comprehension and strategy awareness of Grade 11 English Second Language learners in the Eastern Cape. Reading & Writing 3(1), Art. #23. https://doi.org/10.4102/rw.v3i1.23

article_title: Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory
citation: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85
title: Six pedagogical conditions for environmental education of senior pupils through a foreign language
description: The article organizes its forming experiment around six conditions: accounting for age peculiarities, updating the axiological core content of the foreign-language course, didactically justified selection of material, creative use of foreign teaching materials, use of technologies forming intellectual communicative activity, and integrating curricular and extracurricular work. The first condition holds that effectiveness requires "to take into account the age peculiarities of the students of school age". The conditions were implemented together in experimental classes.
requirements: Conditions are implemented as a complex; the hypothesis concerns compliance with the complex of pedagogical conditions
constraints: Validated only with senior pupils in two Kazan schools learning a foreign language
examples: Experimental classes used business and role plays, discussions, vocabulary cards, problem-type texts, press conferences, debates, and an English-and-ecology fan club
key_sources: Aida G. Sadykova, Marianna E. Yashina & Luiza R. Zakirova. (2014). Implementing Environmental Culture in the Language Learning Laboratory. English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p85

article_title: Learning Environments as Basis for Cognitive Achievements of Students in Basic Science Classrooms in Nigeria
citation: Atomatofa, R., Okoye, N., & Igwebuike, T. (2016). Learning Environments as Basis for Cognitive Achievements of Students in Basic Science Classrooms in Nigeria. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(6): 1471-1478. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040627
title: Six-step constructivist lesson format alternating group exploration, discussion, teacher elaboration and evaluation
description: The article operationalized its constructivist learning environment through a fixed 45-minute lesson format of six steps: revision and grouping into groups of 8-10, group activities with "explorations and sharing of ideas", reconvened group discussion facilitated by the teacher, teacher elaboration correcting "students' misconceptions", further development of major concepts with student questions, and evaluation with chalkboard summary and assignments. The same content was taught in both environments; only the presentation differed.
requirements: Teachers were personally trained by the researcher for 2 weeks before the study to create the environment and follow the guides
constraints: The format was applied to junior secondary basic science topics in intact classes in Delta State, Nigeria
target_learners: junior secondary school students in Nigeria
target_learning_goals: basic science content knowledge (living things, human body systems, changes in matter)
examples: Each group was given activities to do and materials to use, based on the objectives of the lesson; students discovered ideas and recorded observations while the teacher moved from group to group
key_sources: Atomatofa, R., Okoye, N., & Igwebuike, T. (2016). Learning Environments as Basis for Cognitive Achievements of Students in Basic Science Classrooms in Nigeria. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(6): 1471-1478. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.040627

article_title: Effects of 6 Weeks Psychological Skill Training on Team Cohesion, Self-Confidence & Anxiety: A Case of Youth Basketball Players
citation: Bülent Okan Miçooğullari, Sadettin Kirazci. (2016). Effects of 6 Weeks Psychological Skill Training on Team Cohesion, Self-confidence & Anxiety: A Case of Youth Basketball Players. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(12): 2761-2768. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041210
title: Six-week multi-technique PST program for an intact youth basketball team
description: The intervention combined team building, goal setting, relaxation, imagery, self-talk, pep-talk, converting thoughts, autogenic training, and progressive relaxation techniques, targeting three skills chosen with coaches: anxiety control, self-confidence, and team cohesion. It "consisted of twenty four sessions totally" delivered during the season, with each skill's processes lasting two weeks. Effects were measured with the GEQ, TSCI, and STAI at pretest, posttest, and three follow-ups (2, 6, and 20 weeks).
requirements: Written approval from the club and institutional review board
Informed consent from participants
Baseline and repeated measurement with validated instruments
constraints: Performed in the middle of the basketball league season, whereas the literature advises pre-season or off-season starts
Six-week duration, while sport psychology literature advises at least 3 months for meaningful differences
examples: Each skill received eight sessions over two weeks; follow-up tests were timed at 2, 6, and 20 weeks after the intervention to assess short- and long-term effects.
key_sources: Bülent Okan Miçooğullari, Sadettin Kirazci. (2016). Effects of 6 Weeks Psychological Skill Training on Team Cohesion, Self-confidence & Anxiety: A Case of Youth Basketball Players. Universal Journal of Educational Research 4(12): 2761-2768. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2016.041210

article_title: Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps
citation: Nadezhda M. Andreeva, Ivan P. Artyukhov, Elena G. Myagkova, Nikolay I. Pak, Zhamilya K. Akkasynova. (2018). Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 47-64. http://www.jsser.org
title: Subject information environment for learning computer science
description: The subject information environment (SIE) is the digital infrastructure the authors built to bring the methodological system to life. Its main element is the Interactive digital course, which includes "the methodological support of academic classes, the communication component, and the interactive check and measurement complex". Structural elements cover requirements for discipline acquisition results, an initial test, types of academic classes, modular and competency-based learning technology, and the schedule of the academic process. For independent work, reproductive, productive and creative assignments are offered at various levels, and MOOCs serve as interactive study guides on individual sections without compulsory result checking.
requirements: The SIE must provide a mechanism for seamless inclusion of MOOC elements into the students' independent work
constraints: MOOCs are used without any compulsory requirements for checking the results of mastering the courses
target_learners: university students studying computer science at Russian and Kazakh institutions
target_learning_goals: mastering computer science content in a blended format
development of information and communication competency
examples: The created SIE allowed drawing up individual learning roadmaps and controlled the process of their fulfilment
key_sources: Nadezhda M. Andreeva, Ivan P. Artyukhov, Elena G. Myagkova, Nikolay I. Pak, Zhamilya K. Akkasynova. (2018). Organizing Blended Learning for Students on the Basis of Learning Roadmaps. Journal of Social Studies Education Research, 9(2), 47-64. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1181973

article_title: Valuing a More Rigorous Review of Formative Assessment's Effectiveness
citation: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/
title: Six-type typology of formative assessment interventions based on who or what leads the process
description: The review refines and updates Black and Wiliam's (1998a) original three broad categories into "six mutually exclusive types base d on who or what primarily leads or takes ownership of the process". The types are student-directed, teacher-directed, computer-directed, teacher/student-directed, teacher/computer-directed, and student/computer-directed, each defined by who appraises or monitors work and who reflects on the assessment information to determine next steps. The typology is used to classify interventions so effectiveness variation can be related to intervention type.
requirements: Interventions must be classifiable into mutually exclusive types based on who or what primarily leads or takes ownership of the formative assessment process
constraints: The article notes the teacher term is used broadly to include any adult in charge of the teaching-learning event(s)
target_learners: students in grades 1-6, including regular education students and students with disabilities
target_learning_goals: improving academic achievement through formative assessment
examples: Figure B.2 defines each type, e.g., computer-directed: digital responses are "analyzed by programmed algorithms which generate an assessment score and/or other feedback"
key_sources: Apthorp, H., Klute, M., Petrites, T., Harlacher, J., & Reale, M. (2016). Valuing a more rigorous review of formative assessment's effectiveness. SREE Spring 2016 Conference Proposal. https://www.relcentral.org/news-and-events/the-essence-of-formative-assessment-creating-a-common-understanding-of-the-formative-assessment-process/

article_title: Effects of Second Step Curriculum on Behavioral and Academic Outcomes in 5th and 8th Grade Students: A Longitudinal Study on Character Development
citation: Top, N., Liew, J., & Luo, W. (2016). Effects of Second Step curriculum on behavioral and academic outcomes in 5th and 8th grade students: A longitudinal study on character development. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 10(1), 24-47.
title: Social information processing (SIP) theory and Bronfenbrenner's bioecological model as theoretical grounding for SEL interventions
description: The study is grounded in social information processing (SIP) theory and Bronfenbrenner's bioecological model. According to SIP theory, "the way a person encodes and interprets social cues in a situation will guide how the person reacts or responds to that situation". The bioecological model includes four defining properties: "process, person, context and time". SEL programs that teach emotion recognition, expression, and regulation skills help children avoid hostile attributions and aggressive reactions to socially ambiguous situations.
requirements: Understanding of the interrelated environmental and societal influences on individuals
constraints: The school environment was the primary focus as potential influence on students' outcomes across 4 school semesters
target_learners: children and youth in school settings
examples: The study applied the bioecological model's four components (process, person, context, time) to frame how school environment influences behavioral and academic outcomes over approximately 2 years
key_sources: Top, N., Liew, J., & Luo, W. (2016). Effects of Second Step curriculum on behavioral and academic outcomes in 5th and 8th grade students: A longitudinal study on character development. Novitas-ROYAL (Research on Youth and Language), 10(1), 24-47. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1167262

article_title: An Approach to Integration: The Integration of Language and Content to Promote L2 Learner Autonomy at the College Level (Un Acercamiento a la Integración: El Aprendizaje Integrado de Lengua y Contenidos para Promover la Autonomía del Estudiante de Lengua Extranjera en la Universidad)
citation: Oliva Parera, P. M., & Núñez Delgado, M. P. (2015). An Approach to Integration: The Integration of Language and Content to promote L2 Learner Autonomy at the College Level. Gist Education and Learning Research Journal, 10, 92-112. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1692-5777
title: Sinclair's three-level categorization of learners' metacognitive knowledge (largely unaware, becoming aware, largely aware)
description: The study operationalizes autonomy as "the ability to justify or make informed decisions about learning" and codes learners' survey answers using Sinclair's three-level categorization of metacognitive knowledge. Level 1 is "largely unaware" (little justification, improper metalanguage, no logical arguments), level 2 "becoming aware" (anecdotes, self-analysis, metaphors), and level 3 "largely aware" (providing alternatives for how one could have worked). The authors applied this framework to responses collected in learners' L1 after oral presentations.
requirements: Survey answers collected in the learners' L1 after oral presentations, so the construct of autonomy rather than interlanguage is analyzed
Raters trained to categorize responses using the level descriptors
constraints: The framework was applied to graduate students at the low/mid intermediate ACTFL level in a single semester Spanish course
target_learners: postgraduate university students learning Spanish as a foreign language
examples: Survey answers after each oral presentation were coded level 1-3; student extracts at each level are printed in the Results section
key_sources: Oliva Parera, P. M., & Núñez Delgado, M. P. (2015). An Approach to Integration: The Integration of Language and Content to promote L2 Learner Autonomy at the College Level. Gist Education and Learning Research Journal, 10, 92-112. https://portal.issn.org/resource/ISSN/1692-5777

article_title: The Effect of Situated Learning on Students Vocational English Learning
citation: Melike Özüdoğru, Fatma Özüdoğru. (2017). The Effect of Situated Learning on Students' Vocational English Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2037-2044. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051120
title: Four-week situated vocational English curriculum pairing in-class authentic tasks with parallel out-class video and e-mail activities
description: A unit-level instructional pattern in which each week anchors target vocabulary in a realistic accounting situation: a balance sheet video with group problem-solving, analyzing a cash flow statement and writing a response e-mail as an accountant, discussing a real local shop's weekly sales report, and computing financial ratios from self-found statements. Students prepared videos outside class, shared them in a class whatsapp group, and gave peer feedback while the instructor provided instructional support. The article states this design "included out-class authentic activities which were parallel to in-class activities", which the authors say minimized misunderstandings.
requirements: access to video-recording tools and a class communication group for sharing and peer feedback
instructor availability to model vocabulary and provide feedback
constraints: students perceived weekly assignments as time consuming and overloaded
target_learners: undergraduate Accounting Information Systems students in vocational English courses
target_learning_goals: communicating about financial statements in English
examples: Week 2: students acted as accountants and wrote a response e-mail to the manager about complicated numbers on the income statement and cash flow statement
key_sources: Melike Özüdoğru, Fatma Özüdoğru. (2017). The Effect of Situated Learning on Students' Vocational English Learning. Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(11): 2037-2044. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.051120

article_title: Communicatively Developing Technology of Speech Activation of Tatar Schools' Teachers
citation: Irina V. Khairova & Nodira M. Egamberdieva. (2016). Communicatively Developing Technology of Speech Activation of Tatar Schools` Teachers. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-451.
title: Six-phase pattern of academic work for speech-action formation in advanced training
description: The article describes a phased organization of advanced-training academic work grounded in the theory of internalization, moving from external practical activity to internal mental action. The printed pattern runs: "1) lection – the phase of prior acquaintance with the aim of the action: 2) practicum – the phase of pattern composition approximate base of action; 3) seminar – the phase of action execution in material and materialized form; 4) lesson modeling – the phase of forming the action as produced speech; 5) examination – the phase of speech presentation; 6) giving the lesson – the phase of action execution in intellectual plain."
requirements: Programming the process of academic work taking into account all internalization phases
target_learning_goals: Formation of professional literate speech actions with set characteristics
examples: The communicatively developing program was realized through these phases on advanced study courses in Kazan, Bugulma, Nizhnekamsk, Zelenodolsk and rural Tatarstan districts
key_sources: Irina V. Khairova & Nodira M. Egamberdieva. (2016). Communicatively Developing Technology of Speech Activation of Tatar Schools` Teachers. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 11(4), 433-451. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1094593

article_title: Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions
citation: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446
title: Provide explanations in simple language and require students to restate them to compensate for listening comprehension limitations
description: Because orally presented explanations of fraction concepts or procedures are typically involved and lengthy, thereby taxing listening comprehension ability, the intervention provided explanations in simple language with short sentences, active voice, and unambiguous pronoun antecedents. Students were required to repeat explanations in their own words while incorporating terminology, and explanations were punctuated with frequent checks for understanding.
requirements: Explanations in simple language with short sentences, active voice, and unambiguous pronoun antecedents; frequent checks for understanding
target_learners: at-risk students with listening comprehension limitations
target_learning_goals: fraction concepts and procedures conveyed through oral explanation
examples: Students repeated explanations in their own words while incorporating terminology such as numerator, denominator, and unit.
key_sources: Fuchs, L. S., Schumacher, R. F., Long, J., Namkung, J., Hamlett, C. L., Cirino, P. T., Jordan, N. C., Siegler, R., Gersten, R., & Changas, P. (2013). Improving At-Risk Learners' Understanding of Fractions. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0032446

article_title: The Formation of Students' Foreign Language Communicative Competence during the Learning Process of the English Language through Interactive Learning Technologies (The Study on the Basis of Kazan Federal University)
citation: Fahrutdinova, R. A., Yarmakeev, I. E., & Fakhrutdinov, R. R. (2014). The Formation of Students’ Foreign Language Communicative Competence during the Learning Process of the English Language through Interactive Learning Technologies (The Study on the Basis of Kazan Federal University). English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p36
title: Six-block pedagogical model of foreign language communicative competence formation through interactive learning
description: The article proposes a model of formation of students' foreign language communicative competence consisting of six interconnected blocks: "linguistic, discursive, socio-cultural, strategic, social, sociolinguistic competence". Interactive technologies are assigned to building the linguistic and discursive blocks through nine elaborated task types (questioning, completion, drill, expansion, gap-filling, jigsaw, matching, odd word, prediction). The model was tested on the forming step via an educational-methodical complex on "Speech practice".
requirements: Formation must be based on the development of the FLCC components: linguistic, social, sociocultural, strategic, discursive and linguoprofessional
constraints: Tested at a single institution (Kazan Federal University) with 54 students
target_learners: University students training as teachers of English
target_learning_goals: Foreign language communicative competence across linguistic, discursive, socio-cultural, strategic, social and sociolinguistic components
examples: The forming step used the author's educational-methodical complex on the subject of "Speech practice", including own elaboration of the training tasks
key_sources: Fahrutdinova, R. A., Yarmakeev, I. E., & Fakhrutdinov, R. R. (2014). The Formation of Students’ Foreign Language Communicative Competence during the Learning Process of the English Language through Interactive Learning Technologies (The Study on the Basis of Kazan Federal University). English Language Teaching, 7(12). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v7n12p36

article_title: Effect of Web Assisted Education Supported by Six Thinking Hats on Students' Academic Achievement in Science and Technology Classes
citation: Ercan, O., & Bilen, K. (2008). Effect of Web Assisted Education Supported by Six Thinking Hats on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science and Technology Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 3(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1092413
title: Six thinking hats technique as a multi-directional thinking framework
description: De Bono's six thinking hats technique separates thinking into six modes represented by colored hats: white (objective facts), red (emotions and intuition), black (logical negativity), yellow (constructive benefits), green (creative alternatives), and blue (control of the thinking process). The technique "provides individuals with specific thought patterns and allows them to observe events from different angles", aiming to separate emotions from logic and creativity from knowledge accumulation.
requirements: Students or participants must understand the role of each hat
A facilitator or structured material must guide hat selection and sequencing
constraints: Achievements in this technique depend on how individuals think, per the article
examples: Applied in problem-based learning with university students (Smith & Cook, 2012)
Used in nursing education to improve critical thinking (Karadag, Saritas & Erginer, 2009)
key_sources: Ercan, O., & Bilen, K. (2008). Effect of Web Assisted Education Supported by Six Thinking Hats on Students’ Academic Achievement in Science and Technology Classes. International Journal of Environmental & Science Education, 3(3). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1092413

article_title: Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers
citation: Geerts, W. M., Steenbeek, H. W., & van Geert, P. L. C. (2018). Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers. International Education Studies, 11(1), 64. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p64
title: Situated knowledge as the theoretical framework for teacher expertise development.
description: The article defines situated knowledge as knowledge that arises from and is connected to interactions between the teacher's material body and the physical environment. It is triggered by the situation, contains all relevant aspects of that situation holistically, applies only to that specific situation, and grows with every interaction. The framework explains why expert teachers act intuitively and effectively, and why transfer of this knowledge is difficult since it is implicit and embedded in the social context of the classroom.
requirements: Long-term iterative process of acquiring situated knowledge through repeated interactions in authentic situations
constraints: Transfer is difficult because the knowledge is implicit and embedded in the social context of the classroom
target_learning_goals: Development of situated knowledge for classroom management
key_sources: Geerts, W. M., Steenbeek, H. W., & van Geert, P. L. C. (2018). Effect of Video-Cases on the Acquisition of Situated Knowledge of Teachers. International Education Studies, 11(1), 64. https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v11n1p64

article_title: Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes
citation: Lewis, M., Steele, J. L., Santibañez, L., Stecher, B. M., Hamilton, L., Faxon-Mills, S., & Rudnick, M. (2013). Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes. SREE Fall 2013 Conference.
title: Site A intervention: online mathematics games and teacher-developed videos for flipped classrooms within a district-wide competency-based system
description: Site A's intervention centers on "the development and roll-out of four online mathematics games and of teacher-developed instructional videos" used to flip classrooms so students watch lectures outside class and receive personalized instruction during class. This occurs within a competency-based model the district adopted district-wide in 2008-09, serving about 651 grade 8-9 mathematics students in one middle and one high school.
requirements: Teacher-developed instructional videos and online games must be available for students to watch lectures outside of class
constraints: The authors judged the games and videos to have too low a dosage to yield a detectable effect on mathematics performance individually
target_learners: grade 8-9 mathematics students in a suburban district
examples: The district adopted a competency-based model for the entire district in 2008-09, providing the context for the pilot
key_sources: Lewis, M., Steele, J. L., Santibañez, L., Stecher, B. M., Hamilton, L., Faxon-Mills, S., & Rudnick, M. (2013). Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED564063

article_title: Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes
citation: Lewis, M., Steele, J. L., Santibañez, L., Stecher, B. M., Hamilton, L., Faxon-Mills, S., & Rudnick, M. (2013). Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes. SREE Fall 2013 Conference.
title: Site B intervention: portfolio-based demonstrations of proficiency with rubric-based grading
description: Site B, an intermediary organization working with four high schools, implements an intervention focused on "portfolio-based demonstrations of proficiency and rubric-based grading for clear and frequent feedback." It applies to social studies and ELA classes in the participating schools, serving about 2,369 students in grades 9-12, with evaluation via matched school-by-grade test score comparisons within district or state.
requirements: Rubrics must support clear and frequent feedback on portfolio demonstrations of proficiency
constraints: For two new schools, comparisons cannot incorporate pre-intervention performance data
target_learners: grades 9-12 social studies and ELA students
target_learning_goals: social studies and English language arts proficiency
examples: Matched within-district comparison schools were drawn for three schools, with a statewide pool for the one-high-school district
key_sources: Lewis, M., Steele, J. L., Santibañez, L., Stecher, B. M., Hamilton, L., Faxon-Mills, S., & Rudnick, M. (2013). Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED564063

article_title: Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes
citation: Lewis, M., Steele, J. L., Santibañez, L., Stecher, B. M., Hamilton, L., Faxon-Mills, S., & Rudnick, M. (2013). Proficiency-Based Pathways in Three Pilot Programs: Examining Implementation and Outcomes. SREE Fall 2013 Conference.
title: Site C intervention: five technology-enhanced, project-and-rubric-based ninth-grade language arts units
description: Site C's intervention is "a set of five technology-enhanced, project-and-rubric-based ninth-grade language arts units that encourage proficiency-based teaching and learning," implemented in classrooms of seven teachers across six high schools, serving about 528 ninth-grade students. Outcomes are evaluated against student-level benchmark assessment data and attendance within the same schools, grades, and years.
requirements: Rubric-based evaluation of project work within technology-enhanced units
constraints: Ninth grade is not part of the state accountability testing system, so state test scores cannot be examined; comparison teachers often differ from treatment teachers, limiting ability to separate teacher and curriculum effects
target_learners: ninth-grade English language arts students in a large urban district
examples: All sites also built out learning management systems allowing teachers and parents to track learning progressions

article_title: Effects of Agricultural Sales CDE Modules on Content Knowledge and Argumentation Skill
citation: Sapp, S. B., & Thoron, A. C. (2014). Effects of Agricultural Sales CDE Modules on Content Knowledge and Argumentation Skill. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(5), 93-110. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.05093
title: Situated cognition as the framework for CDE-based skill development
description: The study is grounded in situated cognition, the idea that "learning is specific to the situation in which it occurs" (Anderson, Reder, & Simon, 1996). Within this framework, learning is a by-product of a learner being engaged within a context where knowledge is naturally embedded, such as preparing for and competing in an agricultural sales Career Development Event. The authors also draw on constructivism, which assumes that "people are active learners and must construct knowledge for themselves."
requirements: Learning contexts must authentically embed the knowledge and skills being developed, such as through cognitive apprenticeships integrated in social and functional contexts.
constraints: The framework was applied specifically to agricultural sales CDE preparation; the authors note the study was not linked directly to a specific agriculture course.
examples: Students learned sales content and argumentation within the authentic context of preparing for an agricultural sales competition.
key_sources: Sapp, S. B., & Thoron, A. C. (2014). Effects of Agricultural Sales CDE Modules on Content Knowledge and Argumentation Skill. Journal of Agricultural Education, 55(5), 93-110. https://doi.org/10.5032/jae.2014.05093

article_title: Getting to the Bottom of L2 Listening Instruction: Making a Case for Bottom-Up Activities
citation: Siegel, J., & Siegel, A. (2015). Getting to the bottom of L2 listening instruction: Making a case for bottom-up activities. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 5(4), 637-662. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2015.5.4.6
title: Six bottom-up listening activities for EFL classrooms
description: The article describes a set of six classroom activities targeting different levels of bottom-up processing: counting words, identifying lexical differences, syntactic predicting, highlighting connected speech, fill-in-the-blanks, and short transcriptions. Each was employed for approximately 10 minutes during three classes throughout the semester, using the same textbook audio as the contrast group. The activities address phoneme recognition, lexical segmentation, and chunking.
requirements: A source text such as textbook audio or authentic video from which sentences can be selected
Teacher guidance to select sentences with problematic sound combinations or connected speech features
constraints: The six activities were used as a collective set, so the study could not determine whether one particular activity is more beneficial than another
The short transcription activity may have affected dictation test results through task familiarity
target_learners: Lower-intermediate (A2 CEFR) Japanese university EFL students
target_learning_goals: Lexical segmentation of the speech stream
examples: Counting words: learners count the number of words they hear in teacher-read sentences, typically counting on their fingers
Short transcriptions: students listen to brief question and answer combinations of 15-25 words and attempt to write what they hear
key_sources: Siegel, J., & Siegel, A. (2015). Getting to the bottom of L2 listening instruction: Making a case for bottom-up activities. Studies in Second Language Learning and Teaching, 5(4), 637-662. https://doi.org/10.14746/ssllt.2015.5.4.6

article_title: Weight Loss Self-Efficacy and Modelled Behaviour: Gaining Competence through Example
citation: Schulz, B. R., & McDonald, M. J. (2011). Weight Loss Self-Efficacy and Modelled Behaviour: Gaining Competence through Example. Canadian Journal of Counselling and Psychotherapy, 45(1), 53-67. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ925521
title: Use video models of similar others to strengthen self-efficacy before behavioural commitment
description: The article recommends showing successful, non-expert models (average individuals who lost weight through diet and exercise) to clients not yet engaged in behaviour change, strengthening contemplation and preparation stages. As the authors note, "friends, neighbours, and family members may be as helpful as famous athletes or stars." This supports early-stage self-efficacy enhancement for mixed-weight groups.
requirements: Access to video recordings of relatable successful models
constraints: Effect demonstrated on self-efficacy, not on physical activity behaviour
examples: A 20-minute Body-for-LIFE success stories segment shown in a workshop format
key_sources: Schulz, B. R., & McDonald, M. J. (2011). Weight Loss Self-Efficacy and Modelled Behaviour: Gaining Competence through Example. Canadian Journal of Counselling and Psychotherapy, 45(1), 53-67. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ930789

article_title: The Effectiveness of Training Program Based on the Six Hats Model in Developing Creative Thinking Skills and Academic Achievements in the Arabic Language Course for Gifted and Talented Jordanian Students
citation: Ziadat, A. H., & Al Ziyadat, M. T. (2016). The Effectiveness of Training Program Based on the Six Hats Model in Developing Creative Thinking Skills and Academic Achievements in the Arabic Language Course for Gifted and Talented Jordanian Students. International Education Studies, 9(6). https://doi.org/10.5539/ies.v9n6p150
title: De Bono's Six Thinking Hats Model
description: De Bono's Six Thinking Hats Model is an approach in which "the human thinking would follow six patterns; each pattern is represented by one hat." Learners "put on one hat at a time in one situation and put another on as the situation changes," with each hat representing one pattern of thinking. In this study, students expressed what they learned while reading according to a specified hat's color and meaning — for example, the black hat for analysis and criticism, the yellow hat for optimism, and the green hat for generating new ideas beyond the text.
requirements: Training in the rules of applying the Six Hats Model and the meaning of each hat before use
constraints: The model was applied to gifted seventh-grade Arabic language students; effectiveness at other levels was not established in this study
examples: The experimental group completed 29 training sessions over six weeks (5.25 hours per week) applying the hats to Arabic units 11 and 12

article_title: Reading and Deafness: State of the Evidence and Implications for Research and Practice
citation: Beverly Trezek and Connie Mayer. (2019). Reading and Deafness: State of the Evidence and Implications for Research and Practice. Educ. Sci. 2019, 9, 216. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci9030216
title: Simple View of Reading: reading comprehension is the product of decoding and language comprehension
description: The SVR is a model in which reading comprehension (R) is the product of decoding (D) and language comprehension (C), expressed as R = D × C, with each variable ranging from 0 to 1. The article states that "both decoding and language comprehension are necessary components, but alone are not sufficient, for reading comprehension to occur." The review uses the SVR as its organizing framework for interpreting evidence in reading and deafness and for evaluating the qualitative similarity hypothesis.
requirements: Both decoding and language comprehension must be present; if either is nil, reading comprehension is zero
constraints: The article notes the SVR "is neither a full theory of reading nor a blueprint for instruction" and has been critiqued for focusing on reader-based variables and not accounting for text variation
target_learners: deaf and hearing learners across grade levels
key_sources: Beverly Trezek and Connie Mayer. (2019). Reading and Deafness: State of the Evidence and Implications for Research and Practice. Educ. Sci. 2019, 9, 216. https://doi.org/10.3390/educsci9030216

article_title: Bridging the gap in adrenal crisis management: a pilot simulation-based pre post educational intervention to improve resident knowledge.
citation: Resnick Ortal, Matalka Leen, Foster Christy. (2026). Bridging the gap in adrenal crisis management: a pilot simulation-based pre post educational intervention to improve resident knowledge. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09924-y
title: Use high-fidelity simulation with structured advocacy-inquiry debriefing to teach rare high-acuity clinical scenarios
description: The article used a 45-minute mannequin-based adrenal crisis scenario followed by a 15-minute structured debriefing using advocacy-inquiry techniques, grounded in Kolb's Experiential Learning Theory. The debriefing "emphasized reflective observation and conceptualization following the concrete clinical experience" and focused on four domains including recognition, stress-dose glucocorticoids, electrolytes, and sick-day management. Simulation offers a controlled, experiential environment for rare, high-acuity scenarios trainees infrequently encounter.
requirements: Faculty facilitators trained in advocacy-inquiry debriefing methodology
A high-fidelity mannequin and standardized emergency care environment
constraints: Single-center pilot with small sample; no comparator intervention, so gains from less resource-intensive approaches cannot be ruled out
target_learning_goals: Recognition and acute management of adrenal crisis
Outpatient sick-day management education for families
examples: The scenario involved a previously healthy 14-year-old female with diagnostic uncertainty and dynamic physiologic deterioration if fluids were delayed
key_sources: Resnick Ortal, Matalka Leen, Foster Christy. (2026). Bridging the gap in adrenal crisis management: a pilot simulation-based pre post educational intervention to improve resident knowledge. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09924-y

article_title: Simulated-patient evaluations during formative interviews predict exam performance better than self-reported empathy and the ability to recognize others' emotions.
citation: Carrard Valerie, Bourquin Céline, Félix Sylvie, Viret Francine, Takeuchi Yusuke L., Berney Alexandre. (2026). Simulated-patient evaluations during formative interviews predict exam performance better than self-reported empathy and the ability to recognize others’ emotions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09934-w
title: Use structured simulated-patient programs within competency-based curricula to help identify students struggling to meet communication competency standards
description: The article recommends integrating structured simulated-patient programs not only as formative training but as contributors to competency-based assessment. It states these findings "underscore the practical value of structured simulated‑patient programs within competency‑based medical curricula, as they may help identify students who have difficulty attaining required communication competencies." Because simulated-patient evaluations predicted later OSCE performance, early ratings could flag students needing pedagogical support before qualifying exams.
requirements: Simulated patients must be comprehensively trained, including theoretical introductions, role-plays, feedback giving skills, debriefing, and regular evaluations, as done at the University of Lausanne
constraints: The study was conducted at a single institution, which may limit generalizability to other medical schools or cultural contexts
Translating early identification into action is complex because causes of underperformance vary substantially across students, requiring tailored interventions
examples: The ETMED-L project collected simulated-patient evaluations during mandatory formative interviews in curriculum years 3 and 5 using a standardized form including the JSPPPE and the OSCE communication skills grid
key_sources: Carrard Valerie, Bourquin Céline, Félix Sylvie, Viret Francine, Takeuchi Yusuke L., Berney Alexandre. (2026). Simulated-patient evaluations during formative interviews predict exam performance better than self-reported empathy and the ability to recognize others’ emotions. citation: Carrard Valerie, Bourquin Céline, Félix Sylvie, Viret Francine, Takeuchi Yusuke L., Berney Alexandre. (2026). Simulated-patient evaluations during formative interviews predict exam performance better than self-reported empathy and the ability to recognize others’ emotions. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09934-w
title: Standardized simulated-patient evaluation form combining the JSPPPE, a satisfaction item, and the OSCE communication skills grid
description: A paper-pencil form developed for this study was completed by simulated patients after each formative interview. It "included the 5-item Jefferson Scale of Patient Perception of Physician Empathy (JSPPPE), a single item regarding general satisfaction with the communication, and the communication skills grid used during the OSCEs" with four items covering response to patient feelings and needs, interview structure, verbal expression, and non-verbal expression rated 1 to 5. Reusing the OSCE grid aligns the formative and exam rating schemes.
requirements: Simulated patients complete the form after each formative interview as part of a structured program
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in formative communication skills interviews

article_title: Simulation-Based Radiology Training for Medical Technical Assistant Trainees: Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Witti MJ, Coleman J-C, Richters C, Schönberger J, de Ruijter M-A, Stortz A, Bauer M, Kiriakidou R, Stadler M. (2026). Simulation-Based Radiology Training for Medical Technical Assistant Trainees: Quasi-Experimental Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/97489
title: High-quality, feedback-rich simulations can serve as effective equalizers supporting procedural knowledge acquisition across learners with varying perceived task relevance
description: The article's practical implication is that "high-quality, feedback-rich simulations can be effective equalizers, supporting procedural knowledge acquisition even among learners who perceive the content as less directly relevant to their career." For heterogeneous cohorts, this means "simulation-based training need not be restricted to those with the most obvious career alignment." This principle is grounded in the finding that learning gains were equivalent across specializations despite large differences in perceived utility value.
requirements: The simulation must be well designed, engaging, and instructionally scaffolded, with features such as interactive hands-on tasks, immediate feedback, and clinical authenticity.
constraints: Evidence is limited to short-term procedural learning in a single session; longer-term retention and clinical transfer remain beyond the study's scope.
target_learners: Medical technical assistant trainees in radiology and laboratory medicine specializations
target_learning_goals: Procedural knowledge of the CT contrast injection workflow
examples: Both radiology-specialized (MTRA) and laboratory-specialized (MTLA) trainees benefited substantially and equally from the simulation despite the latter perceiving it as less relevant to their future work.
key_sources: Witti MJ, Coleman J-C, Richters C, Schönberger J, de Ruijter M-A, Stortz A, Bauer M, Kiriakidou R, Stadler M. (2026). Simulation-Based Radiology Training for Medical Technical Assistant Trainees: Quasi-Experimental Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/97489

article_title: Trainee Access to Major Procedures in an Academic Emergency Department: Are We Doing Enough?
citation: Jones C. L., Rienks S., Verbossche F. (2026). Trainee Access to Major Procedures in an Academic Emergency Department: Are We Doing Enough? Emergency Medicine Australasia. https://doi.org/10.1111/1742-6723.70372
title: Incorporate simulation into education programmes for infrequently performed procedures
description: The article recommends simulation as a complement to clinical exposure where procedure volumes are too low for competency development. It notes "Simulation is an option for procedures performed less frequently" but cautions it "works best when incorporated into a curriculum based on defined objectives". The authors' own data showing low trainee exposure motivated this recommendation for their department.
requirements: Simulation must be incorporated into a curriculum based on defined objectives
constraints: Simulation has disadvantages including resourcing and difficulty replacing real-life patient experiences such as consent and responding to patient cues
target_learning_goals: Procedural competency in infrequently performed emergency procedures
examples: The department's data highlighted the need to introduce simulated experiences for several procedures beyond those ACEM already accepts (thoracotomy, pericardiocentesis)
key_sources: Jones C. L., Rienks S., Verbossche F. (2026). Trainee Access to Major Procedures in an Academic Emergency Department: Are We Doing Enough? Emergency Medicine Australasia. https://doi.org/10.1111/1742-6723.70372

article_title: Medical students' experiences of mixed-reality-based anatomy instruction in a non-cadaveric curriculum: a qualitative case study.
citation: Lin Joseph, Ghazi Sarmad, Kuss Ethan, Shehata Sarah. (2026). Medical students’ experiences of mixed-reality-based anatomy instruction in a non-cadaveric curriculum: a qualitative case study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09881-6
title: Situated Learning Theory as an analytic framework for mixed-reality anatomy instruction
description: The study was informed by Situated Learning Theory, which "conceptualizes learning as shaped by participation, context, and social interaction." This framework sensitized the analysis to students' descriptions of shared viewing, instructor guidance, collaborative meaning-making, and context-dependent engagement while learning anatomy through HoloLens 2. In the discussion, the authors interpret HoloAnatomy as functioning not only as a visualization tool but also as a medium for guided participation and shared meaning-making.
requirements: Analysis must attend to the social and instructional conditions surrounding the technology, not only visual novelty
constraints: Applied here to a single bounded case of mixed-reality anatomy instruction at one osteopathic medical school
target_learning_goals: collaborative anatomical understanding through shared viewing and instructor guidance
key_sources: Lin Joseph, Ghazi Sarmad, Kuss Ethan, Shehata Sarah. (2026). Medical students’ experiences of mixed-reality-based anatomy instruction in a non-cadaveric curriculum: a qualitative case study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09881-6

article_title: The role of problem-solving and decision-making skills in linking critical thinking dispositions to perceptions of success.
citation: Akçay Ahmet Oğuz, Karahan Engin, Kara Ahmet. (2026). The role of problem-solving and decision-making skills in linking critical thinking dispositions to perceptions of success. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04918-3
title: Educators should implement curricula that simultaneously develop critical thinking, problem-solving and decision-making skills
description: Because the study found these competencies are interconnected and jointly predict students' perceptions of success, the authors encourage educators to "implement comprehensive curricula that simultaneously develop these skills to prepare students for real-world challenges". The recommendation rests on the correlational mediation findings rather than on an intervention test.
requirements: Curricula must address critical thinking, problem-solving and decision-making together rather than in isolation
constraints: The supporting evidence is cross-sectional and correlational; the mediating roles should be viewed as statistical associations rather than proof of causality
examples: The study administered four validated self-report scales to 285 third- and fourth-grade students and tested the parallel mediation model with path analysis and bootstrapping
key_sources: Akçay Ahmet Oğuz, Karahan Engin, Kara Ahmet. (2026). The role of problem-solving and decision-making skills in linking critical thinking dispositions to perceptions of success. BMC Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40359-026-04918-3

article_title: Dynamic CBME in action: rule-based digital case-based learning to evaluate antibiotic-stewardship reasoning in MBBS learners.
citation: Sunil Kumar D, Sucheta Dandekar, G. Hari Prakash. (2026). Dynamic CBME in action: rule-based digital case-based learning to evaluate antibiotic-stewardship reasoning in MBBS learners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09810-7
title: Brief single-session digital interventions are best treated as feasibility evidence, not effectiveness evidence, for complex clinical reasoning outcomes
description: The authors argue that a single 45-60 minute educational exposure is unlikely to shift a complex cognitive outcome like SCT-measured reasoning, citing evidence that technology-enhanced interventions produce larger gains with "repeated, spaced exposures rather than a single encounter". They recommend interpreting such results as preliminary feasibility and acceptability evidence rather than effectiveness evidence.
requirements: Controlled, multisite, longitudinal studies are needed to confirm preliminary findings
constraints: The single-group pre-post design without a control group means causal attribution to the DCBL intervention is not warranted
examples: Three micro-cases with two to three decision nodes each, completed in a single 45-60 minute sitting
key_sources: Sunil Kumar D, Sucheta Dandekar, G. Hari Prakash. (2026). Dynamic CBME in action: rule-based digital case-based learning to evaluate antibiotic-stewardship reasoning in MBBS learners. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09810-7

article_title: Application of the modified Mini-CEX combined with the SBAR model in the experimental teaching of health assessment course: a quasi-experimental study.
citation: Wang Le, Wang Miao, Zhang Feng-ling, Liu Ning, Wang Hui-xue, Yu Miao, Chen Shenglin. (2026). Application of the modified Mini-CEX combined with the SBAR model in the experimental teaching of health assessment course: a quasi-experimental study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-10086-0
title: Classroom scenario simulation plus clinical apprenticeship teaching sequence
description: The intervention's teaching process "included classroom scenario simulation and clinical apprenticeship." In classroom sessions, teachers demonstrate the modified Mini-CEX and SBAR, then students in six-member groups complete case studies with role-playing and SBAR-based reporting, followed by faculty assessment and feedback. In clinical probation, students "were required to proactively apply the SBAR model in practice to communicate effectively with mentors," with instructors providing timely feedback and students sharing experiences afterward.
requirements: A clinical case bank derived from real cases and collaboration between nursing faculty and clinical specialists
examples: Case bank covered emergency, internal medicine, and surgery diseases such as drug-allergic shock, lobar pneumonia, and acute myocardial infarction

article_title: The Role of the Simulation in Supporting Newly Graduated Nurses in Their First 5 Months of Working Transition: Findings From a Mixed-Method Study.
citation: Mesaglio, M., Dentice, S., Grassetti, L., Achil, I., Bernardinis, A., Caruzzo, D., Inserra, A., Mansutti, I., Mattiussi, E., Menegoz, S., Piani, T., Vanzo, E., Chiappinotto, S., Palese, A. Journal of Clinical Nursing, 35(10), 4210–4220. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocn.17617
title: Simulation for newly graduated nurses should be accessible, intensity-modulated, unit-integrated, and part of a comprehensive supportive strategy
description: The study identifies four conditions under which simulation in the transition phase is effective: it should be "fully accessible to NGRNs", delivered "from high (during the work initiation phase) to lower intensity (in the following months)", "integrated within each unit", and offered "as an element of a comprehensive strategy creating a supportive environment welcoming new graduate". These conditions emerged from preceptor focus groups and are recommended to ensure effective learning targeted at transition challenges.
requirements: Simulation must be accessible to NGRNs, including structured and unstructured opportunities
Simulation intensity should be modulated from high at work initiation to lower in following months
Simulation should be integrated within each operational unit
Simulation should be embedded in a comprehensive supportive strategy including preceptorship
constraints: Effectiveness conditions were identified through preceptor perceptions rather than tested experimentally
target_learners: newly graduated registered nurses in their first 5 months of work
target_learning_goals: development of clinical and transversal competencies during work transition
examples: Preceptors recommended integrating the simulation centre within operational units to develop an educational alliance allowing skills application in the real working environment

article_title: Improving operational preparedness for armored vehicle casualty rescue: effectiveness of simulation-based training with a novel extrication device.
citation: Segura-Fornieles, A. J., Márquez-Hernández, V. V., García-Viola, A., Rodríguez-García, M. C., & Garrido-Molina, J. M. (2026). Improving operational preparedness for armored vehicle casualty rescue: effectiveness of simulation-based training with a novel extrication device. Frontiers in Public Health, 14. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpubh.2026.1910210
title: Structured simulation-based device-specific extrication training should be incorporated into standard military medical education curricula
description: The article recommends incorporating structured, device-specific extrication training into standard military medical education curricula to institutionalize skills ahead of deployment. The training intervention included a two-hour theoretical-practical session with videos, XABCDE training, hands-on practice "following the manufacturer's recommendations and steps," and "individualized performance feedback" during practical training.
requirements: A structured training script and protocol reviewed and agreed upon by all members of the research team
Training conducted by a qualified military nurse
Individualized performance feedback during practical training
constraints: The quasi-experimental one-group pretest-posttest design and absence of a control group limit causal inference
The controlled training environment may not fully reflect the stressful and variable conditions of a real accident scenario
target_learners: Active military personnel in armored infantry battalions
target_learning_goals: Correct use of the Snaid® rapid extrication device for casualty rescue from armored vehicles
Procedural performance of XABCDE assessment and spinal motion restriction during extrication
examples: The study divided 156 participants into groups of 4 following actual crew configuration of battle tanks and monitored device placement in two turret positions
key_sources: Segura-Fornieles, A. J., Márquez-Hernández, V. V., García-Viola, A., Rodríguez-García, M. C., & Garrido-Molina, J. M. (2026).
