article_title: Bridging the gap in pre-hospital maternity care: emergency personnel's knowledge and clinical skills in managing obstetric emergencies.
citation: Shahbazi Sighaldeh S, Norollahpour Z, Nekoolaltak M, Khosravi S, Saberian P, Rahimi Foroushani A, Shateranni F. (2026). Bridging the gap in pre-hospital maternity care: emergency personnel’s knowledge and clinical skills in managing obstetric emergencies. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09636-3
title: Integrate simulation-based obstetric emergency training into continuing professional education for pre-hospital personnel
description: The article recommends that pre-hospital emergency personnel receive ongoing simulation-based training in obstetric emergencies because such emergencies are high-acuity but low-frequency, causing knowledge and skills to decay without regular practice. The article states that "regular simulation-based in-service training allows P-HEP to practice technical and communication skills in realistic scenarios without compromising patient safety." This addresses identified gaps in childbirth and postpartum hemorrhage management.
requirements: Trained simulation facilitators and realistic obstetric emergency scenarios
Integration into continuing professional education programs
constraints: Obstetric emergencies occur too infrequently for providers to maintain competency without ongoing simulation-based education
target_learners: Pre-hospital emergency personnel (paramedics, emergency medical technicians, nurses, anesthetists)
target_learning_goals: Managing obstetric emergencies including childbirth and postpartum hemorrhage
Maintaining clinical competency in rarely encountered emergencies
examples: The study identified the lowest OSCE scores in managing complicated child delivery (33.3%) and postpartum bleeding (23.3%), motivating the recommendation
key_sources: Shahbazi Sighaldeh S, Norollahpour Z, Nekoolaltak M, Khosravi S, Saberian P, Rahimi Foroushani A, Shateranni F. (2026). article_title: Advancing health equity through simulation-based education for pre-health students.
citation: Tomobi Oluwakemi, DeFazio Sarah, Lin Dena, Brashear Alyssa, Smart Klint, Epps Gregory, Woodberry Kerri. (2026). Advancing health equity through simulation-based education for pre-health students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354377
title: Incorporate hands-on clinical simulation as an adjunct to lecture to make basic science relevant for pre-health students.
description: The article recommends that undergraduate curricula incorporate experiential simulation opportunities alongside traditional lecture. The authors state that "undergraduate curricula can incorporate similar experiential opportunities to further demonstrate the relevance of basic science topics to healthcare," positioning simulation as a practical, engaging complement that connects classroom content to clinical application for pre-health learners.
requirements: Access to a simulation center with manikins, equipment, and trained facilitators
Scenarios with learning objectives aligned to underlying basic science concepts
A structured debriefing process (the authors used the PEARLS framework)
constraints: Evidence comes from a single-institution, single-group pretest-posttest study without a comparison group
The authors note a single simulation day may not be enough for certain concepts, which may benefit from long-term study
target_learning_goals: clinical decision-making and emergency response skills
confidence in clinical identification and procedures
examples: A one-day program with four scenarios (cardiac arrest, opioid overdose, malignant hyperthermia, stroke) following a traditional lecture, with team-based role-play and facilitator feedback
key_sources: Tomobi Oluwakemi, DeFazio Sarah, Lin Dena, Brashear Alyssa, Smart Klint, Epps Gregory, Woodberry Kerri. (2026). Advancing health equity through simulation-based education for pre-health students. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0354377

article_title: Virtual reality simulation for tracheostomy emergencies: a randomized educational intervention.
citation: Talan JW, Adelman MH, Forster M, Reuland B, Kaufman B, Hafiz A, Nair SS, Kramer VE, Mendelson JS, Andriotis A. (2026). Virtual reality simulation for tracheostomy emergencies: a randomized educational intervention. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.1093/atsscholar/aapag023
title: Immersive VR tracheostomy emergency curriculum with SimX cases and novel modular task trainer
description: An immersive VR curriculum of 4 tracheostomy emergency cases (cuff leak, occluded inner cannula, accidental decannulation, false passage) programmed in the SimX platform for the Oculus Quest 2, preceded by a 15-minute Sandbox orientation to "eliminate this cognitive load from the cases". Skills were assessed on a novel modular task trainer with 4 anatomical attachments developed with Pulse Medical Demonstration Models.
requirements: 15-minute VR environment orientation before cases
1:1 faculty debriefing after each case
constraints: Cases remain available within the SimX catalog; two additional curriculum cases (chronic decannulation, TI fistula) were not yet assessed
target_learning_goals: recognition and management of tracheostomy emergencies
examples: Each case was debriefed in-person by a simulation center faculty member with a 1:1 ratio
key_sources: Talan JW, Adelman MH, Forster M, Reuland B, Kaufman B, Hafiz A, Nair SS, Kramer VE, Mendelson JS, Andriotis A. (2026). Virtual reality simulation for tracheostomy emergencies: a randomized educational intervention. ATS Scholar. https://doi.org/10.1093/atsscholar/aapag023

article_title: Feasibility of Self-Directed Learning of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills Using Interactive Video in SimZone 0: Pilot Randomized Educational Trial.
citation: Trampal Ramos Á, Charneco Salguero G, González-Tejerina B, Moreno-Palacios E, Leal-Costa C. (2026). Feasibility of Self-Directed Learning of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills Using Interactive Video in SimZone 0: Pilot Randomized Educational Trial. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/95529
title: SimZones framework: five progressive zones organizing simulation-based education
description: The SimZones model, proposed by Roussin and Weinstock, is an organizational framework for simulation-based education that structures learning across five progressive zones. As the article states, "Zone 0 focuses on self-directed learning with automated feedback tools such as interactive video (IV); zone 1 delivers instructor-led basic skill training; zone 2 engages learners in acute simulation scenarios; zone 3 is aimed at team and systems development; and zone 4 is intended for briefings associated with actual patient care." The article tests the pedagogical value of zone 0, which many programs skip.
requirements: Zone 0 requires automated feedback tools such as interactive video and hands-on practice with feedback devices
constraints: Empirical evidence on the impact of zone 0 regarding procedural skill acquisition and retention remains limited
target_learners: health care professionals in simulation programs
key_sources: Trampal Ramos Á, Charneco Salguero G, González-Tejerina B, Moreno-Palacios E, Leal-Costa C. (2026). Feasibility of Self-Directed Learning of Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation Skills Using Interactive Video in SimZone 0: Pilot Randomized Educational Trial. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/95529

article_title: Competences for Providing Oral Health Care to Care-Dependent Older Adults-Defining Learning Objectives for the German Undergraduate Dental Curriculum Through a Delphi Study.
citation: Hillebrecht Anna‐Lena, Barbe Anna Greta, Krämer Susanne, Auerbacher Marc, Semper‐Hogg Wiebke, Spies Benedikt C., Linde Philipp, Erfurt‐Berge Cornelia, Kossioni Anastassia, Farin‐Glattacker Erik, Bitter Kerstin. (2026). Competences for Providing Oral Health Care to Care‐Dependent Older Adults—Defining Learning Objectives for the German Undergraduate Dental Curriculum Through a Delphi Study. European Journal of Dental Education. https://doi.org/10.1111/eje.70094
title: Six‐competence‐area framework for dental care of care‐dependent older people
description: The article establishes a framework of six competence areas for the dental curriculum concerning care‐dependent older people (DOP): "(1) Care dependency in older individuals, (2) Access & barriers to oral health, (3) Legal aspects, (4) Communication, (5) Effects of medical and functional condition on oral health, (6) Clinical management of DOP". These areas organize 43 consensus learning objectives and structure the graduate profile, providing the organizing taxonomy for gerodontology teaching content in the German undergraduate dental curriculum.
requirements: Developed through a Delphi consensus process with dental education experts in gerodontology or special care dentistry at German universities
constraints: Derived from alignment of international special care dentistry and gerodontology guidelines with the German examination catalogue (CES), so scope is the German undergraduate dental curriculum
target_learning_goals: Providing oral health care to care‐dependent older adults

article_title: Enhancing Community Health Worker Communication: Evaluating Simulation-Based Training in Motivational Interviewing.
citation: Chance-Revels, R., Phan, Q., Crawford, K., Steiger, L., & Swan, B. A. (2026). Enhancing Community Health Worker Communication: Evaluating Simulation-Based Training in Motivational Interviewing. Journal of Community Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10900-025-01543-w
title: Integrate simulation-based MI training with SPs, authentic scenarios, and immediate feedback into CHW education programs
description: The article recommends integrating simulation-enhanced MI training into CHW workforce development, using standardized patients, authentic scenarios, and immediate feedback to create a psychologically safe learning environment. The authors state that "Using SPs, authentic scenarios, and immediate feedback creates a psychologically safe environment for CHWs to develop and refine their MI skills." This approach can be adapted for other public health and clinical environments where concise, impactful communication training is necessary.
requirements: Trained standardized patients able to role-play scenarios and provide targeted feedback
A pre-briefing session explaining expectations and simulation objectives
A faculty-led debriefing session for reflection and peer feedback
constraints: A single day may restrict the depth of skill development; the authors note SP-based simulations are expensive to implement, especially in low-resource settings
Long-term retention and transfer of MI skills to practice remain unknown
target_learners: Community health worker trainees in a structured workforce program
target_learning_goals: Confidence engaging with people holding different opinions
Using culturally appropriate resources to combat health misinformation
examples: Trainees rotated through three 15-minute scenarios on vaccine confidence, smoking cessation, and childhood obesity, each followed by 5 minutes of direct SP feedback and a one-hour faculty-led debriefing
key_sources: Chance-Revels, R., Phan, Q., Crawford, K., Steiger, L., & Swan, B. A. (2026). Enhancing Community Health Worker Communication: Evaluating Simulation-Based Training in Motivational Interviewing. Journal of Community Health. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10900-025-01543-w

article_title: Artificially Intelligent Simulated Patients in Undergraduate Surgical Teaching: A Single Blinded Randomized Controlled Study.
citation: Baraza W., Staples G., Wells C., Barbier L., Tonga I., Singh P., Puttick M., Webster C. (2026). Artificially Intelligent Simulated Patients in Undergraduate Surgical Teaching: A Single Blinded Randomized Controlled Study. The Clinical Teacher. https://doi.org/10.1111/tct.70486
title: SimConverse AI simulated patient platform for surgical history-taking practice
description: A commercial, web-based AISP platform (SimConverse, Dymaxion Technologies Pty. Ltd.) that "uses a model-agnostic approach", combining user speech-to-text, curated large language models and generative voice synthesis to create a simulated patient. Medical educators script the patient's history, laboratory results and personality, and the AISP is "constrained to stay within these designated settings". Built-in automated rubrics evaluate learner performance, and the platform outputs a full transcript and an AI-powered feedback summary.
requirements: Pedagogical coding and case scripting by medical educators to define the patient's history, laboratory results and personality
constraints: No facility to question participants interactively on test results or investigations in the studied configuration
Licences required funding; short-term AI-powered education likely requires additional financial outlay
examples: In the study, intervention participants completed two or three consultations with one of two AISPs (cholecystitis or biliary colic) and received AI-generated feedback on history taking and communication

article_title: Group performance differences in reading, math, and science by fourth graders with and without communication disorders.
citation: Karasinski Courtney. (2026). Group performance differences in reading, math, and science by fourth graders with and without communication disorders. CoDAS. https://doi.org/10.1590/2317-1782/e20250322en
title: The simple view of reading
description: The simple view of reading posits that reading consists of two dissociable processes: decoding, which is phonologically based word recognition, and linguistic comprehension, which involves semantic and syntactic knowledge for discourse-level interpretation. The article notes it "has been used to inform the differential diagnosis of dyslexia, poor reading comprehension, and specific language impairment, and is the basis of the national curriculum in the United Kingdom."
requirements: both decoding and linguistic comprehension must be assessed to characterize reading profiles
examples: The article uses the framework to distinguish profiles of dyslexia, specific language impairment, and poor reading comprehension.
key_sources: Karasinski Courtney. (2026). Group performance differences in reading, math, and science by fourth graders with and without communication disorders. CoDAS. https://doi.org/10.1590/2317-1782/e20250322en

article_title: Is procrastination among students lower in group work? Evidence from a registered field experiment.
citation: Koppenborg, Markus, Hüffmeier, Joachim, & Klingsieck, Katrin B. (2026). Is procrastination among students lower in group work? Evidence from a registered field experiment. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70069
title: Reduce procrastination by changing the learning environment, using group work that induces perceived indispensability of each member's contribution
description: The article advocates complementing person-centred procrastination interventions with targeted changes in the learning environment, shifting from "treating individuals' procrastination to preventing it on a larger scale by changes in the context". Group work in which each member's contribution is perceived as indispensable is the concrete mechanism proposed, and if the findings are corroborated, "teachers and counsellors" should consider "situational factors in general, and group work with perceived indispensability in particular".
requirements: Interventions must monitor emotional consequences, since measures that raise negative task-related affect may be counterproductive.
constraints: Legal and ethical reasons may prohibit conjunctive task structures in practice; the evidence for procrastination reduction is mixed and awaits corroboration by future research.
target_learners: higher education students with high levels of trait procrastination
examples: In the field experiment, participants led to believe their group's compensation depended on the worst or average bibliography procrastinated less (conjunctive condition, exploratory analyses) but reported higher prospective negative affect than individual workers.
key_sources: Koppenborg, Markus, Hüffmeier, Joachim, & Klingsieck, Katrin B. (2026). Is procrastination among students lower in group work? Evidence from a registered field experiment. British Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70069

article_title: Service learning in dental education: enhancing student competence through an oral health training programme for children with autism spectrum disorder.
citation: Cao Yina, Pang Liangyue, Meng Wenhua, Tao Ye, Yu Lixia, Liang Jingheng, Zhou Yang, Lin Huancai, Zhou Yan, Zhi Qinghui. (2026). Service learning in dental education: enhancing student competence through an oral health training programme for children with autism spectrum disorder. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09647-0
title: Six-module service learning programme integrating theory, field service, and reflective evaluation
description: The programme was "structured into six sequential modules that integrated theoretical knowledge with community service focused specifically on the ASD population": theoretical teaching, field investigation, data analysis and reporting, educational material development, health education implementation, and programme evaluation and reflection. Each module pairs an academic activity with a service or reflective component, culminating in pre-post assessment.
requirements: A partner institution specializing in education and rehabilitation for children with ASD, supervising lecturers, and faculty formative feedback on student-produced materials.
constraints: Evaluated at one dental school in China with a single-group pretest-posttest design, which the authors state may limit generalizability.
target_learning_goals: Oral epidemiology and examination skills, ASD-specific communication, and health education delivery for children with ASD
key_sources: Cao Yina, Pang Liangyue, Meng Wenhua, Tao Ye, Yu Lixia, Liang Jingheng, Zhou Yang, Lin Huancai, Zhou Yan, Zhi Qinghui. (2026). article_title: Digital Simulation-Based Ultrasound Training for Physiotherapy Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Fernández-Carnero Samuel, Diaz-Pulido Belen, Méndez-Rodriguez Jorge, Pecos-Martin Daniel, Garcia-Miguel Santiago, Achalandabaso-Ochoa Alexander, Cuenca-Zaldívar Nicolas, Naranjo-Cinto Sr Fermín. (2026). Digital Simulation–Based Ultrasound Training for Physiotherapy Students: Prospective Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/87897
title: Use simulation-based online ultrasound training as a scalable and accessible alternative to on-site instruction
description: The article supports using digital simulation-based platforms for ultrasound education where on-site training resources are limited. The study found that "Simulation-based online ultrasound training provides comparable theoretical and practical outcomes to traditional on-site instruction, supporting its use as a scalable and accessible educational alternative." This principle applies to health science education seeking to expand access to ultrasound competency training.
requirements: Learners need access to the online simulation platform and a brief hands-on device contact before practical examination
constraints: A single training session in either modality is insufficient for achieving clinical-grade proficiency
target_learning_goals: probe handling and image optimization skills
examples: Second-year physiotherapy students in the online group accessed the WAZO platform without instructor questions or scanner handling until 2 hours before examination

article_title: External validity of task-specific metrics for performance assessment in laparoscopic crural repair.
citation: Garces-Palacios S, Desir A, Pise A, Holcomb C, Scott DJ, Sankaranarayanan G. (2026). External validity of task-specific metrics for performance assessment in laparoscopic crural repair. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-026-12767-9
title: Inanimate silicone crural repair model in laparoscopic trainer box
description: A physical simulation model constructed from silicone with an embedded mesh to generate tissue tension, closely replicating the tissue mechanics of the diaphragmatic crura. A foam tube simulates the esophagus passing through an intentionally enlarged esophageal hiatus. The model is mounted on a custom 3D-printed stand angled to reproduce operative positioning with the reverse Trendelenburg position and housed within an ATLAS box trainer with a fixed camera for consistent visualization.
requirements: Laparoscopic trainer box with fixed roof camera for consistent visualization
constraints: Designed for crural repair practice; esophageal hiatus intentionally enlarged to reflect clinically relevant scenarios
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic suturing and crural closure technique
examples: Used by 30 participants at the Education and Innovation Center during the 2024 SAGES Annual Meeting

article_title: The effect of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation on training outcomes and insecurities in psychotherapy education.
citation: Cecil Julia, Kokje Eesha, Kleine Anne-Kathrin, Schaffernak Insa, Vogel Lea, Angerer Selina, Lermer Eva, Gaube Susanne. (2026). The effect of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation on training outcomes and insecurities in psychotherapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09917-x
title: Simulation-related factors framework: satisfaction, usability, presence, and technology acceptance as determinants of VP effectiveness
description: The article organizes potential determinants of VP training effectiveness into four simulation-related factors: "user satisfaction with the simulation experience, perceived usability, perceived presence and immersion, and the degree of technology acceptance". Satisfaction promotes engagement and motivation, good usability reduces cognitive load, presence is "the state when virtual objects are perceived as actual objects", and technology acceptance depends on perceived usefulness and ease of use. In this study these factors were measured after the final VP session and tested as predictors of training gains.
requirements: Measurement of satisfaction (SSE Scale), presence (Makransky Presence Scale), usability (SUS), and technology acceptance (TAM) following the final session
constraints: In this study, none of these variables significantly predicted changes in training outcomes, indicating little to no influence
target_learning_goals: Understanding determinants of simulation-based learning effectiveness
examples: The framework drew on the Technology Acceptance Model, the System Usability Scale, the Satisfaction with Simulation Experience Scale, and the Makransky Presence Scale.
key_sources: Cecil Julia, Kokje Eesha, Kleine Anne-Kathrin, Schaffernak Insa, Vogel Lea, Angerer Selina, Lermer Eva, Gaube Susanne. (2026). The effect of AI-enabled virtual patient simulation on training outcomes and insecurities in psychotherapy education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09917-x

article_title: Enhancing patient interview and clinical examination training: the impact of the Simroid dental training robot.
citation: Chen Yao, Peng Wentao, Dai Yanmei, Lin Xin, Zou Huiru. (2026). Enhancing patient interview and clinical examination training: the impact of the Simroid dental training robot. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09520-0
title: Simroid dental training robot
description: The Simroid is a highly realistic humanoid robot designed specifically for dental training, capable of simulating a wide range of oral conditions and patient responses. It can mimic facial expressions, vocalizations, and body movements, providing students with a realistic and immersive training experience. The robot engages in structured interactions through verbal communication and facial expressions, with pre-programmed medical history scripts and preset verbal responses. It can display specific pathological signs for students to identify and can be interviewed to collect medical history information.
requirements: Clinical instructors pre-compile medical record scripts for the robot, including diseases such as dental caries, acute pulpitis, and acute periapical periodontitis
constraints: The Simroid patient robot has limitations in replicating the full spectrum of human emotional responses and spontaneous interactions
High initial cost for equipment acquisition and maintenance
examples: Students interacted with the Simroid in 20-minute simulated consultation practice, 20-minute medical record documentation, and 20-minute assessment sessions
key_sources: Chen Yao, Peng Wentao, Dai Yanmei, Lin Xin, Zou Huiru. (2026). Enhancing patient interview and clinical examination training: the impact of the Simroid dental training robot. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09520-0

article_title: What makes a good simulation technician? A Polish nationwide study.
citation: Korulczyk Jan, Horodeńska Magdalena, Bartoszczyk Martyna, Biskupski Maciej, Dzikowski Wojciech, Majewski Marek, Torres Anna, Torres Kamil. (2026). What makes a good simulation technician? A Polish nationwide study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09323-3
title: Three-domain competency profile of medical simulation technicians: attributes, skills, and knowledge
description: The article organizes the simulation technician's professional profile into three competency domains — attributes, skills, and knowledge — derived from Nominal Group Technique sessions and rated in an 88-item questionnaire. It concludes that "Effective performance of simulation technicians requires a combination of technical proficiency, contextual knowledge, and strong interpersonal attributes," positioning the technician as both a technical expert and an educational collaborator. The framework underpins the study's recommendations for standardized training pathways and competency evaluation.
requirements: Items were generated via NGT sessions with stakeholders and retained only when rated ≥ 4 on a 5-point Likert scale
constraints: The profile reflects the Polish national context and self-reported importance ratings rather than observed performance
target_learning_goals: professional competency development for simulation center staff
key_sources: Korulczyk Jan, Horodeńska Magdalena, Bartoszczyk Martyna, Biskupski Maciej, Dzikowski Wojciech, Majewski Marek, Torres Anna, Torres Kamil. (2026). What makes a good simulation technician? A Polish nationwide study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09323-3

article_title: Improvement of learner's preclinical skill in occlusal rest seat preparation using digital and conventional training.
citation: Thai NP, Hoang HT, Vu CTB, Nguyen ATN, Doan TM. (2026). Improvement of learner’s preclinical skill in occlusal rest seat preparation using digital and conventional training. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08402-7
title: Six-criterion weighted rubric with overall 0–4 score for assessing occlusal rest seat preparation
description: The study assessed each occlusal rest seat using "six component scores corresponding to six criteria with specific weights and an overall score from 0 to 4 points." The criteria—Shape (10%), Width (20%), Length (20%), Depth (20%), Angle (10%), and Smoothness (20%)—were each scored 0–4 against printed acceptable ranges (e.g., width 2.25–2.75 mm, depth 1.25–1.75 mm, angle 80–90 degrees). Rubrics were uniform across groups except smoothness, measured as surface percentage conventionally versus cross-section counts digitally.
requirements: Assessment requires digitized preparations graded by a blinded examiner for reliability; intra-examiner ICC was 0.96 (95% CI: 0.94–0.98)
constraints: The two smoothness measurement approaches (visual–tactile percentage estimation versus cross-sectional counts) are not strictly equivalent and may introduce measurement bias, as the authors state
target_learners: fourth-year dental students in preclinical laboratory training
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of psychomotor skills in occlusal rest seat preparation
examples: The rubric was developed from the department's occlusal rest evaluation standards combined with criteria proposed by Fernandes, with ideal dimensions of 2.5 mm width and length and 1.5 mm depth
key_sources: Thai NP, Hoang HT, Vu CTB, Nguyen ATN, Doan TM. (2026). Improvement of learner’s preclinical skill in occlusal rest seat preparation using digital and conventional training. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-026-08402-7

article_title: The role of AI-mediated learning contexts in the personality-self-directed learning relationship among Chinese medical undergraduates: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Li Chenrui, Hu Fan, Qiao Yongxia, Zhang Meihui, Gao Quyige, Wang Fengyi, Du Naiya, Xia Yunyi, Pan Meizhu, Cai Yong, Wang Ying. (2026). The role of AI-mediated learning contexts in the personality–self-directed learning relationship among Chinese medical undergraduates: a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09414-1
title: Situational strength of AI-mediated learning contexts as a moderator of the personality–self-directed learning relationship
description: The article frames generative AI environments through Social Cognitive Theory's triadic reciprocal determinism and Situational Strength Theory, which "proposes that environments vary in the strength of cues, constraints, and incentives they provide, thereby determining whether and to what extent personality traits are expressed in behavior." Perceived situational strength is operationalized via two indicator sets from the Technology Acceptance Model: AI cognition (perceived usefulness, ease of use, risk, attitude) at the person–technology interface, and AI subjective norms (academic expectations, institutional regulations, peer pressures) at the social level. The framework predicts that AI-mediated contexts can amplify or compensate trait effects, and the study's moderated-mediation finding extends situational strength theory beyond organizational behavior into learning contexts.
requirements: Measurement of AI cognition and AI subjective norms as indicators of perceived situational strength
constraints: SCT does not specify how a technological environment relates to the strength of personality traits; SST is invoked to fill this gap
target_learners: Medical undergraduates using generative AI in their learning
key_sources: Li Chenrui, Hu Fan, Qiao Yongxia, Zhang Meihui, Gao Quyige, Wang Fengyi, Du Naiya, Xia Yunyi, Pan Meizhu, Cai Yong, Wang Ying. (2026). The role of AI-mediated learning contexts in the personality–self-directed learning relationship among Chinese medical undergraduates: a cross-sectional study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09414-1

article_title: Efficacy of laparoscopic simulator training in standardized obstetrics and gynecology residents: a prospective study demonstrating skill convergence.
citation: Li Congqing, Song Fei, Xu Youjiang, Zhang Liwei, Wang Wenyan. (2026). Efficacy of laparoscopic simulator training in standardized obstetrics and gynecology residents: a prospective study demonstrating skill convergence. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-46957-1
title: Simulator training should be used to automate fundamental skills in novices, reducing extraneous cognitive load and freeing resources for higher-order tasks during live surgery.
description: Drawing on cognitive load theory, the article posits that novice surgeons face overwhelming cognitive demands during live surgery. Simulator training reduces extraneous cognitive load by automating fundamental skills, and the progressive skill automation observed in PGY-1 and PGY-2 cohorts (reflected in decreasing completion times) likely represents this cognitive load reduction.
requirements: Structured, deliberate practice in a low-stakes environment allowing repetition of basic psychomotor tasks until automated.
constraints: The cognitive load interpretation is a theoretical framing offered by the authors; the study measured task completion time, not cognitive load directly.
target_learners: novice surgeons and junior residents (PGY-1 and PGY-2)
target_learning_goals: automation of fundamental laparoscopic psychomotor skills
examples: PGY-1 and PGY-2 cohorts showed decreasing completion times across the four weeks, which the authors interpret as progressive skill automation consistent with cognitive load reduction.
key_sources: Li Congqing, Song Fei, Xu Youjiang, Zhang Liwei, Wang Wenyan. (2026). Efficacy of laparoscopic simulator training in standardized obstetrics and gynecology residents: a prospective study demonstrating skill convergence. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-46957-1

article_title: Digitalization and Gamification to Improve Pathology Education: The SIAPeC Quiz Experience.
citation: Caputo Alessandro, Cima Luca, L'Imperio Vincenzo, Alecci Giuseppe, Ascione Andrea, Facchetti Mattia, Eren Özgür Can, Baskovich Brett, Mirza Kamran M., Bonert Michael, Fadda Guido, Fraggetta Filippo. (2026). Digitalization and Gamification to Improve Pathology Education: The SIAPeC Quiz Experience. Pathologica. https://doi.org/10.32074/1591-951X-N980
title: The SIAPeC Quiz: a gamified, case-based pathology quiz session for junior pathologists
description: The SIAPeC Quiz was an interactive session at the 2024 SIAPeC annual congress designed to "evaluate the utility of gamification in pathology education" for junior pathologists. It used case-based challenges simulating real-world diagnostic scenarios, immediate feedback, and digital tools including whole-slide images and multimedia platforms. Questions spanned histology, general pathology, subspecialties, and information-constrained formats, allowing trainees to "safely encounter and learn from errors in a simulated environment".
requirements: A web-based quiz platform compatible with text, static images, links to whole-slide images, multiple-choice and open-text answers, and real-time pacing
Participants need personal smartphones or similar devices to access the quiz
constraints: Open-text answers caused spelling-variation problems in answer recognition (e.g., "spiroadenoma" vs. "spiradenoma")
A minority of participants experienced initial connection difficulties via smartphones
target_learners: Junior pathologists (residents and fellows under 35 years)
target_learning_goals: Engagement with digital tools including whole-slide images
examples: 27 questions: 12 multiple-choice and 15 open-text; 15 with static images, 12 with WSIs, 7 with interactive ancillary technique requests
Information-constrained question formats based on the Twitter hashtags #TooCloseToDiagnose and #TooFarToDiagnose
Deployed on Quizizz; participants accessed via personal smartphones

(2026). Digitalization and Gamification to Improve Pathology Education: The SIAPeC Quiz Experience. Pathologica. https://doi.org/10.32074/1591-951X-N980

article_title: Construction and validation of the Salus-Ed questionnaire for measuring teaching competencies among nurse educators.
citation: Quintana-Alonso R, García JAC, Chamorro-Rebollo E, Redondo EG, Rebordinos-Hernando FJ, Fuster-Linares P. (2026). Construction and validation of the Salus-Ed questionnaire for measuring teaching competencies among nurse educators. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09009-w
title: Six-domain competency model of nurse educator teaching competence
description: The article proposes a six-domain model of nurse educator teaching competence derived empirically through exploratory factor analysis. The domains are relationship and communication competence, self-management and teaching planning competence, methodological competence, teamwork and collaborative management competence, disciplinary competence, and ethical and reflective competence. The article states that 'the resulting six-factor solution preserves the core elements of the original framework while providing a more parsimonious and empirically robust structure for assessing teaching competence among nurse educators.'
requirements: Each of the six extracted competencies was defined on the basis of existing literature to support conceptual clarity and strengthen construct validity
constraints: Derived from exploratory factor analysis in the Spanish context; confirmatory factor analysis with an independent sample is proposed for future research
key_sources: Quintana-Alonso R, García JAC, Chamorro-Rebollo E, Redondo EG, Rebordinos-Hernando FJ, Fuster-Linares P. (2026). Construction and validation of the Salus-Ed questionnaire for measuring teaching competencies among nurse educators. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09009-w

article_title: Pilot study: the impact of simulation-based pediatric basic life support training on the performance of caregivers of children with Rett syndrome.
citation: Kocyigit S, Akgun-Dogan O, Hatirnaz Ng O, Alanay Y, Guven F. (2026). Pilot study: the impact of simulation-based pediatric basic life support training on the performance of caregivers of children with Rett syndrome. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09158-y
title: Simulation centers can serve as community-based resources for caregiver education and emergency preparedness beyond the hospital
description: The article proposes that university-based medical simulation centers, typically used for training healthcare professionals, can be repurposed to train lay caregivers of medically vulnerable children. This approach provides a safe and controlled learning environment where caregivers can practice emergency response skills without patient risk. The authors frame this as a novel form of community engagement with broader public health applications.
requirements: Access to a university-based simulation center with pediatric mannequins and CPR feedback devices
Structured training program with standardized assessment criteria aligned to established guidelines (e.g., 2021 ERC PBLS Guidelines)
constraints: Training in a simulation center may not fully reflect real-life home or community emergencies
The study assessed short-term outcomes only at a single center
target_learners: Primary caregivers (parents or legal guardians) of children with Rett syndrome
Laypersons without clinical experience or prior PBLS training
target_learning_goals: Pediatric basic life support skills including airway management, rescue breathing, and chest compressions
Emergency preparedness and response for life-threatening events in medically vulnerable children
examples: A one-day simulation-based training program at the Acıbadem University Clinical Simulation and Advanced Training Center (CASE) in Istanbul combined PBLS, seizure first aid, airway protection, and choking management for ten caregivers recruited through the Turkish Rett Syndrome Federation
key_sources: Kocyigit S, Akgun-Dogan O, Hatirnaz Ng O, Alanay Y, Guven F. (2026). Pilot study: the impact of simulation-based pediatric basic life support training on the performance of caregivers of children with Rett syndrome. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09158-y

article_title: Effectiveness and retention of extremity and junctional tourniquet training among medical interns.
citation: Sahin Abdul Samet, Yilmaz Mutlu, Imamoglu Melih, Beser Muhammet Fatih, Karaca Yunus, Pasli Sinan, Gunduz Abdulkadir. (2026). Effectiveness and retention of extremity and junctional tourniquet training among medical interns. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09111-z
title: Integrate structured simulation-based hemorrhage control training into medical curricula with periodic refresher sessions
description: The article recommends integrating structured hemorrhage control and tourniquet training into medical school curricula, noting that a three-hour program combining one hour of theory and two hours of hands-on simulation with 1:1 instructor ratio produced significant gains. Because extremity skills and self-confidence declined over two months, the authors state that "integrating intermittent review videos or hands-on booster sessions into the longitudinal medical curriculum is recommended to mitigate long-term skill decay."
requirements: Hands-on practical stations with immediate corrective feedback at a 1:1 instructor-to-participant ratio
constraints: A single training exposure may not fully mitigate skill decay in extremity tourniquet application and self-confidence
Results reflect simulated efficacy and may not fully translate to real-world clinical performance
examples: The study delivered three hours of ATLS/TCCC/Stop the Bleed-based training using commercial extremity and SAM Junctional tourniquets on manikins
key_sources: Sahin Abdul Samet, Yilmaz Mutlu, Imamoglu Melih, Beser Muhammet Fatih, Karaca Yunus, Pasli Sinan, Gunduz Abdulkadir. (2026). article_title: Newly Graduated Nurses' Professional Competency and Caring Perception: A Cross-Sectional Correlational Study.
citation: Yilmaz Merve, Korkmaz Fatos. (2026). Newly Graduated Nurses' Professional Competency and Caring Perception: A Cross‐Sectional Correlational Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70614
title: Strengthen clinical readiness through simulation-based training, structured orientation programmes and supportive mentorship
description: The article recommends that nursing education programmes address the gap between strong caring competencies and weaker clinical biomedical knowledge and general clinical skills. It states that "strengthening clinical readiness through simulation‐based training, structured orientation programmes and supportive mentorship may help bridge this gap." This principle targets the transition from education to professional practice.
requirements: Nursing curricula should integrate competency-based and caring-focused educational strategies
constraints: Cross-sectional design limits ability to examine changes over time; effectiveness of these strategies not directly tested in this study
target_learners: Newly graduated nurses transitioning into clinical practice
target_learning_goals: Clinical judgement and interpretation of clinical data
examples: The study found newly graduated nurses felt confident addressing psychological and emotional needs yet reported limitations in areas requiring clinical judgement, interpretation of clinical data and foundational technical skills
key_sources: Yilmaz Merve, Korkmaz Fatos. (2026). Newly Graduated Nurses' Professional Competency and Caring Perception: A Cross‐Sectional Correlational Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70614

article_title: "I can do math!": A self-regulated learning intervention to enhance math-related motivational factors and performance in middle school.
citation: Granello, F., Cuder, A., Doz, E., Pellizzoni, S., & Passolunghi, M. C. (2026). “I can do math!”: A self‐regulated learning intervention to enhance math‐related motivational factors and performance in middle school. The British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96(2), 501–521. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70034
title: Six-week classroom SRL intervention for middle school math (planning, monitoring and evaluation checklists)
description: A six-session classroom intervention structured around the three phases of the SRL Cyclical Model, each phase spanning two weekly 60-min sessions. Sessions combined researcher-led discussion, strategy checklists, and practice on word problems, algebraic expressions, mental calculation and reasoning tasks. The control group "practiced on the same mathematics exercises as the SRL intervention group" without the SRL-specific activities. Delivered by a researcher to whole classes between October and November 2023.
requirements: Whole-class delivery with strategy checklists for goal setting, monitoring (including error handling, help seeking and time constraints) and self-evaluation, plus math exercises aligned across phases
constraints: The intervention consisted of "only six sessions spread over a month and a half"; the authors note a more intensive or extended programme might yield broader effects, and that researcher-delivered interventions often yield larger effects than teacher-delivered ones
target_learners: Year 6 and Year 7 middle school students
target_learning_goals: Math performance and math-related motivational factors (perseverance, self-efficacy, utility value, STEM vocational interest, theory of intelligence)
examples: In the evaluation sessions, students solved math tasks and then classified their mistakes as calculation, knowledge or time-management errors, followed by metacognitive reflection on weaknesses
key_sources: Granello, F., Cuder, A., Doz, E., Pellizzoni, S., & Passolunghi, M. C. (2026). “I can do math!”: A self‐regulated learning intervention to enhance math‐related motivational factors and performance in middle school. The British Journal of Educational Psychology, 96(2), 501–521. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.70034

article_title: Effectiveness of highand medium-fidelity simulation in nursing education: randomized controlled trial.
citation: Luiz Franciane Silva, Leite Isabel Cristina Gonçalves, Toledo Luana Vieira, dos Santos Kelli Borges, Alvim André Luiz Silva, Prado Roberta Teixeira, Coelho Angélica da Conceição Oliveira, Carbogim Fábio da Costa. (2026). Effectiveness of highand medium-fidelity simulation in nursing education: randomized controlled trial. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2025-0134
title: Design simulation for immersion, objective alignment, and instructional-design quality rather than relying on technological fidelity level
description: The article argues that simulation effectiveness depends on participant immersion, alignment with learning objectives, and instructional-design quality rather than manikin complexity alone, and its trial supports this: high- and medium-fidelity groups learned equally well. It states that "high-quality simulations can be delivered with simple resources when they are carefully planned and aligned with educational goals", and that clear objectives, briefing/debriefing quality, and well-designed scenarios are more decisive than realism. This broadens access to active methodologies in resource-constrained settings.
requirements: Careful planning and alignment of the scenario with educational goals
Clear objectives, high-quality briefing and debriefing, and well-designed scenarios
Standardized instructor training and delivery to ensure comparable pedagogy across conditions
constraints: Evidence comes from a small (n = 32), single-center trial with a fixed instructor team, an immediate posttest with no long-term follow-up, and pressure-injury content in sixth-semester nursing students; generalization should be cautious
target_learning_goals: clinical skills for pressure-injury assessment and treatment
theoretical knowledge of pressure-injury prevention and management
examples: In the trial, the control group trained with a Pressure Injury Stage Simulator manikin (TZJ-4009-U) plus clinical cases and matched the experimental group's standardized-patient scenario on skills (p = 0.853) and knowledge gains
key_sources: Luiz Franciane Silva, Leite Isabel Cristina Gonçalves, Toledo Luana Vieira, dos Santos Kelli Borges, Alvim André Luiz Silva, Prado Roberta Teixeira, Coelho Angélica da Conceição Oliveira, Carbogim Fábio da Costa. (2026). Effectiveness of highand medium-fidelity simulation in nursing education: randomized controlled trial. Revista Brasileira de Enfermagem. https://doi.org/10.1590/0034-7167-2025-0134

article_title: Simulation training for invasive cardiovascular procedures: the Heart-SIMS-1 randomized trial.
citation: Oliveira-Santos Manuel, Guerreiro Cláudio, Lobo Bárbara, Marinho Ana Vera, Borges-Rosa João, Guardado Jorge, Santos Eduardo Oliveira, Costa Marco, Gonçalves Lino, Bogle Richard, Dudek Dariusz, Pires-Morais Gustavo, Marques João Silva, Khokhar Arif A. (2026). Simulation training for invasive cardiovascular procedures: the Heart-SIMS-1 randomized trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-08831-6
title: SimulHeart 3D-printed coronary simulator
description: SimulHeart® (3D CardioSolutions, Coimbra, Portugal) is a custom-made 3D-printed simulator in which "a clear acrylic tank filled with water" holds "standard 3D-printed vascular anatomical structures" including the aorta and coronaries, connected to a simulated radial access and a pulsatile pumping system. It enables the use of standard diagnostic and interventional devices with realistic haptics feedback, was used radiation-free for training and under fluoroscopy for assessment, and had been validated for content and appearance in simulated coronary procedures.
requirements: Standard catheterization laboratory tools and catheters/wires must be compatible with the simulator for realistic hands-on practice.
constraints: The same simulator was used for training and evaluation in this trial, which the authors acknowledge may have favoured the simulation group; the simulator had been validated for face and content validity in simulated procedures.
target_learning_goals: procedural skills in invasive coronary angiography
theoretical knowledge of coronary anatomy and ICA steps
examples: In Heart-SIMS-1, pairs of students completed a 20-minute mentored hands-on session on SimulHeart® using a Judkins Left JL3.5, Judkins Right JR4, and a J-tip 0.035 150 cm wire.

article_title: Simulation-based education in paramedic training: effects of perceived competence and practice frequency on clinical skills.
citation: Turan D, Pekmezci H. (2026). Simulation-based education in paramedic training: effects of perceived competence and practice frequency on clinical skills. BMC Medical Education, 26:487. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08541-5
title: Integrate structured, high-fidelity simulation with repeated practice and simulation-based assessment as a core component of paramedic curricula
description: The article recommends that simulation-based training be treated as a core curricular component rather than a supplement, because it was associated with gains in skills, practice frequency, and perceived competence. It states the improvements "support the integration of structured, simulation-based training as a core component of paramedic curricula rather than as a supplementary learning activity." It also recommends ongoing faculty development in simulation facilitation, debriefing, and standardized assessment tools.
requirements: Faculty trained in simulation facilitation, debriefing strategies, and the use of standardized assessment tools
constraints: Findings come from a single-group pretest–posttest design without a control group, limiting causal inference
target_learners: Paramedic students in vocational higher education
examples: Students completed approximately 992 hours of theoretical instruction and 704 hours of practical training including laboratory sessions, in-ambulance training, and simulation activities at a Clinical Simulation Training Center.
key_sources: Turan D, Pekmezci H. (2026). Simulation-based education in paramedic training: effects of perceived competence and practice frequency on clinical skills. BMC Medical Education, 26:487. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08541-5

article_title: Comparative Efficacy of Simulation-Based and Traditional Training in Ultrasound-Assisted Regional Anesthesia for Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial.
citation: Sánchez-Poveda D, Vicente-Mampel J, Curto B, Moreno V, García-Esteban JA, Hernández-Zaballos F, Alonso-Hernández P. (2026). Comparative Efficacy of Simulation-Based and Traditional Training in Ultrasound-Assisted Regional Anesthesia for Medical Students: Randomized Controlled Trial. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/77702
title: Integrate simulation-based ultrasound training into medical curricula as a safe, scalable alternative that can standardize training
description: The article recommends integrating simulators such as HUSP into medical curricula because simulation "offers a practical, safe, and scalable alternative to traditional educational methods". Beyond individual skill acquisition, the authors argue curricular integration "could standardize training, reduce variability in learner performance, and enhance patient safety by preparing students for clinical practice in a controlled environment". The recommendation rests on the trial's finding of comparable success rates between simulation and traditional teaching.
requirements: Access to the simulator hardware and software license; instructors experienced in ultrasound-guided regional anesthesia following standardized teaching protocols
constraints: Evidence base is a single-center pilot with a small fixed cohort; the authors state further multicenter studies with larger, more diverse cohorts are needed to validate the benefits
target_learners: undergraduate medical students in preclinical training
target_learning_goals: ultrasound-guided nerve identification and regional anesthesia competencies
examples: The trial allocated 34 students equally to a 2-hour HUSP practical session or a theoretical lecture with curated audiovisual materials, then assessed both groups with a blinded live ultrasound assessment 2 days later

article_title: Exploring the role of high-fidelity simulation for pre-foundation assistantship students to improve preparedness for practice.
citation: Moore Amber Jennifer Sara, Dhas Kallpana, Karunaratne Dilroshini, Dasigan Krishna, Brennan-Davies Ailie, Sahni Ankita, Patrick James, Rasool Lisa Saleh, Hridi Syeda, Carter Sef, Patel Shiras, Fakes Lianne, Kelada Mary, Shohayeb Ammar, Baptista Ana, Bartholomew Brent. (2025). Exploring the role of high-fidelity simulation for pre-foundation assistantship students to improve preparedness for practice. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08477-w
title: Use simulation to supplement variable clinical experiential learning in the pre-foundation period, providing a psychologically safe environment to practise acute care
description: Because clinical experiential learning during pre-foundation placements is opportunistic and variable, the article argues simulation offers a consistent learning environment for scenarios students rarely encounter, such as managing acutely unwell patients. Simulation "provides a psychologically safe environment to practice, reflect, debrief and learn", allowing students to make and learn from mistakes without fear of harming real patients, which is essential for building confidence.
requirements: Authenticity and psychological fidelity to establish a fiction contract and engagement
Pre-briefing elements such as respect for learners and clear expectations
constraints: Self-reported confidence gains do not consistently demonstrate improved simulated or real-life competence
Single-centre design involving students from one medical school limits generalisability
The study provides only a short-term view of preparedness for practice
target_learners: final-year medical students on pre-foundation assistantship placements
target_learning_goals: confidence in managing acutely unwell patients
examples: The course supplemented the PFA placement, where clinical experiential learning was described as often opportunistic and variable, with 13 standardised half-day simulation sessions

article_title: Simulation-based training intervention using artificial intelligence to improve clinical bronchoscopy performance: a pre-postintervention study.
citation: Cold Kristoffer M, Arshad Arman, Kildegaard Christian, Laursen Christian B, Konge Lars, Nielsen Anders B. (2025). Simulation-based training intervention using artificial intelligence to improve clinical bronchoscopy performance: a pre–postintervention study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2025-109756
title: General efficacy model of simulation-based training effect by experience level
description: The article proposes, via figure 3, a "general efficacy model of a simulation-based training intervention based on experience level", in which the training effect decreases with experience: previous studies "detected a decreased effect ... of similar simulation-based training interventions ... with experience". The model explains why novices gain most, intermediates less, and experienced operators least, and frames the current null result as the intervention being too small, experience too high, or the sample too small.
requirements: Experience level must be characterised to predict expected training gains
constraints: In the current study the intervention was too small, experience level too high and/or participant number too low to detect significant improvement
target_learners: bronchoscopists across experience levels, from novices to experienced consultants
examples: Figure 3 illustrates decreasing gains with experience, supported by a similar VR cataract surgery study where only novices and intermediates improved

article_title: Co-creation and delivery of a simulation-based learning model for locally employed doctors: Findings from the SIMBA-LED study.
citation: Palanichamy Swetha, Malhotra Kashish, Sin Yun S, Philip Nevil C, Arshad Amynta, Balakrishnan Harshin, Johal Haneesh, Kauser-Malik Saima, Khan Sahrish, Moodalbyle Shreyas, Elhariry Maiar, Narayanan Lakshmi, Kempegowda Punith, DEVI Collaboration. (2025). Co-creation and delivery of a simulation-based learning model for locally employed doctors: Findings from the SIMBA-LED study. Clinical Medicine 25(6). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinme.2025.100524
title: SIMBA-LED programme: an instant-messaging simulation-based learning model for locally employed doctors
description: SIMBA-LED is an online simulation-based learning programme delivered through "WhatsApp and Zoom to create an interactive, accessible and resource-efficient learning environment". It comprises four phases (preparation with consultant-validated anonymised real-life case transcripts; registration; interactive 20-minute case-solving sessions moderated by trained medical students followed by Zoom debriefs with an acute medical consultant; post-session feedback with Pendleton's model and GRS-based assessment). Eleven sessions covering 44 real-life cases aligned with the JRCPTB curriculum were delivered, with pre- and post-session confidence surveys.
requirements: Voluntary registration with email addresses and WhatsApp numbers; moderators recruited and trained from medical students and resident doctors; cases validated by acute medical consultants for clinical accuracy
constraints: Delivered with LEDs whose jobs were equivalent to foundation years 1–3 at a single NHS trust; participation voluntary and free of charge
target_learners: Locally employed doctors (LEDs), including international medical graduates, working in acute medical settings
target_learning_goals: Confidence and skills in managing acute medical scenarios aligned with JRCPTB internal medicine training competencies and ACGME core competencies
examples: A total of 11 SIMBA sessions were conducted, ensuring at least two iterations of each acute medical competency recommended by the JRCPTB; each session included four real-life medical case scenarios, each lasting 20 minutes
key_sources: Palanichamy Swetha, Malhotra Kashish, Sin Yun S, Philip Nevil C, Arshad Amynta, Balakrishnan Harshin, Johal Haneesh, Kauser-Malik Saima, Khan Sahrish, Moodalbyle Shreyas, Elhariry Maiar, Narayanan Lakshmi, Kempegowda Punith, DEVI Collaboration. article_title: Co-creation and delivery of a simulation-based learning model for locally employed doctors: Findings from the SIMBA-LED study.
citation: Palanichamy Swetha, Malhotra Kashish, Sin Yun S, Philip Nevil C, Arshad Amynta, Balakrishnan Harshin, Johal Haneesh, Kauser-Malik Saima, Khan Sahrish, Moodalbyle Shreyas, Elhariry Maiar, Narayanan Lakshmi, Kempegowda Punith, DEVI Collaboration. (2025). Co-creation and delivery of a simulation-based learning model for locally employed doctors: Findings from the SIMBA-LED study. Clinical Medicine 25(6). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clinme.2025.100524
title: SIMBA model: simulation via instant messaging grounded in Kolb's experiential learning theory and Kern's six-step curriculum framework
description: SIMBA (Simulation via Instant Messaging for Bedside Application) is a simulation-based learning model that "leverages simulation gaming and Kolb's experiential learning theory to enhance the educational experience", using widely available digital platforms (WhatsApp and Zoom) for flexible, cost-effective, remote delivery of realistic clinical scenarios. In this study the model was adapted through "Kern et al's six-step curriculum development framework", a systematic approach for creating high-quality healthcare training curricula, in which stakeholder and participant interviews informed an LED-specific intervention. The model is presented as scalable and accessible for learners balancing clinical duties with limited protected teaching time.
requirements: Anonymised, consultant-validated case transcripts; trained moderators; structured pre-, during- and post-session survey and feedback mechanisms
constraints: Unlike resource-intensive, in-person simulation models, SIMBA is explicitly positioned as a remote, instant-messaging format; the article notes future iterations could incorporate AI-driven feedback, adaptive learning pathways and augmented reality features
target_learners: Healthcare professionals in postgraduate medical settings, here LEDs including IMGs
target_learning_goals: Improving knowledge, confidence and skills in managing acute medical scenarios
examples: The four-phase structure (preparation, registration, simulation sessions, post-session feedback) was used to deliver 11 sessions with 44 cases over July 2023–January 2024
key_sources: Palanichamy Swetha, Malhotra Kashish, Sin Yun S, Philip Nevil C, Arshad Amynta, Balakrishnan Harshin, Johal Haneesh, Kauser-Malik Saima, Khan Sahrish, Moodalbyle Shreyas, Elhariry Maiar, Narayanan Lakshmi, Kempegowda Punith, DEVI Collaboration.
