article_title: Development and evaluation of the SimArena Magdeburg (SAM): A randomized controlled trial of the impact of a low-cost 180° simulation arena for emergency medical simulation training on stress perception and the associated resuscitation quality in medical students.
citation: Leschowski N, Brinkema H, Darius S, Wolter J, Böckelmann I, Borucki K, Sauer D, Braun-Dullaeus RC. (2025). Development and evaluation of the SimArena Magdeburg (SAM): A randomized controlled trial of the impact of a low-cost 180° simulation arena for emergency medical simulation training on stress perception and the associated resuscitation quality in medical students. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume42/zma001784
title: SimArena Magdeburg (SAM): a low-cost 180° simulation arena for emergency medical simulation
description: The SimArena Magdeburg (SAM) is a semi-circular 180° curved wooden projection screen on which two synchronized short-throw projectors display panoramic video, with ambient sound, a fan, fog machine and flash strobe to represent emergency scenarios. It was developed at Otto-von-Guericke University Magdeburg for "a realistic, secure, quickly interchangeable, and standardized environment" for emergency medical simulations and exams, and is used regularly in curricular and optional emergency medicine courses.
requirements: Requires two synchronized short-throw projectors, NVIDIA Surround synchronization, Immersive Display software, 360° panoramic video footage cropped to 180°, and playback via QuickTime or VLC player.
constraints: Development quality trade-off: "the quality of the video recordings, video projections and ambient sounds will be lower" than high-cost arenas, and the diameter is slightly smaller with a 180° rather than 270° screen due to spatial conditions.
target_learners: medical students (third to sixth year) in emergency medical education
target_learning_goals: emergency medical simulation training, lay resuscitation skills, stress resistance under realistic conditions
examples: Built for 7,726.50 euros; simulated a forest scene and a busy-road scene in pilot courses at the MAMBA Skillslab.
key_sources: Leschowski N, Brinkema H, Darius S, Wolter J, Böckelmann I, Borucki K, Sauer D, Braun-Dullaeus RC. (2025). Development and evaluation of the SimArena Magdeburg (SAM): A randomized controlled trial of the impact of a low-cost 180° simulation arena for emergency medical simulation training on stress perception and the associated resuscitation quality in medical students. GMS Journal for Medical Education. https://journals.publisso.de/en/journals/jme/volume42/zma001784

article_title: Implementation and evaluation of a Sim + LBL hybrid teaching model in dermatology and venereology: a prospective study.
citation: Li Jialan, Wu Ningling, Lu Jianyun, Tong Xiaoliang, Gao Lihua, Zeng Jinrong. (2025). Implementation and evaluation of a Sim + LBL hybrid teaching model in dermatology and venereology: a prospective study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08440-9
title: Sim + LBL four-phase hybrid lesson pattern: preparation, scenario simulation, structured feedback, and post-session assessment
description: A lesson-level instructional pattern combining scenario-based simulation with lecture-based learning in four sequential phases. Students first collaboratively develop and rehearse case scripts, then perform a timed simulation, then receive instructor-facilitated structured feedback with peer assessment, and finally complete a closed-book test and questionnaire. The article states the model "required students to preview core concepts before class and to engage in structured role-play during simulated outpatient consultations", embedding real-time simulation within lecture sessions.
requirements: Cases must be designed to curriculum guidelines and reviewed by senior faculty to ensure consistent difficulty and learning objectives across groups
Instructors act as non-intervening observers during simulation, interrupting only if performance deviates significantly from the intended theme
constraints: Evidence base is a single-site, non-randomized two-cohort comparison in one course module; the authors call for randomized trials and multi-center validation
examples: Each subgroup was assigned a representative STD case simulating an outpatient consultation; simulations ran within a 10-minute timeframe covering patient interviewing, ethical decision-making, privacy protection, and patient education, followed by feedback capped at 8 minutes per group
key_sources: Li Jialan, Wu Ningling, Lu Jianyun, Tong Xiaoliang, Gao Lihua, Zeng Jinrong. (2025). Implementation and evaluation of a Sim + LBL hybrid teaching model in dermatology and venereology: a prospective study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08440-9

article_title: Evaluation of 3D-Printed Models in Dentoalveolar Trauma Simulation: A Randomized Trial in Undergraduate Dental Training.
citation: Koç Cemre, Akyıldız Bahar Melis, Taş Ayşe. (2025). Evaluation of 3D‐Printed Models in Dentoalveolar Trauma Simulation: A Randomized Trial in Undergraduate Dental Training. Dental Traumatology. https://doi.org/10.1111/edt.13065
title: Six 3D-printed models simulating four dentoalveolar trauma types in permanent and mixed dentition
description: The article describes six 3D-printed models built from an existing educational maxilla design modified in Solidworks and Zbrush, printed as separate components so teeth can be displaced with finger pressure. "Six 3D‐printed models were used in the simulations, consisting of three models representing permanent dentition and three models representing mixed dentition." They simulate uncomplicated crown fracture, complicated crown fracture, intrusive luxation, and avulsion, with intrusion depths of 2, 5, and 8 mm across models.
requirements: Requires CBCT-derived or designed digital data processed in design software to replicate injury patterns, since a single real case containing all scenarios is nearly impossible
constraints: The models do not replicate clinical variables such as bleeding, which can complicate procedures like isolation and repositioning
target_learning_goals: diagnosis and treatment of dentoalveolar trauma (crown fractures, intrusive luxation, avulsion) in permanent and mixed dentition
examples: Students performed covering exposed dentin, direct pulp capping, and repositioning and splinting of displaced teeth under two experts, following IADT guidelines
key_sources: Koç Cemre, Akyıldız Bahar Melis, Taş Ayşe. (2025). Evaluation of 3D‐Printed Models in Dentoalveolar Trauma Simulation: A Randomized Trial in Undergraduate Dental Training. Dental Traumatology. https://doi.org/10.1111/edt.13065

article_title: Web-Based AI-Driven Virtual Patient Simulator Versus Actor-Based Simulation for Teaching Consultation Skills: Multicenter Randomized Crossover Study.
citation: Tyrrell Edward G, Sandhu Sardip K, Berry Kathryn, Ghannam Suzan F, Lewis Sarah A, Crowfoot Daniel, Sahota Gurvinder Singh, Carson Julie, Wilson Emma E, Taggar Jaspal. (2025). Web-Based AI-Driven Virtual Patient Simulator Versus Actor-Based Simulation for Teaching Consultation Skills: Multicenter Randomized Crossover Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/71667
title: SimConverse: web-based AI-driven voice-recognition virtual patient simulator for communication skills training
description: SimConverse is a "purpose-built web-based artificial-intelligence VPS platform designed to develop communication skills in health care professionals," accessed via any computer with a microphone and speaker. It supports "fully automated high-fidelity audio conversations in real time using voice recognition," speaks back with text-to-voice, anchors conversations with a virtual patient static image, and provides "immediate objective grading and personalized feedback" against a predeveloped rubric. Faculty can author their own feedback rubrics; the study used a preexisting rubric adapted to the session's intended learning outcomes covering consultation stages from introduction to closure.
requirements: A computer with a microphone and speaker and internet access; the study assumed basic computer and internet literacy for all participants
Feedback rubrics aligned to the intended learning outcomes, authored or adapted within the platform's rubric system
constraints: The exact wording of the rubrics is commercially sensitive data
Costs depend on the licensing plan agreed with the commercial provider and may vary for other organizations
target_learning_goals: Medical consultation and history-taking communication skills
Responding to patient cues and integrating biopsychosocial factors
examples: In the study, participants consulted with 3 virtual patients (each with 2 compulsory attempts and a third optional attempt), receiving feedback then repeating consultations, within a nominally 3-hour asynchronous session
key_sources: Tyrrell Edward G, Sandhu Sardip K, Berry Kathryn, Ghannam Suzan F, Lewis Sarah A, Crowfoot Daniel, Sahota Gurvinder Singh, Carson Julie, Wilson Emma E, Taggar Jaspal. (2025). Web-Based AI-Driven Virtual Patient Simulator Versus Actor-Based Simulation for Teaching Consultation Skills: Multicenter Randomized Crossover Study. JMIR Formative Research. https://doi.org/10.2196/71667

article_title: A single-group pre-post OSCE evaluation of a simulation-based clinical readiness module in pediatric dentistry.
citation: Güdük Ömer Faruk, Berberoğlu İpek Nur, Akturan Selçuk. (2025). A single-group pre–post OSCE evaluation of a simulation-based clinical readiness module in pediatric dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08215-2
title: Learner-centered readiness pattern combining simulation practice, role-play, scenario analysis, peer feedback, and reflective debriefing
description: The module's instructional design cycles students through active, learner-centered strategies around each station theme: clinical scenario analysis of realistic skills-based cases, structured small-group discussions with checklist-based peer observation, simulation-based skill practice on models and with standardized patients, and instructor-led reflective debriefing. Students alternated between "practitioner" and "observer/evaluator" roles, which the authors state "encouraged self-assessment, critical thinking, and peer feedback skills". Debriefing is described as helping learners close the gap between knowledge and performance.
requirements: Scenarios developed or standardized from previously validated pediatric OSCE stations
Instructor-led debriefing at each simulation station
Peer observation using structured checklists
constraints: Some weeks covered two themes due to content density and time constraints
target_learners: third-year undergraduate dental students preparing for clinical rotations
examples: Each training week paired pre-shared videos and brochures with live sessions: e.g., the fluoride/sealant week used paired practice with peer feedback followed by one-on-one role-plays with expert feedback
key_sources: Güdük Ömer Faruk, Berberoğlu İpek Nur, Akturan Selçuk. (2025). A single-group pre–post OSCE evaluation of a simulation-based clinical readiness module in pediatric dentistry. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08215-2

article_title: Early detection of at-risk health sciences students: a machine learning-based predictive study using midterm grades.
citation: Al Hashmi Reem A. M., Ozturk Ilhan, Elmehdi Hussein M. (2025). Early detection of at-risk health sciences students: a machine learning-based predictive study using midterm grades. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08192-6
title: Interpretable ML early-warning pipeline built on institutional SIS and LMS data (Ellucian Banner and Blackboard)
description: A replicable predictive pipeline that extracts student-level data from the Student Information System (Ellucian Banner) and Learning Management System (Blackboard), balances classes with ROSE, trains five supervised classifiers under 5-fold cross-validation, and adds interpretability layers (variable importance, SHAP, F1-threshold curves). The article states it "demonstrates how existing institutional data pipelines, particularly the Student Information System (SIS) and Learning Management System (LMS), can be leveraged to develop early warning systems in the UAE context." The pipeline is organized into data preparation, model training and threshold optimization, and evaluation stages.
requirements: Institutional SIS and LMS data pipelines with course-level midterm scores
ROSE over-sampling on the training set to address class imbalance (123 at-risk vs 223 not at-risk)
constraints: Thresholds were tuned post-hoc on the hold-out test set, which the authors note risks optimistic bias; ROSE applied outside cross-validation folds may slightly inflate performance
target_learners: First-year undergraduate health sciences students in block-registered common courses
target_learning_goals: Early identification of at-risk students to support timely academic intervention and retention
examples: The study analyzed 346 first-year students across seven programs, all enrolled in Biology, English for Medical Sciences, and Introduction to Health Sciences, using RStudio with caret, ROSE, pROC, xgboost, randomForest, gbm, e1071, and naivebayes packages.
key_sources: Al Hashmi Reem A. M., Ozturk Ilhan, Elmehdi Hussein M. (2025). Early detection of at-risk health sciences students: a machine learning-based predictive study using midterm grades. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08192-6

article_title: First Contact With Care Through Clinical Simulation in Nursing Students: Qualitative Study.
citation: García Carpintero-Blas E, Del Pozo-Herce P, Hernández-Cediel MDC, Rodríguez-García M, Navas-Echazarreta N, Chover-Sierra E, Martínez-Sabater A, Juárez-Vela R, Tovar-Reinoso A. (2025). First Contact With Care Through Clinical Simulation in Nursing Students: Qualitative Study. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/81617
title: Progressive SimZones-based simulation design moving from low-complexity technical zones to realistic Zone 3 scenarios within a four-phase session structure
description: A lesson-level simulation design in which sessions follow the International Nursing Association of Clinical Simulation and Learning's "4 key phases": prebriefing, development of the simulated scenario, debriefing, and final debriefing. Complexity progresses through SimZones: in Zones 1 and 2 the focus is technical skills in a controlled environment with teachers acting as instructors, while Zone 3 adds environmental noise, assistance pressure, and nontechnical skills, with the teacher becoming a facilitator of inquiry using structured debriefing. In this study the pattern was applied to four basic-care scenarios with standardized patients for first-year nursing students.
requirements: Prebriefing emphasizing a psychologically safe environment following Rudolph et al's guidelines
Debriefing following the principles of the good judgment model
Experienced, scripted standardized actors with knowledge of caregiving
constraints: The article reports the design as implemented in one first-year basic-care course at a single Spanish university
examples: Four scenarios were used: cardiology ward admission assessment, infected venous ulcer wound care, pressure ulcer hygiene and postural changes, and postoperative pain assessment and medication administration
key_sources: García Carpintero-Blas E, Del Pozo-Herce P, Hernández-Cediel MDC, Rodríguez-García M, Navas-Echazarreta N, Chover-Sierra E, Martínez-Sabater A, Juárez-Vela R, Tovar-Reinoso A. (2025). First Contact With Care Through Clinical Simulation in Nursing Students: Qualitative Study. JMIR Nursing. https://doi.org/10.2196/81617

article_title: Clinical simulation as an effective teaching model in the Special Needs Dentistry course.
citation: Mellinas-Martínez Irene, Pecci-Lloret María Pilar, Pecci-Lloret Miguel Ramón, Adánez-Martínez María Gracia, Guerrero-Gironés Julia. (2025). Clinical simulation as an effective teaching model in the Special Needs Dentistry course. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07882-5
title: SimMan Essential high-fidelity simulator combined with standardized patients across six clinical scenarios
description: The study's simulation element combines a high-fidelity adult mannequin with standardized patients across six clinical scenarios. Students "carried out practical sessions using a high-fidelity simulators, the SimMan Essential simulator (Laerdal, Stavanger, Norway) (Fig. 1), as well as standardized patients", while instructors in the control room "manage the physiological parameters of the simulator and/or standardized patient" and observe performance in real time.
requirements: A simulation room with a dental chair connected to a control room through a one-way mirror
Instructors able to manage the simulator's physiological parameters and provide verbal responses from the control room
constraints: Scenarios typically last between 10 and 15 min, preceded by about five minutes for team familiarization
target_learning_goals: recognition and management of medical emergencies during dental procedures
communication with patients and accompanying persons
examples: Four scenarios used the SimMan Essential simulator with programmed emergency events such as hypertensive crisis, hypoglycemia, asthma attack and epileptic seizure; three scenarios used standardized patients
key_sources: Mellinas-Martínez Irene, Pecci-Lloret María Pilar, Pecci-Lloret Miguel Ramón, Adánez-Martínez María Gracia, Guerrero-Gironés Julia. (2025). article_title: Analysis of acquisition and retention of cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills according to training frequency.
citation: Joyce Kelly Barreto Silva, Thomaz Bittencourt Couto, Andreia Melo Coriolano, Alex Aquino, Júlio Cesar Martins Monte. (2025). Analysis of acquisition and retention of cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills according to training frequency. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2025AO1257
title: Schedule CPR refresher training every 6 months rather than every 3 months when using feedback-equipped simulators
description: The article's trial found no performance difference between students trained every 3 months and every 6 months, leading the authors to conclude that "a 6-month interval may be sufficient for maintaining proficiency". Because the 6-month schedule halves session frequency without measurable performance loss, it is the more economical choice for programs using feedback-equipped simulators.
requirements: Learners must hold valid BLS certification and train with a feedback-equipped simulator that scores compression depth, recoil, rate, and hand position
constraints: The trial observed students for only 6 months, and the authors attribute the null interval difference partly to the short observation period, pandemic-era clinical exposure, or the medical school curriculum
target_learners: fifth- and sixth-year medical students with BLS/ACLS certification
target_learning_goals: acquisition and retention of high-quality CPR psychomotor skills
examples: In the trial, 43 medical students were randomized to train every 3 or every 6 months, and both groups reached similar overall performance medians of 98%
key_sources: Joyce Kelly Barreto Silva, Thomaz Bittencourt Couto, Andreia Melo Coriolano, Alex Aquino, Júlio Cesar Martins Monte. (2025). Analysis of acquisition and retention of cardiopulmonary resuscitation skills according to training frequency. Einstein (Sao Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2025AO1257

article_title: The effects of stressors on readiness for clinical practice in novice nursing students: a path analysis.
citation: Ozdemir Nur Guven, Dalcali Berna Kokturk, Berse Soner. (2025). The effects of stressors on readiness for clinical practice in novice nursing students: a path analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08079-6
title: SINS-T: Turkish Stressors in Nursing Students scale (41 items, four factors)
description: The SINS-T is a 5-point Likert instrument (1 = not stressful at all to 5 = extremely stressful) with 41 items across four factors: Education (14 items), Relationships (13 items), Confidence (9 items), and Uncertainties (5 items). Scores range from 41 to 205, and "as the score increases, nursing students' stress levels also increase." In this study its Cronbach's α was 0.99, which the authors note may reflect item redundancy.
requirements: Used with first-year nursing students before clinical practice; Turkish validity and reliability established by Akansel, Watson and colleagues
constraints: The authors caution that Cronbach's α near 1.00 frequently reflects item redundancy or overly homogeneous content, and suggest a brief version could be designed
target_learning_goals: measuring stress levels and stressor domains in nursing education
examples: Administered to 553 first-year nursing students in the cross-sectional survey; mean total score 109.76 ± 41.52
key_sources: Ozdemir Nur Guven, Dalcali Berna Kokturk, Berse Soner. (2025). The effects of stressors on readiness for clinical practice in novice nursing students: a path analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08079-6

article_title: A mixed methods study of self-directed learning in clinical practice using a mobile skills training system.
citation: Södersved Källestedt, M.-L., & Hidefjäll, P. (2025). A mixed methods study of self-directed learning in clinical practice using a mobile skills training system. BMC Medical Education, 25, 1515. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08127-1
title: SimCapture for Skills mobile training system for clinical peer-to-peer SDL
description: A mobile e-learning platform combining simulators (mobile skills trainer), evaluation apps on mobile phones, and an administrative backbone to manage training activities distributed at healthcare workplaces. The system, SimCapture for Skills from Laerdal, integrates checklists aligned with evidence-based practices for care tasks including CPR, tracheostomy care, and urinary catheterization. Educational coordinators created checklists following national and/or clinical guidelines, and completed checklists record peer-observed performance of care tasks.
requirements: Educational coordinators to create and maintain checklists following national and/or clinical guidelines
Access to training materials borrowed from a clinical skills centre
Support from clinical educators for technical problems
constraints: Concerns raised about mixed Swedish and English text; suggested improvements included text-to-speech and simplified learner onboarding
examples: Healthcare professionals practiced in pairs, alternating roles as performers and facilitators using the system checklist
key_sources: Södersved Källestedt, M.-L., & Hidefjäll, P. (2025). A mixed methods study of self-directed learning in clinical practice using a mobile skills training system. BMC Medical Education, 25, 1515. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08127-1

article_title: Evaluating the effectiveness of problem-based learning combined with six thinking hats in oral pathology education.
citation: Das Reena, Ramani Pratibha, Sukumaran Gheena, Ramasubramanian Abilasha, Veeraiyan Deepak Nallasamy. (2025). Evaluating the effectiveness of problem-based learning combined with six thinking hats in oral pathology education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-06554-6
title: Six Thinking Hats as a multi-perspective framework for structured diagnostic reasoning
description: The Six Thinking Hats (STH) method, developed by Edward De Bono, is a problem-solving and decision-making tool in which six coloured hats each represent one perspective applied in turn to a case. The article describes it as encouraging "looking at a case from multiple perspectives", with white hat covering facts and information, red hat emotions and intuitions, black hat caution and critical thinking, yellow hat optimism and benefits, green hat creativity and innovation, and blue hat process and control. In this study it structures group discussion of a histopathology case within PBL.
requirements: A moderator (faculty) guides the hat-by-hat discussion and the questionnaire/table outlining the six hats used in the session
constraints: The article states PBL alone has at times produced redundant, prejudiced and partial argument owing to the lack of a holistic thinking framework, which STH is presented as addressing
examples: Residents wore each hat in turn during DLBCL case analysis: facts under the white hat, intuitive impressions under the red hat, supporting evidence under the yellow hat, risks and alternative diagnoses under the black hat, ancillary-test brainstorming under the green hat, and consensus synthesis under the blue hat
key_sources: Das Reena, Ramani Pratibha, Sukumaran Gheena, Ramasubramanian Abilasha, Veeraiyan Deepak Nallasamy. (2025). Evaluating the effectiveness of problem-based learning combined with six thinking hats in oral pathology education. BMC Oral Health. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12903-025-06554-6

article_title: Evaluation of dental students' tooth preparation skills using conventional phantom labs versus advanced simulation technologies: a comparative study.
citation: Kızılırmak Burcu, Gözen Mehmet, Güntekin Neslihan. (2025). Evaluation of dental students’ tooth preparation skills using conventional phantom labs versus advanced simulation technologies: a comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08020-x
title: SIMtoCARE Dente VR haptic dental simulation system
description: The SIMtoCARE Dente® system (SIMtoCARE B.V., Vreeland, The Netherlands) is a VR-based dental simulator used as the intervention in this trial. The article states it "offers real time force feedback and 3D visualization, and is equipped with sensors designed to assess manual dexterity". Its tooth preparation modules let students compare preparations with predefined ideal models, providing color-coded visual feedback and standardized assessment of taper, occlusal reduction, and finish line standardization.
requirements: Requires VR-based simulation laboratory infrastructure and calibrated equipment for standardized assessment
constraints: The article notes the system cannot fully reflect clinical variables such as patient movement or soft tissue resistance, and its tactile feedback is more limited than natural tooth tissue
examples: Used as the simulation intervention: 20 students trained 10 h on the system before post-testing on tooth 46
key_sources: Kızılırmak Burcu, Gözen Mehmet, Güntekin Neslihan. (2025). Evaluation of dental students’ tooth preparation skills using conventional phantom labs versus advanced simulation technologies: a comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08020-x

article_title: Assessing competency in less invasive surfactant administration: simulation-based validity evidence for the LISA-AT scores.
citation: Breindahl Niklas, Bay Emma Therese, Heiring Christian, MacLean-Nyegaard Ingrid Rose, Gudiksen Amalie, Frithioff Andreas, Henriksen Tine Brink, Tolsgaard Martin Grønnebæk, Aunsholt Lise. (2025). Assessing competency in less invasive surfactant administration: simulation-based validity evidence for the LISA-AT scores. Pediatric Research. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-025-03868-7
title: Train procedural novices in simulation to a predefined minimum passing score with per-attempt feedback before supervised clinical practice
description: The article supports competency-based, mastery-style procedural training: novices practise a rare procedure in a safe simulated environment, receive brief structured feedback after each attempt, and continue until they reach a predefined minimum passing score set from expert performance (the experts' lowest quartile). The authors state that using the LISA-AT score "can ensure competence in the simulated setting before advancing to supervised clinical procedures", and that a minimum passing score is required in competency-based learning to guarantee essential skills for safe practice.
requirements: A validity-evidence-supported assessment tool with a set passing standard
Trained raters able to give immediate feedback after each attempt
Simulation equipment and a session length sufficient for novices to reach the standard (here up to 90 min)
constraints: Passing the score did not eliminate all expert–novice differences: laryngoscopy skill and time remained significantly different, suggesting a need for continued and periodic re-training
The study did not evaluate skill retention or transfer of skills from the simulated to the clinical setting
target_learners: Medical students and junior doctors learning invasive neonatal procedures
target_learning_goals: Reaching a predefined mastery standard in LISA performance
Identifying and remediating procedural deficiencies through structured feedback
examples: 23 novices trained with one minute of feedback per attempt until passing twice consecutively; all reached the 39/40 standard within one 90-minute session at a median cost of USD 68 each
key_sources: Breindahl Niklas, Bay Emma Therese, Heiring Christian, MacLean-Nyegaard Ingrid Rose, Gudiksen Amalie, Frithioff Andreas, Henriksen Tine Brink, Tolsgaard Martin Grønnebæk, Aunsholt Lise. (2025). Assessing competency in less invasive surfactant administration: simulation-based validity evidence for the LISA-AT scores. Pediatric Research. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41390-025-03868-7

article_title: The Role of Educational Interactive Virtual Simulation App in Aesthetic Medicine and Cosmetic Dermatology Preclinical Skills.
citation: Hassan Haidar, Khalil Hassan, Shatta Bashar, Magrin Anna Maria Fenech, Novo Pereira Ines, Matin Atif. (2025). The Role of Educational Interactive Virtual Simulation App in Aesthetic Medicine and Cosmetic Dermatology Preclinical Skills. Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocd.70496
title: Use interactive simulation as an enhancement to, rather than a substitute for, conventional clinical training
description: The article's discussion states that although "simulation can emulate numerous elements of clinical practice", it "falls short of fully encompassing the intricacies and unpredictability inherent in real patient care". The authors therefore recommend "utilizing simulation as an enhancement to, rather than a substitute for, conventional clinical training". In their study, the 3D app supplemented postgraduate aesthetic medicine coursework by providing risk-free practice of botulinum toxin planning and injection patterns before real-patient contact.
requirements: Access to conventional supervised clinical training alongside the simulation
constraints: Simulation does not fully encompass the intricacies and unpredictability of real patient care
target_learners: postgraduate healthcare trainees in procedural specialties
examples: The QMUL app was integrated into the training curriculum of first- and second-year aesthetic medicine postgraduate students as a complement to their existing program
key_sources: Hassan Haidar, Khalil Hassan, Shatta Bashar, Magrin Anna Maria Fenech, Novo Pereira Ines, Matin Atif. (2025). The Role of Educational Interactive Virtual Simulation App in Aesthetic Medicine and Cosmetic Dermatology Preclinical Skills. Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology. https://doi.org/10.1111/jocd.70496

article_title: Advancing medical training with augmented reality and haptic feedback simulator: outcomes of a randomized controlled trial on lumbar puncture.
citation: Felten Renaud, Bigaut Kevin, Wirth Thomas, Kremer Laurent, Gauer Lucas, Arnold Cécile, Ollivier Irène, Godet Julien, Scherlinger Marc, Dubois Maxime, Sebbag Eden, De Sèze Jerome, Gottenberg Jacques-Eric. (2025). Advancing medical training with augmented reality and haptic feedback simulator: outcomes of a randomized controlled trial on lumbar puncture. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07536-6
title: Sim&Care AR and haptic feedback lumbar puncture simulator
description: Sim&Care is a lumbar puncture training simulator combining a PC running the software, a Microsoft HoloLens 2 for the AR environment, a haptic interface (the Touch from 3D Systems) for force feedback, and a manikin as physical support. Force feedback is generated through a real-time interactive biomechanical simulation using finite elements, transmitting calculated forces and friction to the haptic interface. It offers four patient cases (standard, scoliosis, osteoarthritis, pediatric) and customization features including patient positioning, needle selection, adjustable difficulty, anatomical transparency display, and a needle-trajectory visual aid. Developed by InSimo with the Strasbourg rheumatology team; this trial was the first randomized evaluation of its educational impact.
requirements: Requires a doctor to be present to explain the procedure and provide medical instructions before students use the simulator; it does not replace learning with an experienced physician.
constraints: The haptic device does not fully replicate the ergonomics of handling a real spinal needle; the stylus differs in form and weight from actual lumbar puncture instruments.
target_learners: Medical students in their clinical years who have not previously performed a lumbar puncture
target_learning_goals: Technical mastery of the lumbar puncture procedure
examples: In the trial, simulation-group students completed a 2-hour structured session progressing from a standard patient with all aids, to scoliosis or osteoarthritis cases, to a challenging scenario with AR anatomical visualization disabled, using only the seated configuration.
key_sources: Felten Renaud, Bigaut Kevin, Wirth Thomas, Kremer Laurent, Gauer Lucas, Arnold Cécile, Ollivier Irène, Godet Julien, Scherlinger Marc, Dubois Maxime, Sebbag Eden, De Sèze Jerome, Gottenberg Jacques-Eric. (2025). Advancing medical training with augmented reality and haptic feedback simulator: outcomes of a randomized controlled trial on lumbar puncture. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07536-6

article_title: An adaptive simulation intervention decreases emergency physician physiologic stress while caring for patients during COVID-19: A randomized clinical trial.
citation: Evans LV, Bonz JW, Buck S, Gerwin JN, Bonner S, Ikejiani S, Moylan T, Joseph M, de Oliveira Almeida G, Ray JM, Dziura JD, Venkatesh AK, Wong AH. (2025). An adaptive simulation intervention decreases emergency physician physiologic stress while caring for patients during COVID-19: A randomized clinical trial. PLOS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0331488
title: Pair simulation-based training with structured debriefing led by an experienced clinician to build confidence and process emotional reactions
description: The article attributes the stress-reduction effect partly to the debriefing component: participants reflected on their clinical experiences, received constructive feedback in "a safe and supportive environment by a seasoned clinician", and processed emotional reactions from scenarios such as vaccine hesitancy and comfort-measures-only care. The authors suggest this helped participants build competence, resilience, and confidence.
requirements: A debriefer trained in debriefing skills who is also a practicing clinician with shared clinical experience with the learners.

article_title: Performance on classroom simulations enhances preservice teachers' motivation in teaching: A latent change perspective.
citation: Wang, H., Thompson‐Lee, S., & Klassen, R. M. (2025). Performance on classroom simulations enhances preservice teachers' motivation in teaching: A latent change perspective. British Journal of Educational Psychology, 95(Suppl. 1), S239–S255. https://doi.org/10.1111/bjep.12761
title: Simulation‐based situated learning builds preservice teacher motivation through mastery experiences
description: The article frames classroom simulations as approximations of practice grounded in situated learning theory, pedagogical reasoning and Bandura's social cognitive theory, which hypothesise that competence develops through interaction of personal, environmental and behavioural factors. Within this account, "such mastery experiences are crucial for developing self‐efficacy, as they allow preservice teachers to practice and refine their skills in a supportive environment". Simulation tasks are also aligned with the competence need in self‐determination theory, and repeated, accumulated enactive experience is expected to explain why effects strengthen across sessions.
requirements: Simulations accompanied by reflection and feedback; the article notes simulations by themselves are not sufficient to change motivation, but simulations accompanied by reflections and feedback make a significant difference
constraints: The article notes one session alone was not associated with significant change in its own outcome variables, and it does not offer definitive findings about the optimal intensity of interventions
target_learners: Preservice teachers at the beginning of their teaching journey with limited exposure to realistic classroom situations
target_learning_goals: Teaching self‐efficacy, career intentions, perceived person–vocation fit, and classroom readiness
examples: The study's three‐session simulation intervention operationalised this framework, with performance in later sessions progressively predicting self‐efficacy change, consistent with Bandura's account of accumulated enactive experience

citation: Atsukawa Natsuko, Tatekawa Hiroyuki, Oura Tatsushi, Matsushita Shu, Horiuchi Daisuke, Takita Hirotaka, Mitsuyama Yasuhito, Omori Ayako, Shimono Taro, Miki Yukio, Ueda Daiju. (2025). title: Six-criterion LLM-based framework for evaluating radiology resident report revisions
description: The article develops a prompt-based evaluation framework in which paired initial and finalized resident reports are input to an LLM, which scores six revision criteria: addition of missing positive findings, deletion of findings, addition of negative findings, correction of expression, correction of diagnosis, and proposal of additional tests or treatments. Each criterion is scored "either positive (1) or negative (0), with a brief rationale provided for each criterion". The framework was tuned on 40 reports, validated on 100 reports against two radiologists, and applied to 900 reports to track skill growth.
requirements: Reports must include findings and diagnosis/impression sections; a tuned prompt specifying the six criteria is needed, and the LLM output is run three times with the most frequent answer taken
constraints: Agreement was only fair to moderate for C3, C4, and C5; no fine-tuning was applied; multiple revisions of the same criterion within one report count as a single revision
examples: The framework was applied to 900 reports (450 CT, 450 MRI) from nine residents' first and last 3-month terms, with results shown in radar charts

description: The article argues that simulation quality determines its usefulness in CEP teaching and assessment: "it is vital that any simulated learning activities used in CEP teaching and assessments are as close to real-world scenarios as possible, to retain relevance and usefulness." Effective forms described include mock wards with mannequins, background noises and actors briefed with scripts and physical constraints such as wheelchairs and weighted vests, and facilitation by practising CEPs or professional actors trained in healthcare simulation, rather than unscripted peer-to-peer role play.

Briefing and scripting of simulated patients with realistic physical constraints
constraints: Peer-to-peer role play was found ineffective; bringing in patients or actors can be equally challenging to organise

target_learning_goals: Exercise delivery, behaviour change communication, and assessment readiness for clinical practice
examples: In practical exams, student actors are briefed with scripts and limitations such as wheelchairs, vision goggles and weighted vests so students must think on the spot for exercise delivery

citation: Hindorf, M., Bäckström, D., Jonson, C.-O., Jonsson, A., & Berggren, P. (2024). Decision-making during training of a Swedish navy command and control team: a quantitative study of workload effects. Cognitive Processing. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10339-024-01242-9
title: Simulation fidelity as the degree of similarity between simulated and operational situations.
description: The article frames fidelity as "the degree of similarity between the simulated and the operational situation", created through the simulation equipment, setting, and scenario. It distinguishes low-fidelity simulation (builds knowledge), mid-fidelity simulation (builds competence), and high-fidelity simulation (builds performance). Low-fidelity simulations are described as simple, while high-fidelity simulations are described as complex and close to reality. The article also notes three primary types of fidelity: physical, conceptual, and psychological.
requirements: Simulation-based training requires a safe method to practise complex tasks, with simulations designed to be as close to reality as possible.
constraints: The perception of higher levels of fidelity as being superior to lower levels is common among participants and instructors, but there is no clear evidence to support this statement.
target_learners: Naval command and control team members
examples: The study compared a low-fidelity tabletop exercise (ETS) with a high-fidelity container-based training facility (Vulcanus II) using the same escalating scenario.

title: Situated learning and communities of practice as the explanatory frame for group-based competence development
description: The article draws on Lave and Wenger's 'Situated Learning' theory, which "posits that learning is not merely an individual intellectual process; instead, it is a social process that occurs in collaboration with other individuals who possess different competencies in a community of practice". Learning is situated in specific contexts and occurs through collaboration rooted in sociocultural situations. The authors combine this with Aase's system perspective on patient safety to interpret how group-learning in the ClinObsMunicipality programme built shared competence and improved interprofessional communication.
requirements: Learning occurs in collaboration with others of differing competencies within a community of practice, in the specific clinical context
constraints: The article uses the theory interpretively to explain qualitative findings, not as a tested mechanism
target_learners: Primary healthcare professionals (registered nurses, assistant nurses, social educators)
target_learning_goals: Observational competence for recognising and responding to clinical deterioration
examples: The study interprets participants' experiences of learning with familiar colleagues and instructors as instances of situated learning within a community of practice.

The applicability of a structured learning programme focusing on improving observational competencies to strengthen patient safety: a qualitative study with professionals in primary healthcare services. title: Small-group session structure pairing a computer simulation with a manual of guided physiologic experiments
description: The instructional pattern places students in groups of two or three within larger facilitated groups, working through a manual of prepared experiments in an interactive computer program, with facilitator-initiated pauses for review among the larger group. The manual included "instructions on how to use the program, a lexicon of terms and reference ranges, and seven sets of experiments". Piloting with 12 learners led to revisions for readability, blank answer spaces, and an added two-compartment model illustration.
requirements: A facilitator manual with answers, key teaching points, and common student questions; facilitators prepared via email and a presession virtual briefing
A 2-hour session with approximately 24 students per facilitator group
constraints: Some respondents felt overwhelmed by the amount of content relative to the session duration; the ICU simulator portion was left as optional out-of-class work
target_learners: second-year medical students in an integrated organ systems course
target_learning_goals: causal reasoning about pulmonary gas exchange and prediction and explanation of physiologic variable changes
examples: Five groups of approximately 24 students each were facilitated by faculty; students worked in pairs or threes with pauses for whole-group synthesis

title: Multi-modality simulation session pattern: didactic lecture, pre-briefing, set induction, model demonstration, and case-based discussion
description: The teaching–learning intervention layered multiple modalities around a 2-hour didactic lecture: a 10-minute pre-briefing outlining learning outcomes with a video recap, a set-induction demonstration of surfactant using a bowl of water and objects of varied density, hands-on lung-model demonstrations of altered pathology, and discussion of "5 case histories along with pulmonary function tests on obstructive and restrictive disorders." The authors state the strategy "combined multiple learning modalities—reading, visual, auditory, and kinesthetic."

article_title: Exploring medical error taxonomies and human factors in simulation-based healthcare education.
citation: Skrisovska T, Schwarz D, Kosinova M, Stourac P. (2025). Exploring medical error taxonomies and human factors in simulation-based healthcare education. PLoS One. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0317128
title: Survey instrument linking simulated and daily-practice medical errors in postgraduate Critical Care simulation courses
description: A survey administered at Masaryk University's Simulation Centre (SIMU) in Brno collected data from 124 participants and 13 tutors on the types and occurrence of medical errors observed or performed during simulations and their frequency in daily practice. Participants answered binary yes/no questions about observing error types and classified them using predefined categories from both Reason's and Round's taxonomies, and could describe specific errors from their own clinical experience. Each session was preceded by a standard briefing introducing the survey and error-type definitions.
requirements: A standard briefing before each simulation session introducing the survey and the error-type definitions
Informed consent and anonymized data handling
constraints: The survey was conducted between March 1, 2021, and October 27, 2022, at a single simulation centre
Reliance on survey data introduces the possibility of subjective bias, as responses may have been influenced by personal perceptions or the safe learning environment
target_learners: Postgraduate healthcare professionals attending high-fidelity Critical Care simulation courses
target_learning_goals: Awareness and categorization of medical errors in simulation and daily clinical practice
examples: Participants were asked whether they observed any type of medical error during the simulation course, with binary yes or no responses, and to specify the error types using predefined categories from both Reason's and Round's taxonomies

article_title: Exploring factors of physicians' preferences for continuing medical education.
citation: Mandic Ruzica Nikolic, Bjegovic-Mikanovic Vesna, Bukumiric Zoran, Terzic-Supic Zorica, Todorovic Jovana, Grujicic Sandra, Nesic Dejan, Laaser Ulrich. (2024). Exploring factors of physicians' preferences for continuing medical education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-06374-2
title: Six-domain physician competency taxonomy for CME/CPD developed by Delphi consensus
description: The article develops a competency framework for physicians' continuing professional development through a three-round Delphi process with 51 experts from CME Centres at all five Serbian medical faculties, starting from an Irish CME-needs instrument. "All listed competencies were classified into six domains: management, clinical practice, communication, public health, essential, and clinical emergency." The classification triangulated exploratory factor analysis, correlation coefficients between competencies, and competency concepts, yielding 74 competencies with 75%-or-more expert agreement. The framework is intended to focus CME/CPD on learning outcomes and support self-assessment and program organization.
requirements: Expert consensus via a Delphi process, triangulated with factor analysis and correlation of individual competencies
constraints: Developed for and validated with physicians in Serbia; the article notes no comprehensive European competency model for physicians of all specialties previously existed
target_learning_goals: continuing medical education and professional development competencies across management, clinical practice, communication, public health, essentials and clinical emergency
examples: The Delphi panel rated an initial list of 53 competencies, added new ones, and the final instrument included 74 competencies with a median rating of 5 or more

article_title: An integrated communication and technical skills educational intervention in critical healthcare situations: A qualitative method.
citation: Juliá‐Sanchis, R., Escribano, S., Sánchez‐Marco, M., García‐Aracil, N., Perpiñá‐Galvañ, J., & Cabañero‐Martínez, M. J. (2025). An integrated communication and technical skills educational intervention in critical healthcare situations: A qualitative method. Nursing Open, 12, e70002. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70002
title: Sim-IPE postgraduate intervention integrating communication and technical skills via high-fidelity simulation with hybrid patients
description: A postgraduate master's intervention in which nurses and physicians train together in critical-care scenarios using simulation-based clinical education with mannequins and hybrid patients—standardized patients fitted with anatomical parts and make-up who adapt their behaviour to team responses. The program comprised "12 simulation sessions", with eight technical, three communication, and one integrated session combining a prebriefing, a 15-minute video-recorded simulation, and a 40-minute good-judgement debriefing. It is patient-centered and designed for interprofessional teams in emergencies and disasters training.
requirements: Students need prior experience with high-fidelity simulation and informed consent; lecturers need at least 10 years of clinical experience and 5 years teaching high-fidelity simulation scenarios
constraints: Hybrid patient portrayal has a limited representation of vital-sign changes; finding suitably trained actors and cost uncertainty limit extension to all faculties
target_learners: postgraduate nursing and medical students in emergencies and disasters training
target_learning_goals: integrated technical and communication skills in critical healthcare situations
examples: The final integrated session simulated an out-of-hospital multi-victim road traffic accident or an unconscious patient due to self-inflicted intoxication, with teams working in full protective equipment under natural light and ambient noise

title: Six-item PtBL assessment rubric covering interdisciplinary integration, interpersonal skills, and media quality
description: A scoring rubric adapted from the AMEE guide framework, comprising six items across three course learning objectives: interdisciplinary data and evidence-based medicine integration, interpersonal and communication skills, and media quality, delivery, and change-agent capacity. Each item is scored 0–10 for a sixty-point total. Content validation by three professors using the item-objective congruence method yielded "an IOC index range between 0.67 and 1.00". It was used simultaneously by peer and teacher raters.
requirements: Rater familiarization with every rubric item and illustrative scenarios before use; content validation by expert review
constraints: The article notes media-quality and change-agent criteria may be especially challenging to interpret, and suggests integrating a checklist for media quality could simplify scoring
target_learning_goals: assessing video-based health-promotion projects across clinical knowledge, communication, and digital-media skills
examples: Used by nineteen raters per group (nine student groups, five MDs, five health professors) in paper-based, non-anonymous format with qualitative comments

article_title: Potential for reducing confirmation bias using the OMP model "6-microskills" with verbalizing discordance: a cross-sectional study.
citation: Kojima J, Uehara T, Ohira Y, Tsukamoto T, Shikino K, Yokokawa D, Li Y, Yanagita Y, Sato R, Ikusaka M. (2025). Potential for reducing confirmation bias using the OMP model “6-microskills” with verbalizing discordance: a cross-sectional study. BMC Med Educ. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06869-6
title: The “6-microskills” method: adding a learner-performed “does not fit” step to the one-minute preceptor model
description: The 6-microskills method extends the 5-microskills (one-minute preceptor) model of outpatient clinical teaching by inserting a third learner-performed step. The article states it developed the method "with an additional step performed by the learner, namely Step 3 (“does not fit”), to encourage critical reflection on the predicted diagnosis". In Step 1 learners state the most likely diagnosis, in Step 2 ("fit") the points fitting it, and in Step 3 the points that did not fit, rating confidence at each step on a 1–10 scale. The method is designed to be administered "with only a minimal addition of time over the 5-microskills".
requirements: Learners state a predicted hypothesis and verbalize both fitting and non-fitting evidence, rating confidence at each step; facilitators guide the one-on-one exercise.
constraints: The study evaluated it on vignettes under a 15-minute time limit with students new to the method; diagnostic accuracy did not improve in that setting.
examples: In the study, 108 students each reasoned on one of eight clinical vignettes, performing Steps 1–3 with confidence ratings after each step.

title: Two-minute simulated animated video for digestive endoscopy patient education

The article states "The video includes key topics such as preoperative diet and water ban requirements, surgical steps, expected feelings, risks and complications, postoperative diet and activity guidance, and how to communicate with doctors about doubts and concerns before and after surgery". It presents a flow chart, a schematic of the procedure, and a simulated procedure within the body, and patients watched it before examination.

Patients instructed to watch the animation before the examination

article_title: Simulation in admissions interviews: applicant experiences and programmatic performance prediction Simulation dans les entrevues d'admission : expériences des candidats et prédiction du rendement au sein des programmes de formation.
citation: Wildermuth Anne, Battista Alexis, Anderson LaKesha N. (2024). Simulation in admissions interviews: applicant experiences and programmatic performance prediction. Canadian Medical Education Journal. https://doi.org/10.36834/cmej.78961
title: Simulation-based MMI admissions stations with standardized patients and attribute-focused rubric scoring
description: The admissions process used station-based multiple mini-interviews in which applicants rotated through timed stations, two of which used simulation with standardized patients in a simulation lab. Applicants had two minutes to read a scenario and eight minutes to navigate it with a standardized patient while a trained evaluator scored the encounter on a rubric. The article states "The rubric evaluated personal attributes of the applicant that the station was specifically intended to elicit," and evaluators did not consider medical, legal, or scientific accuracy. Evaluators from eight health professions were trained on implicit bias, holistic admissions, and the interview process.
requirements: Trained evaluators scoring on a rubric targeting the personal attributes each station is intended to elicit
Standardized patients trained for the encounter who do not assess the applicant
Evaluator training on implicit bias, holistic admissions, and the specific interview process
constraints: Evaluators did not consider medical, legal, or scientific accuracy, even if the applicant was wrong
The station design deliberately excludes assessment of medical knowledge
target_learning_goals: assessment of personal and interpersonal attributes such as integrity, humility, professionalism, empathy, and ability to accept feedback
examples: The Wrong Medication Station in Appendix A asks the applicant to inform a standardized patient that a wrong medication was prescribed, assessing integrity, humility, professionalism, empathy, and ability to accept feedback

title: Six-month multi-technique remedial program for underperforming first-year biochemistry students with rubric-based incentives
description: A structured remedial program in which the Biochemistry faculty "designed an exclusive teaching methodology for the remedial students": daily one-hour sessions over six months, spanning mind maps, role play, viva, seminars, quizzes, small group discussions, weekly tests, quick revisions, assignments, grade incentives in FA, summarization, open- and closed-book tests, poster making, underlining and highlighting, leader-led group reading, independent study, and solving previous years' papers. Sessions ran in addition to the standard curriculum, mentors were trained beforehand, and modules were "continuously tailored based on the feedback and ongoing evaluation of students by their mentors". examples: Over six months, daily one-hour sessions included mind maps, role play, viva, seminars, quizzes, small group discussions, weekly tests, quick revisions, assignments, grade incentives in FA, and other activities detailed in Annexure 1

article_title: Student perspectives of simulated learning to improve their dysphagia management.
citation: Adams, S.N., Kater, K-A., & Seedat, J. (2024). Student perspectives of simulated learning to improve their dysphagia management. South African Journal of Communication Disorders, 71(1), a1060. https://doi.org/10.4102/sajcd.v71i1.1060
title: Use simulation as an adjunct to real-life clinical exposure, not as a replacement
description: The article's central design recommendation is that a simulated learning environment for dysphagia must supplement, not substitute for, genuine patient contact. Students noted the lab's inability to replicate hospital noise, distractions and unstructured interactions, and the mannequin could not display physical signs such as facial weakness or drooling. The authors state "it is important that the simulation lab is used as an adjunct to real-life exposure and not in isolation", positioning simulation as a bridge within the student's learning continuum.
requirements: Simulation should be integrated with real-life clinical placements so students also encounter genuine patient interactions
constraints: The simulation lab cannot fully replicate real-life clinical noises, distractions and unstructured patient interactions
examples: Students reported the sim lab environment 'didn't replicate' hospital noise and distractions, and that they could not see signs such as pocketing or drooling

article_title: Situational simulation teaching effectively improves dental students' non-operational clinical competency and objective structured clinical examination performance.
citation: Wu Ju-Hui, Lin Pei Chen, Lee Kun-Tsung, Liu Hsin-Liang, Lu Peih-Ying, Lee Chen-Yi. (2024). Situational simulation teaching effectively improves dental students’ non-operational clinical competency and objective structured clinical examination performance. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05546-4
title: Learning theories underpinning simulation-based education, and Miller's Pyramid as an explanatory framework
description: The article grounds simulation-based education in several learning theories: "constructivism, cognitivism, experiential learning, active learning, and Miller's Pyramid". Constructivism treats knowledge as built through learner-environment interaction; cognitivism frames simulation as retrieving and organizing prior knowledge for problem-solving; experiential learning locates learning in experience and reflection-on-action, with debriefing as "an essential element in simulations". The authors also use Miller's Pyramid to interpret their findings, placing academic performance at the knowledge level, SSC and OSCE at the shows-how level, and clerkship performance at the does level.
requirements: Debriefing and reflection sessions to consolidate learning after the simulation activity
Pre-briefing that imparts the intended learning outcomes and activates prior knowledge
constraints: The framework is used by the authors to interpret findings from one cohort of fifth-year dental students at a single university
target_learners: fifth-year undergraduate dental students during clerkship training
target_learning_goals: non-operational clinical competency including communication and cognitive skills
examples: The authors use Miller's Pyramid to explain why academic performance predicted both OSCE and clerkship performance while SSC participation affected only OSCE performance

article_title: Controlled prospective study on ultrasound simulation training in fetal echocardiography: FESIM II.
citation: Janzing Paul, Nourkami-Tutdibi Nasenien, Tutdibi Erol, Freundt Paula, von Ostrowski Thomas, Langer Martin, Zemlin Michael, Steinhard Johannes. (2023). Controlled prospective study on ultrasound simulation training in fetal echocardiography: FESIM II. Archives of Gynecology and Obstetrics. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00404-023-07133-2
title: Structure simulation-based ultrasound training as scaffolded practice with aids that can be switched off for examination-like testing
description: The article describes a training design in which beginners first practice with extensive aids — a 3D map of the fetus, anatomic labels, written instructions and live correctness feedback — and then are tested with all aids removed under real-life examination conditions. "Trainees can independently switch aids on or off ensuring that basic and advanced sonographers can adjust difficulty of training to their personal skill level." In FESIM II this design supported novices reaching over 95% correct standard planes within 2 weeks and expert-level speed within 6 weeks.
requirements: A simulator offering both an aided learning mode and an aid-free examination mode with automated assessment of obtained planes.
constraints: The study tested only standard-plane acquisition on a virtual fetus; the students' ability to recognize abnormal findings was not tested.
Transfer of simulation-trained skill to real patients was not examined in this study.
target_learners: Ob/Gyn physicians seeking to improve screening skills
target_learning_goals: correct acquisition of fetal echocardiography standard planes
development of visuo-spatial skills and mental mapping
examples: Students attended a 90-min introductory seminar, two tutor-supervised sessions, then trained alone twice weekly for 12 h, with biweekly standardized aid-free tests on a randomly moving virtual fetus.

citation: Der Sahakian Guillaume et al. (2024). The 2024 French guidelines for scenario design in simulation-based education: manikin-based immersive simulation, simulated participant-based immersive simulation and procedural simulation. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2024.2363006
title: Six parts required to adequately describe a simulation scenario, derived from the literature and published templates
description: From their literature review and analysis of published templates, the authors identify six required parts of a scenario description: a complete layout with a concise title; practical elements; a well-identified learner population with curriculum context; clear, limited, observable and measurable learning objectives for technical and non-technical competencies; all material and human resources for an authentic case; and a detailed session timeline including a section suggesting improvements for future sessions. The article reports that "the literature review and the various published templates highlighted 6 parts required to adequately describe a scenario."
requirements: Learning objectives should be clear, limited, descriptive, easily observable and measurable
A timeline including concise briefing, sequence of events, and main debriefing points linked to the learning objectives
target_learners: simulation educators writing scenarios for healthcare students and professionals
target_learning_goals: effective scenario design supporting targeted learning objectives
examples: The review cites prior frameworks including the Tupass scenario script with its 'scenario life savers' section

description: A commercially available, fully immersive semi-automated VR trauma training scenario (by SimX Inc.) run on a Meta Quest 2 headset and controllers, applying ATLS principles to a polytraumatized virtual patient. Participants had "45 min to complete the case or retry" and the scenario "could be repeated as often as desired". A study investigator moderated the scenario, giving prerecorded verbal responses and initiating automated physiological responses.

A moderator controlling scenario progression and prerecorded verbal responses

primary survey and recognition of life-threatening situations

article_title: Proficiency in performing radiofrequency ablation procedure for non-functioning benign thyroid nodules: a qualitative rather than quantitative matter.
citation: Chytiris S, Teliti M, Croce L, Coperchini F, Grillini B, Cerutti M, Fonte R, Magri F, Rotondi M. (2024). Proficiency in performing radiofrequency ablation procedure for non-functioning benign thyroid nodules: a qualitative rather than quantitative matter. Frontiers in Endocrinology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2024.1399912
title: Size-specific learning curves: procedural proficiency is a qualitative, task-dependent matter, and experience on easier task variants does not transfer to harder variants
description: The article proposes that learning curves for a procedural skill are not a single quantity tied to cumulative case count but are specific to the difficulty of the case variant treated. Its CUSUM analyses show "specific LCs exist concerning the size of the nodule treated", and that "previously achieved experience (as assessed by the number of total procedures performed) on small-intermediate nodules does not provide advantages" when treating large nodules. Proficiency assessment should therefore match the training case mix to the target task, and therapeutic success should be distinguished from technical efficacy, since a 50% volume reduction "is most often sufficient to improve patients' symptoms".
requirements: Requires a proficiency marker for the procedure (here 6-month VRR ≥50%) and a case-mix stratification variable (baseline nodule volume) against which learning curves are separately charted
constraints: Derived from a single-center retrospective single-operator cohort, which the authors state "inherently restricts external generalizability"
The article states the study "lacks an evaluation of the initial ablation ratio (IAR)", a parameter whose value for documenting operator skills it attributes to prior work
target_learners: Physicians in procedural training (endocrinologists performing thyroid RFA)
target_learning_goals: Acquiring safe, proficient procedural performance in radiofrequency ablation of benign thyroid nodules
examples: The single operator performed 179 consecutive procedures; CUSUM charts were drawn separately for small (<10 ml), intermediate (10–25 ml), and large (>25 ml) nodule groups, revealing proficiency shifts at case 10, 59, and none, respectively

article_title: Surgical quality assessment of critical view of safety in 283 laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos by surgical residents and surgeons.
citation: Grüter Alexander A. J., Daams Freek, Bonjer Hendrik J., van Duijvendijk Peter, Tuynman Jurriaan B. (2024). Surgical quality assessment of critical view of safety in 283 laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos by surgical residents and surgeons. Surgical Endoscopy. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00464-024-10873-0
title: 6-point critical view of safety competency assessment tool (adapted from Sanford et al.)
description: A 6-point competency assessment tool (CAT) for scoring the critical view of safety in laparoscopic cholecystectomy videos, adapted from Sanford et al. It comprises three criteria — "1. clearance of hepatocystic triangle, 2. cystic plate, and 3. two structures connect to the gallbladder" — each scored 0 to 2 for a maximum total of 6, where a higher score indicates superior surgical performance and a score of 5 or 6 indicates a favorable CVS.
requirements: Video (or photographic) record of the operative field in which the CVS is visible; the study excluded videos where the CVS was not adequately assessable
constraints: The study used it without a comprehensive explanation or training session on how to exactly use the tool and when to assign specific scores
target_learning_goals: assessing attainment of the critical view of safety during laparoscopic cholecystectomy
examples: Each criterion of CVS could receive a score ranging from 0 to 2 points, resulting in a total potential score of 6 points, as printed in Table 1

article_title: The impact of simulation-based learning on the knowledge, attitude and performance of physiotherapy students on practice placement.
citation: Dairo Yetunde M., Hunter Kirsty, Ishaku Timothy. (2024). The impact of simulation-based learning on the knowledge, attitude and performance of physiotherapy students on practice placement. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-024-05718-2
title: Four-week simulation placement structured as five daily stations led in rotation by students, with daily practice-educator debriefs using Pendleton's rules
description: The pattern organises a four-week simulation placement as an immersive practice environment. Students work in groups of four to five, covering five stations a day, each student leading a station with responsibilities including "taking patient history, leading the peer discussions on assessment and treatment planning, writing patient notes". Each station has a service user or scripted model, students spend about 60 minutes per station, and a 60-minute daily debrief with an HCPC-registered physiotherapist provides feedback modelled on Pendleton's rules encouraging self-reflection.
requirements: A practice facilitator pre-selects patient models who read from scripts provided by the physiotherapy practice placement team
A qualified, HCPC-registered practice educator observes student work and leads the daily debrief
constraints: Groups of four to five were felt by some participants to be larger than typical real-world physiotherapy staffing ratios for one patient
Groups did not change periodically across the four weeks, which some participants felt limited learning from different cohort peers
target_learners: Year 2 students on a 2-year MSc pre-registration physiotherapy programme in the UK
target_learning_goals: Teamwork and communication with peers and service users
Professional behaviours including time management and reflection
examples: Students spent five hours with patients, one hour with the practice educator, and one hour in peer group discussion each placement day, with an induction day covering moving and handling and infection control

title: Six-session MS self-care education program covering self-care importance, diet, pain and fatigue management, urinary disorders, stress coping, and exercise

Session 1 covers familiarization and "talking about self-care and its importance in controlling disease complications"; later sessions address proper diet in MS, "pain management methods and fatigue reduction and muscle relaxation methods," improving urinary disorders, coping with stress, anxiety and depression, and exercise in MS disease. Appropriate Delivery Project: Impact of Simulation Training on the Increase in Vaginal Births in Hospitals in Brazil. Einstein (São Paulo). https://doi.org/10.31744/einstein_journal/2024AO0783
title: Include simulation-based training as a component of broader quality improvement initiatives in obstetric practice, integrated within a curriculum rather than in isolation
description: The article recommends that hospital managers treat simulation-based training as one valid strategy within multi-component obstetric improvement projects. It argues that "simulation is likely to show the maximum effect when it is integrated within a curriculum, not when it is performed in isolation", and reports that the pilot findings "provide important evidence for hospital managers to include simulation-based training as a valid strategy in improvement projects in obstetric practice."
requirements: Integration within a broader curriculum or improvement initiative with concurrent organizational actions
constraints: The study could not attribute the observed changes exclusively to simulation training because several other initiatives took place simultaneously

article_title: Virtual reality vs. physical models in surgical skills training. An update of the evidence.
citation: Chahal Baldev, Aydin Abdullatif, Ahmed Kamran. (2023). Virtual reality vs. physical models in surgical skills training. An update of the evidence. Current Opinion in Urology. https://doi.org/10.1097/MOU.0000000000001145
title: Face, content and construct validity framework for evaluating surgical simulators
description: The review adopts a three-part validity framework as the minimum criteria a simulator should meet to justify widespread use. "Face validity refers to user opinion of a simulator's realism while content validity is based on expert opinion as to how well the simulator's content reflects the necessary skills and knowledge required. Construct validity is demonstrated when nonexperts are outperformed by experts in standardised tasks." The framework is applied throughout to rate VR, bench, cadaveric and 3D-printed simulators, alongside cost-effectiveness and availability considerations.
requirements: Validation studies demonstrating face, content and construct validity, which the review calls the minimum criteria for widespread use
constraints: The framework does not by itself capture cost-effectiveness and availability, which the review names as additional evaluation considerations
target_learning_goals: technical surgical skills acquisition in a safe environment
examples: The review rates the FlexBlad bladder phantom as demonstrating content, face and construct validity, and a high-fidelity VR TURBT simulator as failing construct validity

title: Recognize sex differences and emphasize the simultaneous development of cognition and physical well-being to support primary school students' academic development
description: Because sex, body mass index, muscle strength, cardiorespiratory function, and the executive function aspects of inhibition, working memory, and shifting jointly emerged as key factors of academic achievement, the article concludes educators should not treat cognitive and physical development in isolation. It underscores "the importance of recognizing sex differences and highlighting the interconnected development of cognition and the body, which can positively impact the academic development of primary school students."

Recognition of sex differences in academic performance

examples: The study identified body mass index, muscle strength (push-up, sit-up, standing long-jump), and vital capacity among key factors alongside executive function measures

article_title: User Perceptions of Visual Clot in a High-Fidelity Simulation Study: Mixed Qualitative-Quantitative Study.
citation: Gasciauskaite G, Castellucci C, Malorgio A, Budowski AD, Schweiger G, Kolbe M, Fries D, Grande B, Nöthiger CB, Spahn DR, Roche TR, Tscholl DW, Akbas S. (2024). User Perceptions of Visual Clot in a High-Fidelity Simulation Study: Mixed Qualitative-Quantitative Study. JMIR Human Factors. https://doi.org/10.2196/47991
title: Situation awareness-oriented, user-centered design as the conceptual basis of Visual Clot
description: The article grounds Visual Clot in Endsley's user-centered design principles, Wittgenstein's philosophy of logical representation, and NASA's guidance on organization of information. Situation awareness "breaks down into three separate phases (1) the perception of environmental elements in the current situation within a volume of time and space, (2) understanding their meaning, and (3) their projection in the near future." Based on this, Visual Clot data are visually represented, preprocessed, and simplified, with the goal of providing situational information quickly and with minimal cognitive load.
requirements: Data must be presented as direct visual representations that meaningfully correspond to the reality they represent, consolidating essential data into a single display
constraints: The article notes such information presentation increases diagnostic confidence, but numeric indicators are needed for precise data analysis and targeted treatment initiation
target_learners: health care professionals managing complex dynamic clinical situations such as anesthesia care providers
target_learning_goals: maintaining situation awareness and interpreting complex physiological monitoring information during critical events
examples: Other technologies the article names as based on situation awareness and user-centered design principles include Philips Visual Patient Avatar, AlertWatch, Dynamic Lung Panel and PulmoSight, HemoSight and Physiology Screen, and Alarm Status Visualizer
