article_title: Difficult airway simulation-based training for anaesthesiologists: efficacy and skills retention within six months.
citation: Bielka Kateryna, Kuchyn Iurii, Fomina Hanna, Khomenko Olena, Kyselova Iryna, Frank Michael. (2024). Difficult airway simulation-based training for anaesthesiologists: efficacy and skills retention within six months. BMC Anesthesiology. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12871-024-02423-x
title: Simulation-based training as a mechanism for improving guideline adherence and retaining emergency procedural skills in practising clinicians
description: The article operates on the premise that simulation-based training "gives better outcomes compared to non-simulation and non-intervention education", and that rehearsing protocol-driven management of rare critical events in a controlled setting produces durable behavioural change in practising clinicians — not only trainees. The authors frame acquired skills as retained at least six months, and suggest "certain elements of correct difficult airway management are being retained for longer periods, warranting less frequent repetition of costly full simulations", implying different decay rates for different skill elements.
requirements: Rehearsal on equipment identical to that used in the assessed scenarios
Structured debriefing connecting scenario performance to guideline learning
constraints: Retention beyond six months was not evaluated; a cited prior study (Kuduvalli et al.) found knowledge decay and higher protocol deviation one year after mannequin training
High cost, technical problems, and variety of approaches limit widespread use in low- and middle-income settings, though low- vs high-fidelity comparisons found similar results
target_learners: experienced clinicians with established management preferences
target_learning_goals: clinical decision-making in rare critical events
examples: The authors note one similar study found no significant pre–post difference in ASA algorithm adherence, suggesting personal clinical experience and available devices also shape emergency airway decisions.

citation: Dupont A, Ciener D, Monteilh C, Bharath A, Thomas A, Wolpert K, Pearce J. (2024). Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11384
title: Simulation session structure pairing two complication cases with an immediate PEARLS debrief and a reinforcing didactic presentation
description: The session pattern runs two ~30-minute simulation cases, an immediate ~30-40 minute debrief, and a PowerPoint didactic distributed before or after: "The simulations and debrief required around 2 hours to complete; each case ran around 30 minutes, and the debrief sessions required around 30 minutes." During the debrief "learning objectives were reviewed, and any objectives that had required a prompt or had been missed were discussed in detail," and "The educational PowerPoint was used to augment any missed learning objectives." Critical actions tied to educational objectives were tracked throughout both simulations with prompts embedded so objectives would be completed.
requirements: One to two simulation instructors, ideally PEM providers with experience in simulation, to run the scenario and debrief
A critical actions checklist modeled on institutional procedural sedation standards to track objective completion
constraints: Cases must be discussed and reviewed amongst the running physicians prior to simulation to help standardize scenarios across institutions
Debriefing allotted time was around 40 minutes per simulation
examples: The team moved directly from the propofol case to the ketamine case, then debriefed both immediately with Appendix F materials modeled after the PEARLS approach
key_sources: Dupont A, Ciener D, Monteilh C, Bharath A, Thomas A, Wolpert K, Pearce J. (2024). Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11384

article_title: Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications.
citation: Dupont A, Ciener D, Monteilh C, Bharath A, Thomas A, Wolpert K, Pearce J. (2024). Pediatric Emergency Medicine Didactics and Simulation (PEMDAS): Pediatric Sedation Complications. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.11384
title: Use simulation to practice low-frequency, high-acuity sedation complications so providers are ready when they occur in real time
description: The article's rationale is that rare but life-threatening sedation complications are hard to rehearse clinically, so simulation is the appropriate practice venue: "Interventions for these low-frequency but higher-acuity situations can be adequately practiced via simulation." In the discussion the authors reiterate that "These simulations are effective ways to practice high-acuity events so that, when they occur in real time, the provider is ready." The cases operationalize this by embedding laryngospasm with hypoxia to 45% and propofol-induced apnea requiring bag valve mask ventilation into otherwise routine procedural sedation scenarios.

Cues throughout the cases to guide learners who get stuck
constraints: The article presents this as the authors' rationale; it did not directly assess changes in comfort level or medical knowledge beyond the debriefing session
Some typical medication side effects such as nystagmus and hypersalivation cannot be portrayed with a high-fidelity mannequin
target_learners: PED providers including fellows, residents, APPs, and faculty
target_learning_goals: prompt recognition and management of life-threatening sedation complications such as laryngospasm and apnea
examples: Case 1 simulated progressive propofol-induced apnea requiring bag valve mask ventilation and worsening hypotension requiring a fluid bolus

article_title: Pre-clerkship procedural training in venipuncture: a prospective cohort study on skills acquisition and durability.
citation: Kodikara Kaumudee, Seneviratne Thilanka, Premaratna Ranjan. (2023). Pre-clerkship procedural training in venipuncture: a prospective cohort study on skills acquisition and durability. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-023-04722-2
title: Situated learning account of transfer from simulated to clinical procedural performance
description: The authors use situated learning theory to interpret why students performed well on real patients despite differences from the skills laboratory. In the lab, students "could just insert the needle without manipulating the mannequin's skin", whereas in the clinical setting they met soft skin and differently positioned veins, requiring them to assess the patient's vein by touching, checking, and choosing. Through these differing conditions "the students were able to grasp new experiences and construct new knowledge".
requirements: Authentic clinical conditions that differ from the simulation and require adaptive assessment of the patient's anatomy
constraints: Offered by the authors as an interpretive account of their delayed-assessment findings, not a tested mechanism
target_learners: Pre-clerkship medical students transitioning from skills laboratory to ward-based practice

description: The article's explanatory account is that a simulation cannot be reduced to the manikin: perceived quality and educational impact depend on equipment reliability, environment, script relevance, and briefing and debriefing quality, whose contribution to fidelity likely exceeds the manikin's technical features. The article states "Multiple factors are likely to influence the quality of a simulation such as the reliability of the equipment, the environment, the relevance of the script, or the quality of the briefing and debriefing." This account explains why substituting a low-cost manikin did not change learner perception. Reflective feedback during debriefing is described as the main component linking concrete experience to abstract conceptualization.

constraints: Results are valid only for the described scenarios, per the article's stated limitation

target_learning_goals: technical and non-technical crisis resource management skills
examples: Both groups shared identical environment, scenarios, briefing, and debriefing by the same instructor, isolating manikin fidelity as the only difference

title: Simplify VR technical procedures and elements to reduce cognitive load toward the learning goal
description: The article's lesson from development was to reduce cognitive load by simplifying technical procedures and removing elements that distract from the learning goal. Citing a serious-game study finding that "having high fidelity (many features) in the game produced too high a cognitive load", the developers used only one controller button, a digital blood pressure gauge instead of manual cuff inflation, yellow circles marking interactable objects, and a stripped-down wardroom.
requirements: Identify the single learning goal (here, the ABCDE order) and remove features unrelated to it
constraints: Simplification limits the application to a basic introduction; advanced practice needs more options and scenarios
target_learners: Inexperienced health students and professionals new to VR
target_learning_goals: Learning the order of the ABCDE observations
examples: Manual blood pressure measurement was replaced with a digital gauge after testing showed it was too complex; a mirror, window view, and teleportation were removed as distractions

article_title: Effect of different teaching/learning approaches using virtual patients on student's situational interest and cognitive load: a comparative study.
citation: Fuoad Sura Ali, El-Sayed Walid, Marei Hesham. (2022). Effect of different teaching/learning approaches using virtual patients on student’s situational interest and cognitive load: a comparative study. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-022-03831-8
title: Knowledge-deprivation and trigger-maintenance accounts of situational interest development during learning sessions
description: The article invokes two accounts of how situational interest arises and fades. Under the knowledge-deprivation account (attributed to Rotgans and Schmidt), the main trigger is "a lack of knowledge to solve specific problems", so interest rises while the gap persists and "will go down as soon as the learner’s gap of knowledge is filled". Under the trigger-maintenance account, repeated triggering through novelty, challenge, relevance, and active mental engagement such as peer discussion maintains interest across a session. The authors use these to explain the decline of interest in independent VPs and its stability in collaborative VPs.
requirements: Instructional activities that repeatedly trigger interest (novelty, knowledge gaps, relevance, active engagement) to maintain situational interest
constraints: The article treats situational interest as "a short-lived psychological, cognitive and physiological status", requiring repeated triggering within a session
target_learning_goals: Sustaining engagement and motivation during learning activities
examples: The authors interpret the significant end-of-session interest drop in independent VPs as satisfaction of students' knowledge gap, consistent with knowledge-deprivation theory

title: Simulated patient intervention for burns and stroke topics in occupational first aid training
description: A simulated patient — a Belgian Red Cross employee professionally involved in patient simulation — unexpectedly entered the room during practical exercises for the topics burns and stroke, "combining acting distress and pain with make-up" to mimic an ill or injured person as truthfully as possible. For burns the actor wore a large second-degree burn on the lower arm; for stroke the actor feigned hemiparalysis with a positive face-arm-speech-time test. Two participants actively provided first aid, followed by a group discussion with the simulated patient and instructor on what went well and what could be improved. Control trainings were identical except that video clips and case photographs were shown with no participant interaction.

The intervention is embedded in the regular curriculum topics (burns and stroke) after theoretical explanations are given
constraints: Used specifically for the topics burns and stroke because it is not feasible to use a simulated patient for all topics taught during a 3-day certification training
target_learners: laypeople in occupational first aid certification training (employees, 16 years or older)
target_learning_goals: first aid knowledge for stroke and burns
practical first aid skills for stroke and burns
examples: In 46 trainings involving 403 participants a simulated patient was used, while 83 trainings with 710 participants received the video-and-photograph control condition

title: Simian@3G high-fidelity asthma exacerbation simulation course with 22-item checklist and global rating scale assessment

title: Three-level fidelity taxonomy for clinical simulators (low, medium, high)
description: The article organises clinical simulators by 'fidelity', defined as "the degree of realism of the models and the intended experience", into three categories. Low-fidelity simulation covers basic psychomotor skills on a single body part; medium-fidelity adds a mannequin with pre-established software letting instructors manage basic physiological variables for decision-making practice; high-fidelity integrates multiple physiological variables with life-size mannequins that have personality, aimed at advanced techniques and critical-situation management. The study applies this taxonomy by comparing an MFS intervention (Seville) with an HFS intervention (Cantabria).

constraints: The taxonomy classifies simulators by technological complexity; the article notes HFS's high cost and that technological complexity is an inherent obstacle.

examples: The Cantabria intervention used METIman and SimMan 3G high-fidelity mannequins; the Seville intervention used the Resusci Anne SkillReporter mannequin with visual feedback for CPR practice.

non-technical skills such as active listening, communication, empathy, and generating confidence

citation: Faulkner Nicholas, Wright Breanna, Lennox Alyse, Bismark Marie, Boag Jane, Boffa Sophie, Waxman Bruce, Watson-Kruse Janet, Paine Geoff, Bragge Peter. (2020). Simulation-based training for increasing health service board members' effectiveness: a cluster randomised controlled trial. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-034994
title: Two-hour simulation-based board communication workshop with scenario role-plays and three-part structured debrief
description: A simulation-based training intervention for health service boards in which "Training sessions ran for 2 hours and involved all board members". Each participant completed a short scenario-based simulation with a facilitator and trained actor, observed by other members, and "divided into three parts: part 1 was the initial simulation/challenge, part 2 was facilitated reflections and feedback and part 3 was a repeat simulation where the participant could try new strategies". It was developed through a four-step process (expert panel, evidence review, stakeholder dialogue, scenario development) and informed by the agenda-led, outcome-based analysis technique.
requirements: A facilitator and trained actor per simulation; pre-workshop conversations with the board chair to select scenarios; confidentiality of workshop content to preserve a safe space
constraints: Workshops were 2 hours; a number of participants suggested increasing the length of the session and providing a follow-up session
target_learning_goals: Skills and confidence in communicating during board meetings, including asking difficult questions, dealing with pushback and refocusing conversations
examples: Participants chose between prepared scenarios or one they wanted to explore; simulations were conducted as improvisations between the participant and the actor

description: Simulation-based training "places learners in realistic situations that provide an opportunity to practice and learn in a safe environment". Debriefing is integral: practice, facilitated reflection and feedback, then a repeat attempt with new strategies.

title: Six-function model of medical communication as a framework for focusing OSCE scenarios and selecting validated communication models
description: The discussion presents a framework by De Haes and colleagues, "named the Six-function model of medical communication", which provides opportunities to focus on six functions: fostering the relationship, gathering information, information provision, decision making, enabling disease and treatment-related behavior, and responding to emotions. For each function, validated specific communication models such as SPIKES or VRCoDES can be used.
requirements: Models used to ensure validity and transparency should be validated models, used during training, and developed with communication experts.
target_learners: medical students and graduates assessed in high-stakes OSCEs
target_learning_goals: physician-patient communication across six medical communication functions
examples: The VRCoDES classifies clinicians' responses to patients' cues and emotions by explicitness of the response and provision of space.

article_title: How do we teach surgical residents in the COVID-19 era?
citation: Okland Tyler S. MD, Pepper Jon-Paul MD, Valdez Tulio A. MD, MSc. (2020). How do we teach surgical residents in the COVID-19 era? Journal of Surgical Education. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jsurg.2020.05.030
title: Treat surgical training and prevention of skill decay as a priority when operative volume collapses, using simulation to fill training gaps
description: The article argues that when elective operations are suspended, "Surgical training and prevention of skill decay should be a priority for any training center," and that simulation "appears to offer utility of both safety and procedural training for the surgical resident." Because nonuse of procedural skills risks decay, programs should deliberately substitute simulation-based training when residents are not operating.
requirements: training centers must allocate effort and resources to simulation when operative volume is restricted
constraints: the article is a perspective; it does not itself test whether simulation prevents decay in this setting
target_learning_goals: maintenance of surgical training during reduced caseloads
examples: an otolaryngology program distributed weekly take-home surgical kits to junior residents during COVID-19 elective-case delays

title: SIMISGEST-VR: a portable, low-cost, gesture-mediated 3D VR simulator for basic MIS psychomotor skills
description: SIMISGEST-VR is a web-based 3D virtual reality simulator mediated by a Leap Motion Controller, built in Unity3D with two nonfunctional laparoscopic forceps, support devices reproducing the fulcrum effect, and a mounting pad with a 45-degree LMC tilt. It supports 6 MIST-VR-adapted tasks, records metrics (time, efficiency of movement, economy of diathermy, errors, final score), and provides concurrent, immediate, and terminal feedback via an integrated SQLite database. The article reports a total hardware cost of approximately US $200, against US $2000-US $100,000 for market VR simulators.
requirements: A Leap Motion Controller, a computer running the web-based environment on PC or iOS, nonfunctional MIS forceps, support devices, and a mounting pad
constraints: The cut skill of the basic psychomotor skills construct is underrepresented because of technical reasons associated with the LMC
Some ergonomic principles applied to MIS were disregarded to keep the simulator portable
target_learning_goals: basic psychomotor skills in minimally invasive surgery
examples: The final prototype used white-painted forceps shafts after black shafts impeded LMC detection, and support devices were added after the fulcrum effect was not reproduced in the initial version

title: Six-theme framework of nursing students' experience of the abrupt shift to e-learning during COVID-19 confinement
description: An inductive thematic framework organizing nursing students' experiences of emergency e-learning into six major themes: "(1) practicing care; (2) uncertainty; (3) time; (4) teaching methodologies; (5) context of confinement and added difficulties; (6) face-to-face win." It was derived from semi-structured interviews with 32 Bachelor's and Master's nursing students at two Spanish public universities, analyzed through the six phases of thematic analysis with MAXQDA 12. constraints: Results center on the first month of confinement, with very specific cognitive and social states; the sample cannot be representative of the reference population, affecting generalization

examples: At the University of Granada, a list of 4th-year volunteers was created during the pandemic

article_title: SimLife model: introducing a new teaching device in endocrine surgery simulation.
citation: Donatini G., Bakkar S., Leclere F. M., Dib W., Suaud S., Oriot D., Breque C., Richer J. P., Faure J. P., Danion J. (2020). SimLife model: introducing a new teaching device in endocrine surgery simulation. Updates in Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-020-00871-x
title: SimLife: a hyper-realistic dynamic cadaveric simulator for endocrine surgery training
description: SimLife is a human cadaver-based surgical simulator developed at Poitiers University's ABS Lab. The body is "dynamized by pulsatile vascularization with simulated blood warmed to 37 °C" and is ventilated, using the P4P (Pulse for Practice) module that perfuses a blood-mimicking fluid in a pulsating manner and allows computer-monitored hemodynamic responses to simulated adverse scenarios such as hemorrhage. It was evaluated for adrenal, thyroid and neck dissection training.
requirements: Cadavers donated to science retrieved within the SimLife protocol timeframe and meeting inclusion criteria (BMI below 25 kg/m2, no previous major surgery, no contamination risk)
The dedicated P4P power module and a dedicated budget to run the system
constraints: The revascularized model lacks hemostatic mechanisms, so intraoperative hemostasis cannot be achieved
The model was set for senior trainees
Availability depends on cadaver supply
Cost is about 2000 euros per body
target_learners: Senior surgical trainees in endocrine surgery
target_learning_goals: Technical skill acquisition in adrenal surgery, thyroid surgery and lateral compartment neck dissection
examples: 32 training sessions were hosted, including 24 adrenal surgeries and 4 hemithyroidectomies with concomitant functional lateral compartment neck dissection; artificial lymph node metastases were injected and identifiable on preoperative neck ultrasound

title: Procedure-specific competency scoring broken into essential executional steps with fault penalties
description: The authors designed a performance assessment pattern following the Downing method: each surgical procedure "was broken down into essential executional steps" with a task-fulfillment scoring system where correct execution earns 1 point and surgical faults incur penalties from -1 to -3. Scales were built by the nominal group method with six national experts, tested on six senior expert surgeons, and psychometrically assessed on trainees, with validity and interobserver reliability checked by two external observers.
requirements: Expert panel to construct the scale by the nominal group method
Two external observers to establish validity and interobserver reproducibility
constraints: Scales are procedure specific and differ in essential steps and maximum score, so scores are not comparable across procedures
target_learners: Surgical trainees of variable levels of experience

examples: Figure 3 demonstrates the application of the scale for right transperitoneal adrenalectomy as an example

title: Simulated STEMI OSCE station with professional actors and a 12-item guideline-based checklist
description: An assessment element in which applicants manage a simulated STEMI patient in a standard doctor's office staffed by a trained professional actor and an electronic checklist evaluator, within a five-minute time limit. The checklist, developed by an experienced cardiologist and revised by five physicians, included 12 items scored 0-10 covering six treatment items and six diagnosis/transfer items, including a two-point penalty for "delaying treatment to wait for myocardial necrosis markers". The authors consider the simulation highly reliable because it was performed in a hospital environment with trained actors and realistic emotional stress.
requirements: Trained professional actors and trained evaluators with a centralized external evaluator for interpretation doubts
A printed scenario instruction, available medication list, and a provided anterior-wall STEMI ECG tracing
constraints: Fibrinolytic therapy and coronary angioplasty were not available on site in the scenario
The five-minute time limit led evaluators to prioritize diagnosis and treatment items over history and physical examination
The tool needs external validation in other training centers
target_learners: recently graduated physicians applying for medical residency
target_learning_goals: diagnosis and initial management of STEMI
transfer management within an urgency network
examples: 771 applicants completed the station in the 2016 HC-FMRP-USP residency selection, evaluated by 16 trained doctors

description: A structured, pragmatic process guiding researchers to develop implementable, evidence-based sports injury prevention interventions. It involves establishing a research–stakeholder collaborative partnership that moves through six steps: synthesising evidence and clinical experience, consulting experts, engaging end users, testing feasibility and acceptability, evaluating against theory, and obtaining feedback from early implementers. The article applies it to develop the I-PROTECT model, with stakeholder input revising draft models at every step.
requirements: A research–stakeholder collaborative partnership spanning researchers, programme deliverers and end users
Stakeholder advice and input available throughout all six steps
constraints: Described for sports injury prevention interventions in community sport settings
target_learning_goals: adopting and sustaining evidence-based injury prevention training routines
examples: Applied to develop the I-PROTECT model across literature review, expert workshops, end-user workshops, 3–4 weeks of pilot testing, theory evaluation and a one-season feasibility trial

citation: Ming Jin-Lain, Huang Hui-Mei, Hung Shiao-Pei, Chang Ching-I, Hsu Yueh-Shuang, Tzeng Yuann-Meei, Huang Hsin-Yi, Hsu Teh-Fu. (2019). International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph16193648
title: Simulation as participatory learning that builds transferable problem-solving strategies
description: The article frames simulation as "learning activities in a range of mimicked real-world clinical environments, through role play or immersive devices, to reach the goal of demonstration procedures, decision-making, and critical thinking". It presents simulation as a participatory experience in which participants build their own problem-solving strategies during learning, transform and apply these strategies to relevant situations, and thereby improve awareness and problem-solving capability. The workplace violence course instantiates this account by having nurses construct coping strategies in simulated aggression scenarios.
requirements: Mimicked real-world clinical environments with role play or immersive devices
Participatory engagement so learners construct their own strategies
constraints: The article notes studies on simulation training for workplace violence prevention specifically are still limited

article_title: Stress response in the daily lives of simulation repeaters. A randomized controlled trial assessing stress evolution over one year of repetitive immersive simulations.
citation: Ghazali Daniel Aiham, Breque Cyril, Sosner Philippe, Lesbordes Mathieu, Chavagnat Jean-Jacques, Ragot Stéphanie, Oriot Denis. (2019). title: Schedule repeated simulation sessions about every six weeks so trainees habituate and simulation stress ceases to spill into daily life
description: The article's 24-hour Holter data showed that teams repeating simulations every 6 weeks showed declining sympathetic activity on simulation days, whereas teams repeating every 6 months did not. The authors conclude that "a standardized simulation with a full briefing and debriefing with good judgment [26] allowed participants to get used to simulation sessions when they were repeated every 6 weeks," while at 6-month spacing "habituation did not occur and ANS activity remained identical." This supports spacing repeated high-fidelity sessions at roughly six-week intervals.

constraints: The finding comes from one scenario type (infant shock) with one EMS team composition; the authors note LF/HF does not constantly represent sympathetic dominance

target_learning_goals: managing life-threatening pediatric emergencies under stress
examples: Six experimental teams completed 9 sessions over one year (every 6 weeks) while six control teams completed only 3 common sessions; 24-hour Holter LF/HF was lower in the experimental group at the intermediate and final sessions

title: Three-category taxonomy of simulation fidelity: environmental, equipment and psychological
description: The article organises simulation fidelity into three categories, where fidelity refers to "how closely the simulation resembles the actual situation being replicated". Environmental fidelity concerns the situation in which the simulation takes place, equipment fidelity how closely tools resemble clinical practice, and psychological fidelity how faithfully the simulation mimics emotional and behavioural aspects. The article uses this taxonomy to orient novices to simulation terminology.
requirements: Educationalists designing simulation scenarios should attend to all three fidelity categories as the article frames them
target_learning_goals: clinical and procedural skills training in simulated environments
examples: The article distinguishes simulation modalities including human cadavers, simulated patients, screen-based simulation, part-task trainers and virtual reality.

article_title: Simulation-based Education and Human Factors Training in Postgraduate Medical Education: A Northern Ireland Perspective.
citation: Lawson Sara, Reid James, Morrow Michael, Gardiner Keith. (2018). Simulation-based Education and Human Factors Training in Postgraduate Medical Education: A Northern Ireland Perspective. The Ulster Medical Journal 87(3):163-167. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6169420/
title: Realism framework: physical, semantic and phenomenological realism in simulation design
description: Beyond fidelity, the article presents realism as "the extent to which the simulation feels and/or behaves the same way as the real-life system", decomposed into physical realism (how much it appears to be a real-life patient), semantic realism (whether the scenario would play out like this in the real world) and phenomenological realism (how the candidate feels in the scenario). It cites Owen's qualitative study showing semantic realism issues are most poorly tolerated.
requirements: Scenario designers should consider all three realism dimensions when building simulations
constraints: The article reports that issues with semantic realism, such as sequencing of events and acting out of role, are the most poorly tolerated by learners
examples: Owen's qualitative research study with medical students and post-graduate trainees found semantic realism problems, e.g. the sequencing of events in the scenario, availability of help and acting out of role, are most poorly tolerated.

article_title: Using electronic patient records: defining learning outcomes for undergraduate education.
citation: Pontefract S. K., Wilson K. (2019). Using electronic patient records: defining learning outcomes for undergraduate education. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1466-5
title: Six domains of competence for using Electronic Patient Records in undergraduate healthcare education
description: The article defines six domains of competence needed by healthcare graduates to work in a digital healthcare environment: "1) Digital Health: work as a practitioner in the digital healthcare environment; 2) Accessing Data: access and interpret patient data to inform clinical decision-making; 3) Communication: communicate effectively with healthcare professionals and patients in the digital environment; 4) Generating data: generate data for and about patients within the EPR; 5) Multidisciplinary working: work with healthcare professionals with and alongside EPRs; and 6) Monitoring and audit: monitor and improve the quality and safety of healthcare." constraints: All participants from both the working group and the eDelphi were UK-based, and therefore the results may not be entirely transferable to other countries

The competencies defined here will require regular review to ensure relevance to practice

target_learning_goals: monitoring and audit for quality and safety

article_title: Paracentesis Simulation: A Comprehensive Approach to Procedural Education.
citation: Sall D, Wigger GW, Kinnear B, Kelleher M, Warm E, O'Toole JK. (2018). Paracentesis Simulation: A Comprehensive Approach to Procedural Education. MedEdPORTAL. https://doi.org/10.15766/mep_2374-8265.10747

They view the maintenance opportunity as crucial because learners go prolonged periods without performing many procedures, resulting in skill deterioration and error opportunity. citation: Schelfhout Stijn, Wille Bart, Fonteyne Lot, Roels Elisabeth, De Fruyt Filip, Duyck Wouter. (2019). The effects of vocational interest on study results: Student person – environment fit and program interest diversity. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0214618
title: SIMON-I RIASEC questionnaire for study orientation toward higher education
description: SIMON-I is a RIASEC-based vocational interest questionnaire introduced as a study orientation tool for the transition into higher education. It "measures the interests of (future) higher education students in order to guide the student towards the best fitting study programs", using 153 very short yes/no items describing professions (66) and activities (87), such as Geneticist? (I) or Starting up an enterprise? (E). Dimension scores are recalibrated to a 0–100 scale, rendering a student RIASEC profile. constraints: The authors note their rationale could be applied to any other RIASEC-based instrument, but the reported reliabilities and fit indices are specific to this study's data.

target_learning_goals: study program choice and orientation toward fitting study programs
examples: First-year students completed the questionnaire in about five to ten minutes during the starting week of the academic year 2016–2017.

title: Situational account of nature's stress-buffering effects: benefits accrue during rest, not mental load
description: The article proposes that acute effects of natural environments on the autonomic stress system are situation-dependent rather than uniform. Its pilot data showed higher tonic vagal tone in nature during rest but no event or phasic differences during task performance, leading the authors to state the influence arises "during rest, that is, during break time or mental pauses". The account rests on neurobiological links between stress and attention and frames rest periods as the window in which nature's buffering occurs.

constraints: Findings are provisional from a small pilot; mechanisms remain uncertain and unmeasured confounders such as temperature may contribute

examples: Children performed identical reading, rest and d2 test procedures in a forested area and in classrooms while wearing chest-strapped HR monitors

article_title: Do patient-specific instruments (PSI) for UKA allow non-expert surgeons to achieve the same saw cut accuracy as expert surgeons?
citation: Jones Gareth G., Logishetty K., Clarke S., Collins R., Jaere M., Harris S., Cobb J. P. (2018). Do patient-specific instruments (PSI) for UKA allow non-expert surgeons to achieve the same saw cut accuracy as expert surgeons? Archives of Orthopaedic and Trauma Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00402-018-3031-9
title: Train surgeons in simulation before introducing new surgical technology such as PSI
description: The article recommends that any new surgical technology be rehearsed in simulation before clinical use, because the largest PSI errors in the study arose when surgeons focused on fitting the guide to the bone and overlooked their normal routine of confirming alignment guide parallelity — what the authors call "inattentional blindness due to a focus on the new technology". Simulation practice lets surgeons integrate the new instrument into their routine without patient risk.
requirements: Access to a simulation model replicating the operative setup, as in the study's sawbone model with soft-tissue simulation used in the manufacturer's instructional courses
constraints: The study tested only two guide designs in a sawbone model, so results cannot be generalised to other instrumentation
target_learning_goals: safe and accurate use of patient-specific instrumentation in UKA
examples: Trainees and experts watched a video demonstration and practised tibial saw cuts on a sawbone knee model with stretch tube ligaments replicating the manufacturer's instructional course setup

article_title: Comparison of simulation debriefs with traditional needs assessment methods: a qualitative exploratory study in a critical care community setting.
citation: Sarti Aimee J, Ajjawi Rola, Sutherland Stephanie, Landriault Angele, Kim John, Cardinal Pierre. (2018). Comparison of simulation debriefs with traditional needs assessment methods: a qualitative exploratory study in a critical care community setting. BMJ Open. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6194405/
title: Use simulation debriefs as a dual-purpose needs assessment and education method under certain conditions
description: This principle holds that simulation debriefing sessions can serve simultaneously as an educational activity and as a data collection method for needs assessment. The article found that "Data from VPS and MBS debriefs contributed to 15 of 20 total themes compared with the earlier study", while costing less time and money. The authors conclude that "the dual benefit of being educative and identifying needs is appealing" given fiscal constraints.
requirements: Access to a simulation programme with predeveloped scenarios
A trained simulation facilitator
constraints: Cost analysis excluded initial investment and maintenance costs of a simulation programme
Relatively small sample at a single centre
Cross-sectional design does not permit generalisations
target_learners: Critical care healthcare professionals in community hospital settings
target_learning_goals: Identifying system, team and individual level learning needs in critical care
examples: Each team completed two MBS and two VPS sessions followed by 20 min debrief sessions that were video-recorded and analysed

article_title: Medical students' knowledge of ultrasonography: effects of a simulation-based ultrasound training program.
citation: Eroglu Oguz & Coskun Figen. (2018). Medical students’ knowledge of ultrasonography: effects of a simulation-based ultrasound training program. The Pan African Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.11604/pamj.2018.30.122.14820
title: Use simulation-based ultrasound devices to teach ultrasonography to medical students in a short training period
description: The article recommends simulation-based ultrasound training as a way for medical students to acquire ultrasound knowledge and skills quickly and safely. The authors state that "simulation-based ultrasound devices provide a safe environment for users" and that repeated practice there decreases shyness and increases self-confidence and motivation. They conclude students "can learn to use an ultrasound device within a short period of time via simulation-based training programs".
requirements: Qualified specialist trainers to deliver theoretical and hands-on instruction
A simulation-based ultrasound training device with a mannequin for realistic hands-on practice
constraints: Due to budgetary limitations, not all ultrasound modules in the simulation device were purchased; the CLUE protocol was used instead of Echocardiography for cardiac evaluation
target_learning_goals: perform ultrasonography including FAST, E-FAST, RUSH and cardiac limited ultrasound examinations
examples: 96 final-year students received 20 hours of training (4h theoretical, 16h hands-on) over four weeks using the Sonosim ultrasound training solution device
key_sources: Eroglu Oguz & Coskun Figen. (2018). Medical students’ knowledge of ultrasonography: effects of a simulation-based ultrasound training program. The Pan African Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.11604/pamj.2018.30.122.14820

article_title: Medical students' knowledge of ultrasonography: effects of a simulation-based ultrasound training program.
citation: Eroglu Oguz & Coskun Figen. (2018). Medical students’ knowledge of ultrasonography: effects of a simulation-based ultrasound training program. The Pan African Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.11604/pamj.2018.30.122.14820
title: Simulation-based devices as safe, repeatable, and accessible alternatives to patient models for ultrasound training
description: The article presents a rationale for why simulation-based ultrasound devices are valuable training resources. It argues that appropriate patient, volunteer, or cadaver models are not always available and that body characteristics or clinical conditions may prevent adequate imaging, whereas simulation devices are "the only applicable and sustainable method for meeting the needs in both pathologic and normal anatomic models". The authors add that these devices are "easily accessible at any time", provide clear pathologic or normal images, and offer a repeatable, safe environment that builds trainee self-confidence and motivation.
requirements: Access to a simulation-based ultrasound training device
constraints: Budgetary limitations may restrict which ultrasound modules can be purchased
target_learning_goals: safe and repeatable practice of ultrasonography skills
examples: The authors cite McGraw et al. finding assistants trained via simulation were faster and more successful in subsequent venous catheterization, and Turner et al. finding the simulation-trained group better in manner, confidence, knowledge, and skill
key_sources: Eroglu Oguz & Coskun Figen. (2018). Medical students’ knowledge of ultrasonography: effects of a simulation-based ultrasound training program. The Pan African Medical Journal. https://doi.org/10.11604/pamj.2018.30.122.14820

article_title: A program to train medical physicists for direct patient care responsibilities.
citation: Brown DW, Atwood TF, Moore KL, MacAulay R, Murphy JD, Mundt AJ, Pawlicki T. (2018). A program to train medical physicists for direct patient care responsibilities. Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics. https://doi.org/10.1002/acm2.12472
title: Simulated Patient Interactions with two contrasting patient models
description: Two simulated patient models were developed with the Professional Development Center at UC San Diego: "a tech‐savvy and curious breast cancer patient" and "a non‐technical and nervous prostate cancer patient." Two Simulated Patients were hired and trained to play these roles in physicist-patient consults. Patient characteristics and demeanors are withheld from trainees beforehand so trainees practice assessing informational needs and comfort level with technical language. A trainer observes each 30-minute consult, and trainers and Simulated Patients give immediate verbal feedback; consults are videotaped, reviewed, and discussed.
requirements: trained Simulated Patients
a trainer present in the room to assess competencies
videotaping for review and discussion
constraints: implemented in collaboration with the UC San Diego School of Medicine Professional Development Center
examples: Each consult is scheduled for 30 minutes with verbal feedback immediately after

article_title: Enhancing delivery of osteoarthritis care in the general practice consultation: evaluation of a behaviour change intervention.
citation: Porcheret M, Main C, Croft P, Dziedzic K. (2018). Enhancing delivery of osteoarthritis care in the general practice consultation: evaluation of a behaviour change intervention. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-018-0715-8
title: Video-recorded simulated-patient consultations with a 14-task rating tool as a proxy measure of clinician competency
description: The study assessed workshop impact using video-recorded consultations between GPs and trained simulated patients as a proxy measure of competency, defined as what someone is capable of doing in "controlled representations of professional practice". Five simulators each portrayed a patient with a different story, and new scenarios were used at each time-point to limit learning effects. Videos were scored for the presence of 14 predetermined consultation tasks drawn from a Delphi consensus study, assessed by trained assessors blinded to time-point using a rating tool with established validity and reliability.
requirements: Trained simulated patients with detailed realistic scenarios; assessors independent of the intervention, blinded to time-point; a rating tool with established validity and reliability
constraints: The article states this measures competency, not performance in day-to-day practice; the average duration was longer than typical GP consultations, possibly reflecting being observed
target_learners: General practitioners and other clinicians undergoing consultation-skills training
target_learning_goals: Measuring change in consultation behaviours and competency before and after training
examples: 15 GPs video-recorded with simulated patients at baseline, one month and five months, yielding 45 videos assessed for 14 tasks
key_sources: Porcheret M, Main C, Croft P, Dziedzic K. (2018). Enhancing delivery of osteoarthritis care in the general practice consultation: evaluation of a behaviour change intervention. BMC Family Practice. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-018-0715-8

article_title: Education in trauma: An educational alternative that promotes injury prevention.
citation: Charry Jose Daniel, Ochoa Juan Daniel, Tejada Jorman Harvey, Navarro-Parra Sandra Liliana, Esquivel Nicolas, Vasques Yolercy. (2017). Education in trauma: An educational alternative that promotes injury prevention. Chinese Journal of Traumatology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cjtee.2017.04.006
title: Six-month weekly trauma-prevention workshop model for high school seniors
description: The article's educational model consists of "Weekly educational workshops" held "for six months, explaining different trauma mechanism, traffic accidents, car crush images, pre-hospital care, surgery, recovery and sequelae that remain after injury." Individual surveys on safety-device use and attitudes toward alcohol and driving are administered before and after the workshops to measure behavioral impact. Attendance was reported at 100% over the six months.
requirements: Weekly two-hour sessions delivered over six months, with pre- and post-program individual surveys to measure behavioral impact
constraints: Evaluated in Colombian high school senior students; the authors state a more accurate study using multivariate analysis is needed
target_learners: High school senior adolescents (mean age 17.5) in Colombia
target_learning_goals: Road safety attitudes and behaviors, including helmet and seat belt use and avoiding driving under the influence of alcohol
examples: 160 adolescents attended weekly 2-hour sessions for six months with 100% attendance, covering trauma mechanisms, crash images, pre-hospital care, surgery, recovery and sequelae
key_sources: Charry Jose Daniel, Ochoa Juan Daniel, Tejada Jorman Harvey, Navarro-Parra Sandra Liliana, Esquivel Nicolas, Vasques Yolercy. (2017). Education in trauma: An educational alternative that promotes injury prevention. Chinese Journal of Traumatology. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cjtee.2017.04.006

article_title: Medical students' clinical performance of dealing with patients in the context of domestic violence.
citation: Kong Hyun-Hee, Im Sunju, Seo Ji-Hyun, Kim Do-Kyong, Roh HyeRin. (2018). Medical students’ clinical performance of dealing with patients in the context of domestic violence. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2018.79
title: Six-domain framework for a successful domestic violence interview
description: The article categorizes DV interview checklist items into six domains for a successful DV interview: disclosure strategy and trust building (D), DV-related history taking (H), checking the perpetrator's psychosocial state (P), checking the victim's physical and psychological condition (V), negotiation and persuasion about further plans (N), and providing information about ethico-legal issues, diagnosis, treatment, and support services (I). The authors state they "categorized the items of the checklist according to the six domains for a successful DV interview". The framework was used to diagnose medical students' strengths and weaknesses in SP-based DV examinations.
requirements: A DV case checklist whose items can be mapped onto the six domains, with trained standardized patients and standardized scoring criteria
constraints: Developed and applied in the context of Korean undergraduate medical SP examinations with child abuse and elder abuse cases
examples: The consortium's case development committee built a child abuse SP case for 3rd-year students and an elder abuse case for 4th-year students, scoring history taking and patient education items as yes/no
key_sources: Kong Hyun-Hee, Im Sunju, Seo Ji-Hyun, Kim Do-Kyong, Roh HyeRin. (2018). Medical students’ clinical performance of dealing with patients in the context of domestic violence. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2018.79
